papers.title: Cultural invariance in music-evoked emotions
papers.abstract: Worldwide, people produce and listen to music to induce, express, and regulate their own and others' emotions. To what extent culture influences the emotions evoked by music is, however, contested. The documented global variation in musical behaviours and emotion concepts suggests substantial cross-cultural differences in how listeners relate to music emotionally, while shared physiology and evolutionary history would predict broad global agreement on the emotional information extracted from music. Some evidence suggests shared processes but experiments on the subject do not represent global diversity in either music or participants. Here, we report a large citizen-science experiment wherein listeners (N = 124,394 in 189 countries; conducted in English) rated their emotional responses to popular Western music and to vocal music produced in mostly small-scale societies drawn from a globally representative corpus (i.e., songs assumed to be unfamiliar in style). We found strong similarity in listeners' emotional responses to music: Average agreement between pairs of countries' listeners was high. Furthermore, across both popular and unfamiliar types of music, emotional responses were shaped far more by individual listeners and the specific songs than by cultural background: Both between-person differences within a country and within-subject differences across songs explained substantially more variance in emotional responses than country-wise differences. Together, these results indicate that a listener's cultural background has only a marginal influence on the emotions they feel in response to music, raising the possibility of universal structure in emotional responses to music.

papers.title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
papers.abstract: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.

The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) provides a compact description of the training dynamics of neural networks under gradient descent. For a scalar-valued network fθf_{\theta}, the NTK is defined as Θθ​(x,x′):=⟨∇θfθ​(x),∇θfθ​(x′)⟩\Theta_{\theta}(x,x^{\prime}):=\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x),\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x^{\prime})\right\rangle, where θ\theta denotes the network’s trainable parameters and x,x′x,x^{\prime} are data points. In the infinite-width limit at fixed depth, under suitable assumptions, the NTK becomes deterministic at initialization and remains constant during training [1, 2, 3]. This gives rise to the so-called NTK regime, in which training is governed by a fixed kernel and becomes analytically tractable. However, these results do not establish whether the NTK regime persists when width and depth scale jointly.

Prior work on multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) has shown that finite-width effects can accumulate when depth grows proportionally with width, making the depth-to-width ratio a key scaling parameter governing deviations from the infinite-width limit [4, 5, 6, 7]. The effect of this ratio further depends on initialization, with qualitatively different behavior in the ordered and chaotic regimes and at their critical boundary, the edge of chaos (EOC) [8, 9, 10, 11]. Thus, both depth-to-width scaling and initialization determine the applicability of the NTK regime in deep MLPs.

Importantly, deviations from the infinite-width limit are architecture-dependent. Unlike in MLPs, depth and width limits commute in residual networks under suitable residual-branch scaling, with no nontrivial joint scaling limit arising [12, 13, 14]. In contrast, finite-width effects in linear recurrent networks accumulate more rapidly with depth, giving rise to a distinct joint scaling regime where depth grows proportionally to the square root of width [15, 16].

papers.title: Propagation of chaos with singular potentials: A weighted duality approach
papers.abstract: We establish the propagation of chaos and derive the Vlasov equation from a many-body $N$-particle system in the mean-field regime with singular interaction forces bounded by $|x|^{-\alpha-1}$ for $0\le \alpha <(d-1)/2$ in dimensions $d\ge 2$, which in particular include the full range of sub-Coulomb interactions in three dimensions as well as the Coulomb interaction in two dimensions. Our proof is based on an energy-based framework for deriving weighted uniform bounds on cumulants that builds upon the recent duality method developed by Bresch--Duerinckx--Jabin in combination with a new Morawetz-type estimate, allowing us to remove the restriction to locally square-integrable interaction force kernels and handle more singular regimes.

papers.intro:
The rigorous derivation of effective macroscopic equations from the microscopic dynamics of interacting many-body systems stands as a fundamental problem in mathematical physics. In this direction, the derivation of the Vlasov equation starting directly from the deterministic Newton equations governing an NN-particle system is a great challenge for the Coulomb interaction in the kinetic theory of plasmas. Heuristically, the formal derivation relies on the assumption that the constituent particles are statistically independent, naturally leading to the mean-field approximation where the total interaction force experienced by a single particle can be effectively replaced by a self-consistent macroscopic field generated by the system’s one-body reduced spatial density. The mathematical difficulty in justifying this limit lies in proving rigorously that this statistical independence actually holds over macroscopic time scales, a property canonically referred to as the propagation of chaos.

The study of mean-field limits is a classical subject, starting from the pioneering works [18, 2, 5] that treat smooth interaction kernels; see also the excellent surveys [11, 13] on the subject. The problem has recently been studied intensively, focusing on singular interaction kernels, especially the Riesz type potentials (1.2). For the first order particle systems, we mention [23] which treats the full range of Riesz kernels, see also [14, 12, 22, 19, 20]. On the other hand, fewer works on the mean-field limit for the second order systems are available, however we mention the recent important works [4, 3, 6] that treat a class of singular interaction kernels. We also refer to [15] for the derivation of Vlasov-Poisson equation from potentials with suitable cut-off, and [10, 9] for recent refinements.

papers.title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.

papers.intro:
The 6D pose estimation problem in bin picking is subject to the simultaneous presence of heavy occlusion, high inter-class similarity among industrial parts, and challenging attributes such as specularity and symmetry. Single-view observations frequently capture only fragmented evidence, so pose estimates fall short of the sub-centimeter, sub-degree accuracy required by downstream tasks such as robotic grasping [19, 52, 26, 44].

These challenges motivate multi-view acquisition. Surfaces missing in one view are regularly recovered in another, and fusing several calibrated views produces a more consistent and reliable reconstruction [11, 27, 10, 52, 32]. Yet, especially multi-view reconstruction introduces a computational bottleneck. At resolutions sufficient for reliable instance separation, reconstructing and processing the 3D volume incurs substantial computational and memory costs. The reconstruction volume covers the entire workspace while discriminative geometry is localized in small areas, so the task-relevant occupancy is highly sparse. Two paradigms, multi-stage and holistic pipelines, have emerged to handle high-resolution reconstruction differently.

Multi-stage pipelines obtain object hypotheses from an upstream, decoupled detector or segmenter, estimate the 6D pose per crop, and append refinement stages [5, 26, 27, 28, 35, 14]. These methods currently lead the industrial track of the BOP challenge [40] and achieve the highest reported accuracies. However, they are ensembles of independently trained networks. Memory and training-data requirements accumulate across the sub-modules. Inference proceeds sequentially over candidates and views, so runtime scales with the number of objects, views and with the resolution of the crops. Figure 1 plots accuracy against runtime for the leading entries on IPD [25]. The two are coupled. No published entry above 0.800.80 AP runs in under 13.413.4 s, and the fastest entry outperforms the most accurate by 18.618.6 AP. Runtimes are self-reported under differing hardware, modalities and view counts, so the entries can not be compared directly. The trend over the population is nonetheless consistent, and it repeats on the other BOP-industrial dataset, XYZ-IBD [23] and ITODD-MV [9]. We attribute the coupling to the sequential structure. Accuracy in such pipelines is gained by appending stages, and the cost is incurred anew for every hypothesis. The fast and accurate regime is unoccupied.

The authors of [32] proposed to make this reduction step task-dependent via a staged heatmap formulation. A coarse voxelized region-of-interest stage predicts where target objects are plausible, a finer objectness stage focuses towards foreground candidates. Only the retained candidates are forwarded to the 6D pose heads. Allocating computation on task-relevant evidence rather than indiscriminate sampling strategies appears to be a promising way out of the trade-off. We adopt this line of research and address one structural limitation. [32] consumes depth-only, and geometrically degenerate parts are reported as dominant failure mode. We fuse color and depth directly during scene reconstruction. Synchronized RGB-D views are integrated into a sparse truncated signed distance field [56], and the colored surface points from the zero-crossing band are the input to our network. The staged heatmap strategy is applied on the sparse voxelization of that cloud, after which foreground voxel candidates are lifted back to point level through an exact grid lookup. A shared Point Transformer trunk [51] feeds three heads: classification, translation and rotation. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first fully sparse holistic RGB-D framework for 6D pose estimation.

Conventional holistic designs recover the pose in a subsequent object-wise aggregation, commonly a mean-shift clustering of keypoint votes followed by a least-squares fit [16, 17, 10, 11, 34]. Depth-based pipelines frequently append an ICP refinement that dominates the post-processing budget [14, 32]. We remove this time-consuming stage in three steps. First, translation offsets are voted per point, which naturally forms clusters [32]. A single clustering pass over the scene replaces the per-object mode. Only points voting into a cluster are retained, which sharpens the point cloud segments beyond the heatmap accuracy. Second, every point of a cluster predicts its location in the class-conditioned canonical frame together with a learned confidence. Thus, a point and its predicted coordinate form a 3D-3D correspondence. Third, the pose follows in closed form as the confidence-weighted Procrustes solution [20] over the correspondence set that is over-determined by orders of magnitude relative to keypoint voting, batched over all objects of a scene. Assignment and reliability are both predicted rather than inferred from the current pose estimate, so neither correspondence search nor outlier rejection is iterated.

Conventional holistic designs recover the pose in a subsequent object-wise aggregation, commonly a mean-shift clustering of keypoint votes followed by a least-squares fit [16, 17, 10, 11, 34]. Depth-based pipelines frequently append an ICP refinement that dominates the post-processing budget [14, 32]. We remove this time-consuming stage in three steps. First, translation offsets are voted per point, which naturally forms clusters [32]. A single clustering pass over the scene replaces the per-object mode. Only points voting into a cluster are retained, which sharpens the point cloud segments beyond the heatmap accuracy. Second, every point of a cluster predicts its location in the class-conditioned canonical frame together with a learned confidence. Thus, a point and its predicted coordinate form a 3D-3D correspondence. Third, the pose follows in closed form as the confidence-weighted Procrustes solution [20] over the correspondence set that is over-determined by orders of magnitude relative to keypoint voting, batched over all objects of a scene. Assignment and reliability are both predicted rather than inferred from the current pose estimate, so neither correspondence search nor outlier rejection is iterated.

Additionally, we introduce heatmap-guided feature distillation, a novel scheme that improves efficiency while reducing memory consumption. The staged heatmap formulation provides a sparse, task-supervised measure of relevance. We reweight the teacher-student feature alignment by the attention priors assigned by the teacher. The teacher and student share grid construction and network components but differ in capacity. We summarize our contributions as follows. • A holistic, fully sparse multi-view RGB-D framework for 6D pose estimation that fuses appearance and geometry before the first network stage, and recovers poses scene-adaptively in 1.131.13 s, outperforming methods in the same latency regime by a wide margin. • A symmetry-aware canonical coordinate voting head that replaces rotation regression by per-point correspondence votes with learned confidences and a weighted Procrustes solve, yielding poses for an arbitrary number of objects in closed form and without iterative refinement. • A heatmap-guided feature distillation scheme that reuses the attention priors of the pipeline as transfer weights.

papers.title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
papers.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.
papers.intro:
Forest managers need to know which tree species grow where. Species maps are used to plan harvesting and replanting, to find stands at risk from drought or pests [10], and, together with canopy analysis, to support agroforestry and the monitoring of agricultural and forest land. Many agencies fly regular aerial surveys, so recognising species from these images is of clear practical value. The hard cases are the rare species. They have few labels, and they are often the ones that matter most for biodiversity and for planning. Self-supervised foundation models are a promising answer to this problem. DINOv3 [28] includes a vision transformer pretrained without labels on SAT-493M, a set of 493 million satellite images. If its features already separate tree species, a user can run the model once over an image archive and train only a linear classifier on top. This is cheap, and it should need fewer labels. Recent benchmarks, however, find that geospatial foundation models do not consistently beat supervised models [21], and a well-tuned ImageNet model remains a strong baseline [8]. We first ran this comparison on the official split of TreeSatAI [1]. A fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50 beat the frozen DINOv3 model by 0.08 macro F1, also on the rare classes. We then looked at where the test patches are. Forest labels are spatially clustered, and a model can score well by recognising the place rather than the species [14, 25]. In the official split, 28.8% of the test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and the label of the nearest such patch alone is correct for 83.6% of them. Such a test rewards a model that adapts closely to the training stands. It does not tell us how well a model works in a new area, which is how species maps are used in practice. We therefore repeat the comparison on a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares (Fig. 1). On this split, both models lose accuracy, the fine-tuned model more so, and the difference between them is no longer significant. The largest change is on the rarest species. Here the fine-tuned model loses 0.27 F1 and the frozen model only 0.10, although the remaining difference between them is uncertain. This fits earlier findings that fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and hurt out-of-distribution performance [16], and that self-supervised features are less affected by class imbalance [20]. Our design compares two complete strategies, a frozen satellite-pretrained transformer and a fine-tuned ImageNet CNN. It cannot separate the effects of architecture, pretraining data and freezing, so our claims are about the comparison of these strategies and how it depends on the evaluation split, not about self-supervised pretraining being better in general. Our main contributions are: • We show that the official TreeSatAI split overlaps spatially with its training data, and that test patches close to training data favour the fine-tuned model more than the frozen one (Sec. 3.1). • We release a spatial split with 2 km squares and a 200 m buffer. On it, a frozen DINOv3 model with a linear classifier performs on par with a fine-tuned ResNet-50 at every label budget we tested (Sec. 5). • On unseen areas, the frozen model reaches a higher mean F1 on the five rarest species, but the confidence interval of the difference includes zero because these classes have few test locations (Sec. 5.1). • We locate the remaining errors of the frozen features in closely related species. Colour, classifier capacity and pooling do not explain them. A slightly coarser input and a middle layer, chosen on validation data, raise the frozen model to 0.662 macro F1 on the spatial test set (Sec. 6).

papers.title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
papers.abstract: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

papers.intro:
Finding corresponding representations across trained neural networks [Bau et al., 2019, Huh et al., 2024, Gurnee et al., 2024] is an important scientific task for understanding shared internal structure across independently trained models [Li et al., 2015, Morcos et al., 2018, Raghu et al., 2017, Kornblith et al., 2019] and for identifying components that can be reused across networks [Yosinski et al., 2014, Bansal et al., 2021, Csiszárik et al., 2021, Moschella et al., 2023]. These correspondences cannot be determined by layer indices or tensor shapes [Nguyen et al., 2021, Khosla and Williams, 2024, Singh and Jaggi, 2020], since networks may differ in depth and width, and each representation depends on the trained computation that produces it [Yurochkin et al., 2019, Tatro et al., 2020].

Responses from multiple sites can be collected during the same model traversal, and the responses or suitable comparison descriptors can be cached across comparisons. For previously unmeasured models, however, the corresponding responses still need to be acquired. We investigate a different use of these measurements: as supervision for learning how parameterized computations relate to the representations they produce. This leads to our central question:

Can we learn to predict representation similarity scores in unseen models across different sites using only their architecture and trained weights?

In this paper, we demonstrate that this is indeed possible. We study this question as a metanetwork learning task [Unterthiner et al., 2020, Schürholt et al., 2021, Zhou et al., 2023b, Zhou et al., 2023a, Navon et al., 2023]: given two internal sites from different trained models, we aim to predict how their representations are related. To do so, we need to know both which sites we are comparing and which relation we want to predict. The weights of the layer immediately before a site may miss earlier computations that shape its representation. In contrast, a single description of the whole model cannot distinguish between sites without additional information. As such, we represent each site using the computations that lead to it and train the metanetwork to learn relations measured from activations. This allows us to study how well trained computations can predict different properties of representations, including their geometry [Kriegeskorte et al., 2008, Raghu et al., 2017], neighborhood structure [Gwilliam and Shrivastava, 2022], and predictive behavior [Alain and Bengio, 2016, Ding et al., 2021]. However, model parameters do not always make these relations easy to recognize. Parameter symmetries [Hecht-Nielsen, 1990, Godfrey et al., 2022, Zhao et al., 2026] pose one source of challenge for this learning problem (see Fig. 1). Even when tensor shapes match, relabelings of hidden units can yield different parameter configurations that produce the same network function [Sussmann, 1992, Chen et al., 1993, Ainsworth et al., 2023]. Distances computed directly in parameter space can conflate differences in learned computation with differences in coordinate choice [Phuong and Lampert, 2020, Vlačić and Bölcskei, 2021, Stock and Gribonval, 2023, Bona-Pellissier et al., 2023, Simsek et al., 2021]. Representational correspondence can also extend beyond these parameter symmetries. For example, orthogonally rotating features preserves their inner-product geometry while changing the individual feature values [Kornblith et al., 2019]. Different upstream computations may produce similar representation geometry without being connected by these transformations. The learning problem is thus both to recognize equivalent parameterizations and to characterize which differences in trained computations matter for representational correspondence.

In this paper, we demonstrate that this is indeed possible. We study this question as a metanetwork learning task [Unterthiner et al., 2020, Schürholt et al., 2021, Zhou et al., 2023b, Zhou et al., 2023a, Navon et al., 2023]: given two internal sites from different trained models, we aim to predict how their representations are related. However, model parameters do not always make these relations easy to recognize. Parameter symmetries [Hecht-Nielsen, 1990, Godfrey et al., 2022, Zhao et al., 2026] pose one source of challenge for this learning problem (see Fig. 1). Representational correspondence can also extend beyond these parameter symmetries. For example, orthogonally rotating features preserves their inner-product geometry while changing the individual feature values [Kornblith et al., 2019]. Different upstream computations may produce similar representation geometry without being connected by these transformations. The learning problem is thus both to recognize equivalent parameterizations and to characterize which differences in trained computations matter for representational correspondence.

To this end, we introduce Parameter-based Analysis for Relational Inference of Sites (𝖯𝖠𝖱𝖨𝖲\mathsf{PARIS}), a framework for learning internal representation relations from the computations that produce them (see Fig. 2). We build on graph metanetworks that encode network parameters with their connectivity [Lim et al., 2024b, Kofinas et al., 2024]. To accommodate variation in architecture, we represent each site’s upstream computation as a graph encoding its architecture, trained parameters, and inference state. To account for permutation symmetries (e.g., hidden-coordinate permutation and head permutation), the encoding maps relabelings of hidden units and channels to graph relabelings while preserving parameter correspondences across successive layers. For attention, we encode the composed query-key and value-output operators, which are invariant to the changes of basis within their internal spaces. To learn representational correspondences beyond those induced by parameter symmetries, we train the graph metanetwork using representation similarity between sites across independently trained models. At search time, it predicts these relations for unseen models from their site graphs, without requiring new base-model forward passes.

papers.title: Semi-global Convergence and Finite-Sample Error Bounds for Model Predictive Path Integral Control
papers.abstract: We investigate the global optimisation behaviour of Model Predictive Path Integral Control (MPPI) in the low-temperature setting. For objective functions with a unique global minimum and under weak additional assumptions, allowing non-convexity and non-smoothness, we establish semi-global convergence of the mean-field or population level MPPI iteration to this global optimum. We also establish finite-sample results that show that with high probability the MPPI iteration comes close to the global optimum and provide sample complexity results. Under slightly stronger assumptions, we make these results more quantitative and provide concrete bounds on the inverse temperature and number of samples. Finally, we illustrate the results on the classic LQR problem.

papers.intro:
Model Predictive Path-Integral Control (MPPI) is one of the major sampling-based control methods used in robotics, autonomous driving, and model-based reinforcement learning (Kazim et al., 2024). While very successful in applications, the theoretical understanding of MPPI is still limited. Introduced originally by information-theoretic arguments connected to stochastic optimal control (Williams et al., 2018), it has since been recognised that MPPI is essentially a zeroth-order sampling-based optimisation method combined with receding-horizon control. In particular, a rigorous theoretical analysis must start with the optimisation behaviour of MPPI. Most existing works have been focused on local perspectives, e.g., interpreting MPPI as a form of gradient descent (Fazlyab et al., 2026), or considering restricted classes of objectives like quadratic functions (Yi et al., 2024). This is a severe limitation, since MPPI is particularly interesting for challenging non-convex and even non-smooth problems arising in control tasks. Motivated by this shortcoming, we investigate MPPI as a sampling-based global optimisation method for non-convex, non-smooth objective functions with a unique global optimum. For this, we build on the recent work Fornasier et al. (2026) that connects MPPI with global non-convex optimisation. More precisely, this work finds that the plain MPPI iteration on the population level corresponds exactly to Consensus Hopping (CH), a limiting case of Consensus-Based Optimisation (CBO), which is a class of popular global optimisation methods based on interacting particle systems (Pinnau et al., 2017) with strong theoretical guarantees (Fornasier et al., 2024; Carrillo et al., 2018). In turn, this connection allows one to prove strong convergence results for CH and hence MPPI. We build on this work and establish semi-global convergence results for MPPI on the population level. While already conceptually insightful, MPPI is a sampling-based method, and hence any result with practical relevance needs to take into account the finite-sample error incurred by the sampling process. To address this important issue, we also prove corresponding high-probability error bounds and establish sample complexity bounds for the actual sampling-based MPPI iteration. Apart from requiring a unique global optimum, our results rely only on rather general assumptions on the objective function, covering in particular non-convex and non-smooth functions. Our work provides a significant step towards a deeper theoretical understanding of MPPI and helps to put it on a solid theoretical foundation, on which reliable sampling-based control approaches can be built.

MPPI was introduced in the context of autonomous driving (Williams et al., 2016) based on information-theoretic considerations (Williams et al., 2018) that connect to stochastic optimal control and path-integral control. However, the connection is mostly heuristic and the rigorous theoretical foundation is lost (Homburger et al., 2025). By now there is a multitude of different MPPI variants, cf. Kazim et al. (2024) for an overview, and similar to most analyses, we focus on the plain MPPI iteration formally introduced in Section 2, and investigate MPPI as a zeroth-order sampling-based optimisation method, cf. Jordana et al. (2025) for more on this perspective. In contrast to previous works like Yi et al. (2024) or Yoon and Kim (2026), we consider general non-convex objective functions. For this, we build on the recent work Fornasier et al. (2026) that identified MPPI on the population level as Consensus Hopping (CH), which is connected to Consensus-Based Optimisation (CBO) (Pinnau et al., 2017). Utilising a quantitative Laplace principle as pioneered by the work Fornasier et al. (2024), one can establish semi-global convergence guarantees for CH and hence for population-level MPPI. The concept of semi-global results is common in nonlinear control, see (Grüne and Pannek, 2017, Chapter 6) for more details. The use of the Laplace principle in connection with MPPI has already been noticed in Homburger et al. (2025); however, a different scaling is used there, and no non-asymptotic results are provided. Note that it is well-known that MPPI has problems with functions having multiple global optima (Liu et al., 2026) due to averaging effects, which motivates our focus on objectives with a unique global optimum. We also provide finite-sample results, which are particularly relevant since in practice MPPI is always sampling-based. Prior works have investigated this in restricted settings like LQR problems, cf. (Yoon et al., 2022; Yoon and Kim, 2026), whereas we work with very general nonconvex objectives. Instead of relying on propagation of chaos techniques as suggested in Fornasier et al. (2026), we directly analyse the estimation error in a single step from the perspective of self-normalised importance weighted sampling, cf. Agapiou et al. (2017) for an overview and similar results. While this has been used in prior works on MPPI like Yoon et al. (2022); Yoon and Kim (2026), our simple but effective estimation error bounds become particularly powerful in connection with our semi-global convergence results. In particular, to the best of our knowledge we achieve the first finite-sample complexity bounds for general nonconvex objective functions with only modest regularity assumptions.

In particular, to the best of our knowledge we achieve the first finite-sample complexity bounds for general nonconvex objective functions with only modest regularity assumptions.

papers.title: Mapping the Wind to Find the Source: Online Physics-Informed Gas Source Localization with Mobile Robots
papers.abstract: Gas Source Localization (GSL) with mobile robots is challenging because wind and gas measurements are spatially sparse, noisy, and potentially affected by robot motion. Indoor airflow can vary substantially across space, while detailed environmental layouts, boundary conditions, or precomputed airflow fields are often unavailable. Moreover, hazardous sources must be localized as quickly as possible, making exhaustive exploration impractical. This paper presents a lightweight physics-informed probabilistic framework for efficient GSL under spatially varying indoor airflow. As the robot navigates, it continuously collects wind and gas measurements and reconstructs the spatially varying airflow field online. The estimated wind field drives a forward dispersion model that predicts the gas pattern for each candidate source location. These predictions are compared with the measured gas pattern to update a probabilistic belief over the source location. As the wind field is reconstructed incrementally, the framework also accounts for the spatially non-uniform reliability of wind field estimation and its influence on the source estimation. The resulting belief map is then used for informative path planning to guide the robot toward informative regions. High-fidelity simulations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the individual components and their integrations within the complete system, while physical indoor experiments assess the system performance under realistic sensing, motion, and airflow conditions. The results demonstrate that incorporating lightweight physical knowledge significantly improves localization robustness under spatially complex airflow and enables more efficient exploration.
papers.intro:
Gas leaks pose serious risks to human health, infrastructure, and the environment [1]. Mobile robots equipped with gas sensors can reduce human exposure by autonomously exploring potentially hazardous areas. GSL refers to the task of inferring the spatial location of a gas source from a limited set of gas measurements. As GSL is often time-critical, exhaustively sampling the entire environment is impractical. Instead, the robot should use the available measurements efficiently and prioritize informative regions. Since gas transport is governed by physical processes, incorporating knowledge of gas dispersion into source inference can constrain the search and guide the robot navigation more efficiently, particularly during the early stages of an emergency when measurements are limited.

papers.title: Kinetic Tomography with Diffuse Interstellar Bands in APOGEE DR17
papers.abstract: Context: Mapping gas flows in the interstellar medium is key to understanding the formation of structure in our Milky Way. Methods that simultaneously reconstruct clouds' distances and line-of-sight velocities are called kinetic tomography (KT). Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are powerful tracers for such maps because they trace the integrated dust density and the dust-weighted velocity. Previous DIB-KT works had small samples with coarse kpc-scale resolution and could not capture vertical disk structure. Aims: Make 4D (3D position + radial velocity) maps of the Milky Way from new, high-quality 15,273 {\AA} DIB detections in APOGEE DR17. Methods: We combine variational inference and Gaussian processes with a mixture likelihood for low signal-to-noise detections and marginalization over distance uncertainties. We calibrate the model on mock fields and spectral injection tests and validate the map against independent tracers of the dust density (3D dust maps) and velocity substructure (masers and young stellar clusters). Results: We recover a posterior distribution over 3D maps of the density and velocity structure of the 15,273 {\AA} DIB within 6 kpc of the Sun. We measure the large-scale structure of the DIB disk (scale length, height and flare) and detect vertical distortions consistent with the warp. On smaller scales, the map resolves distance ambiguities in gas longitude-velocity diagrams. From the second-order velocity structure function, we measure a slope (0.64 $\pm$ 0.04) consistent with Kolmogorov turbulence, amplitude consistent with expectations for molecular clouds, and a preliminary ratio of compressive-to-solenoidal modes. Conclusions: With larger DIB catalogs expected from SDSS-V, this framework should resolve kinematic substructure at the scales needed to constrain the formation and dynamics of individual clouds and voids. papers.intro:
The motion of gas within galaxies is one of the fundamental quantities governing how structure in the interstellar medium (ISM) forms, evolves, and dissipates. The velocity field determines the rate at which diffuse atomic gas is swept up, compressed, and cooled into the dense molecular clouds that form stars, and likewise dictates how those clouds are destroyed by shear and stellar feedback (Ballesteros-Paredes et al., 2020; Chevance et al., 2023). On larger scales, the streaming motions of gas across the Galactic disk encode the gravitational potential of the Milky Way and the nature of its spiral structure. For example, whether the arms are long-lived, quasi-stationary density waves or more transient features leaves a distinct kinematic imprint on the gas as it flows into and out of the arms (Dobbs and Baba, 2014; Shu, 2016). A spatially resolved, 3D view of how the ISM is moving is therefore a prerequisite for connecting the small-scale physics of cloud formation and destruction to the large-scale architecture of the Milky Way.

A spatially resolved, 3D view of how the ISM is moving is therefore a prerequisite for connecting the small-scale physics of cloud formation and destruction to the large-scale architecture of the Milky Way.

Historically, the kinematics of the ISM have been traced almost exclusively through CO and H I spectral-line emission. These surveys provide position–position–velocity (PPV) cubes that map the radial velocity of the gas along the line of sight. They do not, however, indicate where along the line of sight that gas is located. Converting an observed line-of-sight radial velocity into a distance requires the assumption of a Galactic rotation curve (Nakanishi and Sofue, 2016; Roman-Duval et al., 2009), an approach that breaks down where the dynamics are most interesting — in the presence of non-circular motions (Hunter et al., 2024). Toward the inner Galaxy, a single radial velocity can also map to two different distances, constituting the well-known near/far kinematic distance ambiguity within the solar circle (Wienen et al., 2015; Kolpak et al., 2003). As a result, the PPV view of the Milky Way alone makes it difficult to reliably reconstruct the 3D flow of gas. Recent works like Söding et al. (2025) have made progress in this direction by reconstructing the 3D gas density and velocity fields across the disk through forward-modeling gas emission with a Gaussian-process-based velocity field anchored to a rotation curve and maser and YSO parallax constraints.

Two broad approaches to kinetic tomography have been developed.

The first technique couples 3D dust maps to spectral-line emission by assuming an approximately constant gas-to-dust ratio. This approach was introduced by Tchernyshyov and Peek (2017), who fused distance-resolved 3D dust maps with CO and H I emission cubes to solve for the line-of-sight velocity field that self-consistently relates the spatially resolved dust to the velocity-resolved gas across much of the Galactic plane. Building on the advent of parsec-scale 3D dust reconstructions enabled by Gaia (Leike et al., 2020; Edenhofer et al., 2024b), Soler et al. (2023) used the histogram of oriented gradients method to combine the distance information in 3D dust with H I and CO emission to constrain the dynamics of the Taurus molecular cloud. Soler et al. (2025) then extended this approach to the Galactic plane within 1.25 kpc of the Sun using the Edenhofer et al. (2024b) 3D dust map. Shortly thereafter, McCallum et al. (2026b) likewise combined the Edenhofer et al. (2024b) 3D dust map with H I emission from the HI4PI survey within the framework of Information Field Theory (Enßlin et al., 2009; Enßlin, 2019) to infer the local distance-resolved velocity field at even higher angular and distance resolution. These 3D-dust-based spectral-line approaches are powerful, but they rely on morphologically matching two physically distinct tracers – dust seen in extinction and gas seen in emission – across distance and velocity and are particularly limited in the presence of morphological differences (O’Neill et al., 2026, e.g. due to significant variations in the dust-to-gas ratio, as seen locally in recent work;) or if the 3D dust does not trace the full column of gas due to the sensitivity and depth of current maps.

Because a DIB is measured in absorption against a background star, its strength constrains the amount of intervening medium while its central wavelength yields a density-weighted average of the integrated line-of-sight velocity. papers.title: Spiral Pitch Angles in Black Hole Images and Movies
papers.abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has produced images of M87* and Sgr A*, and will soon produce time sequences of images, or movies. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) models predict EHT sources will exhibit brightness fluctuations along the ring. The fluctuations are commonly connected to trailing spiral features. Here, we introduce a method to measure the pitch angle $\psi$ of radially extended features by cross-correlating brightness fluctuations sampled on rings at two distinct impact parameters. Pitch angle can be reliably measured from synthetic movies with BHEX resolution, and can be constrained even at EHT resolution. Single images enable noisy constraints of $\psi$. Pitch angle depends most on the viewing inclination and black hole spin. For constant inclination, the spiral winding direction depends on the sign of spin, with spirals winding more tightly in the direction of frame dragging near the horizon. The pitch angle will complement other observables to reliably constrain both the source inclination and spin in future analysis by EHT, and by expansions to the EHT such as ngEHT and BHEX.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has produced horizon-scale images of the black hole M87* at the center of M87 (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2019a) and the black hole Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) at the heart of our own galaxy (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022a). These images were made by combining data from an array of radio telescopes using very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). For M87*, the result is several snapshot images (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2021a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2024b; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2025a). Meanwhile, repeated observations, improved (u,v)(u,v) coverage, and improved imaging algorithms will enable movies (time sequences of images) for both M87* and Sgr A*. What information can be extracted from larger samples of images and movies, as they become feasible?

We measured this apparent rotation by correlating brightness temperature along the ring. The main result was that rotation was unexpectedly slow—slower than the Keplerian velocity of a feature just subject to gravitation, and slower than the fluid velocity (which can be arrested by pressure gradient and magnetic field forces). Rather than the fast motion of a hot spot, we predicted EHT movies will exhibit a pattern speed Ωp\Omega_{p}, driven by the slow azimuthal phase velocity of ingoing spiral waves.

A central goal of the EHT is to measure black hole spin (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 2024). We define the dimensionless spin a∗≡J​c/G​M2a_{\ast}\equiv Jc/GM^{2}, for black hole angular momentum JJ, speed of light cc, Newtonian gravitational constant GG, and black hole mass MM. Spin is one of the two parameters that describe an uncharged black hole. In an astronomical context, spin can influence the surrounding environment, powering relativistic jets (Blandford and Znajek, 1977), influencing the orbits of nearby stars (Levin and Beloborodov, 2003; Levin, 2022; GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2026, e.g.), and influencing the behavior of the near-horizon accretion flow. Constraints on spin could offer insights into the black hole’s formation, growth history, and host galaxy’s merger history (Gammie et al., 2004; Volonteri et al., 2007; Merloni and Heinz, 2008; Bambi et al., 2021; Reynolds, 2021; Ricarte et al., 2023; Ricarte et al., 2025b, e.g.,). However, the pattern speed in movies depends most strongly on the viewing inclination ii relative to the accretion disk angular momentum, with only a weaker dependence on a∗a_{\ast}.

Spin is one of the two parameters that describe an uncharged black hole. In an astronomical context, spin can influence the surrounding environment, powering relativistic jets (Blandford and Znajek, 1977), influencing the orbits of nearby stars (Levin and Beloborodov, 2003; Levin, 2022; GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2026, e.g.), and influencing the behavior of the near-horizon accretion flow. Constraints on spin could offer insights into the black hole’s formation, growth history, and host galaxy’s merger history (Gammie et al., 2004; Volonteri et al., 2007; Merloni and Heinz, 2008; Bambi et al., 2021; Reynolds, 2021; Ricarte et al., 2023; Ricarte et al., 2025b, e.g.,). However, the pattern speed in movies depends most strongly on the viewing inclination ii relative to the accretion disk angular momentum, with only a weaker dependence on a∗a_{\ast}.

This motivated additional techniques to constrain spin. One promising technique uses polarization, as the linear polarization structure shows a clear spin dependence in models (Palumbo et al., 2020; Chael et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2026; Chael et al., 2026a, e.g.). However, polarized observables are sensitive to additional uncertainties compared to intensity observables, including additional parameters (the magnetic field polarity), observational uncertainties in the compact flux, and intervening Faraday rotation. These uncertainties must be considered when performing polarization-based spin inference (R. Gunturu et al. in preparation).

The magnitude of the asymmetry typically increases with the magnitude of the spin, enabling statistically significant spin constraints (Bernshteyn et al., 2026). papers.title: On the High Eccentricity Orbit of 51 Eri b and Constraints on Interactions with a Second Companion
papers.abstract: The eccentricity of an exoplanet's orbit is a key observational quantity that can be used to infer its dynamical past and predict its future orbital evolution. Planets are expected to emerge from their protoplanetary cradles with roughly circular eccentricities, and non-circular eccentricites to arise from subsequent dynamical processing in the absence of the gas disk. We present an updated orbit for 51 Eridani b based on 5 years of 0.2 mas precision optical interferometry from VLTI/GRAVITY(+). This planet is young (${\sim}20\,\mathrm{Myr}$ old), temperate ($T_{\rm eff}\sim650\,\mathrm{K}$), and on a wide orbit ($a{=}9.36\,\mathrm{au}$) with an uncertain mass ($M_{\rm b}\leq12\,M_{\rm J}$). We measured the planet's motion to an exceptionally high precision, confirming that its orbit is very eccentric ($e_b=0.574\pm0.003$). We observe residuals to the absolute astrometry of the host star based on a single planet orbit that could be attributable to reflex motion from a third body in the system. We construct a two companion orbit model that could explain the apparent reflex motion of 51 Eri A: this model predicts that the putative second companion has $M_c\in[1.0, 2900]_{95\%}\,M_{\rm Jup}$ and $a_c\in[0.3, 3.1]_{95\%}\,\mathrm{au}$. In this framework, a dynamical interaction between b and ``c" could have kicked the exterior, lower mass b out onto its present, eccentric orbit. If this signal is astrophysical, and not due to a systematic error, this candidate should be confirmable with Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry in the near future.

papers.intro:
Gas giants are the dominant dynamical forces in their planetary systems, and are therefore crucial to understanding our own Solar System in a broad context. The distribution of giant planet eccentricity contains clues regarding giant planet formation and dynamical evolution [129, 47, 18, 15, e.g.]. The eccentricities of giant planets detected via radial velocities exhibit a large population of low eccentricity orbits, with a tail towards higher eccentricities [65, 15, 88]. Near-circular orbits are the expected result of formation within a protoplanetary disk, where gas drag damps the initial eccentricity. Subsequent processing, by scattering with other giant planets, interactions with stellar multiples, or stellar close encounters is then expected to increase the eccentricities for a fraction of these systems. Wider separation, directly imaged companions, when sorted by mass, appear to exhibit a preference for low eccentricity orbits [18], although this apparent trend is complicated by the low sample size, choice of priors (and hyper-priors), and limited coverage of orbital arcs [41, 89].

51 Eridani b is one of the lowest mass directly imaged planets known. It was discovered during the Gemini Planet Imager (GPI) Exoplanet Survey [80] and has been subsequently characterized by Gemini/GPI [38, 99, 39], VLT/SPHERE [109, 83, 25], Keck/NIRC2 [99, 81], JWST/NIRCam [7], VLT/HiRISE [40], and JWST/NIRSpec [82]. Atmospheric modeling has indicated that the planet has a cloudy atmosphere in chemical disequilibrium due to vertical mixing [99, 25, 81, 127, 7, 82]. Given the planet’s low luminosity and the system’s apparent age [45] based on its membership in the β\beta-Pic Moving Group (BPMG) [131, 11, e.g.], the planet’s mass has been projected to lie below the deuterium burning limit [80]. The proper motion anomaly between Hipparcos and Gaia for the host star is incongruent with the reflex motion that the planet’s orbit should induce at 1−2​σ1{-}2\,\sigma [39, see Figure 5-9 in]. When this proper motion anomaly is included in the likelihood function of a single planet orbit fit, it implies an upper limit on the mass of the planet of ≤12​MJup{\leq}12\,M_{\rm{Jup}} at 2​σ2\,\sigma [43].

In this paper we seek to confirm the high eccentricity of 51 Eri b, and to place constraints on the processes that could have excited the planet on to such an orbit.

papers.title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
papers.abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

papers.intro:
Graph coloring is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem, which, given a graph and a palette of colors, asks for an assignment of colors to the nodes of the graph such that adjacent nodes receive different colors. Given a palette of kk colors, deciding whether such an assignment exists is NP-complete for every fixed k≥3k\geq 3 (Garey et al., 1974). Moreover, computing the smallest number of colors required to obtain a conflict-free assignment, known as the chromatic number, is NP-hard. Graph coloring has applications in several practical domains, such as register allocation, where a compiler has to choose how to assign the variables of a program to the computer registers (Chaitin et al., 1981), and timetabling problems, where conflicting activities must occupy distinct timeslots (Welsh and Powell, 1967; Carter et al., 1996). Sudoku puzzles can also be seen as graph coloring instances, with cells represented as nodes and digits as colors (Herzberg and Murty, 2007).

Traditional exact approaches include integer programming (Méndez-Díaz and Zabala, 2006), as well as SAT and constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) solvers (Heule et al., 2022). Moreover, classical heuristics, which are generally faster but provide no guarantee of finding a valid coloring, include constructive algorithms such as greedy coloring (Welsh and Powell, 1967) and Dsatur (Brélaz, 1979), as well as local-search methods (Hertz and de Werra, 1987; Malaguti and Toth, 2010).

More generally, neural combinatorial optimization uses learned models as heuristics for constrained optimization problems like the traveling salesman (Bello et al., 2016; Khalil et al., 2017) and knapsack (Drakulic et al., 2023). When trained on instance distributions, these models amortize the cost of learning a heuristic and enable fast inference on new instances (Bengio et al., 2021).

Related Work For graph coloring, neural approaches can optimize instances directly or learn across a distribution. PI-SAGE (Schuetz et al., 2022) casts coloring as unsupervised node classification, using a graph neural network (GNN) to produce soft color assignments, which are then rounded. Building on PI-SAGE, Vanderbush and Weber (2026) improve approximate kk-coloring using recursive warm starts obtained from (k−1)(k\!-\!1)-colorings. ROS (Qiu et al., 2025) similarly relaxes assignments to continuous ones, optimizes a continuous objective, and samples discrete solutions. Other methods learn general procedures across instances. AnyCSP (Tönshoff et al., 2023) trains a GNN with reinforcement learning for solving general CSPs by performing global stochastic updates. Similarly, ConsFormer (Xu et al., 2025) trains a Transformer to improve complete assignments using differentiable relaxations of the constraints, as a learned form of local search. Le et al. (2026) learn color representations with a contrastive loss and decode them by clustering. Li et al. (2022) also propose a color-equivariant model using restricted linear equivariant updates, but predict all node colors simultaneously, without conditioning each assignment on previous ones as in sequential decoding. Instead, Watkins et al. (2023) propose a sequential constructive heuristic that learns node selection, while a fixed rule assigns the lowest permissible color. See Appendix B for additional related work.

Graph tasks often exhibit symmetries (Gilmer et al., 2017). Most commonly, if two graphs are isomorphic via a node permutation, node-level outputs should permute accordingly. In graph coloring, applying the same node permutation to a graph and to a valid coloring preserves validity. Importantly, however, an individual coloring isn’t invariant under node permutations, since nodes in the same automorphism orbit may receive different colors. A solver must therefore be able to break node symmetries. Moreover, graph coloring exhibits a symmetry over its output. Color labels are interchangeable, since permuting them transforms any coloring into an equivalent one. These observations suggest that a learned solver should exploit both forms of symmetry to learn efficiently.

Contributions We introduce Scone (Symmetry-aware COloring via Neural Equivariance), a model that constructs colorings sequentially, one node at a time. At each step, it takes as input the current partial coloring, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate through the graph, which distinguishes any nodes that were previously symmetric. Node colors are scored by a color-equivariant GNN, so relabeling the colors permutes the predictions accordingly without changing the behavior of the model. We show theoretically that equivariance reduces the state space that the model must learn (Theorem 1), and that sequential decoding yields expressive models (Theorems 3, 4). In summary, Scone combines sequential predictions, equivariance and classical search for expressivity and efficiency. We evaluate Scone on real-world coloring applications, including Sudoku, register allocation, and exam timetabling. Here, it achieves state-of-the-art solution quality among neural methods, achieving the best solution quality while also having the lowest solve times.

papers.title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings
papers.abstract: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.

papers.intro:
Understanding language requires recovering not only what is said but also what speakers intend beyond the literal meaning of an utterance (Grice, 1975; Levinson, 1983). The kitchen is a bit warm may function as a request to open a window, and an enthusiastic Wonderful may express reluctant acceptance rather than genuine praise. This ability to infer intended meaning, known as pragmatic competence, is fundamental to conversational language understanding (Sperber and Wilson, 1986; Clark, 1996). As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into conversational systems, recovering intended meaning has become essential for reliable interaction. A model that interprets an indirect refusal literally may comply with a rejected request, while one that treats a complaint as a factual statement may provide information instead of apologising. In both cases, the response may appear appropriate despite the model misjudging the speaker’s intent.

The question matters as LLMs are increasingly deployed across languages, cultures, conversational environments, and model development contexts that differ substantially from those represented in English-centric evaluations. Robust pragmatic performance should not depend on a particular evaluation setup, but generalise across data types, languages, phenomena, and prompting strategies.

Robust pragmatic performance should not depend on a particular evaluation setup, but generalise across data types, languages, phenomena, and prompting strategies.

Testing such generalisation remains difficult because few benchmarks span both purpose-written and dialogue-derived materials, limiting evaluation across data types (Ma et al., 2025). Moreover, because pragmatic interpretation hinges on language-specific idioms, wordplay, and cultural knowledge, cross-linguistic differences on directly translated materials may reflect translation artefacts rather than model deficits (Liu et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025; Brglez and Vintar, 2026). Robust evaluation therefore demands resources that combine varied pragmatic data types with careful cross-linguistic adaptation.

papers.title: Dynamical Variational Theory of Stochastic Reaction Networks
papers.abstract: Discrete stochastic population dynamics describe systems ranging from biochemical reaction networks and gene regulation to epidemic spreading, ecology, and population genetics, where finite populations generate strong intrinsic fluctuations. Predicting their dynamics, including mean populations, fluctuations, time-lagged correlations, response functions, and steady states, remains challenging: the chemical master equation admits no general analytical solution, numerical solutions scale poorly with system size, and standard approximations fail at low copy numbers. Using a field-theoretic representation of the reaction dynamics, we develop a dynamical variational approximation for stochastic reaction networks based on the Plefka expansion from spin-glass physics. For reaction systems with general stoichiometry and time-dependent rates, the expansion yields tractable non-Markovian effective dynamics with self-consistent memory. We further introduce a generalized self-consistent bubble resummation that provides closed predictions for means, correlations, and response functions. The formulation applies broadly to discrete stochastic population dynamics on networks, and we provide a numerical implementation with adaptive time stepping for user-defined systems. We benchmark the method on stochastic gene regulation, enzyme kinetics, and infection dynamics, where it accurately captures both time-dependent behaviour and steady states, including fluctuation-driven effects missed by conventional approximations. Together, these results establish a general analytical framework for stochastic reaction dynamics across transient and stationary regimes in strongly fluctuating low-copy-number systems.

papers.title: A closed-loop agentic research environment for MRI development within Siemens IDEA platform
papers.abstract: Motivation: Testing new ideas in MRI can require substantial effort to learn sequence programming and reconstruction tools and to debug implementations before the scientific question can be addressed. Goals: Reduce the implementation and debugging burden of testing MRI ideas while retaining researcher control of scientific decisions. Approach: We developed an environment where LLM agents develop sequences in the native Siemens IDEA platform, evaluate them through Bloch simulation and reconstruction, and further iteratively refine them using scanner feedback. Results: As test cases, the agentic environment was used to implement and validate a GIRF-based gradient-calibration sequence and reconstruction in approximately 4 hours, and to develop and optimize a rapid 3-second multichannel calibration scan in approximately 12 hours of researcher-guided iteration.

papers.title: Square Kilometre Array Science Data Challenge 3b: EoR inference
papers.abstract: We present and analyse the results of Science Data Challenge 3b (SDC3b; https://sdc3.skao.int/challenges/inference), an Epoch of Reionization (EoR) inference exercise organised by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) using simulated SKA data. The nine-month challenge, running from October 2024 to May 2025, represents the first community-wide comparison of EoR inference pipelines on common simulated datasets. We consider multiple datasets designed to assess performance on both foreground-free and foreground-contaminated cylindrical power spectra and imaging products, adopting different reionization scenarios and EoR simulation models. We include results from 16 teams, which employ a range of methodologies to infer the posterior distribution of the hydrogen neutral fraction across three redshift intervals spanning z=8.41 to z=6.25. The results show significant inter-team variability of the astrophysical constraints even in the simpler case where only instrumental noise is added to the cosmological signal. This underscores the need for further investigation into the relative contributions of signal modelling, the treatment of instrumental effects, and inference methods to the robustness of the resulting conclusions. Although individual methods can produce biased parameter estimates, the combined average of their estimates remains close to the input values, suggesting that independent approaches can offset method-specific biases.

papers.intro:
One of the main science goals for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is to map the distribution of the 21-cm signal from the eras referred to as the Cosmic Dawn and Epoch of Reionization (CD/EoR), roughly corresponding to the first billion years in the history of the Universe (see CD Science Working Group et al., 2026, for an overview). During these times, as well as during the preceding Dark Ages, the hydrogen gas in the Intergalactic Medium (IGM) was mostly atomic and neutral. Non-ionizing radiation produced by the first generations of stars and accreting black holes during the CD/EoR could, through the so-called Wouthuysen-Field effect, decouple the HI quantum state from the background photons of the Cosmic Microwave Background. This led to the generation of an observable 21-cm signal (see e.g. Pritchard and Loeb, 2012, for a review on the 21-cm signal from the CD/EoR). During the reionization process, H-ionizing photons produced by stars and/or accreting black holes turned intergalactic HI into HII, ultimately resulting in a fully reionized Universe in which most HI resides inside galaxies.

By measuring the evolution of the redshifted 21-cm signal over a range of frequencies with the SKA-Low telescope, it should be possible to derive information about the state of the IGM at different times, and through this, about the radiation fields produced by the galaxies. However, these measurements are far from trivial. The radio sky at the relevant frequencies (50–250 MHz) is filled with strong foreground signals both from the Milky Way and from extragalactic radio sources. Separating the redshifted 21-cm signal from these foregrounds is challenging as they are several orders of magnitude brighter and therefore require excellent calibration of instrumental effects. Once a 21-cm signal has been extracted, deriving information is not straightforward either but requires inference based on simulations of the signal. Recent examples of the application of inference to data from 21-cm experiments can be found in Abdurashidova et al. (2026) and Ghara et al. (2025). We refer interested readers to Acharya et al. (2026) for more discussion.

To test the ability of existing frameworks to study the redshifted 21-cm signal from the CD/EoR, the SKA Observatory initiated an SKA Data Challenge, the third of such challenges after SDC1 (Bonaldi et al., 2021) and SDC2 (Hartley et al., 2023). It was decided to split SDC3 into two parts. SDC3a tested the ability to extract the 21-cm signal from simulated SKA-Low data including foreground and telescope effects. Its results were published in Bonaldi et al. (2025) and a description of how the data was created in Bonaldi et al. (2026), henceforth SDC3a1. The second part, SDC3b, tests the ability to derive information about the state of the IGM from an already extracted 21-cm signal. This paper presents the results from SDC3b.

The provided 21-cm data was produced blindly and the correct answers were not provided until after the participating teams had submitted their results. The choice was made to focus on the mean neutral fraction as this is a single parameter that measures the progress of reionization in the IGM. It is also a quantity which is well defined and does not depend on the details of the reionization model used.

papers.title: The origin of the apparent ULX deficit in NGC 3256
papers.abstract: Ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources are bright, off-nuclear X-ray point sources, mostly associated with high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs), with a compact object accreting from a donor star at super-Eddington luminosities. Although their HMXB nature implies a connection to star formation processes, previous works have found that luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) appear to have a deficit of ULXs compared to their very high star formation rates (SFRs). Here, we analyze three Chandra observations of NGC 3256, a merging LIRG with SFR ~50-60 Msun/yr. Based on local scaling relations, it could be expected to host between 100-120 individual ULXs, which could have a non-negligible impact on the energetics and feedback processes of the galaxy. We aim to characterize all its detected X-ray point sources to determine if there is a ULX deficit in this galaxy. We also aim to explore the potential impact of host-galaxy obscuration and metallicity in said deficit. We characterize the luminosity of each X-ray point source in each Chandra observation, and use all observations to determine their potential ULX nature and the fraction of transient ULXs, as well as construct a ULX luminosity function for this galaxy. We find that the galaxy hosts 10-15 ULXs, making it one of the most ULX-rich galaxies known to date. While comparison with the ULX/SFR ratio of nearby galaxies predicted as many as ~100 ULXs, we show that, when accounting for its very high metallicity, NGC 3256 does not have a ULX deficit; and may even present an excess. While the high obscuration in LIRGs has previously been invoked to explain the ULX deficit, we conclude that it is not required to explain the ULX to SFR ratio in NGC 3256. If obscuration still plays a role, then LIRGs may actually be significantly more efficient at producing ULXs than normal galaxies (of the same metallicity), in disagreement with previous results.

Ultra-luminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are defined as off-nuclear point sources with X-ray luminosities Lx>1039L_{x}>10^{39} erg s-1 (Kaaret et al., 2017; King et al., 2023, e.g.,), which can only be achieved as a result of accretion onto a compact object. These sources have garnered the interest of the community since their discovery (Long et al., 1981; Fabbiano and Trinchieri, 1987, e.g.,), given that 103910^{39} erg s-1 is the Eddington luminosity for a 10 M⊙M_{\odot} black hole. Sources with significantly higher luminosity must therefore have significantly higher mass (i.e. potential intermediate mass black holes, IMBHs), or be stellar mass objects accreting at super-Eddington rates.

These sources have garnered the interest of the community since their discovery (Long et al., 1981; Fabbiano and Trinchieri, 1987, e.g.,), given that 103910^{39} erg s-1 is the Eddington luminosity for a 10 M⊙M_{\odot} black hole. Sources with significantly higher luminosity must therefore have significantly higher mass (i.e. potential intermediate mass black holes, IMBHs), or be stellar mass objects accreting at super-Eddington rates.

IMBHs bridge the gap between stellar and supermassive black holes, offering fundamental information about black hole seeding mechanisms and growth (Greene et al., 2020, see e.g.,). Very few are considered reliable candidates, and these tend to have masses in the range of 105−10610^{5}-10^{6} M⊙ (Chilingarian et al., 2018; Zaw et al., 2020, e.g.,). ULX IMBH candidates, however, have candidate black hole masses on the order ∼100−1000\sim 100-1000 M⊙ (Farrell et al., 2009; Davis et al., 2011; Pasham et al., 2014; Mezcua et al., 2015; Mezcua et al., 2018, e.g., HLX-1 in ESO 243-49, M82 X-1, NGC 2276-3c, and NGC 5252 X-1;), making them representative of the low-end tail of the IMBH mass distribution, and potential seeds for supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

Bachetti et al. (2014) identified, for the first time, the ULX M82 X-2 as a high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB), with an accreting neutron star and a donor star. Since then, a handful of ULXs (Walton et al., 2022, out of ∼1800\sim 1800 candidates known to date,) have been firmly identified as neutron stars thanks to the detection of pulsations (Fürst et al., 2016; Israel et al., 2017; Carpano et al., 2018; Sathyaprakash et al., 2019; Rodríguez Castillo et al., 2020; Pintore et al., 2025; Ducci et al., 2025, e.g.,), which further supported the notion that the majority of the population may be comprised of stellar-mass compact objects. An X-ray binary origin of ULXs is also supported by the correlation found between the number of ULXs in nearby, star-forming galaxies and their star formation rate (SFR); with an average of 2 ULXs per unit SFR (Mapelli et al., 2010, e.g.,). If ULXs have a binary origin, they are the ideal site to study super-Eddington accretion. The extreme X-ray luminosity of some sources (Davis et al., 2011; Sutton et al., 2012; Amato et al., 2025, >1041>10^{41} erg s-1; e.g.,) may be more difficult to explain without an IMBH. However, ULX-1 in NGC 5907 has been reported to reach such luminosities, despite its confirmed pulsar nature (Israel et al., 2017; Fürst et al., 2017, e.g.,); and accreting neutron-star models invoking geometrical beaming manage to achieve them (King, 2009; Dauser et al., 2017, e.g.,). As such, ULXs and their nature remain a topic of debate.

Luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) have infrared luminosities LIR>1011L_{\rm IR}>10^{11} L⊙ and SFRs that easily surpass 1010 M⊙ yr-1. In the local Universe, they are often the result of mergers (Sanders and Mirabel, 1996; Larson et al., 2016, e.g.,) and, at the peak of star-formation in the Universe (z∼2−3\sim 2-3), they dominate the infrared luminosity density function (Caputi et al., 2007; Magnelli et al., 2011, e.g.,). At an expected rate of 2 ULXs per unit SFR, LIRGs should be the ideal sites to search for ULXs. However, the most extensive study to date (Luangtip et al., 2015, focusing on 17 systems;) from the Great Observatories All-Sky LIRG Survey (Armus et al., 2009, GOALS,) found that the rate of ULXs per unit SFR was only 0.2, a factor of 10 lower than expected.

LIRGs are inherently gas-rich and dusty (Downes and Solomon, 1998; Herrero-Illana et al., 2019; Chartab et al., 2022, e.g.,), which leads to high levels of extinction (Piqueras López et al., 2013, AV up to 20 mag, e.g.,), even in the X-ray regime (Iwasawa et al., 2011; Torres-Albà et al., 2018, e.g.,) and, particularly, in their nuclear regions (Ricci et al., 2017; Ricci et al., 2021, >1023−1024>10^{23}-10^{24} cm-2, e.g.,). The high levels of extinction make observing sources with a luminosity of ∼1039\sim 10^{39} erg s-1 extremely challenging, and thus Luangtip et al. (2015) propose this as the dominant explanation for the deficit of ULXs in local LIRGs. However, they also suggest two other potential contributors to the deficit.
