The high levels of extinction make observing sources with a luminosity of ∼1039\sim 10^{39} erg s-1 extremely challenging, and thus Luangtip et al. (2015) propose this as the dominant explanation for the deficit of ULXs in local LIRGs. However, they also suggest two other potential contributors to the deficit.

First, the observed dependence of ULX abundance on metallicity. The high SFRs of LIRGs lead to high supernovae rates, which in turn leads to higher-than-solar metallicities (see e.g., Rich et al., 2012, who find super-solar gas metallicities in the inner few kpc of NGC 3256). Previous works indicate that metallicity does have an impact on the abundance of ULXs in galaxies (Mapelli et al., 2011; Prestwich et al., 2013; Lehmer et al., 2021, e.g.,), with higher metallicity leading to reduced formation of high-mass stars, which results in a decrease in the detected number of ULXs.

Previous works indicate that metallicity does have an impact on the abundance of ULXs in galaxies (Mapelli et al., 2011; Prestwich et al., 2013; Lehmer et al., 2021, e.g.,), with higher metallicity leading to reduced formation of high-mass stars, which results in a decrease in the detected number of ULXs.

The second effect could be the age of the starbursts within these systems. That is, if a significant fraction of the star-formation is younger than ∼10\sim 10 Myr (Linden et al., 2010), not enough stars may have died and turned into accreting, compact objects. Estimates of star formation histories (SFHs) in local LIRGs are consistent with a significant fraction of their recent star-formation activity occurring within the last 10 Myr (e.g., Cortijo-Ferrero et al., 2017; Pereira-Santaella et al., 2015, Nagarajan-Swenson in prep.). Although Luangtip et al. (2015) argue that neither of these effects alone is sufficient to fully explain the ULX deficit in LIRGs, it is unclear how much the combination of both can account for. For example, an in-depth study of the high-mass X-ray binary population in another LIRG, NGC 7552, concludes the opposite; that there likely is an intrinsic lack of X-ray binaries, rather than an obscured population (West et al., 2023).

papers.abstract: We prove the Lyons-Pemantle-Peres conjecture for high enough offspring laws, that is we show that the speed satisfies $\ell'(\lambda) < 0 $ for the entire transient regime of the bias $\lambda \in (0, m)$ in the special case that the number of children $Z$ in the Galton-Watson tree satisfies $Z \geq 4$ almost surely.

papers.title: Optimal long-time derivative estimates for underdamped Langevin dynamics
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behaviour of derivatives of the semigroup $P_t=e^{t\mathcal{A}}$ generated by the underdamped Langevin (kinetic Fokker-Planck) operator $\mathcal{A}$ on $L^2(\mu)$, where the Gibbs measure $\mu$ is not required to be finite. Under a weighted relative bound on the Hessian of the potential, we prove that for every integer $m\ge 0$ the squared $L^2(\mu)$ norms of $\mathcal{A}^m P_t h_0$ and of $\nabla_{x,v}\mathcal{A}^m P_t h_0$ are bounded by $C_m t^{-2m}\|h_0\|^2$ and $D_m t^{-(2m+1)}\|h_0\|^2$ respectively for large times, and the free dynamics shows that these exponents are optimal. The proof rests on a resolvent estimate near the imaginary axis, valid for every smooth potential, which follows from the adjoint relation between the generator and the velocity reversal and from the Gaussian Poincar\'e inequality in the velocity variable.

papers.title: Swimming formula in a linearly viscous fluid with anisotropic and odd viscosity tensors at low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: We theoretically investigate the low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics of a microswimmer in a linearly viscous fluid. The fluid is characterized by a viscosity tensor containing both even and odd components, and can therefore exhibit anisotropic and chiral properties absent in an isotropic Newtonian fluid. By employing the generalized Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we establish the Onsager-Casimir reciprocity for the resistance tensors of an arbitrarily shaped rigid body. We then derive a swimming formula that linearly relates the swimming velocities to the prescribed surface velocity of a microswimmer and imposed background flows. As a showcase application of the derived swimming formula, we prove that the scallop theorem holds in this class of linearly viscous fluids. Furthermore, we investigate the equations of motion for a spherical swimmer in a fluid with odd viscosity, as a representative example of the generalized linear constitutive framework. In particular, we reveal that sufficiently strong shear flows destabilize the bimodal chirotactic alignment of a microswimmer. Our results highlight how intrinsic fluid chirality and anisotropy fundamentally alter the orientational dynamics and transport phenomena of microswimmers.

papers.intro:
Microorganisms frequently navigate complex fluids ranging from biological to synthetic structured media (Spagnolie & Underhill, 2023). Unlike a simple isotropic Newtonian fluid, many such media possess a preferred microstructural orientation, giving rise to anisotropic mechanical and rheological responses. In biological contexts, examples of structured biological environments include the extracellular matrix, biopolymer networks, and cervical mucus, whose fibrous microstructure motivates anisotropic models of microorganism transport (Cupples et al., 2017; Shi & Powers, 2017; Cupples et al., 2018). Similar axial ordering also arises in synthetic systems, such as liquid crystals (Aranson, 2018), aligned colloidal suspensions (Snezhko, 2016), actuated magnetic particles (Junot et al., 2023; Beppu & Timonen, 2024), and chiral columnar crystals (Kole et al., 2024; Maitra, 2025). Understanding how orientationally ordered media affect microswimmer motion and particle transport is important for reproductive biology, targeted drug delivery, and the design of microfluidic devices (Ju et al., 2025).

Understanding how orientationally ordered media affect microswimmer motion and particle transport is important for reproductive biology, targeted drug delivery, and the design of microfluidic devices (Ju et al., 2025).

To describe the mechanics of such structured media, continuum theories based on rational mechanics have been developed (Truesdell, 1992; Truesdell & Noll, 2004). Extending the concept of simple materials established in the framework of rational mechanics, Ericksen formulated the fundamental continuum theory for fluids with uniaxial orientational order, known as transversely isotropic fluids (Ericksen, 1960). Under strict invariance conditions required of classical continua, this constitutive relation is uniaxial, characterizing the fluid anisotropy through a single preferred direction that represents the local microstructural orientation. This framework was later extended into the hydrodynamic theory of nematic liquid crystals (Leslie, 1966). Such continuum descriptions have served as a cornerstone for studying complex media, including fiber-reinforced fluids, polymeric suspensions, and the motion of microswimmers in liquid crystals (Daddi-Moussa-Ider & Menzel, 2018; Lin et al., 2022; Mandal et al., 2025). Numerical approaches, including multiparticle collision dynamics, have subsequently been developed to resolve the coupled flow and orientational dynamics (Mandal & Mazza, 2019; Mandal & Mazza, 2021). These descriptions provide a foundation for anisotropic transport, while internally driven chiral media introduce additional constitutive couplings.

In recent years, research on active matter has extended this picture to systems composed of individual units that consume energy locally to perform mechanical work (Marchetti et al., 2013; Gompper et al., 2025). A particularly intriguing subclass comprises chiral active fluids, where active agents break both time-reversal and parity symmetries (Fürthauer et al., 2012; Liebchen & Levis, 2022; Hosaka & Komura, 2022; Fruchart et al., 2023; Mecke et al., 2024). Examples of chiral active fluids range from chiral bacterial vortices (Beppu et al., 2021; Nishiguchi et al., 2025), living chiral crystals (Tan et al., 2022), and cilia-driven tissue surfaces to synthetic micro-rotors and actuated colloidal particles (Soni et al., 2019; López-Castaño et al., 2022; Mecke et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025). In suspensions of driven rotors, internal angular momentum and active torques can generate additional contributions to the macroscopic stress. This coupling between directional order and microscopic chirality fundamentally alters the macroscopic hydrodynamic equations, giving rise to unconventional mechanical behaviors absent in classical fluids (Shankar et al., 2022).

The combination of internal driving, chirality, and axial anisotropy has revealed a spectrum of novel transport phenomena. A prominent consequence is the emergence of odd viscosity, a nondissipative contribution to the viscous stress (Avron, 1998; Banerjee et al., 2017). Odd viscosity is the part of the viscosity tensor that is antisymmetric under exchange of the stress and strain-rate index pairs. Its associated stress makes no direct contribution to the local viscous dissipation, and the odd viscosity therefore gives rise to transverse hydrodynamic responses, unlike the conventional shear viscosity of a Newtonian fluid. This transverse property leads to a range of dynamical phenomena, and recent experimental and theoretical findings have demonstrated that chiral active fluids exhibit topological edge modes (Souslov et al., 2019), unusual interfacial dynamics (Soni et al., 2019; Abanov et al., 2020; França & Jalaal, 2026), and nonreciprocal hydrodynamic responses, including asymmetric Green’s functions for point-force responses (Hosaka et al., 2021b) and lift forces (Hosaka et al., 2021a; Lier et al., 2023; Lier, 2024b).

Although much of the early work on odd viscosity focused on two-dimensional systems, three-dimensional odd-viscous hydrodynamics has also advanced rapidly (Markovich & Lubensky, 2021). In particular, the hydrodynamics of spherical bodies in three-dimensional odd-viscous fluids has been investigated extensively (Khain et al., 2022; Yuan & Olvera de la Cruz, 2023; Hosaka et al., 2023c), and exact solutions for a rigid sphere in models with a single odd viscosity coefficient have recently been obtained (Everts & Cichocki, 2024; Meissner-Oszer et al., 2026). Related studies have also examined the motion of self-propelled particles and microswimmers in odd flows (Lapa & Hughes, 2014; Hosaka et al., 2023a; Hosaka et al., 2023b; Hosaka et al., 2023c; Hosaka et al., 2024; Chatzittofi & Hosaka, 2025), as well as the sedimentation of particles with geometries beyond simple circular or spherical shapes (Khain et al., 2024). Despite these advances, particle transport in fluids described by more general viscosity tensors, including those with two independent odd viscosity coefficients, remains incompletely understood. A recent step in this direction was taken by Lier, who investigated particle transport in weakly odd-viscous fluids with two independent odd viscosity coefficients (Lier, 2026). Beyond extending these studies to more general constitutive models, an important open question is how the surface deformations of an active particle or microswimmer determine its translational and rotational swimming velocities. Surface integral formulas relating swimming velocities to prescribed surface deformations have been derived for Newtonian fluids (Stone & Samuel, 1996; Yariv, 2006; Ishimoto, 2023), whereas their counterparts for fluids with anisotropic and odd viscosity tensors remain to be established. Deriving such formulas requires an understanding of the symmetry relations of the hydrodynamic resistance tensors, whose explicit evaluation can be challenging for bodies of arbitrary shape. Related integral formulas for spherical swimmers have been discussed by one of the present authors (Hosaka et al., 2024; Chatzittofi et al., 2026). These developments lead to a natural question: how do anisotropic and odd contributions to the viscosity tensor modify the symmetry relations of particle resistance tensors and the resulting swimming formulas (figure 1)?

papers.title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry
papers.abstract: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.

A corridor viewed through an open doorway, reflected in a planar mirror, displayed on a screen, or seen through a window can produce the same image. The first physical surface along a camera ray is the nearest surface that would stop a physical probe: corridor structure, mirror glass, the display panel, or the window pane. A depth network may estimate the depicted corridor behind a display even though the physical surface is the panel. When the images are identical, the initial image provides no evidence for choosing among these mechanisms. Camera motion can expose their different light paths. Matched hypotheses produce the same initial image and differ only after motion. Figure 1 summarizes the method and shows, on one real stereo pair, the two hypothesis warps that are compared.

Several lines of work address mirrors, glass, multiple surfaces, and abstention. Multi-layer formulations retain both a transparent interface and the scene behind that interface (Wen et al., 2025; Wen and Deng, 2026; Min et al., 2026). Detectors localize mirrors and glass (Tan et al., 2021; Na et al., 2026). Selective prediction with split conformal prediction (Vovk et al., 2005; Lei et al., 2018) decides when a system should answer. These methods estimate surfaces and confidence from a fixed viewpoint. This work asks whether any available viewpoint can identify the physical mechanism. Identifiability depends on the hypothesis family, the bounded action set, and a separability threshold with units specified by the protocol.

Intervene3D takes one image, its geometry estimate, and candidate camera motions. Real data also supplies an annotated region, camera calibration, and stereo reference disparity outside that region for alignment. A frozen monocular depth network runs on the initial image only. Each hypothesis predicts how image content moves. Warped photographs provide the evidence after motion. The output is a mechanism and the first physical surface, or an abstention. The full family contains direct content (HDH_{D}), a flat emissive panel (HEH_{E}), a planar mirror (HRH_{R}), and a transparent pane (HTH_{T}), all matched at the initial pose. The basic transmission model gives HTH_{T} and HDH_{D} identical image motion, so motion alone cannot distinguish them. The real illusion benchmark (Yao et al., 2025) contains printed sheets, posters, and monitors in photographed scenes. Experiments on it use only HDH_{D} and HEH_{E}. Two selectors choose the motion. Intervene3D-maximin selects the motion that maximizes the smallest separability among separable, contending hypothesis pairs. Intervene3D-sum uses their summed separability. With two hypotheses, maximin and summed selection coincide. Evidence that the selectors differ therefore comes from the synthetic benchmark. After the selected motion, residuals determine the answer. The system also checks whether the action set can separate the remaining alternatives, and applies an adequacy test where enabled. Table 1 states when each protocol performs these checks.

papers.title: Galaxy Bias and Soft Limits from Inflation
papers.abstract: Primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) leaves an imprint on large-scale structure through a scale-dependent galaxy bias, and properly incorporating the effects of higher order PNG into the bias expansion requires a consistent renormalization framework that extends beyond the squeezed limit of the bispectrum. We develop the multi-loop renormalization of bias operators in the presence of non-vanishing primordial n-point functions of arbitrary order, including stochastic contributions. We show that galaxy bias renormalization is determined by the multi-soft limits of primordial correlators and bias kernels. We provide explicit computations for one- and two-loop renormalization of deterministic operators up to fifth order in the bias expansion. Finally, we derive the renormalization group equations for the bias parameters at one and two loops.

papers.title: Burnside Problems for Matrix Semigroup Quotients with Applications to Border Complexity
papers.abstract: The Burnside theorem for matrix semigroups states that a finitely generated matrix semigroup is finite whenever each element has only finitely many distinct powers. We study analogous finiteness questions for quotients of matrix semigroups by congruences, which need not themselves admit faithful finite-dimensional matrix representations. We show three finiteness criteria based on uniform bounds on the quotient images of (rank-)stable subsemigroups and groups in the Zariski closure. Our proofs use exterior algebra and the Ramsey theorem to develop variations of Simon's factorisation forest to matrix semigroups modulo congruences. We also present applications of our results to border complexity. One such involves separating homogeneous algebraic branching programs of fixed width and degree from its Zariski closure.

papers.intro:
In 1902, Burnside asked whether a finitely generated group is necessarily finite if every element has finite order, that is, if some positive power of each element equals the identity. Novikov and Adian showed in 1968 that the answer is negative even when the orders of all elements are bounded by a common constant [1]. By contrast, Schur proved that the answer is positive for groups of invertible matrices over the complex numbers [2]. Kaplansky generalised Schur’s result from the complex numbers to arbitrary fields (see [3]). McNaughton and Zalcstein further extended this conclusion to matrix semigroups over arbitrary fields [4]. They proved that a finitely generated matrix semigroup is finite whenever each element is torsion, meaning that its powers take only finitely many distinct values. Among other things, this shows that infiniteness of finitely generated matrix semigroups is semi-decidable (a witness of infiniteness is a matrix of infinite order) and hence finiteness of finitely generated matrix semigroups is decidable.

The positive answer to the Burnside problem for matrix groups generalises to quotients of matrix groups by Zariski closed normal subgroups, since such quotients can be embedded in matrix groups in higher ambient dimension. This finiteness result is a key ingredient in the first proposed algorithm for computing the Zariski closure of a finitely generated matrix group [5], resolving an open problem in quantum computation. In subsequent joint work, again relying on such a Burnside finiteness theorem, we obtained an elementary algorithm for computing this closure [6].

In this paper, we study Burnside-type questions for quotients of matrix semigroups. Our approach is based on congruences, that is, equivalence relations of matrix semigroups that are compatible with matrix multiplication. Given a finite set XX of rational matrices and a congruence ∼\sim on the semigroup ⟨X⟩\langle X\rangle they generate, we ask for sufficient conditions that • the quotient ⟨X⟩/∼\langle X\rangle/{\sim} be finite, and • there be a uniform bound on the length of the shortest product of generators from XX representing each equivalence class. The classical results on the Burnside problem for matrix semigroups do not apply here, since the quotient need not admit a faithful finite-dimensional representation in a monoid of matrices with entries in a field.11 1 The matrices A=(1101)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} and B=(1011)B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix} generate a free monoid. For the congruence ∼\sim generated by the relation A​B∼IAB\sim I we have B​A≁IBA\not\sim I. Then, in the quotient ⟨A,B⟩/∼\langle A,B\rangle/{\sim}, the image of BB is a right inverse of the image of AA, but not a left inverse. Hence the quotient is not embeddable as a submonoid of a monoid of square matrices with entries in a field. We establish three quantitative finiteness criteria for such quotients and present two applications to border complexity.

Border complexity, also known as approximate complexity, studies polynomials and tensors obtained as limits of parametrised families of bounded complexity. The distinction between exact and approximate computability is central to geometric complexity theory, where questions about computational power are expressed through polynomial and tensor orbit closures [7, 8, 9]. This distinction is already visible in small-width algebraic branching programs, as approximation can increase the expressive power in these models [10]. Our two applications study these distinctions through semigroup congruences: 1. First, for homogeneous algebraic branching programs, we separate the class of polynomials computable by algebraic branching programs of fixed width and degree from its Zariski closure. 2. Second, we construct a finitely generated matrix monoid under whose action the orbit closure of the permanent is not contained in that of the determinant. Curiously, under the congruence of mutual reducibility, the orbit closure of the determinant has a finite quotient whereas that of the permanent is not finite. Both of these applications use the fact that a finitely generated matrix semigroup can have a finite quotient under a congruence, while its Zariski closure has infinitely many classes under the same congruence. These applications connect semigroup theory with border complexity and provide a new toolkit for studying a broader range of algebraic computational models.

The central tool in our proof is the notion of factorisation forest for matrix semigroups, which we developed in recent works [11, 12]. The original notion of factorization forest for semigroups was introduced by Imre Simon [13] and was later used in [14] to give an algorithm for deciding finiteness of matrix semigroups with entries in the tropical semiring. The notion has become central in the algebraic theory of formal languages (see, for example, [15, 16]) and has played a significant role in the resolution of a number of open problems (e.g., the proof of Courcelle’s conjecture that for a class of graphs of bounded treewidth a property is MSO-definable if and only if it is recognisable by a tree automaton [17]). In particular, factorisation forests provide a means to translate results on groups to the setting of semigroups. Our variants generalise Simon’s factorisation from finite semigroups to (infinite) matrix semigroups [11] and matrix semigroup quotients. In our factorisation trees, the role of idempotent elements in the classical version is replaced by (rank-)stable matrices and generalisations. We recently used one of these variants in the context of finite matrix semigroups, to give a polynomial-space algorithm for the finiteness problem for finitely generated matrix semigroups, improving a previous NExp-upper bound. papers.title: How Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity Shape Decentralized Learning: A Spectral Analysis
papers.abstract: Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to consensus dynamics.

papers.intro:
Federated learning (FL) enables multiple devices or organizations to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing their local data. While traditional FL architectures rely on a central server to coordinate training and aggregate model updates [15], decentralized federated learning (DFL) removes this dependency by allowing nodes to exchange model parameters directly with their neighbors [12, 9]. This approach is particularly relevant in environments where centralized coordination is impractical or undesirable, such as peer-to-peer networks, edge computing systems, and distributed sensing infrastructures. However, decentralization also introduces new challenges, as the learning process becomes dependent on the communication network connecting the participating nodes.

Federated learning (FL) enables multiple devices or organizations to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing their local data. While traditional FL architectures rely on a central server to coordinate training and aggregate model updates [15], decentralized federated learning (DFL) removes this dependency by allowing nodes to exchange model parameters directly with their neighbors [12, 9]. This approach is particularly relevant in environments where centralized coordination is impractical or undesirable, such as peer-to-peer networks, edge computing systems, and distributed sensing infrastructures. However, decentralization also introduces new challenges, as the learning process becomes dependent on the communication network connecting the participating nodes.

Understanding how network topology affects decentralized learning has therefore attracted considerable attention. Existing theoretical analyses have investigated how the spectral properties of the communication matrix influence information mixing, model disagreement, and convergence rates [12, 17, 9]. In particular, the spectral gap has traditionally been used to characterize how quickly differences between local models are attenuated, although more recent analyses have shown that the complete eigenvalue spectrum can provide a more accurate characterization of topology-dependent convergence [23]. Several studies have also identified conditions under which the impact of topology becomes limited [21, 19], while others have shown that heterogeneous data distributions can substantially alter its influence on learning [10, 6]. Nevertheless, many of these analyses assume doubly stochastic mixing matrices, which assign equal influence to all nodes in the consensus process. This assumption simplifies the analysis but does not necessarily reflect decentralized averaging over irregular communication networks.

Several studies have also identified conditions under which the impact of topology becomes limited [21, 19], while others have shown that heterogeneous data distributions can substantially alter its influence on learning [10, 6]. Nevertheless, many of these analyses assume doubly stochastic mixing matrices, which assign equal influence to all nodes in the consensus process. This assumption simplifies the analysis but does not necessarily reflect decentralized averaging over irregular communication networks.

Indeed, consider a decentralized system in which each node averages the models received from its neighbors, including its own, assigning equal weight to each contribution. Although the communication graph may be undirected, the resulting mixing matrix is generally not doubly stochastic: nodes with different degrees normalize their incoming contributions differently. Consequently, the consensus component of the learning dynamics does not necessarily correspond to a uniform average of the local models and updates. Instead, individual nodes contribute according to a topology-dependent stationary distribution. Recent work has investigated the theoretical properties of row-stochastic aggregation and its implications for decentralized optimization [13, 14]. However, the consequences of these non-uniform stationary weights for the contribution of heterogeneous information located at different nodes remain less explicitly characterized. This raises a question that convergence-oriented analyses do not fully address: beyond determining how quickly information propagates, how does network topology determine which information has greater influence on the learning process?

The answer becomes particularly relevant when data are heterogeneously distributed. In practical decentralized systems, different nodes may observe different populations, environments, or classes, and some information may be available only at a small subset of nodes. Under these conditions, the influence of local information depends not only on its statistical properties but also on the position of the nodes holding it within the communication network. Previous empirical work has shown that information available at highly connected nodes can propagate more effectively than information located at peripheral nodes, leading to substantial differences in learning performance [20]. At the same time, heterogeneous local gradients can continuously introduce differences between models, whose propagation and attenuation depend on the spectral properties of the network [10, 24]. Understanding decentralized learning therefore requires considering both the influence assigned to individual nodes and the dynamics of disagreement among them.

In this paper, we investigate how network topology and data distribution jointly determine the influence of local information in decentralized learning. While existing spectral analyses primarily characterize convergence and information mixing, they provide less insight into how information held by different nodes contributes to the learning process. We address this question by combining the spectral decomposition of DecAvg dynamics, i.e., the fully decentralized version of FedAvg aggregation function[22], with a class-wise characterization of local gradients. This allows us to distinguish the effects of network mixing from those of topology-dependent node influence, and to quantify how the placement of heterogeneous information shapes the consensus trajectory. In particular, our analysis provides a theoretical explanation for the hub amplification and peripheral dilution effects previously observed empirically, identifying the conditions under which network structure can favor or suppress localized information.

The main contributions of this work are as follows: • Topology-dependent information influence. We characterize how stationary influence weights interact with heterogeneous local data distributions, deriving a class-contribution ratio that quantifies how node position and data placement jointly determine the relative contribution of localized information to the consensus trajectory. • Spectral analysis of learning dynamics. Building on established spectral properties of reversible mixing matrices, we decompose DecAvg dynamics into consensus and disagreement components, characterizing how stationary node influence, spectral mixing, and gradient heterogeneity jointly shape learning dynamics. • Experimental evaluation. Through experiments on regular and heterogeneous network topologies, we investigate the predicted effects of topology and data placement, showing limited topology dependence under IID data and differences in the learning of localized information under non-IID data. Our findings highlight that the impact of network topology on decentralized learning cannot be characterized solely through connectivity or spectral mixing rates. The stationary distribution introduces an additional mechanism through which topology influences learning, particularly when data are not uniformly distributed across nodes. This perspective is especially relevant in decentralized deployments where communication patterns are constrained by the underlying infrastructure and cannot necessarily be optimized or redesigned.

papers.title: Revisiting Finiteness of Matrix Monoids
papers.abstract: This paper concerns decision problems related to finite monoids of rational matrices. We show that determining finiteness of a given finitely presented monoid is in PSPACE, improving the known $\text{co}{-}\text{NEXP}^{\text{NP}}$ bound. We also show that the membership problem for finite matrix monoids is PSPACE-complete, improving the known NEXP-upper bound. Our two complexity results are corollaries of a new polynomial bit-size bound on matrix entries in finite monoids. This is obtained by reduction to the case of matrix groups, using the structure theory of noncommutative algebras and of matrix monoids. Our techniques also give us a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a monoid of rational matrices is conjugate to a monoid of integer matrices.

papers.intro:
The study of decision problems for matrix monoids—and their connections with automata theory—has a long history, spanning more than sixty years; see [13, 3] for a comprehensive survey. The connection between automata and monoids arises from the fact that the transition maps of automata give rise to matrix monoids with entries in a semiring. A particularly important instance is weighted automata over the field ℚ\mathbb{Q} of rational numbers. In this setting, questions about the support and the growth of the formal series recognised by weighted automata reduce to questions about finitely generated matrix monoids over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. In this paper we revisit several classical decision problems for monoids of rational matrices and obtain new complexity results.

papers.title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.

This makes test-time compute a useful scaling axis: a deployment can spend more compute when a problem is difficult or when higher accuracy is required.

A model can look better than its base model at the training budget and become worse when both receive a larger budget.

papers.title: SpatialScout-V2: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore Real-World 3D Scenes and Localize Objects?
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.

papers.intro:
Spatial intelligence enables agents to understand the spatial layout of their surroundings and use that understanding to guide their actions. When observations are partial, this understanding must be built incrementally [41]. Agents need to decide which regions warrant further exploration, recognize the same objects across viewpoints, and integrate local position estimates into a shared three-dimensional representation [15]. As evidence accumulates, this representation must also be revised. Spatial intelligence thus couples exploration and representation: the current scene understanding guides subsequent observations, which in turn update that understanding [6, 13].

papers.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
papers.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

Skills, natural language instructions placed in a model’s context, have become a common way to specialize agents for new tasks, tools and domains. Beyond writing them by hand, recent work refines skills in loops where a large language model (LLM) proposes edits and keeps those that help the agent [1, 3, 20, 32]. Relying on large and capable, often proprietary LLM optimizers is costly, though, compared to gradient-based optimizations, which are much more sample-efficient, as shown in adversarial research [24, 29, 6].

papers.title: Demographic inference in exoplanet chemistry is shaped by retrieval assumptions
papers.abstract: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history. Atmospheric C/O can provide clues about where and how planets form, particularly through the accretion of gas and solids across disk snowlines. Since planetary migration can change orbital distances and hence equilibrium temperatures ($T_{eq}$), investigating C/O across different planetary populations may provide insights into their formation and evolution. As observational precision improves with the JWST, the limits of standard atmospheric retrieval methods that assume altitude-independent molecular abundances have become apparent. We present atmospheric retrievals for 20 transiting planets with published JWST transmission spectra, including complementary HST spectra for targets where such data are available, spanning gas giants, warm Neptunes, and temperate/warm sub-Neptunes, to test how population-level chemical inferences depend on retrieval assumptions. Free-chemistry retrievals show a visually non-monotonic C/O-$T_{eq}$ distribution, but this apparent pattern is not statistically robust and is sensitive to sample composition. When molecular abundances are constrained by a grid of disequilibrium models, the inferred C/O distribution becomes more restricted, showing that demographic chemical trends can depend strongly on the adopted retrieval parameterization. Several hot Jupiters converge to low C/O ($\leq$ 0.05), whereas colder, cloudy planets retain broad posteriors that reflect limited information content of their spectra. Our results suggest that population-level chemical trends inferred from free-chemistry retrievals should be interpreted with caution unless sample selection, residual structure, prior sensitivity, and chemical assumptions are explicitly tested.

papers.intro:
Atmospheric elemental abundances in giant exoplanets provide one of the few direct probes of their formation histories and interior compositions (Öberg et al., 2011; Madhusudhan et al., 2014; Mordasini et al., 2016; Teske, 2024). In our own Solar System, Jupiter’s supersolar enrichments in carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, and noble gases indicate that heavy elements were delivered by solid planetesimals rather than by gas alone (Owen et al., 1999; Atreya and Wong, 2005; Mousis et al., 2019). This link between atmospheric composition and formation has motivated the use of transmission and emission spectra to trace accretion history in exoplanets (Öberg et al., 2011; Madhusudhan et al., 2016; Cridland et al., 2020; Teske, 2024).

Among the various elemental ratios, the carbon-to-oxygen ratio (C/O) has been the most widely investigated. Early models showed that the C/O of a planet’s envelope depends on where it forms relative to the major volatile snowlines of H2​O\mathrm{H_{2}O}, CO2\mathrm{CO_{2}}, and CO, which divide carbon and oxygen between gas and solids (Öberg et al., 2011; Cridland et al., 2020; Öberg and Wordsworth, 2019). In disk-chemistry models, gas inside the H2​O\mathrm{H_{2}O} snowline has approximately stellar or slightly super-stellar C/O. A subsolar atmospheric C/O can therefore indicate enrichment by oxygen-rich solids rather than direct accretion of oxygen-rich gas. Beyond the H2​O\mathrm{H_{2}O} snowline but inside the CO snowline, water ice is removed from the gas phase. This can result in a higher gas-phase C/O, so planets accreting a substantial fraction of their envelopes from this region may also reach higher atmospheric C/O (Öberg et al., 2011; Madhusudhan et al., 2014; Mordasini et al., 2016). Retrieval studies have reported a wide range of atmospheric C/O estimates, from higher or super-solar C/O in systems such as WASP-12 b, WASP-33 b, WASP-103 b, WASP-19 b, HD 149026 b, WASP-69 b, WASP-76 b, and WASP-121 b (Madhusudhan et al., 2011; Haynes et al., 2015; Kreidberg et al., 2018a; Bean et al., 2023; Schlawin et al., 2024a; Weiner Mansfield et al., 2024; Smith et al., 2024; Saha and Jenkins, 2026) to near-solar or intermediate C/O in planets such as WASP-80 b, WASP-77 A b, and WASP-18 b (Wiser et al., 2025; August et al., 2023; Brogi et al., 2023), and lower or subsolar C/O in planets such as HD 209458 b, HD 189733 b, WASP-107 b, and WASP-39 b (Xue et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Welbanks et al., 2024; Alderson et al., 2023). However, C/O alone is not sufficient to trace planet formation pathways, as planets accrete both solids and gas in proportions that vary with time, disk chemistry, and dynamical history (Mordasini, 2018; Cridland et al., 2020; Eistrup et al., 2018; Crossfield, 2023). Robust formation interpretation therefore requires additional context beyond C/O alone, including host-normalized abundance ratios, volatile and refractory elemental ratios, disk chemistry, and migration history.

Sulfur has recently emerged as a complementary tracer of solid accretion (Moses et al., 2011; Zahnle et al., 2016; Laas and Caselli, 2019; Crossfield, 2023). In protoplanetary disks, sulfur is largely stored in refractory or moderately volatile compounds (e.g. FeS, MgS, organosulfur ices), unlike the highly volatile carriers of carbon and oxygen. As a result, the volatile-to-sulfur ratios, such as C/S and O/S, encode the balance between solid and gaseous heavy-element delivery (Laas and Caselli, 2019; Keyte et al., 2024). Pebble-accretion models predict sulfur depletion and super-stellar C/S and O/S, whereas planetesimal-dominated accretion yields near-stellar values (Mordasini et al., 2016; Crossfield, 2023). Until recently, this idea could not be tested because sulfur-bearing molecules were not detected in exoplanet spectra. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has now made sulfur chemistry observable in several systems (Welbanks et al., 2024; Beatty et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025b; Fu et al., 2024), enabling first, albeit tentative, demographic explorations of C/S and O/S.

Early demographic studies based on the Hubble Space Telescope’s Wide Field Camera (HST/WFC3) data pioneered the population approach but also exposed important limitations. The limited 1.1–1.7 μ​m\mathrm{\mu m} band provided access to water vapour and cloud properties but not to key carbon and sulfur-bearing species such as CO, CO2\mathrm{CO_{2}}, CH4\mathrm{CH_{4}}, or SO2\mathrm{SO_{2}} (Barstow and Heng, 2020; Lueber et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025). In addition, non-uniform data reduction, noise treatment, and retrieval assumptions led to different abundance estimates (Mugnai et al., 2024; Barstow et al., 2022). Atmospheric retrievals that assume thermochemical-equilibrium struggle in atmospheres where photochemistry and vertical mixing drive strong deviations from equilibrium scenarios (Moses et al., 2011; Molaverdikhani et al., 2019a; Tsai et al., 2017). Bardet et al. (Bardet et al., 2025) recently re-analyzed ten hot-Jupiter atmospheres with the TauREx-FRECKLL disequilibrium-chemistry retrieval framework. They showed that including kinetic chemistry can significantly change the inferred metallicity and C/O compared to simpler chemistry assumptions, while the retrieved constraints remain sensitive to priors, spectral resolution, and data-reduction choices.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
papers.abstract: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.
papers.intro:
What exactly is a contact model? And what does it mean to formulate one using cone complementarity? Answering these questions requires taking a step back and asking a more fundamental question: where do contact forces come from? The normal contact force arises from the short-range repulsion between atoms that are pushed close together. The frictional contact force arises from the interactions at the microscopic asperities where two surfaces actually touch, which adhere, deform, and interlock as the surfaces slide over each other. Contact is therefore a complex, multiscale effect, and a “mechanistic” approach that tries to numerically simulate these processes directly is intractable at the scale of robots.

Answering these questions requires taking a step back and asking a more fundamental question: where do contact forces come from? The normal contact force arises from the short-range repulsion between atoms that are pushed close together. The frictional contact force arises from the interactions at the microscopic asperities where two surfaces actually touch, which adhere, deform, and interlock as the surfaces slide over each other. Contact is therefore a complex, multiscale effect, and a “mechanistic” approach that tries to numerically simulate these processes directly is intractable at the scale of robots.

Practical contact models used in robotics are therefore “phenomenological”: they reproduce the macroscopic phenomenon (“what contacts do”) without reproducing the underlying microscopic mechanism (“how contacts do it”). The first question any contact model must answer is thus: what do contacts do? They do two things: i) prevent intersections between surfaces that try to pass through each other, and ii) dissipate energy between surfaces that try to slide on top of each other. All contact models, at their core, are therefore mathematical abstractions designed to produce these two effects in a way that makes theoretical analysis and numerical simulation tractable. And cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics are a family of particularly elegant ways of doing so.

Aimed at doctoral students and early-career robotics researchers, this tutorial collates the most common mathematical formulations of contact dynamics based on cone complementarity conditions, along with the key techniques and insights used to solve the resulting problems numerically. The material draws primarily from (Witkin and Baraff, 1997; Google DeepMind, 2022; Stewart, 2000; Acary et al., 2018; Andrews et al., 2022; Le Lidec et al., 2023; Carpentier et al., 2024; Tsounis et al., 2025; Castro et al., 2023; Lynch and Park, 2017; Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004), supplemented by the authors’ own derivations. Upon completing the tutorial, readers should be well prepared to explore the open-source implementations of widely used simulators (e.g., MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012), Bullet (Coumans, 2015), Drake (Tedrake and the Drake Team, 2019), Kamino (Tsounis et al., 2026), Simple (Carpentier et al., 2024), Newton (The Newton Contributors, 2025)), or to extend their understanding beyond forward simulation by investigating the use of cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics in optimal control and trajectory optimization (Mordatch et al., 2012; Posa et al., 2014; Manchester and Kuindersma, 2019; Toussaint et al., 2020; Tassa et al., 2012; Howell et al., 2022a; Pang et al., 2023). To get the most out of the tutorial, readers will benefit from prior familiarity with rigid-body dynamics (Lynch and Park, 2017; Featherstone, 2014; Toussaint, ; Robotic Systems Lab, 2017; Kim, 2012; Tedrake, 2024), convex analysis (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004; Nesterov, 2018; Bertsekas, 2009; Parikh and Boyd, 2014), and numerical methods (Nocedal and Wright, 2006; Solomon, 2015; Strang, 2007).

Several existing resources cover material that overlaps with the contents of this tutorial. The SIGGRAPH course of Andrews, Erleben, and Ferguson (Andrews et al., 2022) is the closest in spirit. Written for computer graphics, it covers collision detection in detail, and focuses on linear complementarity formulations as well as penalty and barrier formulations used for deformable bodies; with a brief mention of cone complementarity formulations used in robotics. This tutorial is complementary: it is written for robotics, focuses on cone complementarity formulations, and provides very brief summaries of collision detection and linear-complementarity formulations (mostly derived from the SIGGRAPH course itself). Acary, Brémond, and Huber (Acary et al., 2018) survey the exact formulations of the frictional contact problem for a computational mechanics audience, and compare the solvers of Siconos numerically on a large benchmark collection. The present tutorial also covers the exact formulations (borrowing several of their mathematical constructions and terminology), and additionally discusses its convex relaxations that are commonly used in robotics. The monograph of Acary and Brogliato (Acary and Brogliato, 2008) and the review of Stewart (Stewart, 2000) treat the mathematical theory of nonsmooth dynamics and its time discretization in a depth and generality that go well beyond the scope of this tutorial. Le Lidec et al. (Le Lidec et al., 2023) provide a comparative analysis of the contact dynamics formulations and solution algorithms used by current robotics simulators, including numerical experiments and discussions on the physical artifacts of the convex relaxations. This tutorial instead provides the pedagogy around the same subject, with step-by-step mathematical derivations, as well as additional formulations and solution algorithms that are no longer commonly employed in the modern simulation landscape of today but do nevertheless provide important context. Finally, the MuJoCo documentation (Google DeepMind, 2022) and the paper introducing Drake’s SAP solver (Castro et al., 2023) present the mathematical formulations of these two simulators in detail, each within its own framework. This tutorial places both within a common family of transcriptions (i.e., the nonlinear least-squares transcription from Section 4), and presents self-contained mathematical derivations.

papers.title: Bridging the Discovery Gap in Solid Dataspaces with a Semantic Data Catalog
papers.abstract: Dataspaces are an emerging concept to enable secure and controlled data sharing between multiple stakeholders. However, most existing dataspace architectures, such as those based on the concepts of IDSA (International Data Spaces Association) and Gaia-X, are heavily concept-driven and require significant effort to implement, making it difficult to quickly build a functional dataspace. Solid (Social Linked Data) offers a compelling alternative by providing a lighter and more practical approach. However, for Solid to function as a true dataspace, like traditional dataspaces, it must be built in a decentralized manner, i.e., the dataspace must consist of more than a single Solid server. However, this decentralization introduces a key challenge: Data Discovery. Unlike traditional dataspace architectures, which often include predefined components such as data catalogs to facilitate data discovery and access, Solid does not inherently provide such mechanisms. As a result, managing and locating relevant data across multiple Solid servers and pods becomes a significant barrier to usability. To address this gap, we present a FAIR-compliant data catalog for Solid. Our catalog follows the FAIR principles (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability) by integrating semantic models that describe all available data sources within the Solid ecosystem. This approach enables enhanced data discovery, improves accessibility through standardized metadata, enhances interoperability between different data sources, and promotes data reuse across applications. By bridging this critical gap, our catalog improves the usability of Solid-based dataspaces, making them a viable option for decentralized and open data ecosystems, such as smart city applications.
papers.intro:
The concept of dataspaces has emerged as a response to the increasing need for decentralized, interoperable, and secure data-sharing ecosystems. Unlike traditional centralized data platforms, dataspaces provide a framework where multiple independent stakeholders can share and access data under defined governance models while maintaining control over their respective data sources Curry and Tuikka (2022). This approach is particularly relevant in domains such as smart cities, where heterogeneous data from various public and private entities must be efficiently shared and utilized.

The concept of dataspaces has emerged as a response to the increasing need for decentralized, interoperable, and secure data-sharing ecosystems. Unlike traditional centralized data platforms, dataspaces provide a framework where multiple independent stakeholders can share and access data under defined governance models while maintaining control over their respective data sources Curry and Tuikka (2022). This approach is particularly relevant in domains such as smart cities, where heterogeneous data from various public and private entities must be efficiently shared and utilized.

However, most existing dataspace architectures, such as IDSA and Gaia-X, are heavily conceptual and complex. They emphasize trust frameworks, policy enforcement, and governance mechanisms, but their technical implementations often require significant effort and infrastructure. Setting up a functional dataspace within these ecosystems is not trivial — it involves establishing a network of trusted entities, integrating identity and access management systems, and deploying dedicated service components like metadata registries and data marketplaces Solmaz et al. (2022). As a result, these architectures are primarily suited for enterprise-level data ecosystems, where formalized governance structures and extensive resources are available.

Setting up a functional dataspace within these ecosystems is not trivial — it involves establishing a network of trusted entities, integrating identity and access management systems, and deploying dedicated service components like metadata registries and data marketplaces Solmaz et al. (2022). As a result, these architectures are primarily suited for enterprise-level data ecosystems, where formalized governance structures and extensive resources are available.

In contrast, Solid provides an alternative approach to decentralized data sharing. Originally conceived by Tim Berners-Lee, Solid focuses on personal data sovereignty, allowing individuals and organizations to store their data in personal data pods while enabling controlled access through standard web technologies. By using Linked Data principles, Solid ensures interoperability across different data sources without requiring a central authority. This makes it an attractive candidate for building lightweight and rapidly deployable dataspaces, particularly in domains where smaller, more flexible data-sharing ecosystems are needed Sambra et al. (2016).

This makes it an attractive candidate for building lightweight and rapidly deployable dataspaces, particularly in domains where smaller, more flexible data-sharing ecosystems are needed Sambra et al. (2016).

While Solid offers a promising foundation for decentralized dataspaces, it introduces a critical challenge: data discovery. Unlike traditional dataspace architectures, which include predefined components such as data catalogs and metadata registries to enable structured data discovery, Solid does not natively provide such mechanisms. This is especially problematic in a fully decentralized Solid ecosystem, where multiple independent Solid servers host fragmented data across different participants as needed for dataspaces. Without a way to efficiently index, describe, and discover available datasets, the practical usability of a Solid-based dataspace remains limited.

Unlike traditional dataspace architectures, which include predefined components such as data catalogs and metadata registries to enable structured data discovery, Solid does not natively provide such mechanisms. This is especially problematic in a fully decentralized Solid ecosystem, where multiple independent Solid servers host fragmented data across different participants as needed for dataspaces. Without a way to efficiently index, describe, and discover available datasets, the practical usability of a Solid-based dataspace remains limited.

In conventional dataspace implementations, data findability is addressed through centralized or federated catalog services, which maintain metadata descriptions of all available datasets within the ecosystem Jahnke et al. (2024). These catalogs enable semantic search, data governance, and automated interoperability by leveraging standardized metadata schemas and ontologies. Without an equivalent component, Solid dataspaces risk becoming fragmented, making it difficult for users and applications to locate relevant datasets efficiently.

papers.title: The Galaxy Activity, Torus, and Outflow Survey: N. Little Red Dots are not dust deficient: constraints from Seyfert 1 JWST spectra
papers.abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, red sources discovered by JWST. Most show broad permitted emission lines characteristic of AGN, but other properties differ from local AGN, such as X-ray and radio weakness and an apparent scarcity of dust. If LRDs at z>4 are indeed dust deficient, the bolometric luminosities and black hole (BH) masses measured from SED fitting would be overestimated, and their red optical continuum would be intrinsic rather than reddened. Here we use rest-frame 3-27 micron JWST spectra of a sample of nearby (D<60 Mpc) Seyfert 1 (Sy1) nuclei to place constraints on the dust emission of LRDs. We normalised the individual Sy1 spectra by their broad H$\alpha$ and 5100 A continuum luminosities and stacked them, obtaining scalings that reproduce, within a factor of three, the rest-frame near-infrared emission of a NIRSpec+MIRI stack of 249 LRDs at 2.3<z<9.3 and the near- and mid-infrared emission of a local LRD at z=0.1, with the 5100 A continuum giving the more reliable prediction when modest extinction is considered (Av<1 mag). However, simultaneously reproducing the optical and infrared SEDs of LRDs requires a more reddened accretion disc (Av ~ 2 mag) and a torus with a lower reprocessing efficiency (Ct ~ 0.1-0.2) than inferred for local Sy1 galaxies. This combination offers an alternative to BH-star scenarios that explain the optical continuum as an unreddened blackbody of T ~ 5000 K. Our model, based on local Sy1s, yields a more plausible infrared-to-optical energy balance, suggesting that LRDs are not dust deficient. From the torus model that reproduces the optical and near-infrared SED of the high-redshift LRD stack, we estimate a dust mass of $M_{\rm dust}\simeq10^4\,M_\odot$, consistent with the dust masses typical of AGN tori.

Interestingly, the population of AGN at z≳\gtrsim4 discovered by JWST show some properties that are substantially different from those of nearby AGN. Despite the broad Balmer lines detected in a significant fraction of them, indicating that they are type-1 AGN, they are extremely weak in the X-rays (Ananna et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2024; Maiolino et al., 2025; Tortosa et al., 2026; Geris et al., 2026b). They are also faint at radio frequencies (Mazzolari et al., 2024; Mazzolari et al., 2025), and they show weak or no significant ultraviolet (UV) to optical variability (Kokubo and Harikane, 2025; Tee et al., 2025), although this aspect has been debated (Furtak et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2025; Lambrides et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a; Secunda et al., 2026).

While many of the broad line AGN found by JWST have blue colors (so-called Little Blue Dots, Hainline et al. 2025; Brazzini et al. 2026; Geris et al. 2026b), a fraction of them (which depends on luminosity and selection band) is characterized by red optical slope and blue UV slope, giving them a characteristic “V-shaped” continuum – these have been named “Little Red Dots” (Matthee et al., 2024; Greene et al., 2024; Kocevski et al., 2025). In addition to the several peculiar properties discussed above, LRDs are often characterized by Balmer absorption lines (Matthee et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2026a; D’Eugenio et al., 2025; Matthee et al., 2026) and also Balmer breaks. The latter were initially interpreted as tracing evolved stellar populations, resulting in extremely large stellar masses (possibly cosmology-breaking; Inayoshi and Ichikawa 2024) and extremely high stellar densities (Baggen et al., 2024). However, subsequent studies have revealed that such features are tracing dense gas along the line of sight (Inayoshi and Maiolino, 2025; Ji et al., 2025; Naidu et al., 2026; de Graaff et al., 2025). papers.title: Two distinct notions of speed in antiferromagnets
papers.abstract: The terahertz resonance frequencies of antiferromagnets characterize their precessional dynamics but do not necessarily imply faster laser-induced quenching of magnetic order. Here, we investigate the distinct roles of magnetic compensation and electronic scattering phase space by comparing ultrafast demagnetization in the antiferromagnetic charge-transfer insulator NiO, the metallic antiferromagnet Mn2Au, and a ferromagnetic Ni reference. The extracted response in Mn2Au is approximately four times faster than in NiO and substantially faster than in Ni. These observations are consistent with exchange-mediated scattering between antiparallel sublattices enabling rapid loss of antiferromagnetic order without requiring net angular-momentum transfer to an external reservoir, provided sufficient electronic scattering phase space is available. In insulating NiO, restricted electronic scattering channels reduces the ultrafast response. Our results distinguish ultrafast demagnetization from exchange-enhanced precession and identify the interplay of spin-flip probability and electronic scattering rate as a key factor governing the nonequilibrium response of compensated magnets.

papers.title: Generic arm separation for planar percolation models
papers.abstract: Arm separation is an important technical tool in the study of critical and near-critical planar percolation systems. When combined with RSW estimates, it proves quasi-multiplicativity of arm-event probabilities, links the derivatives of different events and allows the identification of universal arm exponents. We provide a very generic statement of arm separation that applies to arbitrary planar percolation models. Our argument is based on exploring configurations conditioned on the existence of arms in such a way that "exposed" arms are revealed with positive probability. The exploration algorithm is independent of the percolation model and applies to all polychromatic arm events. As an application, we prove a strong arm-separation result for critical planar FK-percolation.

papers.intro:
Arm separation is a fundamental tool in the study of planar critical and near-critical percolation. An arm event denotes the existence of disjoint paths of prescribed colours joining the two boundaries of an annulus. Informally, arm separation states that, conditional on such an event, the arms can be chosen so that their endpoints on the outer boundary are separated by distances comparable to the outer radius, with uniformly positive probability. An analogous statement applies at the inner boundary.

An analogous statement applies at the inner boundary.

Arm separation was introduced by Kesten [Kes87b] for planar Bernoulli percolation; see [Nol08] for a detailed exposition. Its usefulness lies in the room it provides to extend arms and join them to other paths using Russo–Seymour–Welsh (RSW) estimates. Keeping the endpoints sufficiently far apart allows these connections to be constructed with uniformly positive probability, which is crucial when comparing events across different scales. Arm separation is thus a technical but essential ingredient in a wide range of applications, including quasi-multiplicativity [Kes87b, Nol08, CDCH16, DCMT21], the derivation of scaling relations [Kes87a, Kes87b, Nol08, GPS13, GPS18, DCM22], the construction of incipient infinite clusters [Kes86, Jár03, DS11, BS17], noise sensitivity [SS10, GPS10, TV25] and identification and comparison of arm exponents [SW01, BN11, KSL25, GM25, RT26] to name just a few.

We show how to explore the configuration in order to produce exposed arms. One may then use RSW estimates to glue these arms to desired destinations.

papers.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

papers.intro:
Deployed image classifiers often need small, specific changes: a fine-grained concept has to move to another class, a recurring confusion between two classes has to be repaired, or a rare subgroup is misclassified. Collecting data and fine-tuning is costly and can change behavior far beyond the requested fix. Model editing methods instead compute a targeted weight change for one request [31, 22, 24]. Recently, general-purpose large language models (LLMs) have begun to edit networks directly, a practice called weight-space programming [39]. Here, an LLM agent inspects activations and weights, finds the units that respond to a concept, writes a targeted change and checks its effect with forward passes, all without gradient descent.

papers.title: Beam Model Technical Report
papers.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

papers.title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.

papers.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
papers.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

The European Union’s AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 [1] (hereinafter also referred to as the Act), is the first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. It entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. The general provisions (Art. 1–4) and prohibitions of certain AI practices (Art. 5) have applied since February 2025, and obligations for providers of General-Purpose AI models (GPAI) models have applied since August 2025 (Art. 53). Since August 2026, the transparency rules (Art. 50) apply, and the European Commission can fine GPAI model providers for non-compliance (Art. 101). The remaining requirements follow in later years [2]. The already enforced obligations require providers to document their models and to provide information to downstream users, which directly affects how AI models are shared and reused, among other things.
