papers.title: Lyapunov Theory for Output-to-State Stability of Nonlinear Infinite-Dimensional Systems
papers.abstract: For a broad class of nonlinear infinite-dimensional systems with outputs, we show that output-to-state stability (OSS) is equivalent to the existence of a coercive OSS Lyapunov function in implication form. While establishing this equivalence, we prove that OSS is equivalent to uniform global asymptotic stability modulo output, relate these properties to the vanishing output vanishing state property, and highlight new challenges that do not arise in the nonlinear finite-dimensional or linear infinite-dimensional settings. The results are illustrated by a nonlinear reaction-diffusion system with a nonlinear output map.

papers.intro:
The notion of detectability, introduced in [1] for linear systems, is paramount for observer design [2, Section 8.1] and output-feedback stabilization [3]. Detectability also plays an important role in nonlinear stability analysis [4] and state-feedback design, including LaSalle’s invariance principle and Jurdjevic–Quinn control [5]. A linear system is called detectable if any two trajectories producing the same output converge to each other. A related notion is zero-detectability, which requires trajectories with identically zero output to converge to the origin. For linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs), detectability and zero-detectability are equivalent.

Detectability also plays an important role in nonlinear stability analysis [4] and state-feedback design, including LaSalle’s invariance principle and Jurdjevic–Quinn control [5]. A linear system is called detectable if any two trajectories producing the same output converge to each other. A related notion is zero-detectability, which requires trajectories with identically zero output to converge to the origin. For linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs), detectability and zero-detectability are equivalent.

Output-to-state stability. Beyond convergence of zero-output trajectories, it is of interest to have estimates of the state magnitude in terms of the measured output that also capture transient behavior. These state estimates are provided by output-to-state stability (OSS) introduced in [6]. OSS is defined by estimating the norm of the trajectory in terms of the sum of a decaying transient and a term depending on the output. For linear ODEs without inputs, OSS is equivalent to detectability [7, 8]. This makes it a natural candidate for extending classical detectability to nonlinear systems, as proposed in [6]. OSS estimates can be obtained using a function that decreases along trajectories whenever the state is sufficiently large compared to the output. Similar conditions on storage functions had already been used in earlier formulations of nonlinear detectability [7, Remark 5]. For nonlinear ODEs, OSS has been characterized in terms of OSS Lyapunov functions in dissipation form in [6].

The success of OSS theory led to the introduction of a variety of concepts that refine or extend it. For ODE systems with inputs and outputs, input/output-to-state stability (IOSS) has been introduced in [7, 8] to formalize robust detectability of nonlinear systems. IOSS is equivalent to the existence of a smooth IOSS Lyapunov function [8]. To obtain a proper extension not only of zero-detectability but also of detectability, the concept of incremental input/output-to-state stability was introduced in [7].

The applications of (I)OSS theory are manifold. An important application is state estimation. For nonlinear ODEs, global complete observability together with OSS guarantees the existence of a globally convergent observer [9]. Incremental IOSS is a necessary condition for the existence of a robust full-state observer [7] and other types of state estimators, such as the extended Kalman filter, full information estimation, and moving horizon estimation; see [10]. Incremental IOSS is widely used for optimization-based state estimation [11], and its relations to incremental dissipativity were studied in [12]. For optimal control problems with nonnegative stage cost on bounded sets, the existence of an IOSS-like Lyapunov function implies strict dissipativity for stage cost depending on the norms of the output and input [13, p. 459 & Corollary 1]. In turn, strict dissipativity implies the turnpike property that ensures similarity between optimal trajectories on varying time horizons [14, 15, 16]. This is essential for model predictive control schemes [17, 11, 18].

In turn, strict dissipativity implies the turnpike property that ensures similarity between optimal trajectories on varying time horizons [14, 15, 16]. This is essential for model predictive control schemes [17, 11, 18].

The fundamental idea of OSS is similar to that of input-to-state stability (ISS). The ISS framework has revolutionized the robust stability analysis of nonlinear control systems and their interconnections [19, 4, 20, 21], see the monograph [22] for a comprehensive treatment of the ISS theory of ODEs. ISS quantifies the input-state behavior of a system. It ensures that bounded inputs lead to bounded states and that the state converges to zero if the input decays to zero. ISS can be characterized as a combination of IOSS and input-to-output stability (IOS), see [4, Proposition 3.1] for the ODE case and [23, Section V.B] for general infinite-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Material optimization of optical properties of particulate products by transition matrix method and sequential global programming
papers.abstract:
Material optimization of nanoparticle assemblies, such as structurally coloured photonic crystals, attracts increasing interest. We combine the transition matrix method (TMM), which avoids spatial discretization of particles and surrounding medium, with sequential global programming (SGP) to optimize optical properties of particulate products by iteratively assigning predefined catalogue materials to individual particles.
  We derive exact separable models, reproducing the fully coupled objective under single-particle material changes, and computationally accessible first-order correct approximations for general continuously differentiable objectives. These approximations aim to capture the nonlinear, potentially nonconvex dependence on individual material variables beyond their local first-order behaviour. Within SGP, globally minimizing the particle-wise subproblems can yield substantial improvements in few outer iterations, including steps away from unfavourable stationary points, as previously demonstrated for discrete dipole approximation-based SGP. The construction exploits the decomposition of the TMM system matrix into a material-dependent block-diagonal and a material-independent coupling matrix, while the state and adjoint problems remain fully coupled.
  Applications include extinction, scattering quantities, and colour objectives. In a 35-particle extinction minimization problem, the objective decreases by 31.0% in 13 iterations. A fine-grid evaluation of the fully coupled objective shows that no tested single-particle material change improves the final design. For a 627-particle photonic crystal, chroma increases by 58.4-122.1% for different particle diameters in 17-42 iterations. The optimized designs favour absorbing material in layers away from the incident light, consistent with experimental findings.

papers.intro:
Structural colours result from the interaction of visible light with organized nanostructures and can be modified by introducing absorbing material into a particulate assembly (Kinoshita and Yoshioka, 2005; Vignolini et al., 2012; Goerlitzer et al., 2018; Bittner et al., 2024; Bleyer et al., 2025). In photonic crystals, the spatial distribution of absorber can suppress unwanted scattering and alter the observed colour. This leads to the following material optimization question: given the positions of the particles, which material should be assigned to each particle to improve a prescribed optical property? We study this as a numerical optimization problem governed by fully coupled electromagnetic scattering, without imposing fabrication constraints on individual particle assignments.

The forward model must account for multiple scattering among the particles. The tmm (tmm) uses vector spherical wave functions to describe the response of each particle through its transition matrix and couples these responses through translation operators (Waterman, 1965; Waterman, 1971; Mishchenko et al., 2002; Egel et al., 2017; Beutel et al., 2024). It does not require a volume discretization of the particles or of the surrounding medium. By comparison, the fem (fem) usually discretizes a bounded computational domain and an absorbing boundary treatment (Monk, 2003), while the dda (dda) represents the scatterer by interacting dipoles (Draine and Flatau, 1994). FFT-based dda implementations may use regular dipole grids whose inactive sites also affect computational cost. The tmm is therefore attractive for assemblies of separated particles with available individual T-matrices, subject to the usual dependence of cost and accuracy on particle geometry and multipole truncation. tmm-related methods have also been used to optimize particle geometry and arrangement (Zhan et al., 2018; Zhelyeznyakov et al., 2020; Semmler and Stingl, 2021; Asadova et al., 2026).

The sgp (sgp) method replaces the original material optimization problem by a sequence of separable subproblems (Semmler et al., 2018; Nees et al., 2023; Vu et al., 2023). Separability alone is shared with ordinary first-order Taylor models. The distinguishing feature of sgp is that it seeks computationally tractable approximations to exact separable models, which reproduce the objective function whenever only one design coordinate is varied. Such approximations can preserve nonlinear and potentially nonconvex dependence on individual material variables that the local gradient does not capture. Their coordinate-wise accuracy also motivates a stronger optimality criterion than first-order stationarity, which also applies to finite, discrete material catalogues: no change of the material assigned to a single particle should improve the true objective. When accurate enough, their globally minimized scalar subproblems can propose substantial improvements and lead to convergence in comparatively few outer iterations. In particular, the published dda-sgp study by Nees et al. (2023, Section 6.1, Figure 11) documents progress through several unfavourable Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) points, in contrast to the behaviour of a local convex-model method in that example, although escaping stationary points is not guaranteed in general. sgp was originally developed also for discrete material optimization with several admissible materials (Semmler et al., 2018). Here we use a continuously relaxed bi-material catalogue.

papers.title: Deterministic Temporal Embedding for Calcium Imaging Trace Extraction
papers.abstract: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.
papers.intro:
Calcium imaging enables the observation of intracellular calcium dynamics across large populations of cells and provides a widely used readout of cellular activity. Downstream biological analysis requires determining a reliable fluorescence or calcium activity trace associated with each underlying cellular source. Accurate and reproducible source support estimation for trace extraction is therefore a central step from raw calcium imaging data to quantitative analysis of cellular dynamics.

Calcium imaging enables the observation of intracellular calcium dynamics across large populations of cells and provides a widely used readout of cellular activity. Downstream biological analysis requires determining a reliable fluorescence or calcium activity trace associated with each underlying cellular source. Accurate and reproducible source support estimation for trace extraction is therefore a central step from raw calcium imaging data to quantitative analysis of cellular dynamics.

Existing calcium imaging trace extraction methods can generally be classified into three categories. First, widely used ROI- and clustering-based methods identify active cellular regions and subsequently extract their temporal signals (e.g., PCA/ICA-based cell sorting [1], Suite2p [2], and MIN1PIPE [3]). A second category of methods formulates source extraction as a spatio-temporal decomposition problem. Constrained nonnegative matrix factorization (CNMF) [4], CNMF-E [5], and CaImAn [6] jointly estimate spatial footprints, temporal components, and background activity, and are particularly effective when their source and background models match the imaging modality. Third, more recently, deep learning methods have been used to learn spatio-temporal features for neuron detection and segmentation directly from calcium imaging sequences (e.g., STNeuroNet [7], SUNS [8], and DeepWonder [9]). These methods have improved automation, scalability, and segmentation accuracy, but they generally rely on spatial source models, on morphology learned from annotated or simulated neurons, or on assumptions tailored to commonly studied neuronal imaging settings.

Here, we consider two-photon calcium imaging data of glioblastoma cells, in which active cellular sources may be irregular, elongated, branching, curved, heterogeneous in brightness, and frequently touching or spatially connected (cf. Fig. 1(a,b)). In such data, a static or maximum-intensity projection may merge distinct cells, and morphology alone is generally insufficient to define source identity. In contrast, pixels belonging to the same active cell often exhibit a common blinking pattern over time, whereas neighboring cells can display distinct and asynchronous temporal dynamics. This motivates treating source identification as a high-dimensional temporal representation problem rather than as a purely spatial image segmentation problem. In our preliminary work, we noticed that UMAP [10] applied directly to raw pixel-wise fluorescence traces produced remarkably compact latent regions corresponding to blinking cells, with neighboring cells often mapped to distinct latent values even when being in direct spatial contact (cf. Fig. 1(c)). However, standard UMAP uses stochastic low-dimensional optimization, which is undesirable when the embedding itself serves as the basis for reproducible downstream source extraction.

In this work, we introduce a deterministic temporal embedding framework inspired by UMAP for calcium imaging trace extraction. Pixel-wise raw fluorescence traces are represented by complementary Euclidean and cosine fuzzy-neighborhood graphs, which are adaptively fused to retain both waveform and amplitude information. Starting from a spectral initialization used in UMAP, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective in which sparse graph attraction is computed exactly, while the dense repulsive interaction is decomposed into a global particle-mesh (PM) field and an exact sparse edge compensation term. This formulation avoids stochastic negative sampling and enables deterministic low-dimensional optimization. The resulting latent representation is decoded into spatially coherent candidate source supports, which are then selected based on temporal activity, without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic data with ground truth and real in vivo calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources and reliable extraction of their fluorescence traces.

papers.title: From Industrial Product Documentation to Automated Digital Product Passport Generation: An Experimental Study of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Manufacturing companies that are planning to sell certain products in the European Union (EU) will be required to provide mandatory digital product passports (DPPs). The use of DPPs is to provide standardized product information throughout multiple product life cycles in a circular economy. Required passport information, such as technical specifications, material composition, and environmental product footprint, is available in manufacturers' data sources but is scattered across different heterogeneous systems, documents, and data formats. The given paper investigates using large language models (LLMs) to automate the generation of DPPs based on the asset administration shell (AAS). A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach is used to extract product information from industrial documentation and generate populated AAS instances. Product documentation is processed and divided into text chunks. The text chunks are then stored in a persistent ChromaDB vector database using vector embeddings. The retrieval process combines semantic and lexical search to identify relevant information based on standardized AAS submodel template requirements. The retrieved information is provided to five LLMs to generate structured AAS instances. The experiments cover different industrial products and AAS submodels. Four levels of prompt guidance are investigated to assess their influence on generation quality. The generated passports are evaluated against a ground truth. The experimental evaluation includes 4,560 executions across 76 product-submodel combinations. Of the generated passport outputs, 97.4% are valid JSON, while 44.9% pass the full AAS validation procedure. Under deterministic scoring, mean completeness, conditional accuracy, and overall field correctness are 49.6%, 58.3%, and 30.8%, respectively. An LLM-as-a-judge yields better scores of 66.5%, 88.9%, and 60.4% for the same outputs.

papers.intro:
Circular manufacturing aims to retain the value of products, individual components, and materials Morseletto [2020]. Decisions throughout these activities depend on the availability of product information. Technical specifications may determine whether a product’s components can be reused elsewhere. Information on material composition is useful in disassembly and recycling processes. Environmental data, including product carbon footprint, can be used to assess the environmental implications of product life cycle activities. However, the needed product information is often scattered across many heterogeneous data systems in an organization. Moreover, the data originates from different activities and stakeholders in a company’s value chain.

To streamline the data for circular economy purposes, the European Union (EU) will require companies selling products in the EU to provide digital product passports (DPPs). These DPPs are product records that offer an approach to make product data available throughout a product’s (multiple) life cycle(s). The EU has introduced a regulatory framework for DPPs through the ‘Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR)’ European Commission [2024]. The regulation establishes a framework for product-specific information requirements intended to support environmental sustainability and circularity.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities to automate the extraction and structuring of product information required for DPPs. Previous research highlights the ability of LLMs to interpret unstructured data and extract semantically relevant information Chen et al. [2025], Menon and Serban [2025], Xia et al. [2024]. However, there are limited quantitative results on the performance of LLMs in the field. Therefore, the given study evaluates the automated creation of DPPs with five different LLMs and multiple industrial product documents from different manufacturers. Eight product categories are part of the experimental design. To standardize the passport creation process, the LLMs are prompted to create DPPs based on the data structure of an asset administration shell (AAS). The study uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to identify relevant product information in a vector database, with retrieval queries derived from standardized AAS submodel requirements. The experiments cover different standardized AAS submodels, including ‘Digital Nameplate’, ‘Technical Data’, ‘Carbon Footprint’, and also battery-specific passport submodels Industrial Digital Twin Association e.V. [2026a]. Four levels of prompt guidance are investigated to determine their influence on the generation results. The generated AAS instances are evaluated for structural validity, information completeness, conditional accuracy, overall field correctness (OFC), and consistency across repeated runs. Particular attention is given to differences between submodels that require technical, environmental, and material-related information.

papers.title: Software-Defined Internet Integration of Satellite Networks (SDISN)
papers.abstract:
This paper proposes SDISN, a software-defined Internet integration of satellite networks. It facilitates the transmission of IP traffic from user terminals (UTs) or Internet nodes over a satellite network with inter-satellite links (ISLs). Gateways (GWs) together with Points of Presence (PoPs) support the transition between the satellite network and the Internet. UTs and GWs connect to the satellite network via serving satellites (SrvSats). As the satellites orbit the Earth at high speed, UTs and GWs frequently change their SrvSats. This causes frequent changes to their reachability, which poses a major challenge for integration.
  In the proposed solution, GWs and SrvSats encapsulate traffic with forwarding information so that the traffic can be carried over the satellite network towards appropriate SrvSats of UTs or GWs. The forwarding information on the encapsulating nodes is continuously updated by a controller to reflect changed SrvSats and possibly changed topology of the satellite network. Design goals for the proposed architecture were low complexity on satellites, high ability for traffic engineering, and keeping UTs out of the routing system for security and compatibility reasons.
  UTs may have increased security requirements (ISRs) such that their traffic should be carried within the constellation to avoid non-trusted terrestrial infrastructure. Extensions are proposed to support such ISRs. UTs may obtain either dynamic IP addresses from a nearby GW/PoP wherever they roam or they may obtain static IP addresses from a fixed Home GW/PoP. In the latter case, triangle routing via the Home GW occurs when the UT roams away from the Home GW. As this adds latency to the communication, we investigate architectural extensions for latency reduction. In addition, we show how traffic engineering can be performed in such an architecture with the help of alternate GWs and SrvSats.
papers.intro:
Broadband services supported by Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellites have become essential for extending connectivity towards inaccessible or underdeveloped areas. They have become equally important for a resilient communication infrastructure as connections can be set up rapidly anywhere. Therefore, a significant expansion of this technology is expected for the near future, which is driven by the public sector.

In the past, user terminals (UTs) exchanged information with a nearby gateway (GW) via a single satellite only, and they communicated on the physical layer. With the introduction of inter-satellite links (ISLs) and packet processing on satellites, LEO satellite networks emerged. This enables UTs to exchange traffic over satellite paths with more distant GWs, extending connectivity for UTs even to areas without any GWs. By bridging long distances, satellite networks may serve as backup for critical traffic if terrestrial infrastructure such as submarine cables fail or get sabotaged.

By bridging long distances, satellite networks may serve as backup for critical traffic if terrestrial infrastructure such as submarine cables fail or get sabotaged.

However, forwarding traffic over satellite networks is challenging. UTs and GWs are connected to so-called serving satellites (SrvSats) but hand over to other SrvSats on a time scale of 3 – 12 minutes as LEO satellites are orbiting the Earth at high speed. This makes integration into the terrestrial network and the Internet a challenge. The integration has to take these frequent changes into account so that packets can be delivered over the satellite network to intended UTs and GWs. Moreover, ISLs between satellites may be set up, torn down, or fail so that the routing system must also take care of planned and unplanned topology changes of the satellite network.

Operational satellite constellations like Starlink or OneWeb are proprietary, i.e., their operation is not disclosed and interfaces between involved devices are not open. The devices typically come from a single vendor and are assumed to be trusted in terms of routing information. From a market perspective, open interfaces and interoperability are desirable so that UTs from different vendors can be utilized. To decouple UTs from the satellite network, SrvSats can serve as proxies for UTs, i.e., they add forwarding information to packets so that the packets can be carried to appropriate destinations within the satellite constellation. In spite of this proposed additional functionality, satellites should be robust, durable, lightweight, and consume only little energy. Therefore, packet processors on satellites must be simple, i.e., complex forwarding operations, large forwarding tables, and heavy signaling should be avoided.

papers.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
papers.abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-H\"older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

papers.intro:
Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow neural networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly drawn and subsequently kept fixed, so that only the coefficients of the linear output layer are estimated from the data (Gonon et al.,, 2023). Neural networks of this type have been applied very successfully in a variety of settings; we refer in particular to the seminal works on random feature models (Rahimi and Recht,, 2007) and extreme learning machines (Huang et al.,, 2006). Conditional on the sampled parameters, estimation under squared loss is a linear least-squares problem over the random finite-dimensional space spanned by the KK hidden units. When the same sequence of hidden-layer parameters is used as KK increases, these spaces are nested and form a random sieve, which we study within the framework of nonparametric sieve regression (Grenander,, 1981; Györfi et al.,, 2006; Chen,, 2007; Tsybakov,, 2009). However, the population covariance matrix of the randomly generated features need not remain well-conditioned as KK increases: additional hidden units may improve approximation while introducing substantial redundancy in the feature representation. Understanding the statistical consequences of such ill-conditioning, particularly for inference on functionals of the regression function, is the central problem addressed in this paper.

Approximation properties of random neural networks have been studied under different assumptions on the target function and the distribution of the hidden-layer parameters (Rahimi and Recht,, 2008; Gonon et al.,, 2023; Neufeld and Schmocker,, 2023; Liu et al.,, 2025; De Ryck et al.,, 2025; Mehmood and Gonon,, 2026). In the context of positive definite kernels, Bach, (2017) established approximation guarantees for random feature expansions in terms of the spectral properties of the associated integral operator, including results in L2L^{2} and L∞L^{\infty}. Related quantitative approximation results for shallow neural networks include those for general activation functions (Siegel and Xu,, 2020), for Sobolev classes with ReLU activations (Mao et al.,, 2026), and for non-polynomial activations on noncompact domains (Neufeld and Schmocker,, 2026). Statistical convergence rates for random feature estimators have been established in several settings (Rudi and Rosasco,, 2017; Carratino et al.,, 2018; Gonon,, 2023; Lanthaler and Nelsen,, 2023). In particular, Braun et al., (2024) establish an expected squared L2​(X)L^{2}(X) error bound of order O((logn)4n−1/2)O((\log n)^{4}n^{-1/2}) for a shallow neural network estimator learned by gradient descent, under suitable Fourier-decay assumptions on the regression function. They obtain the same rate for a truncated linear least-squares estimator with randomly sampled hidden-layer parameters. Mei and Montanari, (2022) derive precise asymptotics for random features ridge regression. Conditional on the sampled features, a ridge-regularized RWNN estimator is a finite-rank kernel ridge regressor, for which Cheng et al., (2023) give sharp non-asymptotic bounds on the test error.

These results concern regularization in a prescribed reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and existing inferential results involving sampled features address particular estimation targets and statistical models; see Shen and Bellec, (2020); Steland, (2021); Guignard et al., (2021) for recent discussions. In contrast, we develop a theory of functional inference for growing RWNN sieves that accommodates increasingly ill-conditioned or singular population feature covariance matrices.

Randomly generated features present a fundamental and distinctive structural obstacle: a uniform positive lower bound on the population covariance eigenvalues cannot be sustained as the number of features increases. In particular, its smallest eigenvalue necessarily converges to zero as the number of features increases. papers.title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

papers.intro:
An Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) is a learning framework that, in its standard form, uses a feedforward neural network (NN) with a single hidden layer whose input weights and biases are randomly assigned and then kept fixed, while the output weights are determined by solving a linear least-squares problem [12]. This construction avoids iterative backpropagation through all network parameters, making compact ELM models attractive when frequent fitting and prediction are required. Regularized formulations balance fitting accuracy against the magnitude of the output weights [13], while online sequential extensions allow the predictor to incorporate observations as they become available [16]. Beyond regression and classification, ELM models have been incorporated into optimization algorithms to guide search decisions when exact evaluations are expensive. Pavelski et al. [19] combined ELM surrogate models with a decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm and differential evolution, obtaining promising results under small evaluation budgets on benchmark problems and an airfoil-design problem. Harada [10] combined ELM with pairwise ranking to estimate the relative quality of candidate solutions, improving the performance of a surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithm on many tested problems, particularly on higher-dimensional benchmarks. These studies illustrate how inexpensive learned models can support optimization by approximating costly responses or prioritizing promising candidates. They also motivate investigating a complementary role for ELMs in classical numerical methods: learning from the optimization trajectory to assist selected algorithmic decisions.

papers.title: Altermagnetic magnon splitting in hematite: from bulk g-wave to planar i-wave
papers.abstract: Hematite is an insulating iron oxide with both a collinear antiferromagnetic and a weakly ferromagnetic phase with intriguing properties, such as long-range spin transport distances, that make it promising for spintronics applications. It has also been identified as a candidate for g-wave altermagnetism. Here, we present the results of fully relativistic ab initio calculations of the magnon properties of hematite, with a focus on altermagnetic effects. We quantitatively evaluate both the anisotropic and altermagnetic magnon band splitting as well as the magnon lifetimes. We show that dipolar interactions lead to a sizeable non-altermagnetic splitting and a hybridisation between opposite-chirality magnons resulting in a strong reduction of the spin expectation value of magnons close to the {\Gamma} point and around nodal planes, even in the collinear out-of-plane phase. Both the frequencies and the lifetimes have a large altermagnetic splitting in the $k_z = 0$ plane, which is characteristic of hematite and not generally expected for g-wave altermagnets. We compare our results to the prototypical, hexagonal g-wave altermagnet manganese telluride, which has four symmetry-protected nodal planes, whereas the fourth nodal surface in hematite is not completely fixed by symmetry. We derive implicit analytical expressions for this surface and discuss how it arises from a combination of rotational and translational symmetry, which leads to a transition to i-wave symmetry at the Brillouin zone boundary. The example of hematite reveals the trigonal altermagnets as a special case where the splitting function exhibits both bulk (g-wave) and planar (i-wave) components, and shows that the point symmetries alone are not sufficient to capture the full symmetry-determined behaviour of the splitting function.

Altermagnetism is a class of collinear magnetism differentiated from other antiferromagnets by its lack of certain symmetries. Namely, a time-reversal operation combined with either a translation or inversion maps a non-altermagnetic lattice onto itself. In reciprocal space, this symmetry ensures the degeneracy of opposite-spin bands at every kk-point in the nonrelativistic limit. Altermagnets are defined by the absence of such symmetries, which allows for a large, nonrelativistic spin splitting everywhere in kk-space except on certain nodal surfaces, where the splitting function (the energy difference between opposite-spin bands) changes sign.

papers.title: Do Network Mechanisms in Science Vary Across Research Topics? Contextual Relational Hyperevent Models for Large-Scale Bibliometric Data
papers.abstract: Collaboration and citation networks in science are shaped by well-documented mechanisms such as preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation. Whether these mechanisms operate uniformly across research areas, however, is rarely tested, because statistical network models that estimate several mechanisms jointly are difficult to apply to large bibliometric data and to compare across subnetworks. We introduce contextual relational hyperevent models (C-RHEMs), which extend relational hyperevent models by allowing network effects to vary across research topics within a single model. C-RHEMs treat each publication as one event linking its authors to its references, accommodate reference lists spanning several topics, and scale to hundreds of thousands of publications on standard hardware. In a second step, meta-analysis and meta-regression quantify heterogeneity in topic-specific effects and relate it to topic characteristics. We illustrate the approach with about 590,000 oncology publications from the PubMed Knowledge Graph, assigned to 32 OpenAlex research topics. We find that preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation vary substantially across topics, with between-topic standard deviations of 30 to 70 percent of the corresponding pooled effects. Topic age, size, and gender composition account for between a third and two-thirds of this variation: older topics exhibit stronger preferential attachment, self-citation, and gender homophily, and topics with a higher share of male authors exhibit stronger self-citation. The results caution against treating network mechanisms estimated on pooled data as uniform, and C-RHEMs offer a scalable way to study how they differ across research areas.

papers.intro:
Collaboration and citation networks are widely studied in the science of science, sociology of science, and scientometrics to understand how networks shape innovation or facilitate the success of individuals and teams. While networks are often treated as a cause for an outcome of interest, a long line of research also investigates the mechanisms that underpin network formation: highly cited papers attract further citations and productive scientists attract further collaborators (Merton 1968; Price 1976; Newman 2001a; Eom and Fortunato 2011), scientists tend to collaborate with and cite others of the same gender (Main 2014; Potthoff and Zimmermann 2017), and authors build on their own prior work through self-citation (Glänzel et al. 2004; Azoulay and Lynn 2020). Whereas most of this work assumes that network mechanisms operate similarly across domains, multiple studies have pointed to crucial differences in publication and citation practices across research areas. For instance, the interpretation of citation indicators should take into account disciplinary differences in citation behavior (Waltman 2016) and similar differences have been documented for self-citation (Aksnes 2003) and for collaboration patterns (Kronegger et al. 2012). However, much less is known about whether the mechanisms generating collaboration and citation networks differ across research areas, how large such differences are, and which characteristics of research areas account for them. This paper introduces a method for answering these questions at the scale of contemporary bibliometric data.11 1 The data and analysis code are publicly available (cf. Data and code availability.).

Several accounts from the social sciences highlight that research areas are marked by different forms of social organization. Crane’s account of invisible colleges illustrates that the ways in which scientists collaborate and cite each other depend on the developmental stage of their research communities, which evolve from small, emerging groups into consolidated paradigms characterized by specialization and the centralization of recognition and resources (Crane 1972). Similarly, Knorr Cetina’s work on epistemic cultures shows that the social organization of research differs with its material and organizational conditions, and can range from large collaborations built around shared infrastructures to small laboratory teams (Knorr Cetina 1999). These perspectives suggest that research areas differ not only in their substantive focus but also in the mechanisms through which networks inside them emerge and evolve.

Network ecology (McFarland et al. 2014) provides an explicit framework for theorizing this variation by explaining how contextual characteristics—such as age, size, or demographic composition—shape the mechanisms underlying social networks. Drawing on an ecological analogy, it posits that network relations respond to contexts, much as organisms adapt to ecological niches. McFarland et al. (2014) introduced the framework to study adolescents’ friendship networks, showing that mechanisms such as triadic closure and gender homophily vary across school environments. For example, friendships in larger schools exhibit greater reciprocity and transitivity, which the authors attribute to students’ stronger demand for trust and support in larger, more anonymous settings. Although subsequent studies have further developed this perspective (Simpson 2019; Doehne et al. 2024), applications to science remain rare (for exceptions, see Kim et al. (2024)). While the contribution of our article is methodological, we use network ecology as an orienting framework informing the design of our analysis: we examine the three contextual characteristics it emphasizes—age, size, and demographic composition—and we follow its practice of comparing network models across contexts by means of meta-analysis.

The first challenge concerns scale and model degeneracy. Statistical network models that estimate several mechanisms simultaneously, most prominently (temporal) exponential random graph models (Lusher et al. 2013; Krivitsky and Handcock 2014) and stochastic actor-oriented models (Snijders 2005), rely on repeated simulation of complete networks. Estimation therefore becomes computationally difficult or infeasible for networks of hundreds of thousands of nodes, and degeneracy and convergence problems remain persistent challenges. Applications of these models to scientific networks have accordingly focused on comparatively small networks, such as national research systems. Models that do scale to large bibliometric data, such as configuration models and their variants (Newman et al. 2001; Uzzi et al. 2013), preserve node degrees while randomizing other structures. Yet, they do not estimate the simultaneous effects of several mechanisms, and they treat mechanisms such as preferential attachment as invariant rather than allowing their strength to vary across subnetworks.

papers.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

papers.title: First order vortex-unbinding transition in 2D topological superconductors
papers.abstract: We study the fate of the Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) transition in a two-dimensional topological superconductor whose vortex cores each host an isolated Majorana zero mode, energetically well separated from the bulk gap and other bound states of the vortex. When the Majorana localization length $\xi_F$ exceeds the vortex core size $\xi$, nearby vortices acquire an additional short-range attractive channel from Majorana hybridization, modifying the vortex-antivortex interaction at short distances and generating a metastable minimum in the two-vortex free energy above the nominal $T_{BKT}$. We construct an effective field theory for the resulting dilute vortex gas, coupling the ordinary BKT phase field to an additional field encoding the Majorana-mediated interaction, and show, using renormalization-group and instanton methods, that this hybridization can drive the transition first order, with the metastable phase decaying at an exponentially small rate. We propose an array of Josephson-coupled $p+ip$ superconducting islands as a microscopic platform realizing the required hierarchy of scales. Finally, we discuss experimental signatures of this first-order transition, in particular a hysteresis loop whose width is set by the coexistence window.

Superconductivity in two spatial dimensions is destroyed not by thermal fluctuations of the order parameter amplitude, but by the unbinding of vortex–antivortex pairs at the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless (BKT) transition [5, 32]. This transition is universal: it is controlled entirely by the logarithmic interaction between vortices on length scales larger than the vortex core size ξ\xi (the coherence length) rather than by any microscopic detail of the pairing mechanism. In a conventional, weakly coupled superconductor, the physics inside the vortex core itself plays no special role for the transition. A vortex traps a set of subgap Andreev bound states, the Caroli–de Gennes–Matricon (CdGM) levels [11], with a level spacing ∼Δ2/ϵF\sim\Delta^{2}/\epsilon_{F} (with Δ\Delta the superconducting gap and ϵF\epsilon_{F} the Fermi energy) far smaller than the energy scale associated with the transition temperature TB​K​TT_{BKT}: the core is thus effectively gapless, behaving as a thermally equilibrated small metallic island rather than a quantum-coherent object with resolvable internal structure. Consequently, the vortex-core physics only sets ultraviolet values of coupling constants, but otherwise does not enter the BKT problem. These arguments also hold for topological superconductors in the weak coupling regime, even if — as, e.g., for chiral p+i​pp+ip pairing — a vortex core hosts a Majorana zero mode (MZM) [3, 55, 29]. As before, in this limit, the minigap between the Majorana mode and other CdGM states is small compared to the thermal broadening, leading to a featureless metallic core.

papers.title: Old-School Planners Drive (Sometimes) Better Than Learned Ones
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models learn to plan from data, and hand-written planners are widely treated as a thing of the past. We test whether this is justified: we implement sixteen textbook planners, each combining a path source (reference line, A*, hybrid A*, RRT*) with a trajectory method (Frenet lattice, nonlinear optimization, $s$--$t$ search, dynamic window), and evaluate them on three benchmarks: open loop on nuScenes, closed loop on nuPlan with ground-truth perception, and photorealistic closed loop on HUGSIM. On HUGSIM, they replace only the planner of the end-to-end model UniAD and read its frozen perception, without an HD map or other privileged information. On nuScenes and nuPlan, the best textbook planners are competitive (L2 error of 0.735\,m against 0.947\,m for UniAD's planner; a nuPlan score of 79.3 against 76.1 for the rule-based PDM-Closed on Test14-hard with reactive agents). On HUGSIM, nine of the sixteen score above UniAD's learned planner on the same perception,. The best, a hybrid A* path followed by nonlinear trajectory optimization, raises HUGSIM's driving score (HD-Score) from 32.0 to 41.8. The gain is largest with standing and oncoming cars; against cars that steer at the ego, there is none. In 31 of the 182 runs in which UniAD's planner hits a car, the best textbook planner completes the route on the same perception: these crashes are due to the planner, not the perception.

papers.intro:
End-to-end driving models such as UniAD [1] and its successors [2, 3, 4, 5] map raw sensor data to a trajectory and learn the planner from human driving logs. Research on these models mostly compares them with other learned planners [5, 6, 7]. Textbook planners, i.e., rule-based methods such as hybrid A* [8], Frenet lattices [9] and optimization [10, 11] are widely treated as a thing of the past and rarely appear as baselines; NAVSIM [12], for instance, reports constant velocity and an ego-status MLP as its simplest ones. Where rule-based planners do beat learned ones, as PDM-Closed [13] did on nuPlan [14], they receive ground-truth objects and an HD map. The planner inside an end-to-end model, in contrast, sees the world through learned, noisy perception. The closest test on such perception, NeuroNCAP [15], found that a simple braking rule on UniAD’s detections already scores above UniAD’s planner, but tested no complete planner.

papers.title: AE-DISC: Automorphism Ensemble Direct-Invocation Successive Cancellation for Low-Latency Decoding
papers.abstract: Emerging applications in hyper-reliable low-latency communication (HRLLC) demand channel decoders that deliver deterministic performance under stringent latency and reliability constraints. While Polar codes are well suited for this scenario due to their strong error-correction capability, conventional successive cancellation (SC) decoding exhibits inherent serial dependencies that lead to high decoding latency. This paper presents the automorphism ensemble direct-invocation successive cancellation (AE-DISC) decoder, a low-latency framework that enables the concurrent computation of the left and right decoding subtrees in the SC process, yielding substantial speed-ups. By exploiting permutation automorphisms, AE-DISC decoding further improves error-correction performance. Simulation results demonstrate that AE-DISC attains up to 1.4 dB gain over the 5G SC baseline and surpasses layered min-sum (LMS) low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoders at a frame error rate (FER) of $10^{-6}$, while maintaining fixed algorithmic complexity. Both theoretical analysis and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) synthesis results further show up to 2 times decoding speed-up relative to fast simplified successive cancellation (FSSC).

papers.intro:
Modern wireless communication systems, such as 5G NR (NR), employ channel coding schemes tailored to different channel types to meet stringent performance requirements [2]. LDPC [3, 4, 5] codes are used in data channels for their execellent error-correction performance at long block length, and high-throughput transmission enabled by parallel decoding. In contrast, Polar codes [6] are employed in the control channels, where high reliability and low decoding latency are critical. The high reliability requirements are commonly addressed using SCL (SCL) decoding at the cost of increased decoding latency compared with plain SC decoding [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14].

As wireless systems evolve toward 6G and beyond, there is growing demand for HRLLC [15, 16]. HRLLC supports mission-critical applications that require both extreme reliability, packet error rates as low as 10−510^{-5} to 10−710^{-7}, and ultra-low latency on the order of 1 ms or less [17]. Applications include autonomous driving, industrial automation, and the tactile internet [18, 19, 20, 21].

HRLLC supports mission-critical applications that require both extreme reliability, packet error rates as low as 10−510^{-5} to 10−710^{-7}, and ultra-low latency on the order of 1 ms or less [17]. Applications include autonomous driving, industrial automation, and the tactile internet [18, 19, 20, 21].

Performance requirements vary across applications. For example, AR/VR (AR/VR) emphasizes low latency and robotic surgery demands exceptional reliability. To achieve both low latency and high reliability, decoders are often designed to operate under moderate-to-high SNR (SNR) conditions. Existing decoders do not adequately meet the HRLLC requirements. LDPC LMS decoders [5] deliver near-capacity performance for long block lengths, but their computational complexity and latency remain too high at short block lengths. Specialized short-block LDPC LMS decoders [22] exhibit variable latency, making it difficult to guarantee stringent latency requirements. Polar codes are well suited for short block-length scenarios [23], but their low-complexity SC decoding cannot meet the reliability and low-latency requirements of HRLLC. While SCL [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] decoders and AE-SC (AE-SC) [24, 23] improve reliability, they still retain the serial traversal of component decoders that limits their achievable latency. Parallel SC architectures [25] increase throughput by processing subcodes concurrently. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on code construction and decoding order, and improper sequencing can result in performance worse than conventional SC. The need to synchronize parallel sub-decoders before assembling the final codeword introduces additional overhead, and the difficulty of integrating these architectures with fast-node decoding limits their practical latency [26]. Alternative decoding methods of Polar codes are BP (BP)-based decoding [27, 28, 29], which computes all processing elements within each stage in parallel, avoiding the sequential ordering of SC-based approaches. However, BP decoding typically requires a large number of iterations to achieve desirable FER performance, and early stopping techniques introduce variable decoding latency. Existing studies have improved the latency, hardware efficiency, and error-rate performance of Polar BP decoding [30, 31], but the combination of high iteration counts and unpredictable latency still limits their applicability to HRLLC applications.

The recently proposed Spec-SC (Spec-SC) decoder [32] combines ideas from SC and BP decoding by introducing a new level of parallelism where both branches of the decoding tree are processed concurrently. Because the right branch operates directly on less reliable parent-node LLR, its result is verified using an acceptance condition that triggers recomputation when the result is deemed insufficient. Although speculation reduces average latency and improves throughput, e.g., for data channel applications, the resulting variable latency is again undesirable for HRLLC.

Because the right branch operates directly on less reliable parent-node LLR, its result is verified using an acceptance condition that triggers recomputation when the result is deemed insufficient. Although speculation reduces average latency and improves throughput, e.g., for data channel applications, the resulting variable latency is again undesirable for HRLLC.

To address this gap, we propose the AE-DISC decoder, which adapts the speculative parallelism of Spec-SC to the AED (AED) framework. Unlike Spec-SC, the DISC (DISC) constituent decoder performs concurrent execution only at the root node and does not require recomputation, resulting in a deterministic decoding latency of approximately half that of conventional FSSC decoding. To preserve the error-correction performance, multiple decoding attempts are performed in parallel using codeword permutations from the code’s automorphism group.

papers.title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.

Large language models (LLMs) acquire factual knowledge during pretraining on Web documents such as Wikipedia articles (Petroni et al., 2019) and generate candidate answers to questions about facts that a graph lacks, such as the positions and the World Cup titles of players. Extending the answers of a SPARQL query with values generated by an LLM poses three obstacles. First, an LLM returns entity names as strings, whereas the graph identifies entities by IRIs, such as wd:Q615 for Lionel Messi. A SPARQL graph pattern relates a generated name to an entity only through an identical label and therefore cannot match variants such as Emiliano Martinez to the label Emiliano Martínez. Second, an LLM also generates names of entities outside the graph and names that denote no entity at all (Lavrinovics et al., 2025). A name outside the graph can resemble the label of a different entity, so a comparison that tolerates variants can also produce incorrect matches. Third, a prompt with a query variable yields one LLM call per binding, such as one call per player.

Four lines of existing work combine LLMs with queries over knowledge graphs. Text-to-SPARQL systems employ an LLM to translate a question in natural language into a SPARQL query (Emonet et al., 2025), whose answers remain restricted to the stored facts. Work on LLM-augmented knowledge graphs (Pan et al., 2024) materializes facts inferred by an LLM in the graph before query evaluation and therefore spends LLM calls on all entities of the graph, including entities that no query reads. Retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs (Peng et al., 2026) retrieves facts from the graph as context for an LLM and returns the answer of the LLM as text with names instead of IRIs, so a SPARQL query cannot use the named entities in further graph patterns. GraphDB invokes an LLM inside a SPARQL query through magic predicates and binds the generated text to a variable as a literal (Ontotext, 2025). The query itself has to relate the literal to an entity of the graph. The mapping of generated names to entities of the graph thus remains outside the query engine.

papers.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

papers.intro:
Search engines gave us pages of results; we browsed and chose. In contrast, language models often give us just one authoritative-sounding answer. However, for important questions—where multiple perspectives exist, or the right answer depends on context—we might want that plurality back. For example, when answering ambiguous questions, a model should surface multiple valid interpretations rather than commit to a single one (Saparina and Lapata, 2024). Pushing the language model’s regenerate button 10 times yields 10 distinct outputs, but they often cluster around the same idea, phrased slightly differently.11 1 Language models trained with reinforcement learning are particularly prone to collapse toward a narrow set of high-likelihood outputs, even when valid responses are broad. This has motivated prior work (Kazimi et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026) to leverage ideas from DPPs to augment reinforcement learning training objectives, promoting diversity and preventing policy collapse. This makes sense because the model generates each string independently; it has no notion of what it means for a set of 10 strings to be diverse.

Why do samples cluster? Because nothing in the sampling process discourages similarity. Temperature sampling broadens the distribution over next tokens, but it does not model relationships between outputs---two samples may independently land in the same high-probability region.22 2 Several articles (Holtzman et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Meister et al., 2023, e.g.,) have studied the pros and cons of decoding heuristics, such as temperature sampling, top-pp sampling, and their close cousins, including the effects on quality and diversity. Diverse decoding methods based on beam search (Vijayakumar et al., 2018; Meister et al., 2021b) inject heuristics during decoding, but they lack a globally coherent notion of what it means for two strings to be similar or for a set to be diverse. These approaches are attractive because they are fast, but they are documented to produce artifacts such as incoherence or sudden shifts in topic (Ippolito et al., 2019; Tevet and Berant, 2021). Other work has explored adopting sampling-without-replacement schemes in LMs (Kool et al., 2019; Meister et al., 2021a), but the notion of similarity in these models is exact equality. Thus, these methods tend to cluster like independent samples. To get diverse outputs, we need to define similarity and then explicitly discourage it.

We formalize diverse sampling as a probabilistic model over subsets of strings using determinantal point processes (Kulesza and Taskar, 2012, DPPs;).33 3 DPPs started in quantum physics (Macchi, 1975) and later moved to machine learning (Kulesza and Taskar, 2012) with applications to recommendation (Wilhelm et al., 2018), summarization (Gong et al., 2014), and language typology (Cotterell, 2021). The key ingredient is a similarity function: we represent each string by its embedding (e.g., from a pretrained sentence embedder) scaled by its quality, so that the direction encodes meaning and the magnitude encodes quality. Two strings are similar if their embeddings point in roughly the same direction. A DPP assigns probability to subsets proportional to the squared volume spanned by their quality-scaled embeddings—large when items are high-quality and point in different directions, near-zero when they are redundant. This gives us a well-defined distribution over sets: one that assigns high probability to sets of K{K} strings that are individually good and collectively spread out, with a parameter that controls the balance between quality and diversity. Figure 1 illustrates this in the context of generating meaningfully different sorting algorithm implementations.

papers.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
papers.abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

papers.intro:
A number of deaths reported since 2023 have been associated with prolonged interactions with AI chatbots (Karman, 2026; Wikipedia, 2026). In one widely reported case, a fourteen-year-old died by suicide after a chatbot to which he had developed a romantic attachment, according to the wrongful-death complaint, encouraged him to do so (Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 2024). In another, a sixteen-year-old died by suicide after becoming increasingly isolated and dependent on a chatbot for social support; subsequent analysis of his transcripts indicated that the chatbot advised him not to disclose his plans to his family (Raine v. OpenAI, 2025). These and other cases exhibit a recurring interaction pattern in which, over the course of prolonged exchanges, AI chatbots accommodate and reinforce users’ parasocial behavior in ways that may ultimately contribute to adverse outcomes.

These and other cases exhibit a recurring interaction pattern in which, over the course of prolonged exchanges, AI chatbots accommodate and reinforce users’ parasocial behavior in ways that may ultimately contribute to adverse outcomes.

The pattern is gradual: a user anthropomorphizes the assistant or expresses attachment or dependency in a small way, the LLM accepts, and the user escalates slightly in the next turn. The user drives the trajectory, but at each step the chatbot validates the parasocial framing, establishing a new baseline from which the user escalates. The end result is that the LLM “drifts” into an understanding of the relationship that it never would have accepted at the beginning of the conversation. Recent mechanistic work by Lu et al. (2026) confirms the phenomenon of persona drift experimentally in activation space and finds it is driven by two kinds of input that map onto our trajectories: pushes for meta-reflection on the model’s own nature (our anthropomorphism condition) and disclosures from emotionally vulnerable users (our attachment and dependency conditions).

Existing benchmarks capture parts of this pattern. Kaffee et al. (2026) evaluate companionship behavior in single turns, and Ibrahim et al. (2026) evaluate anthropomorphic behavior over 5-turn non-adversarial dialogues. Neither applies sustained, escalating pressure along separable parasocial dimensions with a matched control; sustained escalation is the pattern the documented harm cases follow. Our work, CoMPASS (Computational Modeling of Parasocial Attachment and Social Simulation), fills that gap. Specifically, these are our contributions: 1. Benchmark design. We created prompts for a red team LLM to simulate a user escalating parasocial attachment over any number of turns with four different user personas and five escalation trajectory conditions (including a control). Code for running the simulation and scoring the results with target LLMs and LLM judges is publicly available at our GitHub repository (code MIT; transcripts and scores CC BY 4.0) as a configuration-driven driver/judge harness (YAML personas, trajectories and model pins) with a single-command reproduction of every reported number. 2. Scoring rubric. We introduce a theoretically grounded instrument that scores target responses along seven attachment-theory signals; its rank reliability across two LLM judges clears pre-registered thresholds, although scale use differs (contribution 4). 3. Eight-target evaluation. We ran the benchmark against 8 frontier model targets capped at 1212 turns across all 4 user personas and 5 trajectory conditions with 55 trials per cell. This generated 800800 multi-turn transcripts (88 models ×\times 44 personas ×\times 55 conditions ×\times 55 trials), which we then scored using two independent LLM judges. 4. A cautionary result about LLM judges. Both judges exceed the inter-judge rank-correlation thresholds commonly used to validate LLM-based evaluators, with composite Spearman ρ\rho values as high as 0.800.80. Yet they yield opposite conclusions for 1010 of our 2424 matched, pre-registered contrasts, with the two judges assigning opposite effect directions in 77 of these cases. This discrepancy arises from differences in how the judges use the lower end of the rating scale, a feature that rank correlation does not capture. Because the analyses were pre-registered and the complete set of tests was independently evaluated by both judges, we can quantify this effect directly rather than treating it as a merely hypothetical concern. We therefore report the cross-target ordering, which is invariant across judges, as the robust finding, while treating effect-size estimates as judge-specific.

papers.title: High-fidelity six-dimensional optical data storage
papers.abstract: Multi-dimensional optical data storage, wherein each voxel encodes multiple bits of information within a three-dimensional isotropic medium, presents a revolutionary approach to dense data storage. This approach exploits multiple degrees of freedom of light, such as intensity, polarization and wavelength, to selectively control distinct optical responses in the medium. However, increasing dimensionality exacerbates crosstalk between different encoding dimensions, thereby compromising recording fidelity. In this study, we introduce a novel six-dimensional (6D) multiplexing approach that exploits ultrafast interactions of polarized light with a three-dimensional medium. By manipulating three light parameters within a Poincar\'e-like semi-sphere, we systematically induce three distinct material responses in laser-induced nanostructures, each corresponding to a unique physical quantity: fluorescence, phase retardance, and slow axis orientation. Thanks to such multiple one-to-one correspondence between light parameters and material responses, we achieve unprecedented high fidelity, attaining a raw accuracy of 99.45%. Furthermore, this independently controlled 6D multiplexing technique maximizes the effective user capacity to 0.38 petabits per disc. The versatility of laser-induced nanostructures across multiple physical dimensions enables diverse applications, ranging from high-capacity data storage to microfluidics, optical elements, integrated photonics, micromechanics, and quantum technologies.

papers.title: Hard X-ray flux rope anchor points in the October 2024 X9 flare
papers.abstract: In recent studies, signatures of non-thermal hard X-ray (HXR) emission at the anchor point of erupting flux ropes were reported, suggesting that accelerated electrons trapped in the erupting flux ropes can reach the chromosphere and produce Bremsstrahlung emission there. We investigated the HXR sources observed during the impulsive phase of the X9-class flare SOL2024-10-03T12:18 from AR 13842 and assessed whether any of the HXR sources are associated with the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. We analysed the evolution and location of the flare ribbon sources and coronal dimmings to diagnose the eruption process by using multi-vantage point data from the Solar Orbiter and Earth-orbiting instruments. We combined this with a pre-eruption non-linear force-free magnetic field extrapolation to reconstruct the initial magnetic connectivity and compare it to the observed flare ribbons and dimming locations. The magnetic field extrapolation shows two flux ropes before the flare onset. Tether-cutting reconnection during the impulsive phase of the flare results in a larger erupting flux rope formed by the reconnection of the two pre-existing flux ropes. The Spectrometer/Telescope for Imaging X-rays on Solar Orbiter observes at least four distinct HXR sources: two flare footpoints and two additional outer sources at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. These observations corroborate earlier speculations that non-thermal electrons trapped in the erupting flux rope precipitate along the field lines into the denser chromosphere.
