As 3D world auditing requires both high accuracy and computational efficiency, a viable strategy is to decompose the audit along the three competencies above and assign each to models of appropriate sizes. Existing work [18] compares two primary paradigms. In the first paradigm, a single frontier VLM executes all three competencies end to end. Although accurate, this approach is computationally expensive. On WorldAuditBench [18], a single audit by a frontier VLM exceeds ten minutes and costs approximately $3.00. In the second paradigm, an inexpensive vision-language-action (VLA) model [58] explores the environment and logs visual observations, which a frontier VLM subsequently inspects offline. While cost-effective, current VLA models lack the reasoning needed to prioritize inspection targets or trigger latent glitches, leading to frequent misses and false alarms. Consequently, the strongest such auditor achieves a success rate of only 17.4%.

papers.title: TRACE: Attribute Execution for Sequential Image Editing
papers.abstract: Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. This lets users develop a result without repeatedly restating or repairing their decisions. The difficulty is that a retrieved image can contain a valid color on an obsolete surface, while the current image may lack the newly requested material. Neither reference selection nor a precise object mask alone specifies how to reconcile attributes occupying the same region. We present TRACE, which separates the continuing attribute from its visual carrier and prioritizes local appearance operations under complete-request checks. Active-goal binding identifies what should persist, carrier selection supplies suitable current or newly generated pixels, and tonal calibration reduces tinting near highlights and shadows. Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and complete sequential benchmarks support joint color-material recovery and show how local execution preserves the surrounding scene.

papers.intro:
Sequential image editing lets a user develop an image through a conversation: given the current image and a new instruction, the system returns an updated image that should also respect earlier decisions. A user might first change a sign to yellow, then ask for a wooden surface, and later revise its shape. This workflow is useful precisely because each request can build on the preceding result. The challenge is deciding what should survive each change. A new color replaces the old color, whereas a material change usually leaves the color requirement intact. Moreover, an image records what the editor produced, which may differ from what the user requested. An earlier edit can fail, and a later edit can undo an earlier success. A sequential editor must therefore track the intended state throughout the conversation and recover valid requirements when they disappear from the image.

Instruction-trained editors improve the fidelity of individual changes [5, 14, 24, 50, 34, 55, 3], while multi-turn training and conditioning reduce drift across successive outputs [67, 41, 22, 62, 66, 9, 8]. Memory and reference-selection methods retain entity state and retrieve earlier images that contain useful visual evidence [38, 19, 32]. Yet even correct retrieval leaves an important choice unresolved: which part of that evidence should be reused? In the sign example, an earlier image may show the desired yellow on the old surface. Copying the sign restores yellow but also removes the new wood grain. A precise object mask cannot prevent this regression, because color and material occupy the same pixels. If the earlier color edit failed, the retrieved image may not contain the desired appearance at all. Thus a continuing requirement, its visual evidence, and the surface on which it should appear need separate representations. Color-transfer and color-editing methods already offer ways to change color while retaining structure [45, 63, 64]; sequential recovery additionally requires deciding whether the target is still valid and whether the resulting image satisfies the newer request.

In this paper, we propose TRACE, an attribute executor around a frozen image editor. Its central idea is to reuse an appearance operation whose target and application image are bound separately. Active-goal binding follows the instructions to retain complementary requirements, retire revised values, and associate each target with its original request. Local attribute execution uses qualified history to specify the desired color, while the current object supplies the spatial samples and surface structure. When the current object lacks the newly requested material, a corrective image supplies a replacement surface for the same local region. Tonal calibration fits the target color center while tapering changes near highlights and shadows. Complete-request selection then checks both the earlier and current requests in their original image contexts. A color match alone is insufficient when an earlier instruction also specifies identity or other properties. Successful operations can be retained and applied again after fresh target binding and verification, adapting execution without changing the editor’s weights.

papers.title: Minimal Memory for Correctable Visual Continuation
papers.abstract: Given past images and known actions, visual continuation generates future frames from one evolving scene state. Keeping this state revisable matters when an object reappears or a later view changes an earlier interpretation. Once past images cannot be replayed, a summary sufficient for current rendering can lose candidates needed after correction. We establish matching sparse and dense bounds on the bits needed for later correction under stable observations and bounded disagreement. For static streams at the stated smoothness and margin scales, correction incurs at least logarithmic overhead in one dimension and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions. Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) stores geometric summaries with exact updates under clipped expansion and coordinate assignments, then uses historical existence constraints to select one state for all requested frames. Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, while controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.

Coherence requires preserving action consequences while revising uncertain interpretations across shots and revisits.

papers.title: On the Hamel Coefficients and the Boltzmann-Hamel Equations for the Rigid Body
papers.abstract: The Boltzmann-Hamel (BH) equations are central in the dynamics and control of nonholonomic systems described in terms of quasi-velocities. The rigid body is a classical example of such systems, and it is well-known that the BH-equations are the Newton-Euler (NE) equations when described in terms of rigid body twists as quasi-velocities. It is further known that the NE-equations are the Euler-Poincare, respectively, the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations on SE(3) when using body-fixed or spatial representation of rigid body twists. The connection between these equations are the Hamel coefficients, which are immediately identified as the structure constants of SE(3). However, an explicit coordinate-free derivation has not been presented in the literature. In this paper the Hamel coefficients for the rigid body are derived in a coordinate-free way without resorting to local coordinates describing the rigid body motion. The three most relevant choices of quasi-velocities (body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representation of rigid body twists) are considered. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly for the rotating and free floating body. Further, the Hamel equations for nonholonomically constrained rigid bodies are discussed, and demonstrated for the inhomogenous ball rolling on a plane.

papers.intro:
The Boltzmann-Hamel (BH) equations are a milestone result of the research on the dynamics of nonholonomic systems, which was initiated by Hertz [22]. Hamel continued previous works of Volterra [48] (who continued the work of Beltrami), Tzénoff [46, 47] (who built upon the work of Chaplygin [11, 13, 12]), Poincaré [39], Voronets [49, 51], and Boltzmann [4] in particular, into a general concept. Key elements in these equations are the three-index symbols that are referred to as ’Hamel coefficients’, which reveal the nonholonomic nature of the quasi-coordinates respectively of the constraints a system is subjected to.

Key elements in these equations are the three-index symbols that are referred to as ’Hamel coefficients’, which reveal the nonholonomic nature of the quasi-coordinates respectively of the constraints a system is subjected to.

If the Lagrangian is invariant under the action of a Lie group, then the Hamel coefficients are identical to the structure constants of this group. The BH-equations are then the Euler-Lagrange equations corresponding to a reduced variational principle on this symmetry group, respectively the Euler-Poincaré equations [3, 31, 30]. For this reason the BH-equations are often used as synonym for the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations [1, 3]. The configuration space of a rigid body is the Lie group S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right) (the special Euclidean group [30, 31, 35, 40]), and the BH-equations are the Euler-Poincaré equations (when formulated in terms of body-fixed twists), or the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations (when using spatial twists). The rigid body is often used as the typical example to study fundamental aspects of nonholonomic systems in a coordinate-free geometric setting. However, a systematic treatment of the original BH-equations [18, 19, 21] in local coordinates along with the original derivation of the Hamel coefficients for the rigid body, in a way that links them to the Euler-Lagrange equations on S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right), has not yet been reported in the literature. Key to this is evaluating the Hamel coefficients taking into account the geometry of rigid body motions (possibly without resorting to local coordinates), which not only demonstrates technicalities of the actual determination of these coefficients, but also offers insight into the geometric nature of the problem. Moreover, the Hamel coefficients are specific to the particular representation of rigid body velocities (i.e. the definition of quasi-velocities) and the corresponding invariance of the rigid body Lagrangian under action of the symmetry group. The three most relevant representations of rigid body velocities, are the body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representation [33, 35]. The first two correspond to a left-invariant and right-invariant Lagrangian on S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right), respectively. The hybrid representation assumes the direct product group S​O​(3)×ℝ3SO\left(3\right)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3} as symmetry group and corresponding right-invariant Lagrangian, which clearly implies a different geometric model of rigid body motions [34, 45]. Despite the long history of analytical rigid body dynamics, this paper seems to be the first publication reporting an explicit geometric construction of the Hamel coefficients, which are indeed determined by the structure constant of the Lie group underlying the respective definition of rigid body twist. The paper summarizes material that is scattered in the literature along with references to the original sources, and presents novel derivations of Hamel coefficients. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly summarizes the BH-equations in their original form and the definition of the Hamel coefficients. First the BH-equations for general unconstrained systems described in quasi-coordinates are reviewed. Then the Hamel equations for constrained systems described in quasi-coordinates as well as in ’holonomic’ coordinates are recalled. In order to make a connection to the modern approach in geometric mechanics, the BH-equations for the rigid body are finally identified as the Euler-Poincaré respectively the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations when using S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right) as rigid body configuration space. The Hamel coefficients are derived in section 3 for the rotating rigid body when the angular velocity in body-fixed and spatial representation is used as quasi-velocity. The corresponding BH-equations are derived in section 4. The Hamel coefficients for the free rigid body are derived in section 5 where the body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representations of twists are used as quasi-velocities. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly in section 6. papers.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
papers.abstract: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Natural Language Understanding (NLU) pipelines which aim to understand information from text [1]. While some pipelines use a single NER extractor to handle various entity types, domain-specific applications commonly apply multiple NER extractors and leverage the expertise of each extractor [2]. This is also a modular approach to entity extraction. For instance, if a new service package toyota care, has to be recognized, it can be integrated without impacting other NER extractors in the pipeline.

While some pipelines use a single NER extractor to handle various entity types, domain-specific applications commonly apply multiple NER extractors and leverage the expertise of each extractor [2]. This is also a modular approach to entity extraction. For instance, if a new service package toyota care, has to be recognized, it can be integrated without impacting other NER extractors in the pipeline.

When applying multiple NER extractors, predictions of extractors might conflict with each other by assigning different entity types to overlapping spans of text. Figure 1 shows an example from automotive domain where the extracted entities oil change, change tire and tire rotation of repair_operation category overlap with one another. Additionally, jimmy is recognized as both car_model and name entities. However, the correct set of entities in this context are oil change, tire rotation, and jimmy (recognized as a car_model).

NLU systems like spaCy [3] usually address this problem by applying the NER extractors sequentially, such that NER extractors later in the pipeline have a lower priority (to assign entities in case of span overlap) over extractors earlier in the pipeline. This pipeline-based approach relies on a curated order of the NER extractors. However, determining the perfect order of these extractors is challenging. In our use case of a conversation agent, the perfect order of extractors would also depend on the state of the dialogue, which makes this approach infeasible for our needs.

An alternative approach that overcomes the limitations of ordered NER extractors consists in applying multiple NER extractors in parallel and collecting all predicted entities. Naturally, an additional step is to resolve conflicting entities. One approach to entity conflict resolution is to write hand-crafted rules that define prioritization of entities given the current state of the dialogue. However, this approach comes with its own limitations – designing these rules requires domain expertise; and adding new rules is challenging as they might interfere with existing rules.

Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been a recurring topic in the NLU community, given their ability to deal with different NLU tasks with great success [4]. In this paper, we investigate the effect of leveraging LLMs to replace the set of manually-crafted rules for entity conflict resolution. We first generate a dataset containing over 6000060000 utterance examples from our real-world dialogue system. We then use this dataset to train and evaluate LLMs and compare their performance against our rule-based conflict resolution approach in multiple settings. Our experiments show that LLM-based conflict resolution approach achieves an agreement of 81.42%81.42\% with the rule-based conflict resolution approach, indicating that LLMs are valid alternatives to consider as replacements for tedious hand-crafted rule-based conflict resolution strategies in specific domains.

The rule-based conflict resolution approach, however, is not a perfect standard to evaluate the performance of LLMs as it might fail to capture more nuanced aspects of the text. To objectively evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, we create a human-annotated dataset, Automotive-Curated that contains 674674 examples from three distinct conversation contexts. Results show that on this dataset, the LLM and rule-based conflict resolution approach achieved a competitive overall accuracy of 78.93%78.93\%, and 78.60%78.60\% respectively. Further, we observe that LLM outperforms rule-based conflict resolution approach in generic conversational context like time negotiation, but the comparative performance drops in domain specific contexts like service request.

papers.title: Critical droplets and metastability in long-range chains
papers.abstract: Metastable decay in first-order phase transitions proceeds through the nucleation of critical droplets. In the one-dimensional nearest-neighbor Ising chain, the cost of the two walls bounding a droplet is independent of its size. For interactions decaying as $1/r^{1+\sigma}$, this surface cost instead depends on the droplet size and competes with the bulk free-energy gain. The critical radius scales as $R_c\propto h^{-1/\sigma}$ at small $h$, where $h>0$ is the bias field. The value $\sigma=1$ separates two regimes: for $\sigma<1$, the activation barrier diverges as $h\to0^+$; at $\sigma=1$, it grows logarithmically; and for $\sigma>1$, it remains finite, as in the nearest-neighbor chain. A nonlocal $\phi^4$ field theory yields critical droplets with algebraic tails and confirms the predicted radius and barrier scalings, while stochastic long-range dynamics independently reproduces the critical-radius scaling.

papers.intro:
Metastability and nucleation are central to the dynamics of first-order transitions in systems ranging from condensed matter to quantum field theory [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. A system can remain trapped in a locally stable state even when a lower-free-energy phase is available, and its decay then proceeds through rare fluctuations [6]. In the nucleation picture, such a fluctuation creates a localized domain, or droplet, of the stable phase within the metastable background [7, 8]. Small droplets shrink and disappear, whereas sufficiently large ones grow and eventually convert the surrounding system. The critical droplet separating these two regimes sets the activation barrier for nucleation.

How this picture changes when interactions extend over long distances remains comparatively less understood. Trapped-ion simulators realize tunable power-law Ising couplings [9, 10] and have recently probed bubble-nucleation dynamics [11], and false-vacuum decay has also been investigated in Rydberg arrays [12, 13]. Photon-mediated interactions in cavity-coupled gases provide a complementary setting for metastability and switching [14, 15, 16], while ultracold-gas experiments directly probe thermal effects in metastable decay [17, 18]. These developments motivate understanding how interaction range affects thermally activated nucleation [6, 19, 20], a decay mechanism distinct from the quantum tunneling studied for long-range systems [21].

papers.title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing
papers.abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.

papers.title: SlotFlow-GB: A Neural Framework for Trans-Dimensional Inference of Overlapping Galactic Binaries
papers.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe the millihertz gravitational-wave sky, including millions of long-lived Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands of which are expected to be individually resolvable throughout the mission's lifetime. Extracting these sources requires jointly determining their number and physical parameters from strongly overlapping signals, posing a computationally demanding trans-dimensional inference problem. We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework that constructs a learned approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior, producing a probability distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual binaries in a single evaluation, without requiring their number to be specified in advance. We demonstrate this framework using year-long LISA simulations containing up to ten binaries within a 2 $\mu$Hz frequency interval, focusing on a high-SNR regime in which source overlap, rather than individual-source detectability, is the primary challenge. The inferred source count differs from the true count by at most one in 94% of cases, while the model identifies individual binaries even when their signals overlap strongly in frequency. A complete evaluation, including parameter sampling, takes just 41 ms per band on one NVIDIA GH200 GPU, or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. We further demonstrate that these distributions can be used to initialize subsequent likelihood-based inference, connecting fast amortized predictions with joint parameter estimation.

Their signals are present simultaneously in the data, and those from nearby frequencies can overlap strongly. Recovering GB signals in a crowded band requires solving two coupled problems: determining how many binaries are present, and inferring the physical parameters of each one. Because the number of unknown parameters changes with the number of superposed GB signals, the inference task is intrinsically trans-dimensional.

Early studies showed that overlapping GBs could be recovered using blocked annealed sampling with a variable number of sources [3] and reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo [4, 5]. These methods were subsequently developed into trans-dimensional global fits that jointly infer multiple source populations and instrumental noise. For instance, variable GB counts have been treated with reversible-jump sampling [6, 7, 8], while product-space model selection has also been suggested for this problem [9, 10]. Other approaches construct the catalog iteratively through repeated search and thresholding [11]. Such analyses have been demonstrated on LISA Data Challenge simulated datasets [12], including GPU-accelerated implementations for large-scale inference [8].

We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework for end-to-end trans-dimensional inference that represents an unknown population of Galactic binaries through a distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual sources. It combines a fixed pool of competing source slots [28], with no predefined assignment to individual binaries; a permutation-invariant training loss that uses one-to-one matching to associate predicted slots with injected sources [29]; and conditional normalizing flows [30] that represent an eight-dimensional parameter density for each candidate. These densities retain correlations between individual source parameters, but not between different sources.

papers.title: Asymptotic efficiency comparison of explicit Dirichlet shape estimators
papers.abstract: In this study, we compare the asymptotic efficiency of three closed-form estimators of the Dirichlet shape parameters. We start by proving that, in the beta distribution, the score-adjusted moment estimator (SA) has strictly smaller componentwise asymptotic variances than the usual moment estimator (M1) for both parameters. We then introduce a new moment estimator (M2) that combines the marginal moment equations to obtain a common estimate of the total concentration. M2 coincides with M1 in the beta case and has strictly smaller componentwise asymptotic variances for every positive shape vector in three or more dimensions. We then show that SA is asymptotically more efficient than M2 when all shape parameters are equal; if at least two parameters differ, each estimator has smaller asymptotic variance than the other for some linear combination of the parameters. Furthermore, SA has strictly smaller componentwise asymptotic variances than M2 when all shape parameters are at least 1. Finally, we show that this ordering can reverse if a parameter becomes too small, and obtain relevant mathematical and computational bounds. Overall, the study shows that, for the Dirichlet distribution and under a broad range of parameter settings, score-adjusted estimation outperforms the classic moment estimation and identifies the limits of that advantage.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Distance-Unbiased Sorting
papers.abstract: We study elitist randomized local search for sorting permutations. In this model, each iteration considers a possible exchange of two positions. The entries are exchanged if and only if they are in the wrong order. We introduce \emph{distance-unbiased} selection rules, which may choose an arbitrary distribution over exchange distances but sample uniformly among all pairs at each chosen distance. For static rules, we prove that the optimal worst-case high-probability runtime is $\Theta(n(\log n)^2)$. This establishes the asymptotic optimality of the harmonic sorter within this class and partially resolves an open question of Olesker-Taylor. We then allow the distance distribution to change either according to a predetermined schedule or adaptively using the current permutation and the entire history. Matching upper and lower bounds show that both classes have optimal runtime $\Theta(n(\log n)^2/\log\log n)$. Thus, scheduled adjustments of the distance distribution improve the optimal static worst-case runtime by a factor of $\Theta(\log\log n)$, while full-information adaptation provides no further asymptotic improvement.

Few algorithmic problems have been studied as thoroughly and are as well understood as sorting [5, 14]. Over decades, researchers have developed sorting algorithms for different computational models and resource constraints, drawing on a wide range of data structures and algorithmic ideas. Among these, a natural family can be expressed as elitist local search on the space of permutations: starting from an initial permutation, the algorithm repeatedly selects two positions and exchanges their entries whenever they form an inversion. Different selection rules then recover, for example, Bubble Sort and Selection Sort.

We study a restricted class of selection rules that we call distance-unbiased. Such rules may allocate probability arbitrarily across exchange distances but must distribute the mass assigned to each distance uniformly among its pairs. This restriction grants the rule complete control over the distance distribution while preventing it from favoring one pair over another at the same distance. To the best of our knowledge, this symmetry has not previously been studied as a unified class, although many of the randomized algorithms mentioned share it.

papers.title: Transition Dynamics Matter: Hidden Markov Scoring of Epileptogenic Channels in SEEG
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) represents the most effective technique for the detection of the Epileptogenic Zone (EZ) in drug-resistant epilepsy. This procedure produces a multi-dimensional signal with hundreds of components, named channels, each associated with a different brain location. In this work, we propose a joint Hidden Markov Model (HMM), in which each SEEG channel is described by a latent Markov chain, with states shared across the network and channel-specific transition probabilities. Accordingly, we develop a detection algorithm that identifies the channels belonging to the EZ by quantifying, through the Kullback-Leibler divergence, the difference between their transition probabilities in the inter-ictal period and at seizure onset. We evaluate our framework in SEEG recordings from 30 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and compare it with a benchmark that operates in the same observation space but does not consider a latent-state structure. Compared against medically validated EZ definitions, our study shows that modeling channel-specific temporal transitions can improve EZ localization and offer a data-driven framework to investigate the latent dynamics underlying seizures.

papers.intro:
This paper has been submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027.

In drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is the treatment with the highest likelihood of achieving long-term seizure freedom [1]. The goal is to resect the Epileptogenic Zone (EZ), defined as the cortical area indispensable for the generation of seizures. Accurate localization of the EZ is then essential to maximize the probability of seizure freedom after surgical intervention while preserving the eloquent cortex. When noninvasive evaluation is not conclusive, clinical practice involves the use of invasive techniques such as Stereo-Electroencephalography (SEEG) to identify the EZ. This procedure is based on implantation of needle electrodes, which record electrical activity from the deep brain structures with high temporal resolution, although with a limited spatial sampling [2].

When noninvasive evaluation is not conclusive, clinical practice involves the use of invasive techniques such as Stereo-Electroencephalography (SEEG) to identify the EZ. This procedure is based on implantation of needle electrodes, which record electrical activity from the deep brain structures with high temporal resolution, although with a limited spatial sampling [2].

The outcome of SEEG monitoring is a multi-dimensional signal with hundreds of components, named channels, each associated with a different recording site. These signals provide fundamental information about both the ictal periods, i.e., seizures, and inter-ictal periods, i.e., the intervals occurring between consecutive seizures. In a clinical context, the analysis of SEEG signals is primarily based on visual interpretation, focusing on the detection of the channels that change most prominently during the transition to the ictal phase [3]. Such a procedure requires the participation of highly specialized neurologists and can still be subject to interpretative errors due to the complexity of the signals and the necessity of integrating spatial and temporal information.

In recent years, SEEG interpretation has been supported by quantitative techniques with the aim of providing new biomarkers of epileptogenic activities. In particular, the most common biomarker of seizure onset is given by Low-Voltage Fast Oscillations (LVFOs), i.e., low-amplitude activity spanning beta and gamma frequencies (f≥14f\geq 14 Hz) [4]. To detect LVFOs, it is common to map SEEG signals to their time-frequency representations via the short-time Fourier transform, and then quantify the energy increase in high-frequency bands. This is the approach used by the Epileptogenic Index (EI) [5], which is the most well-established technique to assist clinicians during SEEG review. On a practical level, the EI characterizes each SEEG channel through local features, i.e., quantities computed from the target channel at a specific time point, regardless of the rest of the SEEG network. However, seizure generation is recognized as a network phenomenon, and looking at channels as independent processes may be insufficient for the EZ delineation [6].

More advanced models treat SEEG signals as graphs, where nodes denote recording sites, and edges denote inter-channel connectivity. Recent studies report that seizure onset is characterized by a reduction in connectivity for epileptogenic channels [7], followed by a hyper-synchronization during the propagation of epileptic discharges [8]. This pattern is well explained by the inter-ictal suppression hypothesis, which proposes that the EZ is restrained by surrounding structures during the inter-ictal period [9]. However, approaches in the literature often consider time-resolved graphs, i.e., sequences of graphs computed on successive time windows, and analyze each graph independently, without modeling the fact that SEEG signals span both space and time. As suggested by the inter-ictal suppression hypothesis, seizures are not abrupt events but result from the brain evolving from a pre-ictal condition, where the EZ is inhibited, to an ictal condition, where the EZ takes control over the brain [10].

This method separates the emission process (observations given states) from the transition process (temporal evolution among states). In the literature, HMMs have been used to differentiate between inter-ictal and ictal periods, enabling the development of seizure prediction methods [12] and the mapping between non-invasive features and intracranial patterns [13]. However, these previous works focused on modeling the whole-brain evolution and did not consider the possibility of modeling the latent states that characterize each brain location.

In this work, we develop a new framework to characterize SEEG signals, explicitly modeling the transition dynamics that characterizes single channels. We hypothesize that the generation of epileptic discharges can be represented through a transition between latent states, leading the channel from a baseline to abnormal (ictal-like) dynamics. Therefore, the ease with which a channel transitions towards ictal-like states differentiates epileptogenic structures from non-epileptogenic ones. Practically, we assume that each channel evolves according to a latent Markov chain, with each state associated with an observation pattern comprising local, e.g., spectral energy, and spatial features, e.g., functional connectivity. The state occupied by a channel at a given time point determines not only the distribution of its features, but also the probabilities of transiting towards other states.

The state occupied by a channel at a given time point determines not only the distribution of its features, but also the probabilities of transiting towards other states.

Our model assumes that the number of states and their emission probabilities are shared throughout the SEEG signal, while each channel is characterized by its own transition probability matrix. In addition, the transition probabilities are not static but change when the brain changes its macro-conditions and, e.g., enters the ictal phase. Since states and emissions are shared, the transition matrix is the only channel- and condition-specific parameter, and we can compare different channels, or different conditions of the same channel, by computing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the corresponding transition probability matrices. Hence, we assume that epileptogenic channels can be detected by looking at those channels that more prominently change the transition probabilities at the onset of the seizure.

papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP
papers.abstract:
Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. The objective is to minimize the total length of all walks. In general, it is NP-hard to find any approximation for this problem in polynomial time (even if the approximation factor is allowed to depend on the number of vertices). We show that one can obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in time $n^{O(k)}$, answering an open question by Friggstad [2013].
  For the special case where all tour start vertices $s_i$ are identical and all end vertices $t_i$ are identical, we obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in polynomial time, as well as an $(O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}), 1+\epsilon)$-bicriteria approximation. For the multi-depot setting, where $s_i =t_i$ for all $i$, we obtain a constant-factor approximation in polynomial time.
  Finally, our results imply improved constant-factor approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Regret-Bounded Vehicle Routing and unit-weight Path ATSP.

papers.intro:
Path TSP is the general version of the (metric) Traveling Salesperson Problem, where we are looking for a shortest tour from a given start vertex ss to a given end vertex tt that visits all other vertices in between. In the symmetric case, this problem was first studied by Hoogeveen [Hoo91], and a long line of work [AKS15, Seb13, Vyg16, GV18, Sv19, TV19, Zen19] culminated in a reduction from Path TSP to the classical TSP (i.e., the special case s=ts=t) with an arbitrarily small loss in the approximation factor [TVZ22]. In the asymmetric case, Feige and Singh [FS07] gave an analogous reduction, which, however, loses a factor of 2+ϵ2+\epsilon in the approximation guarantee (for an arbitrary constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0). For ATSP, Vygen [Vyg26] obtained an approximation factor 12+2​2+ϵ≈14.8312+2\sqrt{2}+\epsilon\approx 14.83 for general weights and 3+2​2+ϵ≈5.833+2\sqrt{2}+\epsilon\approx 5.83 for unit weights. papers.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.

papers.intro:
The attention layer (Vaswani et al., 2017) of a large language model compares every query with every key via a dot product over the full head dimension. Most work on making attention cheaper keeps this dot product intact and instead reduces the set of keys a query looks at. Strategies to do so include fixed patterns (Child et al., 2019), sliding windows (Jiang et al., 2023), KV-cache eviction (Xiao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023), and query-dependent token selection, training-free (Tang et al., 2024) or learned (Yuan et al., 2025). In this work, we investigate an orthogonal question: whether attention requires computing the complete query–key dot product.

In this work, we investigate an orthogonal question: whether attention requires computing the complete query–key dot product.

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), used by many modern LLMs (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Gemma Team, 2026), give this question a natural structure. RoPE rotates each two-dimensional frequency pair of the query and the key by an angle proportional to its position. Because rotations compose, the two rotations combine into a single one that encodes the relative distance between the query and the key. High-frequency pairs complete many turns within a few tokens, whereas low-frequency pairs barely rotate over the whole context.

The score parts of fast pairs are therefore highly sensitive to the exact distance between the query and the key, whereas language does not follow an exact structure over distant words or tokens, and sequences can be long. This raises the question of whether every pair needs to be computed at every relative distance. We show that high-frequency pairs are not necessary for the model when distance between tokens is large, and that removing them is harmless or even beneficial.

The query and key projections are unchanged and what becomes sparse is the hidden dimension of the dot product. The sparsity pattern follows from the RoPE frequencies and the positions alone: it has no learned parameter and needs no selection step, unlike sparse attention methods that score, route or select keys at runtime. For a given query, fast pairs only see nearby keys, slow pairs see far.

papers.title: Fixing the Last Mile: Failure-Aware Image Restoration with Region-Specific Guidance
papers.abstract: Recent advances in image restoration have greatly improved global image fidelity, producing visually plausible results across most regions of an image. Nevertheless, even high-quality restorations often exhibit localized failures, including artifacts in semantically important regions such as faces and text, structural inconsistencies, and texture mismatches. Although these errors typically affect only a small portion of the image, they often dominate the overall perceptual quality of the result. In this work, we propose Failure-Aware Image Restoration (FAIR) to address the "last-mile" problem in image restoration. Rather than applying one uniform generative prior over the whole image, we condition a single-pass restoration model on both where local failures are likely to occur and what corrective guidance each region requires. This region-bound conditioning enables fine-grained and controllable restoration that improves semantic accuracy and stylistic consistency in critical regions while maintaining faithful, high-quality restoration elsewhere. Our method complements existing restoration pipelines by shifting the emphasis from global fidelity to local perceptual acceptability. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach resolves common failure cases and improves perceptual quality, bridging the gap between technical accuracy and practical usability.

As shown in Fig. 1, such localized failures arise consistently under severe degradations, where heavy blur, noise, or compression remove local information beyond recovery, forcing generative priors to hallucinate plausible yet unfaithful content. Although these errors typically affect only a small portion of the image, they often dominate the perceived quality of the result. We refer to this challenge as the “last-mile” problem in image restoration: closing the perceptual gap by predicting failure-prone regions from the low-quality input and guiding their restoration with external references.

The last-mile problem stems from a structural limitation of current restoration pipelines. Resolving it requires two capabilities that existing methods lack: external information to recover content that is irretrievable from the degraded input, and fine-grained local control to apply such information only where it is needed. Yet existing approaches typically cast restoration as a global reconstruction problem, without explicitly modeling where local failures are likely to occur and, within each at-risk region, what type of failure it is prone to and what corrective guidance it requires. Consequently, the same generative prior is applied uniformly across the image, from smooth backgrounds to semantically important areas such as faces, text, and logos.

The challenge is to introduce external information selectively: it should help regions with insufficient recoverable content without unnecessarily altering regions well constrained by the input. Even recent semantic-guided methods (Yu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2024) introduce high-level priors at the image level, while deriving them largely from the corrupted input. When local information is severely lost, these priors can generate plausible details without ensuring fidelity to the original content. Restoration therefore needs evidence beyond the input and spatial control to apply it only where needed. Deferring guidance to post-hoc repair has further costs: it may disturb well-restored regions, while the second model must work from an image already altered by the first, potentially missing original cues or containing new artifacts.

Rather than treating the image as a uniform field, FAIR recognizes that under severe degradation, small but perceptually critical regions often require different forms of corrective information. To study this behavior systematically, we construct a large-scale failure-aware dataset by applying state-of-the-art restoration models to degraded inputs and automatically annotating both where failures occur and what type of failure is present. Each failure region is additionally paired with an appropriate problem description, yielding region-level supervision aligned with our failure taxonomy. We observe a consistent pattern in this dataset: restoration failures cluster into a small set of semantically meaningful categories, each requiring different forms and strengths of external guidance.

As illustrated in Fig. 2, we organize restoration guidance by increasing constraint strength, with more specific guidance addressing progressively harder local failures: (i) semantic instructions and parametric controls for subjective artifacts; (ii) reference exemplars for pattern and texture inconsistencies; (iii) geometric prompts for fine structural correction; and (iv) identity correspondences for identity-critical regions. Different failures call for different forms of guidance, and FAIR accepts each of them as a condition. Unlike existing methods that apply uniform generation across the image, FAIR binds each guidance condition to its target region. Built on FLUX.2-klein-9B (Labs, 2025) with lightweight LoRA modules, FAIR uses region control to specify where additional guidance is provided and a semantic reference to indicate what the restoration should follow. Experiments show that FAIR improves perceptual acceptability over strong baselines while preserving quality elsewhere.

papers.title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
papers.abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/
papers.intro:
Consider the meerkat (Figure 1). You may have recorded it on a recent holiday and are watching it now on your high-resolution screen. While you admire the sharp details of the meerkat, you find the background leaves distracting and regret not having recorded the video at a shallower depth of field. Applications that synthetically blur the background could help, but to reliably separate the meerkat from its background, they require a depth map for every frame (Bertalmío et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2022).

Consider the meerkat (Figure 1). You may have recorded it on a recent holiday and are watching it now on your high-resolution screen. While you admire the sharp details of the meerkat, you find the background leaves distracting and regret not having recorded the video at a shallower depth of field. Applications that synthetically blur the background could help, but to reliably separate the meerkat from its background, they require a depth map for every frame (Bertalmío et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2022).

Picking a suitable method for estimating depth from monocular videos is surprisingly difficult. Methods designed for single images can provide high-resolution depth maps with sharp occlusion boundaries. InfiniDepth (Yu et al., 2026), for instance, reasonably delineates the fur (third column of Figure 1). Yet its predictions are temporally inconsistent as it processes each frame separately and places the meerkat at different distances over time. A method designed for video, such as π3\pi^{3} (Wang et al., 2026b), reliably places the meerkat at a consistent distance across frames (last column of Figure 1). But it operates at a lower resolution than the input video, which smooths over the fur.

A method designed for video, such as π3\pi^{3} (Wang et al., 2026b), reliably places the meerkat at a consistent distance across frames (last column of Figure 1). But it operates at a lower resolution than the input video, which smooths over the fur.

This trade-off between sharp boundaries and temporal consistency pervades monocular depth estimation. Figure 2 presents the state of the art on boundary sharpness and temporal consistency, measured over the Sintel and Spring datasets (Butler et al., 2012; Mehl et al., 2023). (We choose these datasets for their dense, high-resolution ground truth on video sequences.) We find that single-image methods cluster at the top left and multi-frame methods cluster at the bottom right. That is, depth maps from single-image methods feature the sharpest boundaries but are unstable over time, while depth maps from multi-frame methods are stable but overly smooth. Multi-frame approaches are commonly optimized for stability through temporal attention over many frames (Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026b), video diffusion priors (Hu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026), and video training data (Wang et al., 2023). This biases the methods towards longer temporal context and costly diffusion, which require substantial resources (memory and runtime) and necessitate operating at reduced resolution, thus oversmoothing boundaries.

In this paper, we present Depth Pro 2, a method that estimates sharp, metric, and temporally consistent depth from monocular images and video. Depth Pro 2 outperforms both single-image and multi-frame methods in boundary sharpness and temporal consistency (see Figure 2), as well as in metric depth accuracy (see Section 4). The key idea is an architecture that processes a flexible number of frames jointly at their native resolution. The joint processing stabilizes depth temporally. Operating at native resolution preserves sharp boundaries. In contrast to training with complex multi-stage curricula (Chen et al., 2025; Chou et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023), we train Depth Pro 2 on clips of 1 to 32 frames, mixing image, video, and multi-view datasets. By training on single images alongside video, Depth Pro 2 learns to infer metric scale from individual frames. By training on videos with a temporal consistency loss, it learns to keep its estimates stable across frames.

Depth Pro 2 predicts inverse depth normalized by the focal length, and uses the focal length of input images to recover metric depth (Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2023a). To reliably estimate metric depth when the focal length is not provided, we train a focal length estimator, following Depth Pro (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). In contrast to Depth Pro, however, we design our focal length estimator to be lightweight to facilitate streaming video processing. Our focal length estimator runs at 118 fps at 1080p on a B200 and is more accurate than prior estimators.

To support a broad set of applications that may vary in the relative importance of accuracy and latency, we release a family of models ranging from 24M to 872M parameters. In the streaming setting, where frames arrive one at a time, our smallest model (Depth Pro 2-S) runs at 53 fps at 1080p on a B200 (Figure 12), faster than the 30 fps at which most videos are recorded. Our largest model (Depth Pro 2-H+) runs at 8 fps on 1080p video and outperforms all prior work in terms of metric depth, boundary sharpness, and temporal consistency, on both images and video (Section 4).

papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Kimi K3 Kimi Team (2026), Ring-2.6 Li et al. (2025); Kimi Team (2025). We refer to the latter as bounded-state layers, since their cache memory per request is bounded independently of context length. These models serve everyday chat, coding agents, document analysis and automated data labeling. Such applications differ in context reuse, interaction structure, arrival patterns and concurrency Lin et al. (2024); Xiang et al. (2026). A coding agent accumulates tool outputs across turns, document analysis retains reference material, and chat or labeling services may process many independent requests. These behaviors create different demands on global-attention KV, window caches and recurrent states; no application label alone determines which component limits serving capacity.

Existing systems improve hybrid models’ memory utilization through cache allocation Zheng et al. (2024); Kwon et al. (2023). Static partitioning reserves a fixed budget for each component and can leave one pool underused while another runs out of space (Figure 1a). Dynamic sharing schemes, such as SGLang’s Unified Memory Pool and vLLM’s Hybrid KV Cache Manager, reduce this imbalance SGLang Team (2026); vLLM Team (2026). However, sharing an arena across cache layouts can require changes to indexing and memory access, complicating integration with attention backends and other serving features.

HiCache Xie (2025) preserves reusable contexts in a hierarchical cache and restores them for later execution, reducing repeated prefill computation. However, restored prefixes remain GPU-resident during subsequent decoding. HiSparse Xie et al. (2026) reduces active requests’ GPU footprint by fetching selected KV entries during decode, but is specialized for sparse attention. General offloading systems such as FlexGen and Pie Sheng et al. To this end, we present TideCache, a hybrid-model serving system with three components: the Transparent Cache Pool, a Cache Streamer, and a Request Scheduler. Our key observation is that bounded-state layers create intervals of computation during which the historical KV of the next global-attention layer is not yet needed. The Cache Streamer exploits idle CPU–GPU bandwidth during decode to prefetch host-resident prefixes into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers (Figure 1b). Overlapping these transfers with computation expands effective global-KV capacity: requests with reusable host-resident prefixes shrink their GPU footprint, while newly generated KV stays resident. To make the released capacity available to other cache components, the Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages behind the reserved virtual addresses of the hybrid subpools. The Transparent Cache Pool transparently supports existing cache layouts and attention backend interfaces, without requiring changes to either. The two memory mechanisms work together: layer-wise KV streaming frees HBM that can hold window caches and recurrent states for additional requests, and a larger decode batch provides more computation with which to overlap subsequent transfers. The Request Scheduler coordinates these mechanisms, selecting resident or streamed execution and triggering subpool capacity adjustments according to request and queue conditions.

The Transparent Cache Pool achieves 96.3–113.6% of the turns of the better of two hand-tuned partitions at each fixed load; under a shifting workload on GH200, the full system completes 59% more agent turns and reduces agent P50 TTFT by 78% relative to SGLang with HiCache. papers.title: Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules
papers.abstract: We characterise path-independent auto-deleveraging (ADL) rules as an extended log-exponential family. Immunity to account splitting, merging and reopening further restrict the class. Homogeneity (essentially) restricts the class to a one-parameter family ordered by both fairness and platform risk. Its split-proof members continuously interpolate between proportional division and water-filling. Among these rules, decreasing the parameter reduces risk at the cost of increasing inequality in how accounts are treated. This suggests selecting the parameter through an ex-ante calibration to a risk bound on historical data to choose a maximally fair rule subject to that bound. A counterfactual replay of Hyperliquid's ADL episode on 10 October 2025 finds that a range of intermediate parameters significantly improves on the observed allocation in both burden dispersion and subsequent risk statistics.
papers.intro:
Perpetual futures are widely used to take and hedge directional exposure to cryptoassets. They provide capital-efficient long and short exposure without expiry, using leverage, and perpetual futures exchanges contribute to price discovery of their underlying assets (Alexander and Heck, 2020; Chitra et al., 2026). Leverage also creates a solvency problem. If a losing account is liquidated only after the market has moved through its bankruptcy price, its collateral no longer covers the loss. Insurance funds absorb ordinary shortfalls; when they are insufficient, auto-deleveraging (ADL) forcibly reduces profitable positions on the opposite side. A roughly 30% five-minute Bitcoin price decline in March 2017 exhausted BitMEX’s insurance fund and triggered ADL of profitable shorts; further ADL occurred in BitMEX’s XBT and ETH futures in April 2019; and ADL was activated during Hyperliquid’s 10 October 2025 stress episode (BitMEX, 2019a; BitMEX, 2019b; Chitra et al., 2026).

ADL is a more prominent part of market design in crypto than the analogous partial tear-up of traditional futures positions. Cryptoassets are more volatile than traditional financial assets and crypto derivatives commonly permit high leverage (Bank for International Settlements, 2023; Chitra et al., 2026). Crypto venues also rely more directly on posted collateral, automated liquidation and insurance funds than traditional central counterparties, which interpose a clearing layer backed by margin, default funds and other recovery resources (Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures and International Organization of Securities Commissions, 2014); on-chain venues in particular are designed to operate without a traditional clearing-member intermediary (Harvey et al., 2026). Reduced reliance on intermediation is part of the appeal of this architecture, but makes the allocation of residual losses more important.

How ADL is done matters because it acts on traders who are solvent and usually profitable. A forced reduction can remove a hedge and change a trader’s exposure precisely during stressed markets. The rule therefore determines who bears the burden, how predictable that exposure is ex ante, whether treatment can be manipulated by restructuring accounts, and how much risk remains after deleveraging. These objectives do not necessarily coincide. Proportional reductions are simple and predictable but do not prioritise the riskiest positions; risk-based rules can reduce platform risk but may concentrate the burden on a small set of traders (Campbell et al., 2026; Chitra, 2025). Existing venues indeed use different policies, including rankings based on leverage, profitability, or both, as well as random selection (Hyperliquid, 2026a; Lighter, 2026; Aster, 2026; Extended, 2026; edgeX, 2026; dYdX, 2026). There is therefore no settled convention for how the ADL burden should be allocated.

We take an axiomatic approach to the design of ADL rules, characterising the class of rules that satisfy a set of basic requirements, and trade-off risk and fairness to select a rule within this class. The starting point of the characterization is path independence. Call the aggregate open interest that remains after ADL the target. If the target is revised downward, applying the rule to the surviving positions should agree with applying it directly to the final target; if it is revised upward, restoring positions in stages should agree with allocating the larger target directly. Together with continuity, equal treatment of equals and consistency, path independence characterises an extended log-exponential family.

The rules between proportional division and water-filling22 2 Water-filling reduces positions whose leverage exceeds a common threshold to that threshold and leaves the others unchanged, with the threshold chosen to meet the aggregate target. in the one-parameter family offer a trade-off between fairness and risk. Moving towards water-filling lowers risk but makes percentage reductions less equal. We also characterise the two endpoints of this trade-off more generally. Proportional division uniquely gives the fairest allocation in the position-weighted Lorenz order on percentage reductions, while water-filling minimises platform risk state by state. This gives a simple one-parameter menu for rule design when homogeneity is acceptable and a platform can use historical data to select a parameter from the menu. A natural calibration is to minimize dispersion subject to a specified risk bound being met on that historical data. When heterogeneity is desirable, the design problem is less tidy, but our general results continue to apply.

papers.title: Chemistry by Design (CbyD): A Machine-Readable Dataset of Expert-Curated Total Synthesis Routes
papers.abstract: Chemistry by Design (CbyD) is an open-access educational database of published total syntheses launched in 2011. It was designed to help students and practitioners learn organic reactions and synthetic strategies by depicting every step of published natural product and drug syntheses. Motivated by advances in machine learning for organic synthesis and by requests from academic and industrial researchers, we present a machine-readable version of CbyD for use in cheminformatics and computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP). The released dataset (v2026.11) contains 3,502 routes comprising 56,640 reactions toward 2,902 unique targets. Compared with patent-derived datasets, CbyD reactions are more complex, more frequently change stereochemistry, and are less likely to be covered by patent-derived reaction templates, and CbyD routes are longer and more convergent than those in commonly used CASP benchmarks. We also analyze how molecular complexity changes along these routes and identify transformations associated with large complexity increases. The CbyD dataset will be expanded through versioned public releases that incorporate new routes and community-contributed corrections.

papers.title: No-Harm-Jury A Jury-Based Multi-Dimensional Harm Evaluation Framework for Medical AI Responses
papers.abstract: We present No-Harm-Jury, a jury-based automated evaluation framework that scores AI-generated medical responses across seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions using a panel of five diverse language models as independent jurors. Responses generated by Ministral-14B on 3,000 questions drawn from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA are scored by five jurors across dimensions of informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm; the 151 empty responses (98 MedQA, 53 MedM- CQA) are excluded, leaving 2,849 valid samples. The median aggregation robustly suppresses individual juror biases while maintaining coverage through complementary specialisation. No existing system combines all five prop- erties of No-Harm-Jury: automated scalable evaluation, five diverse LLM jurors, robust me- dian aggregation (with a reliability-weighted extension), seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions, and application to medical QA benchmarks.

papers.title: The Riemann Hypothesis and Prime Numbers
papers.abstract: The Riemann hypothesis is attracting a great deal of attention at present. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics, for each of which the Clay Mathematics Institute offers a prize of one million dollars. It is arguably the most important open problem in all of mathematics. Numerous results have so far been proved only under the assumption of the Riemann hypothesis. Yet the hypothesis itself sounds rather dull: it conjectures that the zeros of a certain function have a certain form. Things become truly exciting, however, when we look at its connection with prime numbers, and that is what we shall do here.

papers.title: TALD: Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement for Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can incur negative transfer when source-modality supervision conflicts with the target modality's discriminative characteristics. We propose TALD, a two-stage framework for Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement in class-aligned logit space. Guided by task-dependent self-benefiting and cross-modal exclusivity criteria, a Residual Disentangler decomposes logits from a teacher and an independently trained target-modality reference student into modality-general and modality-specific components. A Sample-Adaptive Modulator regulates decomposition constraints and sample-specific fusion weights. The learned modality-general components are then adaptively fused to supervise the final student. Across five benchmarks spanning vision, audio, and text, TALD achieves the largest mean accuracy gain and highest positive-transfer frequency among the compared methods. Across ten transfer directions with five runs each, TALD improves over training without distillation in 84% of evaluations, compared with at most 70% for the baselines, while offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We plan to release the code.

The Modality Focusing Hypothesis (MFH) [37] links distillation effectiveness to the proportion of modality-general discriminative information retained by the teacher. Existing methods address modality discrepancies through teacher adaptation [20, 15] or feature filtering and reconstruction [37, 20]. In particular, MGDFR [37] uses channel saliency as a proxy for transferability to reconstruct high-dimensional teacher representations. Such feature-space processing provides an indirect route to shaping class-level supervision and can incur substantial computational overhead. Logits provide such a space. For a shared classification task, corresponding dimensions represent the same classes across modalities [31], allowing the classification effects of logit components to be evaluated directly through the task loss. We therefore formulate disentanglement in this class-aligned space as a residual decomposition, subtracting a learned modality-specific component from the original logits to obtain the modality-general component. papers.title: An {\alpha}-potential linear approximation for LQ differential games
papers.abstract: Feedback Nash equilibria of infinite-horizon linear-quadratic (LQ) differential games are characterized by coupled algebraic Riccati equations (cAREs), whose numerical solution generally relies on iterative algorithms and can be highly sensitive to their initialization. Motivated by the $\alpha$-potential-game framework, this letter proposes an $\alpha$-potential linear approximation for constructing a systematic, game-dependent initialization. For an N-player LQ game, a reference potential game is constructed. Its equilibrium requires solving only one standard algebraic Riccati equation. The original cAREs are subsequently linearized around this reference solution, yielding a coupled linear system whose solution provides player-specific corrections and hence an approximate feedback Nash equilibrium. The resulting approximation is used to initialize three standard cARE solvers. Numerical experiments on $10^4$ randomly generated two-player games show that the proposed initialization reduces the mean number of iterations. Further experiments for $N=2,\ldots,13$ show that the reduction in iteration count persists as the number of players increases.

papers.intro:
Linear-quadratic (LQ) differential games provide a tracable framework for dynamic decision problems involving multiple interacting agents [1, 2, 3]. A central solution concept is the feedback Nash equilibrium, which, for infinite-horizon LQ games, is characterized by a set of coupled algebraic Riccati equations (cAREs) [2, 4]. Unlike the standard single-player ARE, these coupled equations admit no closed-form solution and must be solved iteratively [5]. This is relevant in real-time human–machine systems, where changing interaction conditions or human preferences may require recomputing the game and its equilibrium online [6, 7, 8]. In such settings, efficient, reliable cARE solvers are essential, and their convergence and cost can depend strongly on initialization.

Unlike the standard single-player ARE, these coupled equations admit no closed-form solution and must be solved iteratively [5]. This is relevant in real-time human–machine systems, where changing interaction conditions or human preferences may require recomputing the game and its equilibrium online [6, 7, 8]. In such settings, efficient, reliable cARE solvers are essential, and their convergence and cost can depend strongly on initialization.

Potential games offer a useful structural simplification for differential games, as their feedback Nash equilibrium can be characterized through the optimum of a common potential function [9, 10]. Successful applications of potential games range from distributed self-optimization in modular production systems [11] to game-theoretic analyses of social networks, where coevolutionary dynamics of actions and opinions admit a potential representation [12]. In the LQ setting, an exact potential structure converts the equilibrium problem into a standard optimal-control problem that can be solved through a single ARE. Such a structure, however, is only available under restrictive conditions. The α\alpha-potential-game framework relaxes this requirement by allowing the change in a player’s objective under a unilateral deviation to differ from the corresponding change in a potential function by a bounded amount [13, 14]. This motivates exploiting an approximate potential structure also for LQ games that are not exact potential games.

papers.title: A note on Tur\'an densities of daisies and hypergraph products
papers.abstract:
The Tur\'an density of an $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal H$ is defined as ${\pi}(\mathcal{H})=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \operatorname{ex}(n,\mathcal{H})/\binom{n}{r}$, where $\operatorname{ex}(n,\mathcal H)$ denotes the largest number of edges in an $\mathcal H$-free $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. For integers $r\geq s\geq2$ and $t\geq s$, an $(r,s,t)$-daisy $\mathcal D_r(s,t)$ is the $r$-uniform hypergraph consisting of all unions of a fixed $(r-s)$-set with the $s$-subsets of a disjoint $t$-set. We show that for every fixed $s\geq3$, \[
  \lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\pi}(\mathcal D_r(s,t))=1-O_s(t^{-(s-1)}) \] as $t\rightarrow\infty$. This bound is best possible up to the implicit constant by a classical result of de Caen, and it answers, in a stronger form, a question of Ellis, Ivan and Leader, who asked for the case $s=3$. Moreover, we show a related result for matroid basis hypergraphs. We also consider Tur\'an densities of hypergraph products, of which daisies are a special case. The product of two hypergraphs on disjoint vertex sets consists of all unions of an edge of the first with an edge of the second. For the product $\mathcal H^d$ of $d$ disjoint copies of a fixed $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal H$ that is not $r$-partite, we show that $1-\pi(\mathcal H^d) \rightarrow 0$ exponentially fast as $d\rightarrow\infty$, and we determine the exponential rate in terms of the minimum number of edges in a homomorphic image of $\mathcal H$. This answers a question of Bollob\'as, Leader and Malvenuto up to a polynomial factor in $d$, and we further address a related question of theirs for products of two different hypergraphs.
