papers.title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.

papers.title: FAST Burst-Cluster Catalog of FRB 20240114A
papers.abstract: We present the complete FAST burst-cluster catalog of FRB 20240114A, covering its 495-day active episode from January 28, 2024 to June 5, 2025. The catalog contains 13261 burst clusters, 19037 bursts, and 29026 sub-bursts detected in 99 observing sessions. The data reveal distinct organization across temporal scales. Among drifting burst clusters, downward-drifting clusters outnumber upward-drifting ones by approximately $9.4:1$. Between separate burst clusters, previously reported frequency changes show no preferred direction, while our Weibull analysis finds their arrival times broadly consistent with Poisson statistics, suggesting that burst clusters may represent approximately independent emission episodes within observing sessions. The Parkes/Murriyang observations revealed a long-term modulation of the characteristic emission frequency, and the extended FAST measurements show a consistent evolution. Burst energetics increase with cluster multiplicity and activity level, although significant scatter remains. The manually refined dispersion measure increases at $1.29\pm0.11\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}\,yr^{-1}}$, enlarging the still limited but growing sample of repeaters with increasing DM. Overall, these results summarize the spectral--temporal evolution of FRB 20240114A and present a burst-cluster catalog linked to the existing BurstID measurements, providing a basis for future studies of repeating FRBs.

papers.intro:
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients characterized by large dispersion measures (DMs) and extremely high brightness temperatures, requiring coherent emission mechanisms [56]. Comparisons between observed FRB DMs and predictions from Galactic free-electron density models, including NE2001, YMW16, and NE2025, indicate that the vast majority of known FRBs are extragalactic [9, 55, 35]. The association of FRB 20200428 with the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 demonstrated that magnetars can also produce FRB-like radio bursts, although at radio energies much lower than typical cosmological FRBs [2, 6]. Since the discovery of the first FRB source in archival Parkes data [29] and the identification of the first repeating source FRB 20121102A [43, 44], repeating FRBs have enabled systematic investigations of burst properties, population differences, and long-term activity evolution [30, 64, 46, 47, 45, 22, 40, 10, 3]. More than 4500 FRB sources have been reported, including over 120 confirmed repeaters and more than 150 sources with identified host galaxies. These samples are continuously updated through Blinkverse11 1 https://blinkverse.zero2x.org/ and the Transient Name Server (TNS)22 2 https://www.wis-tns.org/search, while CHIME [5] provides the largest homogeneous FRB samples through its Second Catalog [14]. The sensitivity of FAST [33, 19, 39] enables detailed long-term monitoring of repeating sources.

Radio-continuum and high-resolution observations with MeerKAT, uGMRT, e-MERLIN, and VLBA revealed a persistent radio source associated with FRB 20240114A and its long-term variability, suggesting a possible connection between persistent emission and burst activity [4, 61, 27]. The extreme activity of FRB 20240114A was further demonstrated by the detection of an exceptionally energetic burst during a long-term monitoring campaign [37], establishing this source as an important laboratory for studying FRB emission, propagation, and environments.

papers.title: Life-IQA+: Boosting Blind Image Quality Assessment via GCN-enhanced Layer Interaction and Flexible Hierarchical Expert Specialization
papers.abstract: Blind image quality assessment (BIQA) is essential for evaluating and optimizing visual experience. Existing BIQA methods typically aggregate features from multiple backbone stages without accounting for their unequal contributions to quality prediction. Furthermore, uniformly supervising all experts may constrain their flexibility and limit the diversity of the learned quality representations. To address these issues, we present Life-IQA+, a quality representation decoding framework that combines graph convolutional network (GCN) enhanced layer interaction and flexible hierarchical expert specialization. Specifically, the layer interaction module constructs quality queries from GCN-refined deepest-stage features and uses penultimate-stage features as keys and values, thereby enabling cross-layer representation interaction via the cross-attention mechanism. Building on these representations, we further introduce a flexible hierarchical mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising a densely activated shared expert layer and a sparsely activated routed expert layer. To enhance the representation diversity and ability of experts, we apply auxiliary classification supervision to a subset of shared experts using distortion-type labels for synthetic datasets and discretized quality-level labels for authentic datasets. Experiments on synthetic and authentic distortion benchmarks, together with controlled ablations of expert configurations and supervision strategies, show that Life-IQA+ achieves competitive prediction accuracy with a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. The code is available at: https://github.com/TANGLONG2/Life-IQA-PlusPlus.

Among different IQA paradigms, blind image quality assessment (BIQA) estimates image quality without access to pristine reference images [8, 9, 10, 11, 12], making it particularly suitable for practical scenarios where reference images are typically unavailable. Shallow features (s​t​a​g​e​1stage1, s​t​a​g​e​2stage2) primarily capture local details and texture information, whereas deep features (s​t​a​g​e​3stage3, s​t​a​g​e​4stage4) encode global and semantic information. Despite their complementary roles in perceiving features, the relative contributions to quality prediction remain underexplored.

To quantify the actual contribution of features from different stages to the BIQA, six different pretrained backbones are evaluated on the authentic distortion dataset LIVEC [18]. These backbones include three convolutional neural networks (CNNs), i.e., ResNet50 [19], EfficientNet [20], MobileNet [21] and three Transformer models, i.e., Swin Transformer [22], MaxViT [23], PVT [24]. To separately investigate the quality-representation capacity of the features from different layers, the image features from each stage are directly appended with a simple prediction head, which consists of a global average pooling layer (GAP) and a linear regression layer. We also adopt two simple feature pyramid fusion methods for comparison, including an all-stage aggregation method, and a s​t​a​g​e​3stage3 & s​t​a​g​e​4stage4 fusion scheme. These two methods first align the spatial resolution and channel dimension of the features from different stages, then adopt the same simple prediction head to aggregate. As shown in Fig. 1, the shallow features (s​t​a​g​e​1stage1, s​t​a​g​e​2stage2) consistently achieve lower median SRCC values than the deep features (s​t​a​g​e​3stage3, s​t​a​g​e​4stage4) across all six backbones. Moreover, s​t​a​g​e​3stage3 & s​t​a​g​e​4stage4 achieves performance comparable to all stage aggregation. This suggests that directly fusing all stage features is not always beneficial, as shallow features dominated by low-level details may introduce redundancy or noise into quality regression, especially with limited BIQA training data.

Based on the aforementioned analysis, rather than directly adopting the conventional strategy of aggregating all multi-scale features, we focus on achieving efficient interaction among deeper, semantically richer features. To this end, we first propose Life-IQA, an effective quality feature decoding framework built upon GCN-enhanced Layer Interaction and MoE-based Feature Decoupling. In Life-IQA, the deepest-stage features, enhanced through a graph convolutional network (GCN), serve as query tokens that carry high-level quality semantics, while the penultimate-stage features act as keys and values, providing structured local evidence, then the cross-attention-based interaction is performed. Furthermore, a mixture-of-expert (MoE) module decouples the fused representations, allowing different experts to specialize in particular distortion types or quality dimensions. This design yields a dynamic, data-efficient decoding mechanism tailored to BIQA characteristics. However, the original MoE uses only sparsely routed experts and lacks a dedicated pathway for modeling quality information shared across samples.

A natural extension is to introduce densely activated shared experts in parallel with the original routed experts, following the shared expert organization adopted in DeepSeekMoE [25]. In this parallel MoE, the shared experts capture perceptual cues that recur across samples, while the routed experts preserve input-dependent specialization through sparse activation. Although this design specifies the roles of shared and routed experts, how shared experts should be guided to learn quality-relevant common knowledge remains underexplored in BIQA.

Some works have proposed multi-task learning-based BIQA methods[26, 27, 28, 29, 30], which additionally consider learning distortion-type labels for synthetically distorted datasets or quality-level labels for authentically distorted datasets. However, these methods have not jointly consider both distortion-type and quality-level supervision during learning quality score prediction, and have not consider using different experts to learn different attributes. As shown in Fig. 2, different distortion types exhibit substantially overlapping difference mean opinion score (DMOS) distributions on KADID-10K, while images within the same distortion type span a broad range of quality scores. Moreover, different distortion types exhibit significantly different influences on quality levels, further leading to different quality score distributions. This suggests that effectively leveraging MoE for BIQA requires an expert learning strategy that incorporates distortion-related characteristics or coarse quality levels while preserving flexibility for quality regression.

papers.title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
papers.abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

Video generation models are increasingly cast as world models: given an image and a control signal, they simulate how a scene evolves [5, 26, 49, 44, 45, 59]. Yet the physical world rarely evolves in isolation. A robot moves objects on an accelerating base, and an earthquake shakes everything inside a room. In such a forced response, motion follows no preset visual script: it is the system’s own dynamics answering an external excitation. Right now, we cannot tell. Existing physical benchmarks typically follow a scene from an opening prompt or frames and summarize it with overall motion or appearance scores [42, 32, 34, 30]. This leaves two blind spots. First, under realistic shaking, most motion is a small-amplitude linear swing, which dominates the displacement and can hide whether a model violates the geometry of a rigid rod or the nonlinear dynamics. Second, a single score conflates three abilities that mechanics keeps separate: reproducing a governing law, inferring the state from pixels, and propagating that state forward in time.

papers.title: Equality in the clique bound for critical graphs
papers.abstract: A graph is $k$-critical if its chromatic number is $k$ and every proper subgraph is $(k-1)$-colorable. Gao and Ma (2023) proved that every $n$-vertex $k$-critical graph with $n > k \ge 4$ contains at most $n - k + 3$ cliques of size $k - 1$, and asked which graphs attain this bound. We answer this question by showing that equality holds if and only if $n - k + 3$ is odd and the graph is isomorphic to the join of a complete graph on $k - 3$ vertices and a cycle of length $n - k + 3$. More generally, for $n>k\ge3$, we determine when the size of a nonempty family of distinct $(k-1)$-cliques in an $n$-vertex $k$-critical graph attains the upper bound $s-k+3$, where $s$ is the number of vertices covered by the family. Equality holds if and only if the graph is such a join (with the complete part empty when $k = 3$) and the family consists of all its $(k-1)$-cliques.

papers.title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
papers.abstract:
LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity.
  To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by $27$--$31\%$, and raises throughput by $1.34$--$1.40\times$.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that invoke tools (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023) to edit code, run shell commands, query databases, and browse the web to complete multi-step tasks autonomously (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2025; Yang et al., 2024b). Unlike a chat, an agentic task is a long-running program of many LLM calls, each followed by a tool use whose output is appended to the context. Executions of tens to hundreds of LLM calls are common. In production traces (Zhu et al., 2026b) that include Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025) sessions, the 9090th-percentile session issues over 100100 model calls (241241 for Codex), and its context peaks at 186186K tokens (235235K for Codex). Even on frontier mixture-of-experts models with compact attention, the result is a large memory footprint—e.g., we compute that such a session holds 3636-4545 GB of context with Qwen3-235B-A22B (Qwen Team, 2025) and 1313-1717 GB with DeepSeek-V3’s latent attention (DeepSeek-AI, 2024).

To serve multiple requests simultaneously, servers continuously batch requests based on specific scheduling policies (Zheng et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2022) and availability of space in the KV cache. An open problem is how to simultaneously serve agentic and summarization requests under load on a shared server. In general, there are two approaches: synchronous and asynchronous. In synchronous summarization, the agent harness waits until the context approaches a certain threshold, and then stalls the agent while a summarization request executes. In asynchronous summarization (Chen et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a), the harness lets the agent continue while a request summarizes the context. The agent runs on the full long context until the summarization completes. With synchronous summarization, the summarization is in the critical path, raising the mean and P99 latency. papers.title: An Open-Source ROS 2 Framework for Shared Control in Surgical Teleoperation: Integrating the Haply Inverse3 with the da Vinci Research Kit
papers.abstract: Surgical teleoperation deprives surgeons of touch, forcing visual inference of tissue forces; the commercial platforms now restoring force feedback remain closed, preventing open research on haptic shared control. This paper provides a system contribution: it presents an open-source, ROS 2-native framework that integrates the compact, three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the da~Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). The framework includes a novel mapping strategy that combines 3-DOF translational device input with separately tracked VerseGrip orientation into 6-DOF patient-side manipulator commands. Two virtual-fixture-inspired guidance modes serve as reference implementations to evaluate the framework in a within-subjects user study on a teleoperated hot-wire benchmark task in simulation, and the architecture is further demonstrated on physical dVRK hardware. Relative to unassisted manual control, linear guidance significantly reduced both the number of wire contacts and the task completion time, whereas the progressive-stiffness guidance produced consistent but statistically non-significant trends in the same direction. Subjective ratings of workload, agency, and satisfaction showed favorable descriptive trends for the guidance modes. The results demonstrate the feasibility of haptic shared control with a compact device coupled to the dVRK and provide an openly available, reproducible platform for future research. They further suggest that simpler linear feedback may be more robust for inexperienced operators than more complex profiles.

papers.intro:
Robotic surgical systems such as the da Vinci platform have transformed minimally invasive surgery, but a fundamental limitation remains: the physical separation between surgeon and patient removes natural tactile and force feedback. Current clinical systems have therefore relied primarily on visual cues and learned motor strategies to regulate interaction forces [1, 2]. This sensory gap can increase applied forces, elevate the risk of tissue damage, and make it harder to discriminate tissue properties during manipulation [3, 4]. Although da Vinci 5 introduces force feedback, the platform remains closed, which limits experimental access to the feedback architecture, custom control designs, and alternative haptic rendering strategies. Recent studies suggest that force feedback can reduce applied tissue forces and improve task performance, but the available evidence is still limited and does not yet isolate force feedback from all other platform changes in clinical use [5, 6, 7, 8]. Moreover, because human-in-the-loop control is a complex, multidimensional phenomenon, the design of effective haptic shared control strategies for surgical teleoperation remains an open question that requires further investigation [9, 10, 11]. In contrast, research platforms such as the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) provide the openness needed to investigate new control architectures and human-robot interaction concepts [12, 13].

Integrating haptic devices, such as the 3-DOF Haply Inverse3, with the 6-DOF dVRK requires combining secondary orientation sensing with translation and matching coordinate frames. The primary goal of this work is the system integration itself: providing the research community with an open, ROS 2-native solution for using compact haptic devices with the dVRK. The novelty lies in the end-to-end integration of a compact 3-DOF haptic device with a da Vinci-derived teleoperation platform. The haptic shared-control evaluation presented in this paper serves as a means of validating this platform rather than as an end in itself; the evaluated feedback modes are intentionally simple implementations. The hot-wire task is used as a benchmark because it emphasizes path following, speed regulation, and collision avoidance, all of which are relevant to surgical teleoperation.

papers.title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
papers.abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

authors.institution: Else Kröner Fresenius Center for Digital Health

papers.intro:
Large language models are increasingly integrated into healthcare applications, where they support patient education, clinical decision support, and preliminary diagnosis [1], treatment recommendations [2], and image interpretation and documentation [3]; multi-agent configurations, in which each LLM takes on a specialist role, are being explored for more complex medical scenarios [4]. Yet their clinical safety profiles remain poorly characterized, and strong results on knowledge benchmarks cannot stand in for an explicit measurement of safety [5]. Medical LLMs readily comply with harmful requests, and do so more often than their safety-aligned general-purpose counterparts [6]. An evaluation of 31 LLMs on 100 real primary-care-to-specialist consultation cases found potential for severe harm in up to 22% of cases, and safety performance was only moderately correlated with existing AI and medical-knowledge benchmarks (r=0.61r=0.61–0.640.64) [5]. Because the models are generally accurate and their recommendations read as plausible, clinicians tend to default to accepting them, so such errors are prone to go unnoticed through automation bias [5]. A separate vulnerability stems from the models themselves: frontier LLMs comply with up to 100% of illogical medical requests, prioritizing helpfulness over logical consistency and generating false clinical information even when they know the request is flawed [7].

Model limitations are not the only source of error: model behaviour can also be manipulated deliberately. Prompt injection attacks exploit the fact that LLMs operate directly on text and have no formal way to tell instructions from data [8, 9], so an attacker who controls part of the input can override the intended behaviour of the system [10, 9, 11]. Multimodal models have widened this attack surface further [12]. Instructions hidden in medical images at low contrast or in tiny font, not obvious to human observers, can make vision-language models produce harmful output [3], systematically designed image-based injections succeed in up to 64% of attempts under stealth constraints [12], and in multi-agent pipelines a single injected prompt can replicate from agent to agent, enabling coordinated data theft or system-wide disruption [13].

In clinical settings, such attacks carry direct consequences for patient safety [1, 2, 14, 15]. In a controlled evaluation of commercial LLMs giving medical advice, prompt injections succeeded in 94.4% of trials and in 91.7% of dialogues with extreme harm potential, such as recommending thalidomide during pregnancy, and even flagship models with enhanced safety mechanisms remained susceptible in 80–100% of cases [1]. This vulnerability is not confined to a particular model class: open-source and proprietary models alike can be compromised through prompt injection and fine-tuning attacks across prevention, diagnosis, and treatment tasks [2]. At the same time, results from the Medical Prompt Injection Benchmark (MPIB) show that attack-success rate and clinical harm can diverge substantially, which argues for measuring patient-level risk rather than instruction compliance alone [14]. The problem extends beyond explicit instructions: when fabricated clinical details are planted in a prompt, models elaborate on the false information in 50–82% of cases [15].

Most existing defences act on the input, on the surrounding system architecture, or on the model itself, which is then hardened through adversarial training or preference optimization [16]. Input-level filtering detects 60–80% of injection attempts, and advanced architectural protections reach up to 95% protection against known attack patterns, yet substantial gaps remain against attack vectors that have not been seen before [16]. Training-free defences that repurpose attack techniques against the injected instruction can push attack success close to zero, but only in certain scenarios [17]. Different as they are, all of these defences work from the outside. None of them looks at what is happening inside the model while it runs, yet that is exactly where the signal is. A series of recent studies shows that much of what is needed to catch unsafe behaviour can be read directly from an LLM’s hidden states [18, 19, 20, 21]. Because instruction-tuned models represent data containing injected instructions differently from benign data, a linear classifier on residual-stream vectors detects prompt injection with average false-positive and false-negative rates of 0.5% and 1.4%, without fine-tuning the model or generating a response [21]. Jailbreak and benign prompts likewise leave consistent latent-space patterns across several open-source model families [18], vision-language models show distinct activation patterns for unsafe prompts that can be used for detection without extensive fine-tuning [19], and linear probing across layers isolates safety neurons that, once combined, outperform dedicated guard models with 250 times fewer trainable parameters [20]. Sparse autoencoders and representation engineering widen what can be extracted from these activations, decomposing them into interpretable features and steerable directions for high-level properties such as honesty and harmlessness [22, 23, 24]. Yet each of these detectors is trained for one property on one model, and returns a score rather than something a person can read.

papers.title: Off-Nuclear AGN Signatures in MaNGA: Spatially resolved selection using MEGACUBES
papers.abstract: We present a spatially resolved search for off-nuclear active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidates in the MaNGA survey. Using megacubes, we analyze over 10,000 galaxies, separating AGN activity from diffuse ionized gas with refined equivalent-width and surface-brightness thresholds. Combining a spatial radial algorithm with BPT, WHaN, and WHaD diagnostics, we classify 261 nuclear AGNs, 201 off-nuclear AGNs, and 159 'quiet' (composite-spaxel-dominated) sources. We test whether off-nuclear AGNs reside in distinct host galaxies or whether the offset is a local, gas-driven phenomenon. Nuclear and off-nuclear AGN hosts are statistically indistinguishable in stellar mass, age, star formation rate, and gas-phase metallicity. However, the excitation and kinematics of the AGN-ionized gas differ significantly: nuclear AGN spaxels have [O III]$\lambda5007$ luminosities $\sim 0.7$ dex higher than off-nuclear spaxels, whose lower [O III]/H$\beta$ ratios indicate genuinely lower-excitation gas rather than an obscured view of the central engine. We also find an orientation trend: 72% of nuclear hosts are face-on, versus 50% of off-nuclear hosts, so projection effects contribute to, but do not fully explain, off-nuclear detections. The classical WHaN boundary at $\log$([N II]/H$\alpha$) = -0.4 misclassifies high-metallicity diffuse ionized gas in integral field data; an empirical shift to -0.25 removes over 48,000 spurious AGN spaxels. Finally, the off-nuclear fraction implies an episodic AGN phase lifetime of $\sim 5 \times 10^4$ yr, consistent within a factor of a few with independent fading-AGN estimates and supporting short, recurrent accretion bursts.

papers.intro:
Most present-day galaxies are inferred to host a supermassive black hole (SMBH) at their gravitational centers (Magorrian et al., 1998; Ferrarese and Merritt, 2000; Gebhardt et al., 2000; Greene et al., 2020; Caglar et al., 2023). Only a small fraction of SMBHs are observed to be in an actively accreting state at any given cosmic epoch; however, they are expected to experience recurrent episodes of accretion over the course of their host galaxies’ lifetimes (Martini, 2004; Heckman and Best, 2014; Hickox et al., 2014; Schawinski et al., 2015). During these active phases, SMBHs accrete ambient material and can drive powerful outflows and relativistic jets. Such systems, collectively termed active galactic nuclei (AGNs), are among the most luminous and energetic phenomena in the universe and are frequently classified according to their luminosity—distinguishing lower-luminosity Seyfert galaxies from highly luminous quasars (Seyfert, 1943; Schmidt, 1963; Richards et al., 2006, e.g.,). Additionally, AGNs can be classified using a variety of other multi-wavelength observational criteria (Padovani et al., 2017, e.g.,).

Extensive theoretical and observational investigations have been undertaken to characterize the physical nature of AGNs and to quantify their impact on galaxy evolution. Accumulating evidence indicates that SMBHs exert a fundamental influence on the assembly histories of their host galaxies. In particular, AGN feedback—mediated by radiative output, winds, and jets—is widely invoked as a key mechanism capable of suppressing (quenching) star formation and thereby regulating the stellar mass growth of galaxies (e.g., Fabian, 2012; Zubovas and Bourne, 2017; Harrison and Ramos Almeida, 2024, and references therein). Conversely, alternative scenarios propose that AGN-driven outflows can, under certain conditions, compress the surrounding interstellar medium and thereby induce or enhance star formation (Silk, 2005; Hopkins, 2012; Gallagher et al., 2019, e.g.,).

Conversely, alternative scenarios propose that AGN-driven outflows can, under certain conditions, compress the surrounding interstellar medium and thereby induce or enhance star formation (Silk, 2005; Hopkins, 2012; Gallagher et al., 2019, e.g.,).

A central challenge in understanding SMBH-galaxy co-evolution is obtaining an unbiased census of AGN across the full range of luminosities, host morphologies, and spatial configurations. Traditional single-fiber optical spectroscopic surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al., 2000; Gunn et al., 2006, SDSS;), are limited to the central region of each galaxy. Studies employing these surveys and standard narrow emission-line diagnostic diagrams (Baldwin et al., 1981; Kewley et al., 2001; Kauffmann and others, 2003) are inherently biased toward more luminous AGNs (Trump et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2016, e.g.,). Furthermore, single-fiber Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (Baldwin et al., 1981, BPT;) classification can fail to find AGNs for a variety of reasons: active star formation (Birchall et al., 2020); strong host galaxy dust, or nuclear torus obscuration that dilutes the AGN signatures (Moran et al., 2002; Ramos Almeida and Ricci, 2017); contamination by low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINER)-like emission from hot low-mass evolved stars; and low-metallicity or low-mass AGN hosts (Groves et al., 2006).

The major drawback of these single-fiber surveys is that they miss some unique AGN sources, such as off-nuclear and extended AGN signatures, among others. For instance, the integrated spectrum of a galaxy can hide AGN signatures when the central region is dominated by star formation or is heavily obscured by dust (Wylezalek et al., 2017), pushing any detectable AGN emission to the outskirts, beyond the fiber aperture. Single-fiber surveys further miss AGNs that are spatially offset from the galaxy center due to mergers (Greene et al., 2011; Comerford and Greene, 2014; Barrows et al., 2018), or that were recently switched off while relic ionization is still visible in the outskirts (Keel et al., 2012; Keel et al., 2015). Studying these types of sources is important to shed light on the full picture of SMBH-galaxy co-evolution.

The major drawback of these single-fiber surveys is that they miss some unique AGN sources, such as off-nuclear and extended AGN signatures, among others. Although integral field unit (IFU) data are powerful, they also introduce new challenges. A variety of diagnostic diagrams have been proposed to classify emission-line regions, including the BPT diagrams (Baldwin et al., 1981; Veilleux and Osterbrock, 1987), E​WH​αEW_{\mathrm{H}\alpha} vs. [N ii]/Hα\alpha diagram (Cid Fernandes et al., 2010, WHaN;), E​WH​αEW_{\mathrm{H}\alpha} vs.σH​α\sigma_{\mathrm{H}\alpha} diagram (Sánchez et al., 2024, WHaD;), E​WH​αEW_{\mathrm{H}\alpha} vs. [O iii]/[O ii] diagram (Sánchez et al., 2025, WHaO;), to name a few. Moreover, traditional diagnostic methods were initially calibrated using single-fiber spectra, and more recent diagnostics specifically developed for IFU data still lack the extensive validation studies needed to apply them with full confidence. Each of these is sensitive to different parameters, and degeneracies among them can lead to misclassifications, as they do not always yield consistent classifications (Cid Fernandes et al., 2010). The problem is further deepened by the fact that standard optical diagnostics depend on galactocentric distance and aperture size (Sanchez, 2020; Sanchez et al., 2021). In particular, the fraction of fake AGN classifications increases significantly beyond 1 effective radius (ReR_{\rm e}), primarily due to contamination from diffuse ionized gas (Albán and Wylezalek, 2023, DIG;) and extended LINER-like emission (Heckman, 1980; Binette et al., 1994; Stasinska et al., 2006; Cid Fernandes et al., 2010; Belfiore et al., 2016; Lacerda et al., 2018, e.g.,). To address this, we utilize multiple-extension Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) data products known as megacubes (Riffel et al., 2023), which provide robust stellar population and spatially resolved emission-line fitting for every MaNGA galaxy. We pair these data with the AGN selection criteria introduced by Wylezalek et al. (2018), which are aimed at identifying AGN in optical IFS surveys such as MaNGA and have also been shown to uncover off-nuclear AGN signatures. These criteria were developed while the MaNGA survey was still ongoing, based on a sample of ∼2800\sim 2800 galaxies.

papers.title: The SPACE Program IV: Atmospheric Features on the Cold Transiting Sub-Neptune TOI-6478 b
papers.abstract: Among the current population of exoplanets there are very few sub-Neptunes that have their atmospheric composition identified. This is primarily due to sub-Neptunes having high metallicity, clouds, and/or hazes obscuring absorption features. This often produces a spectrum that presents itself as a featureless spectrum especially in the near-IR. However, there are tentative trends that suggest sub-Neptunes with the lowest equilibrium temperatures ($\mathrm{T_{eq} < 400\:K}$) have detectable features, perhaps due to inefficient haze production or cloud sedimentation. TOI-6478 b is a low-density sub-Neptune exoplanet ($\rm <\mathrm{9.9\:M_{\oplus}}$ and $\rm \sim 4.5R_{\oplus}$) with an equilibrium temperature $\mathrm{T_{eq} = 220 \:K}$ assuming zero albedo. In this study, we present the highest S/N spectral feature ($\sim$6) of any sub-Neptune detected using HST/WFC3. We detect this spectral feature using a robust analysis that incorporates the Transit Light Source Effect (TLSE) to rule out false detections due to stellar activity. With the narrow bandpass of HST we were unable to distinguish whether the spectral feature at 1.4$\mu$m is from H$_2$O or CH$_4$ absorption. Meanwhile, self-consistent atmospheric models provide physical motivation for CH$_4$ to be the dominant absorber given that H$_2$O should condense or cold trap at higher pressures. Through our analysis we determine that HST/WFC3 alone cannot distinguish between major absorbers. However, a broader wavelength coverage by JWST will be able to measure the atmospheric composition in detail, due to the high S/N features for this target.

papers.title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
papers.abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.

Global medium-range weather forecasting faces two complementary demands: the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics calls for efficient ensemble generation to characterize uncertainty in future states [33, 27], while downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations require adaptation to specific task objectives. Data-driven models substantially advance medium-range accuracy [41]. Unifying efficient ensemble generation and task-driven policy optimization within a single generative framework is therefore a fundamental challenge for next-generation weather forecasting.

As shown in Fig. 1 (top left), deterministic models, including Pangu-Weather [4], GraphCast [24], FengWu [8], FuXi [9], and OneForecast [15], predict future states through continuous-field regression. These models deliver strong short-range point forecasts, but standard inference outputs a single trajectory rather than an explicit distribution over future states. Continuous generative models, such as diffusion [18] and flow matching [31] (e.g., GenCast [39]), instead construct ensembles by transforming noise into forecasts (Fig. 1, top right). Iterative samplers require repeated network evaluations, increasing inference cost with ensemble size and forecast horizon; one-step flow models such as Tyche [54] reduce this cost, although our daily-resolution evaluation reveals long-range skill degradation and a year-long rollout cold bias (Fig. 6). Moreover, continuous sampling does not directly expose step-wise discrete likelihoods for likelihood-ratio policy optimization.

This limitation is particularly acute in Earth system applications. Evaluating persistent land temperature extremes involves quantile thresholds and multi-day persistence rules. Marine heatwave forecasting tracks extremes in sea surface temperature [44], which can be predicted by forcing an ocean model with atmospheric forecasts [53]. Threshold-based event scores are non-differentiable, and backpropagating through a coupled simulator incurs substantial overhead. Although BeamVQ [51] incorporates task feedback via quantized candidate search and self-training, making direct policy adaptation to extreme-event and coupled-ocean rewards an intrinsic capability of a global multivariate weather generator remains challenging. Autoregressive modeling over discrete tokens [48, 11] provides a natural interface: in the GPT pretraining–post-training paradigm [40, 37, 14], categorical heads yield exact conditional token log-probabilities, allowing scalar rewards to guide policy updates without differentiating through the evaluator or coupled model [52]. Bringing this paradigm to global weather forecasting requires representing planetary circulation and localized gradients across dozens of coupled channels while decoding tens of thousands of tokens in parallel.

We introduce WeatherCraft (Fig. 1, bottom), unifying probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment via discrete weather tokens. WeatherCraft uses a multi-branch, multiscale spatial residual tokenizer based on finite scalar quantization (FSQ) [34] to encode atmospheric states into a high-capacity coarse-to-fine token hierarchy without learning a vector codebook. Following next-scale prediction [47], a conditional Transformer takes the preceding two days of latents as context and generates the next-day token hierarchy causally across time and scale while predicting all spatial tokens within each scale in parallel; multi-day rollouts feed generated representations back directly in latent space without repeated field decoding and re-encoding. This design supports fast ensemble sampling and yields exact token log-probabilities for every trajectory. Building on this interface, we treat the pretrained dynamics model as a generative policy and perform post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [42] over branching rollout trees, directly optimizing land extreme-event metrics or coupled responses of a frozen ocean model without differentiating through downstream evaluators.

papers.title: An improved Moore bound for girths seven and eleven
papers.abstract: Let $n(d,k)$ be the minimum number of vertices of a graph of minimum degree $d$ and girth at least $g=2k+1$. A simple counting argument gives the classical lower bound $n(d,k)\ge m(d,k)=1+d\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(d-1)^i$, known as the Moore bound and dating back at least to 1960. Apart from complete graphs and odd cycles, graphs attaining this lower bound can exist only for girth $5$ and degrees $3,7$ and $57$ (Hoffman and Singleton 1960; Bannai and Ito 1973; Damerell 1973). Nevertheless, for more than sixty years this lower bound has not been substantially improved beyond an additive constant. For $k\geq 3$, i.e. girth at least $7$, the best general bound was $n(d,k)\ge m(d,k)+2$, due to Bannai and Ito (1981). We show that for fixed girth $7$ and growing degree $d$ we have $n(d,3)\ge m(d,3)+(1-o(1))d/8$. Furthermore, for girth $11$ we have $n(d,5)\ge m(d,5)+\Omega(d^{3/5})$. In particular, the excess $n(d,k)-m(d,k)$, for $k\in\{3,5\}$, tends to infinity with $d$ and is therefore generally unbounded, which answers a question of Bollob\'as from 1978. For the degree/diameter problem we obtain similar bounds. A graph of maximum degree $d$ and diameter $3$ or $5$ has at most $m(d,3)-\Omega(\sqrt{d})$ or $m(d,5)-\Omega(d^{3/10})$ vertices, respectively. This answers a question of Bermond and Bollob\'as from 1981: for every constant $c$ there are $d$ and $k$ such that every graph of maximum degree $d$ and diameter $k$ has at least $c$ fewer vertices than the Moore bound.

papers.title: Dynamics of spinning supermassive black hole binaries: I. A direct $N$-body study
papers.abstract: The dynamical evolution of supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries in dense stellar environments may be influenced by the individual and mutual spin configurations of the black hole through spin-orbit and spin-spin couplings. We investigate the impact of spin on key dynamical properties, including binary hardening, orbital evolution, and energy exchange with the surrounding stellar population of an SMBH binary with masses $m_1=3\cdot10^8\,M_\odot$ and $m_2=8\cdot10^7\,M_\odot$, corresponding to a mass ratio $q\simeq3.75$. We perform direct $N$-body simulations including post-Newtonian (PN) corrections up to 2.5PN order between the black hole-black hole interactions, considering seven spin configurations, including a non-spinning model, and examine the effects of numerical resolution on the energy transferred to the stars. For the adopted initial conditions, the binary merger times vary only by $1.7\%$ of the $\sim3.8$ Myr total inspiral time. The hardening rates and cumulative energy transferred to the stellar population also show modest, non-monotonic variations across the spin configurations, with no clear systematic dependence on spin magnitude or orientation. The energy gained by the stars is consistent with the corresponding energy lost by the binary during the same encounters, including that radiated in gravitational waves, to within approximately $1\%$, which sets the level of the energy error of the balance. We further find that prograde stellar orbits account for roughly three quarters of the cumulative energy gain, a preference that is also present in the non-spinning model and therefore cannot be attributed to black-hole spin. Our results indicate that, for the binary parameters and stellar model considered here, spin has a limited influence on the global merger timescale and overall energy redistribution, while stellar interactions remain central to the hardening process.

papers.intro:
It is now well known that most massive galaxies host in their center a supermassive black hole (SMBH) (Kormendy and Ho, 2013). These SMBHs have masses in the range of 10510^{5}-1010​M⊙10^{10}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}, which correlate strongly with the velocity dispersion of their host galaxy, implying that the host galaxies and their central SMBHs grow together and suggest a co-evolutionary connection between them such as the empirical MBHM_{\mathrm{BH}}–σ\sigma relation which links the SMBH mass MBHM_{\mathrm{BH}} to the stellar velocity dispersion σ\sigma of the galactic bulge (Ferrarese and Merritt, 2000; Gebhardt et al., 2000; McConnell and Ma, 2013). When the galaxy grows, σ\sigma increases and hence subsequently the MBHM_{\mathrm{BH}} also increases.

When the galaxy grows, σ\sigma increases and hence subsequently the MBHM_{\mathrm{BH}} also increases.

Various studies have been carried out using large-scale Hydrodynamical cosmological simulations to study the properties of black holes present inside the gravitationally bound galaxies such as the IllustrisTNG (Vogelsberger et al., 2014; Springel et al., 2018) or EAGLE (Schaye et al., 2015) simulations. Cosmological simulations are in general excellent for studying large-scale structure formation (e.g., galaxies and dark matter halos), galaxy evolution, and SMBH growth over the cosmic time of billions of years. However, they struggle when it comes to resolving the detailed dynamics of SMBH binaries (Volonteri, 2010; Kelley et al., 2017b; Tremmel et al., 2017). They typically cover tens to hundreds of Mpc in size, meaning their smallest resolved scales are typically kpc or at best tens of parsecs in high resolution zoom-in runs, but this is insufficient to resolve the sub-parsec separations of SMBH binaries. Similarly, the temporal resolution is too poor to track the rapid dynamical interactions (Tremmel et al., 2019; Pfister et al., 2019). In these simulations the SMBHs are usually repositioned to the minimum of the local potential well to avoid artificial wandering caused by limited resolution (Tremmel et al., 2015). The SMBHs are artificially seeded in halos, where their masses exceed a threshold of ∼105​M⊙\sim 10^{5}\,\text{M}_{\odot} and their growth and feedback are primarily driven by gas accretion, modeled using semi-analytic subgrid prescriptions (Springel et al., 2005; Booth and Schaye, 2009), which often assume simple accretion and feedback models. Such simulations cannot capture the full complexity of SMBH binary interactions, but instead apply simple recipes to merge the SMBHs when their separation falls below values at which the simulation can still resolve the dynamics (Kelley et al., 2017a). Khan et al. (2016) was the first to perform a full simulation starting with initial conditions drawn from a cosmological simulation of galaxy formation until the final merger of the SMBH binary by gravitational wave (GW) emission.

When two galaxies merge, their central SMBHs eventually form a binary system (Begelman et al., 1980; Mayer et al., 2007). This process occurs in multiple stages. Firstly, as the two galaxies merge, their SMBHs, embedded in their respective stellar bulges, sink toward the center of the newly merged galaxy. This first stage is driven by dynamical friction (Chandrasekhar, 1943) against the background stars and dark matter, which is efficient at separations of 1-10 kpc and helps in bringing the SMBHs close to the galactic nucleus by extracting energy from them (Chandrasekhar, 1943; Milosavljević and Merritt, 2001). Once the separation reaches ∼10−100\sim 10-100\,pc, the two SMBHs form a gravitationally bound binary orbiting within a dense stellar background, where continued interactions with stars remove energy and angular momentum from the bound system (Quinlan, 1996; Sesana, 2010).

The next phase is accompanied by the three-body interactions, or the hardening phase, where the binary hardens as stellar particles interact with it and are then ejected from the system via gravitational slingshot, shrinking the binary further as it loses angular momentum (Merritt and Poon, 2004; Merritt and Milosavljević, 2005; Berczik et al., 2006). For spherical systems, stellar angular momenta are conserved and only stars with sufficiently small values come close to the SMBHs. Once this reservoir is depleted, no more slingshot interactions occur and the hardening of the SMBH binary stalls at ∼1\sim 1\,pc, an effect known as the ‘final parsec problem’ (Milosavljević and Merritt, 2003; Berczik et al., 2005). However, real systems deviate from spherical symmetry and the stellar angular momenta are not conserved, such that the reservoir of stars that eventually come close to the SMBHs is large and is not depleted (Berczik et al., 2006; Khan et al., 2011; Preto et al., 2011; Khan et al., 2013; Holley-Bockelmann and Khan, 2015; Rantala et al., 2017; Gualandris et al., 2017; Kelley et al., 2017b; Bortolas et al., 2018).

GW emission extracts energy and angular momentum, shrinking the orbit and leading to coalescence within a timescale that depends on the binary’s mass ratio, eccentricity, and spin (Peters, 1964; Barack and Cutler, 2004; Sesana et al., 2004). papers.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
papers.abstract: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

Egocentric video records how people act in and interact with their surroundings, making it a valuable source of data for embodied AI and video generation [10, 48, 37, 15, 40]. Captions make these recordings searchable and allow downstream systems to identify when particular actions occur. For example, personal assistants retrieve captions as memory to answer questions about the wearer’s day [48], and robot learning uses timestamped action captions to curate pretraining data [15]. Both applications depend on captions that preserve the details of an activity and associate them with the right moments.

Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [29, 3, 36, 44, 43, 52, 35, 45, 54, 22] can produce detailed video descriptions [52, 56, 18, 4, 6]. On egocentric footage, however, they often overlook brief actions, confuse their order, misinterpret the wearer’s movements, or omit objects central to an event [34, 26, 39, 20, 32].

Part of the problem is that current captioners struggle to decide what to describe and how much detail each activity needs. General captioners [52, 4] cover the visible scene broadly without binding the narrative to the wearer’s actions. Current egocentric captioners, meanwhile, typically produce a brief narration or specialize in hand–object manipulation [57, 23, 47, 21], leaving activities such as navigation and social interaction less fully described. A second challenge is that detail and timing are rarely achieved together. Dense paragraphs often leave unclear when individual actions begin and end, while timestamped captions typically summarize each event in a sentence [31, 12] or group details by scene [50]. Furthermore, the wearer’s motion is difficult to interpret from the first-person viewpoint, because the body is often only partially visible, and the captioner must infer travel direction from changes in the scene [39], cues that can be misleading when head motion diverges from body motion [19].

To address these challenges, we present EgoCaptioner, which describes an egocentric video on two levels (Figure ). A video-level overview establishes the setting and spatial layout, introduces the people and objects involved, and summarizes the wearer’s activities and any purpose supported by the footage. Detailed steps then narrate how the activity unfolds: EgoCaptioner segments the video into temporally bounded events, divides each event into ordered steps with start and end times, and marks key moments, such as object state changes, with timestamps. This two-level structure supports three tasks: full-video captioning, overview captioning, and event-conditioned captioning, in which the model localizes and describes an event named in the instruction. papers.title: Chemical Cartography Across Time: The Age-Dependent Chemical Structure of the Milky Way with a Homogeneous Sample of 580,000 Giants from Five Surveys
papers.abstract: Mapping the distribution of elements in the Milky Way and understanding how that distribution has changed over time can give us insight into the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. Here we use homogeneously estimated atmospheric parameters, elemental abundances, distances, and ages for ~580,000 giants from five major spectroscopic surveys---all simultaneously placed on a single, self-consistent scale by one model---allowing us, for the first time, to use a large sample of stars with uniform labels and ages that cumulatively span much of the disk to trace how the metallicity structure of the Milky Way depends on stellar age. Our chrono-chemical analysis shows that the radial metallicity gradient of the disk depends non-monotonically on age: it is shallow for the youngest stars, steepening to a maximum of ~-0.07 dex/kpc at intermediate ages (~5-6 Gyr), and flattening to near zero for the oldest stars. This "U-shaped" age dependence is driven largely by the low-alpha (thin-disk) population, with the high-alpha (thick-disk) sequence having weak gradients at all ages. In contrast to [Fe/H], the radial [Mg/Fe] gradient is weak (<~0.01 dex/kpc) at all ages. Together, these trends are consistent with an inside-out formation scenario in which the gradient of the star-forming gas has flattened over at least the last ~6 Gyr, while the near-zero gradient of the oldest stars reflects their formation in a well-mixed disk, efficient radial migration, or both.

papers.intro:
The composition of a star is largely determined by the chemistry of the gas cloud that it was born from, and for most elements, this does not change significantly over a star’s lifetime [24]. As such, mapping the distribution of stellar abundances across the Galaxy—chemical cartography—along with how this distribution changes with age, traces how the Milky Way has assembled and evolved over cosmic time. Such analyses can provide direct constraints on the physical processes that shaped the disk: the inside-out growth of the Galactic disk, radial migration and dynamical heating, and the imprint of past mergers [35, 21, 22, 6, 26, 38, e.g.,]. The radial and vertical gradients of metallicity are particularly useful diagnostics, encoding the information about in-situ enrichment, the spatial growth of the disk, and the subsequent redistribution of stars.

As such, mapping the distribution of stellar abundances across the Galaxy—chemical cartography—along with how this distribution changes with age, traces how the Milky Way has assembled and evolved over cosmic time. Such analyses can provide direct constraints on the physical processes that shaped the disk: the inside-out growth of the Galactic disk, radial migration and dynamical heating, and the imprint of past mergers [35, 21, 22, 6, 26, 38, e.g.,]. The radial and vertical gradients of metallicity are particularly useful diagnostics, encoding the information about in-situ enrichment, the spatial growth of the disk, and the subsequent redistribution of stars.

Metallicity gradients in the Galactic disk have been measured extensively. In the radial direction, the present-day [Fe/H] gradient near the Galactic midplane is negative, of order −0.06-0.06 dex kpc-1, and flattens with height above the midplane [13, 9, 33, 32, 30, 38, e.g.,]. In the vertical direction, it is negative and steepens toward the inner Galaxy. These trends reflect the superposition of chemically and kinematically distinct populations—the younger, metal-rich, α\alpha-poor, thin disk and the older, metal-poor, α\alpha-rich thick disk [28, e.g.,]. Interpretation for age-mixed samples, however, is complicated by the fact that gradients measured for such a sample can correspond to one that is not reproduced by any coeval subsample and can differ systematically from each of them. The age-mixed radial gradient is shallower, and the vertical gradient steeper, than those of the underlying mono-age populations, due to differences in the spatial distribution of stars of different ages [70]; this can obscure the very time evolution that we are interested in. Where stellar ages are available, the gradients can instead be measured for the underlying mono-age populations forming the sample, revealing that the metallicity gradients themselves evolve with time.

Prior analyses on the evolution of the chemical structure have been limited by two obstacles: lack of reliable ages for large, spatially-extended samples, and the heterogeneity of the surveys that provide the elemental abundances. Age-resolved measurements of metallicity gradients have thus far come from large single-survey samples or from smaller samples with more precise ages but limited spatial coverage. M. S. Xiang et al. [70] use ∼300,000{\sim}300{,}000 LAMOST main-sequence turn-off stars with isochrone ages, but their sample contains no stars younger than ∼2{\sim}2 Gyr. F. Anders et al. [1] trace the gradient evolution with CoRoT–APOGEE red giants, and I. Ciucă et al. [16] with ∼18,000{\sim}18{,}000 TGAS–RAVE dwarfs. The latter sample is confined to 7.6<R<8.47.6<R<8.4 kpc and |Z|<0.5|Z|<0.5 kpc, and so has difficulty separating radial structure from vertical structure. Expanding the sample by combining surveys has the issue of heterogeneity. W. Sun et al. [60], for example, combine LAMOST and APOGEE red clump stars and find that the two pipelines place stars on systematically different scales, so one survey must be recalibrated onto the other post hoc (e.g., by fitting linear corrections) before the two can be combined. Different spectroscopic surveys probe different regions of the Galaxy with different selection functions and, critically, place abundances on different scales due to differences in processing pipelines, so naively combining the different abundances straight from output catalogs can result in spurious spatial gradients. A solution to this will only be more important as the number of surveys increases if we are to exploit the synergies between them [40, 15, 18, e.g., SDSS-V, MOONS, 4MOST;].

[60], for example, combine LAMOST and APOGEE red clump stars and find that the two pipelines place stars on systematically different scales, so one survey must be recalibrated onto the other post hoc (e.g., by fitting linear corrections) before the two can be combined. Different spectroscopic surveys probe different regions of the Galaxy with different selection functions and, critically, place abundances on different scales due to differences in processing pipelines, so naively combining the different abundances straight from output catalogs can result in spurious spatial gradients. A solution to this will only be more important as the number of surveys increases if we are to exploit the synergies between them [40, 15, 18, e.g., SDSS-V, MOONS, 4MOST;].

papers.title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
papers.abstract: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

Yet following detailed instructions, preserving scene state over time, and producing physically plausible interactions remain challenging. Code2Video approaches, including VideoCoCo [13] and Code Video Model [14], address these challenges through executable scene programs. In this paradigm, a coding agent constructs and renders a 3D proxy whose structure and motion guide a video model in synthesizing the final video. This explicit scene representation helps maintain scene state across camera revisits, as shown in Figure 1(a).

The benefits of Code2Video depend on the task and on how the proxy is constructed and used. Scene programs provide precise control over layout and trajectories, but detailed modeling can introduce geometric or motion errors that may carry over to the final video. When motion naturalness is central and explicit scene control offers limited benefit, an imperfect proxy may yield less natural results than direct generation. Proxies for the same task can differ substantially in their level of detail. Physical interactions also require choosing between scripted motion and physics simulation. The synthesis prompt must then align the intended appearance and finer actions with the rendered proxy. These considerations raise two central questions: How can we achieve the best video generation performance within the Code2Video paradigm, and how far can Code2Video extend the capabilities of video generation?

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Source O-RAN and 5G NTN Stacks on Embedded ARM Platforms for Space Payloads
papers.abstract: Regenerative satellite payloads, which host the 5G Next Generation Node B (gNB) onboard instead of transparently relaying the radio signal, are a key building block of the Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) integration that 3GPP started in Release 17. Combining them with the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture adds software-defined control through RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs), enabling in-orbit reconfiguration, multi-tenancy, and data-driven radio resource management. Open-source implementations make this vision accessible to research institutions and New Space missions, yet there is little quantitative evidence on how they behave on the embedded processors that a satellite can actually carry. This paper presents an out-of-the-box experimental benchmark of two open-source gNB stacks (i.e., OpenAirInterface/Duranta and srsRAN/OCUDU), and two Near-Real-Time RICs (i.e., the ORAN-SC Near-RT RIC and FlexRIC). All components are deployed on an ARMv8 platform representative of the processing units used in small-satellite payloads, driving a USRP B210 software-defined radio. We compare them in terms of functional compliance (3GPP NTN features, O-RAN interfaces, multi-tenancy), resource efficiency, real-time behavior, and engineering suitability. Results show that these platforms can host a joint gNB + near-RT RIC deployment using any of the considered components, although further optimizations are still required for carrier-grade performance. However, the performance and standards compliance vary significantly among them. Building on these results, we derive a decision framework that maps mission profiles and Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) budgets to gNB/near-RT RIC combinations. Finally, we discuss the open gaps remaining before these stacks can be flown in NTN regenerative payloads.

papers.intro:
Satellite systems are becoming an integral part of mobile networks. Since Release 17, 3GPP has specified support for 5G New Radio (NR) over Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN), addressing the long propagation delays, large Doppler shifts, and dynamic cell management characteristic of satellite gNBs [1, 2, 3]. The first NTN deployments standardized by 3GPP in Release 17 rely on transparent payloads, where the satellite acts as a bent-pipe relay, and the gNB remains on the ground. The regenerative payload concept was then standardized in Release 19, proposing hosting the gNB or part of it onboard. This shortens the radio control loops and decouples them from the feeder-link availability, paving the way for inter-satellite routing and in-orbit edge processing [4].

Since Release 17, 3GPP has specified support for 5G New Radio (NR) over Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN), addressing the long propagation delays, large Doppler shifts, and dynamic cell management characteristic of satellite gNBs [1, 2, 3]. The first NTN deployments standardized by 3GPP in Release 17 rely on transparent payloads, where the satellite acts as a bent-pipe relay, and the gNB remains on the ground. The regenerative payload concept was then standardized in Release 19, proposing hosting the gNB or part of it onboard. This shortens the radio control loops and decouples them from the feeder-link availability, paving the way for inter-satellite routing and in-orbit edge processing [4].

Hosting the gNBs onboard also raises the question of how the Radio Access Network (RAN) is operated in space. The Open RAN (O-RAN) architecture already answers this question for terrestrial networks by disaggregating the gNB through open interfaces and exposing it to RICs [5]. Applied to a regenerative satellite, O-RAN enables three major levers: flexible reconfiguration of network functions after launch; sharing of the gNB payload among third parties, either as tenants (multi-tenancy) or as providers of xApps; and fast closed-loop radio resource management and mobility optimization that adapts to orbital dynamics.Where the Radio Intelligent Controllers (RICs) run is equally important. The Non-Real-Time RIC (Non-RT RIC) sets policies through the A1 interface on time scales above one second, which tolerates the space–ground link, whereas the Near-Real-Time RIC (Near-RT RIC) controls the RAN through the E2 interface with loops between 10 ms and 1 s. For a geostationary satellite, the payload–gateway round trip alone may take about a quarter of a second [1], and a low Earth orbit satellite sees a given gateway for only a few minutes per pass. Closing near-real-time loops from the ground is therefore impractical, which motivates hosting the Near-RT RIC onboard next to the gNB, while the Non-RT RIC remains on the ground.

Open-source projects have become the de facto platforms to prototype such systems. OpenAirInterface (OAI) [6] (now Duranta) and srsRAN Project [7] (now OCUDU) provide complete 5G gNB implementations with NTN extensions and E2 agents, while FlexRIC [8] and the O-RAN Software Community (ORAN-SC) Near-RT RIC [9] provide two very different Near-RT RIC implementations: a lightweight, monolithic software development kit and a cloud-native reference platform composed of microservices, respectively. These projects are, however, usually developed and evaluated on x86 servers with abundant computing, memory, and power resources [10, 11]. Satellite payload processors are embedded Systems-on-Chip, typically based on ARM cores, with a few cores, limited memory and storage, and a strict power budget that must be shared with the rest of the payload software [12]. While some recent works have tested OAI to study different NTN architectures [13, 14] , to the best of our knowledge, no work has yet compared alternative gNB stacks and RIC platforms, and their combinations, on the same embedded hardware, nor quantified the cost of hosting the Near-RT RICs onboard the satellite.

papers.title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
papers.abstract: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.

Road safety is one of the strongest motivations for self-driving technology. Traffic accidents cause about 1.3 million deaths and 20–50 million injuries every year [1], and more than 90% of crashes are linked to human error [2]. A self-driving system is usually described as a pipeline of sensing, perception and decision making [3]. Perception is a part where deep learning can help a lot: a vehicle can only take safe decisions if it understands the road, the lane markings, the traffic signs, and the vehicles and pedestrians around it.

The encoder, called the backbone, extracts features from the image; the decoder turns these features back into a full-resolution label map. Many different backbones exist, but in practice one is often chosen in advance and the comparison focuses on the decoder.

papers.title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution.
  Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models.
  Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

papers.intro:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1] introduced an explicit scene representation based on anisotropic Gaussian primitives and efficient α\alpha-compositing rasterization, enabling real-time novel view synthesis at competitive visual quality. Subsequent work has improved its robustness, scalability, and rendering quality [2]. A fundamental limitation persists: the projected covariance of each Gaussian determines its screen-space footprint and therefore influences the local frequency response of the rasterized representation. Although the complete alpha-composited renderer is nonlinear, larger projected footprints attenuate high-frequency image content by increasing the spatial support of individual Gaussian kernels [2, 3]. Consequently, high-frequency scene content, including sharp boundaries, fine surface texture, and sub-pixel geometric structure, can be attenuated by the finite spatial support of projected Gaussian primitives [3, 4]. Addressing this limitation, therefore, requires either increasing the representational capacity of the underlying scene model, often at additional computational and memory cost, or exploiting residual high-frequency cues that remain implicitly encoded within the rendered observations.
