The most direct response to this limitation is primitive densification [1], which introduces additional Gaussian primitives to increase local representational capacity. While effective in principle, densification scales poorly: capturing increasingly fine geometric detail typically requires substantially more primitives, resulting in higher memory consumption, storage requirements, and rendering overhead [5, 6, 7]. Recent 3DGS super-resolution methods [8, 9, 10, 11] improve reconstruction fidelity through additional scene-level optimization and the incorporation of learned super-resolution priors. Although effective, these approaches increase reconstruction complexity, optimization time, and training overhead, limiting their practicality as lightweight inference-time solutions. Alternatively, lightweight 2D super-resolution networks [12, 13, 14] can enhance rendered views with relatively modest inference overhead. However, because they operate solely in image space, they lack explicit geometric constraints and may produce perceptually plausible yet geometrically unconstrained high-frequency detail [15, 16].

To probe this behavior, we systematically contract Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} during rasterization, generating a hierarchy of renderings with progressively smaller Gaussian footprints. We refer to this hierarchy as a multi-aperture rendering sequence, where the term aperture denotes the effective screen-space footprint scale of the rendering primitives, drawing inspiration from the role of aperture in controlling blur scale within optical imaging systems [3]. The resulting image variations are not uniformly distributed across the scene: some regions remain comparatively stable across scales, whereas others exhibit pronounced sensitivity to footprint perturbations. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • A bandwidth-aware interpretation of Gaussian rasterization. We provide a bandwidth-oriented interpretation of Gaussian rasterization, showing how projected Gaussian covariances influence the effective frequency response of individual rasterization kernels and how covariance contraction can probe bandwidth-sensitive scene structure. • A structural uncertainty field from multi-aperture rendering. We introduce a parameter-free uncertainty measure derived from cross-aperture rendering variation that localizes potentially under-resolved scene regions and provides a compact geometric prior for reconstruction. • Aperture-guided super-resolution for Gaussian Splatting. We propose a lightweight architecture that progressively fuses multi-aperture observations conditioned on uncertainty, transmittance, and positional-encoded depth cues to enhance rendered 3DGS views without modifying the underlying representation. • Validation across degradation and rendering scales. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360 demonstrate increasing improvements under moderate and severe representation degradation.

papers.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
papers.abstract:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes.
  In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code.
  We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance.
  In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

papers.intro:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a common practice regularly used in many software projects [1] and has become a popular approach to frequently integrate changes into the source code repository [2]. It supports all activities that comprise the software development process including the compilation, dependency resolution, testing, and deployment of software products. Consequently, development teams benefit from this practice mainly because they receive faster feedback for the proposed source code changes [3].

Continuous Integration (CI) is a common practice regularly used in many software projects [1] and has become a popular approach to frequently integrate changes into the source code repository [2]. It supports all activities that comprise the software development process including the compilation, dependency resolution, testing, and deployment of software products. Consequently, development teams benefit from this practice mainly because they receive faster feedback for the proposed source code changes [3].

However, this benefit also implies that developers need to accept trade-offs [4]. For example, the increase in the speed of the build can impact the quality of it as well as the configuration effort conflicts the simplicity of the configuration. In particular, the development can suffer from long build durations [3, 5] which lowers the benefit of frequent code integration because developers need to wait for the build to finish before they can proceed with their planned implementation tasks. Moreover, these waiting phases can lead to context switches [6] because developers may want to use the time they are waiting for the build to finish. This poses the risk of developers getting distracted and loosing focus of their current work, which can negatively impact the quality of the produced code. Finally, the frequent execution of the build entails a significant resource usage [4, 7] which can also lead to high costs [8, 9].

Prior work proposed approaches that aim at reducing the load of the frequent builds by tackling the problem from different perspectives. First, test selection [10, 11, 12, 13] and prioritization [13, 14, 15, 16] approaches focus on reducing the number of tests that are executed during a build which reduces the overall build time [17]. While these approaches can reduce the time that is spent on testing the software, they do not consider other activities during build execution, such as dependency resolution and compiling. Addressing this issue, other approaches aim at reducing the load by avoiding unnecessary build executions. Abdalkareem et al. Other approaches focus on forecasting the prospective build outcome without executing the build [20, 21]. This helps to save resources while still retrieving feedback on the submitted change set. We perform two experiments in an intra-project setting. First, we evaluate our model with each of the 25 selected projects separately using 100-times stratified random sampling and measure well-known metrics. BuildPredictor performs well on most of the projects showing a median F1-Score, AUC, and MCC of 0.98, 0.98, and 0.82, respectively, which also outperforms other state-of-the-art models. Moreover, the most important attributes concern information about historical build outcomes (e.g., the last build outcome) and properties of the contributor (e.g., the experience of the developer). Second, we investigate how our model evolves over time when only information that was available at the time the commit was contributed is used. We observe a short ramp-up phase where the model jitters a lot until it settles and shows a stable performance. We also observe that the overall performance is lower with the time-sensitive approach compared to the random sampling approach. Moreover, we see a substantial variance in the performance of each project. Hence, we hypothesize that a build outcome prediction in an isolated project setting does not work for all projects, and suggest that a more holistic view on the prediction might help to improve the prediction power, leading to our second research question:

papers.title: Nilpotent skew-symmetric tridiagonal Bohemian matrices: a proof of Corless's conjecture
papers.abstract: Corless studied the skew-symmetric tridiagonal matrices $T_m(u)$ with superdiagonal $u \in \{1, i\}^{m-1}$. He showed that $T_m(u)$ can be nilpotent only if $m = 2^K - 1$ and that the $2^{K-1}$ vectors $u$ obtained from the empty vector by repeated application of $u \mapsto (u, 1, i, \rev u)$ and $u \mapsto (u, i, 1, \rev u)$ give nilpotent matrices, and he conjectured that there are no others. We prove this conjecture. Reducing the characteristic polynomial modulo $4$ gives a necessary condition for nilpotency that is linear over $\F$. For $m > 1$ it forces $u = (v, 1, i, \rev v)$ or $u = (v, i, 1, \rev v)$, and an identity implicit in Corless's proof then reduces the problem to $v$. Since $T_m(u)$ is diagonally similar to a finite section of the Feinberg--Zee hopping matrix, the theorem also determines the nilpotent tridiagonal sign matrices. We further show that the $(1,1)$ entry of the resolvent of a nilpotent $T_m(u)$ is $\lambda^{-1} \pm \lambda^{-3} \pm \lambda^{-7} \pm \dots \pm \lambda^{-(2^K - 1)}$, with signs that determine $u$. The proof of the main theorem has been formalised in Lean~4.

papers.title: Thermal investigation of buffer and transition layers in AlGaN HEMT stacks
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate thermal transport in a set of thin-film layers used in modern HEMT designs. Our theoretical analysis employs three phonon-transport models of increasing sophistication, ranging from a relatively simple Debye-approximation model to a first-principles framework that incorporates Density Functional Theory (DFT)-derived harmonic and anharmonic phonon properties. To describe ternary semiconductors, alloy scattering is also considered, and to account for the properties of non-ideal, polycrystalline thin films, scattering at grain and film boundaries is taken into account. For modeling the specific samples at hand, the latter are fitted to thermal conductivity data measured with Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR). Overall, we find that the first-principles model performs best and produces the most physically consistent results. Special emphasis is placed on establishing a reliable procedure for determining intrinsic transport properties dominated by Umklapp scattering. Building on these, it is then possible to systematically add additional scattering terms to the models and assess how model-inherent factors, such as the treatment of scattering rates or the description of the phonon dispersion, affect model accuracy and overall predictive capabilities.

papers.intro:
GaN-based high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) are among the most intensively researched technologies in microelectronics [1] due to their promising properties for power and optoelectronics applications, such as high breakdown field strength, high operating frequency, large band gap, good thermal conductivity, and small thermal expansion coefficient. Moreover, the high mobility of electrons in the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) at the AlGaN/GaN junction enables very high switching frequencies, making these transistors well suited for high-frequency amplifiers [1]. However, the small dimensions of modern devices and the use of layered materials introduce additional thermal resistances arising from geometric confinement of phonon states (phonon confinement), reduced phonon mean free paths due to boundary scattering (finite-size effects), and thermal boundary resistance at material interfaces. These effects collectively reduce the effective thermal conductivity. Therefore, a detailed understanding of the thermal properties of the involved materials is essential. The present study combines experiments and simulations to investigate phonon thermal transport in three samples containing thin-film layers commonly used in AlGaN high-electron-mobility transistors [1][2]. The thermal conductivity of the samples was measured at different temperatures using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) and then described using three different phonon transport models of increasing complexity. These include (1) the relatively simple Debye-approximation model [3], which assumes a Debye-like linear dispersion; (2) a model that uses the ab initio calculated dispersion for the three acoustic phonon branches branches, but still ignores optical phonons; and (3) a fully ab initio-based model that incorporates both the full phonon dispersion and phonon scattering rates derived from first principles. We compare the three models to identify their shortcomings, rank their performance, and contrast our findings with experimental data from the literature. To that aim, additional scattering processes like alloy scattering and boundary scattering at grain boundaries and thin-film surfaces are also considered. The measurements and modelling show that thermal conductivities of the investigated AlGaN HEMT layers are strongly affected by their microstructure, alloy composition, and thickness. The low conductivity of the AlN transition layer is attributed primarily to its highly polycrystalline structure, whereas the AlGaN layers exhibit pronounced size effects arising from the combined influence of alloy and boundary scattering. Comparison of different transport models further demonstrates that simplified descriptions of scattering can, to some extent, compensate for their inherent limitations through fitted parameters, whereas a fully ab initio treatment, supplemented by appropriate sample-specific corrections, provides a more consistent and robust description across the investigated layers.

papers.title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system
papers.abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically. Using density functional theory (DFT), we compute rigid-body separation (RBS) curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni GBs, extracting the work of separation $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and maximum traction $\sigma_{\max}$ via the universal binding energy relation (UBER). We find that substitution of Cr or Fe into the GB plane increases both quantities relative to pure Ni GBs. To overcome the size limitations of DFT, we compare several machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) foundation models against the DFT dataset and identify a model achieving quantitative agreement with DFT for $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $\sigma_{\max}$. This MLIP enables systematic sampling of alloying configurations at finer concentration steps. We show that alloying-induced changes in GB cohesion depend on both, element type and local structures, revealing trends that are inaccessible with DFT alone. Extending the analysis to a ternary $\mathrm{Ni}_{56}\mathrm{Fe}_{20}\mathrm{Cr}_{24}$ composition, inspired by the principal constituents of the widely used commercial Alloy 718, shows that the binary trends provide a useful basis for interpreting the combined effect of both substitutes, while explicit ternary calculations are required to capture their interplay quantitatively. Together, these results provide a validated workflow for quantifying the effect of alloying elements on GB cohesion in multicomponent alloys. The resulting values may serve as input for continuum-scale fracture models, paving the way toward atomistically informed multiscale modeling.

Nickel-based alloys are a cornerstone of modern high-performance materials, owing to their ability to maintain mechanical integrity and chemical stability under extreme operating conditions [28, 36]. They are widely deployed in energy conversion systems, chemical processing, and aerospace applications, where high temperatures, complex stress states, and aggressive environments are routinely encountered [13, 41]. These multicomponent Ni-based alloys provide an ideal platform for investigating the interplay between chemistry, microstructure, and mechanical response. In particular, ternary Ni–Fe–Cr alloys are frequently used as model systems for oxidation- and corrosion-resistant materials and serve as a simplified representation of more complex commercial alloys, such as Alloy 718 [22, 23, 43, 16]. The Ni–Fe–Cr system is employed here as a representative, technologically relevant test case for developing and validating atomistic methodologies applicable to complex alloys and their interface mechanics.

Density functional theory (DFT) provides a reliable description of interfacial cohesion at the electronic-structure level and, as a first-principles method, is not restricted to a specific chemical subspace, making it a powerful tool for describing multicomponent materials and complex local structural motifs [39, 21]. However, its computational cost severely restricts the accessible system size and configurational sampling. This limitation is especially problematic for multicomponent alloys, where realistic grain boundaries exhibit chemical disorder, segregation, and structural complexity that require large simulation cells far beyond what is feasible with DFT.

To address these challenges, we employ a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) based on the Graph Atomic Cluster Expansion (GRACE) framework [6]. Within this framework, several foundation models are available, which have been trained on large datasets of DFT calculations, such as OMAT [2] or Alexandria [7], and which differ in complexity and the training dataset used [30]. Using our own DFT reference data, we select the foundation model that achieves the best agreement with the DFT results. The resulting MLIP enables an accuracy comparable to DFT while allowing simulations of large, chemically complex GB structures. By combining GRACE with RBS calculations, we demonstrate how MLIPs can be used to systematically study GB cohesion in multicomponent alloys at scales inaccessible to first-principles methods. The workflow presented here, which includes calculating DFT reference data, performing large-scale GB separation simulations with a MLIP, and extracting energy–separation data, is fully transferable to a wide range of alloy systems and establishes a framework for linking atomistic modeling to continuum-scale fracture simulations.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
papers.abstract: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.

papers.intro:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a versatile and powerful imaging technique that allows the acquisition of high-resolution qualitative images of the internal anatomy of the human body. In quantitative MRI (qMRI), various quantitative parameters with specific biophysical correspondences can then be estimated from the image data. MR Elastography (MRE) [1, 2, 3] is a qMRI technique that provides detailed maps of biomechanical properties, enabling a non-invasive assessment of tissue stiffness. Externally induced mechanical waves result in tissue displacements, which are encoded as proportional phase shifts in the MR signal by motion encoding gradients (MEG) that are incorporated into specially designed MRI sequences. These phase shifts are tracked over time, enabling the calculation of shear wave speed (SWS)[4], which generally involves three steps: acquisition of kk-space data, reconstruction of complex-valued MR images from the data, and estimation of quantitative SWS maps from these images with an inversion method.

The brain is a fascinating target for MRE, particularly for detecting and monitoring neurological disorders that are associated with localized changes in tissue stiffness, such as Alzheimer’s disease[5]. Conventional MRE techniques typically require multiple time-resolved acquisitions, resulting in extended acquisition protocols with prolonged scan times and vibration exposure. These factors can increase patient discomfort, reduce clinical efficiency, and limit temporal resolution, making it difficult to investigate dynamic physiological processes that require fast, continuous measurements. Real-time MRE addresses these limitations by enabling high frame-rate stiffness mapping[6]. This approach improves patient comfort, reduces motion-related artifacts, and enables the monitoring of dynamic changes in brain tissue properties – such as those occurring during the Valsalva maneuver[7] or cardiac-cycle-related brain pulsations, as demonstrated in ultrasound elastography[8]. Recent studies have shown the feasibility and clinical value of rapid MRE in various applications, including subsecond mapping of liver stiffness[9], evaluation of the response in skeletal muscle to loading at frame rates of ∼6​Hz\sim 6\,\text{Hz}[6], and functional brain MRE[10].

Real-time stiffness mapping can be achieved by reducing scan time through undersampled data acquisition. In this work, we utilize a motion-robust single-shot spiral readout for MRE data acquisition, enabling the capture of all required data in a single shot per timestep and MEG. However, data undersampling introduces challenges into MRI reconstruction, yielding an ill-posed inverse problem necessitating the use of regularization techniques to stabilize the reconstruction. Importantly, the subsequent generation of MRE maps from wave images is itself inherently ill-posed due to noise and unknown boundary conditions.

Undersampled MRE images have been reconstructed using established non-learning approaches, which are typically applied prior to elastography inversion. These include parallel imaging and compressed sensing with sparsity priors, such as MRE-specific phase or displacement regularization [11], as well as Bayesian models that impose inter–offset constraints [12]. Further, machine learning (ML) has significantly influenced and improved MR image reconstruction [13] in recent years and currently defines the state-of-the-art both in MRI and qMRI reconstruction, see e.g. [14] for an extensive review. Despite these advances, several challenges persist. Frame rates in current rapid MRE techniques are still limited, and developments in neural network (NN)-based reconstruction methods and real-time MRE have largely progressed as separate fields. This work integrates both approaches to enhance the stiffness mapping frame rate while maintaining the accuracy of the reconstructed MR images and SWS maps. So far, ML in MRE has been applied to segmentation tasks [15], phase unwrapping optimization [16], and learning the inversion method for the calculation of stiffness maps[17, 18, 19, 20].

papers.title: Feedback-Free FDD Cell-Free Massive MIMO With Sparse AP Activation and Dual-Mode Precoding
papers.abstract: This correspondence enables practical frequency-division duplex (FDD) operation in cell-free massive MIMO via two mechanisms. Sparse access-point (AP) activation reduces downlink pilot overhead to enable coherent detection, while angle-reciprocity precoding steers beams using only uplink-estimated angles, eliminating channel feedback entirely. A load-adaptive dual-mode optimizer further enhances performance: closed-form signal-to-leakage-and-noise-ratio precoding for high-load rate boosting, or semidefinite relaxation for low-load power minimization. Simulations verify its superiority over existing feedback-free FDD solutions in spectral and energy efficiency, and its robustness to angle errors, reciprocity mismatch, and multipath.

papers.intro:
Cell-free massive MIMO (CFmMIMO) delivers uniform service quality by distributing a large number of access points (APs). In frequency-division duplex (FDD) systems, downlink (DL) precoding requires channel state information (CSI) at the APs, whose acquisition demands both DL pilots for user equipment (UE)-side estimation and feedback—a twofold overhead that has led FDD to be widely perceived as infeasible for massive MIMO, steering most CFmMIMO research to time-division duplex (TDD) leveraging channel reciprocity. Nevertheless, FDD remains indispensable: paired bands dominate global spectrum allocations and cannot readily migrate to TDD for economic and regulatory reasons [1].

Prior work deals with the two overheads separately. For training, compressed-sensing techniques exploit the sparse angle-domain structure to reduce the pilot dimension [2]. For feedback, angular reciprocity—the approximate invariance of the angle of departure (AoD) and the angle of arrival (AoA) across paired bands—allows DL CSI to be inferred from uplink (UL) measurements [3, 4]; yet these schemes either limit precoding to channel statistics and send no DL pilots [3] or still feed back instantaneous path gains for coherent operation [4]. Other approaches shrink, rather than remove, the feedback—quantizing it [5] or acquiring the channel through selected ports that are still trained and fed back [6].

This correspondence proposes a framework built from four components: (i) sparse AP activation (SAA) assigns each user its strongest available AP, collapsing the DL pilot dimension so that orthogonal training and coherent detection become affordable while the idle APs’ circuits are switched off (Section III); (ii) angle-reciprocity precoding (ARP) steers each DL beam solely by UL-estimated angles, eliminating the need for CSI feedback completely (Section III); (iii) a load-adaptive dual-mode optimizer refines the ARP beams—closed-form signal-to-leakage-and-noise ratio (SLNR) precoding boosts the data rate at high traffic load, while semidefinite relaxation (SDR)-based power minimization meets per-user average signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) targets at low traffic load (Section IV); and (iv) a closed-form achievable rate, valid even under angle-estimation errors, reciprocity mismatch, and multipath (Sections III and V).

papers.title: Preconditioning for quadratic matrix optimization via constraint reshaping
papers.abstract: We study quadratic optimization over orthogonality or symplectic constraints, a problem arising in eigenvalue computation, subspace analysis, and reduced-order modeling. Ill-conditioned problems have a wide positive Hessian spectrum at a minimizer, which slows first-order Riemannian methods. Existing preconditioned-metric approaches choose a Riemannian metric, which determines the resulting Hessian spectrum. We instead redesign the problem itself to find the narrowest possible spectrum. We reshape the constraints into equivalent formulations that preserve the optimal value and the solution set, giving a family of preconditioned problems parametrized by positive constraint weights. We derive a closed form for the positive Hessian spectrum in terms of these weights. Minimizing the condition number then reduces to a linear program (LP) in the logarithms of the weights. The LP attains a globally optimal design within the paired equal-block family, and its strong duality gives matching lower bounds on the condition number. On tested instances, the optimized formulation substantially reduces the local condition number, with returned spectra matching predictions on both orthogonal and symplectic instances. We also benchmark the design against Lagrangian and left-right preconditioned metrics. The method thus provides an exact, optimization-based alternative to heuristic preconditioned metrics.

papers.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
papers.abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.

papers.intro:
Artificial intelligence is taking on a growing share of materials discovery [1, 2, 3]. Generative models for crystals propose compounds that have not been seen before [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. They can be steered toward a prescribed symmetry or structural motif [9, 10] or toward a computed property [11, 12], and such steering has already produced candidate superconductors [13, 14]. Autonomous laboratories and AI agents now carry out parts of the research loop itself [15, 16]. Yet, despite these advances, AI-driven discovery remains fundamentally constrained by how its objectives are defined. When materials are generated using predefined numerical rewards, the search inevitably favors what those rewards are designed to recognize, potentially overlooking scientifically valuable candidates that fall outside their definitions.

They can be steered toward a prescribed symmetry or structural motif [9, 10] or toward a computed property [11, 12], and such steering has already produced candidate superconductors [13, 14]. Autonomous laboratories and AI agents now carry out parts of the research loop itself [15, 16]. Yet, despite these advances, AI-driven discovery remains fundamentally constrained by how its objectives are defined. When materials are generated using predefined numerical rewards, the search inevitably favors what those rewards are designed to recognize, potentially overlooking scientifically valuable candidates that fall outside their definitions.

Defining an appropriate reward is particularly challenging in scientific discovery, where the significance of a material is not always known in advance. Researchers often recognize promising features through their accumulated experience and physical intuition, even when these judgments cannot be expressed as simple numerical criteria [17, 18]. Whether a compound can be synthesized is judged from experience, and stand-ins such as the distance from the convex hull capture only part of that judgment [19, 20]. Features of an electronic structure, such as a flat band, a Dirac cone or a van Hove singularity, are recognized as patterns in a band diagram, and there is no accepted score for them. In machine learning, alignment means making a system pursue what people actually intend, and misalignment is a gap between the objective that a system optimizes and that intent [21]. In materials discovery, the objective is often a reward written by researchers themselves, such as a score for flat bands, while their intent shows in the judgments they make. Misalignment here is therefore a gap between what researchers can write down and what they actually prefer. A reward can favor candidates that experts would not choose and pass over candidates that they would. In conventional AI applications, reward misalignment is generally regarded as a problem to be corrected, as it can lead systems to pursue unintended outcomes [22, 23]. Scientific discovery, however, suggests another possibility. What if the disagreement between expert judgment and numerical rewards could itself reveal scientific opportunities that predefined objectives fail to capture? Rather than merely correcting the discrepancy, identifying and exploring it may provide a route toward unexpected materials discovery.

Here, we investigate this possibility using the discovery of electronic flat-band materials as a representative case. A flat band near the Fermi level enhances the role of electron interactions, which makes flat-band materials platforms for unconventional superconductivity, magnetism and other correlated phenomena [24]. Flatness is therefore a useful indicator for identifying potentially interesting electronic structures, although it does not by itself establish their physical properties. Several numerical descriptors have been proposed to quantify flat bands [25, 26], incorporating features such as bandwidth, proximity to the Fermi level, and the extent of flatness in momentum space. However, these descriptors necessarily impose predefined criteria on what constitutes a desirable flat band. We examine whether such criteria adequately capture expert judgment by comparing a hand-designed bandwidth score with pairwise evaluations collected from researchers in materials science and condensed-matter physics. The researchers choose between two structures rather than scoring each, because people judge more reliably by comparison [27, 28]. Such pairwise choices have been used to learn the intuition of medicinal chemists about molecules [29].

papers.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
papers.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

papers.title: An A $\infty$ -algebra structure for enriched Morse complexes
papers.abstract: We construct a homotopy coherent product structure extending the Chas-Sullivan product on chains of the free loop space of a manifold. Our construction uses the framework of Morse homology with DG coefficients and perturbed Morse gradient trees. We define an operad given by moduli spaces of Morse gradient trees with a twisted differential. This Morse tree operad receives a map from a suspended A$\infty$-operad and in turn acts on Morse homology with DG coefficients associated to a fibration over a manifold with a fibrewise monoidal structure.

papers.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.
papers.intro:
Large language models are increasingly working in domains where they are far from perfectly accurate, yet can be trusted to solve a substantial fraction of the tasks they encounter. Confidence prediction allows these systems to identify the tasks that are hardest for the model, and defer them to a human expert or a stronger model, therefore increasing automation without sacrificing low risk. High stakes scenarios where automation is practical yet hardest tasks may be deferred to experts include visual question answering assistance for blind people [5, 25, 29], autonomous driving vehicles [38, 30, 3], or even coding agents, where orchestrators can decompose a problem, delegate and supervise work from specialized or cheaper worker agents [19, 2, 42, 11].

Autoregressive language models generate answers by sampling from next-token likelihoods, making sequence likelihood a natural source of a model’s confidence in its own answer. However, common state-of-the-art post-training and inference techniques can severely degrade likelihood-based confidence as a predictor of answer correctness [41]. Specifically, Nakkiran et al. [41] show that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) post-training [43, 17] moves models away from the likelihood-optimization mechanism that links likelihood to correctness by sharpening the distribution toward sequences rewarded by the verification mechanism, while chain-of-thought makes final-answer likelihood reflect consistency with a sampled reasoning path rather than uncertainty about the answer itself. Prior work estimates confidence with external signals or auxiliary modules: scoring rules built on model outputs [27, 24], probes on internal representations [4, 8], or selector models trained alongside the answerer [21, 37, 39, 53, 48]. More recently, LLMs themselves have been used for selective prediction by asking them to verbalize a confidence score alongside their answer [35, 33, 50, 56]. Without explicit training, models verbalize confidence poorly, so reinforcement learning that explicitly targets confidence prediction has therefore become the leading approach to obtain more reliable responses from models [15, 57, 54]. The rewards used to date score each confidence in isolation, pushing it toward 11 when the answer is correct and toward 00 when it is wrong [15, 57, 54]. At inference, confidence is used to select only the most confident answers to improve task coverage at a chosen risk. What matters is therefore how each value ranks relative to that threshold rather than where it lands on the unit interval. Risk tolerances vary across applications and evaluation settings (a coding orchestrator may accept a worker agent’s lower-confidence patch when downstream tests will catch errors, whereas a VQA assistant for blind users or an autonomous vehicle can only act on high-confidence outputs), so the same confidence value can clear the abstention threshold under one operating point and fall short under another. A reward that scores each confidence in isolation therefore reduces the supervision to a push toward 00 or 11, and in practice produces polarized confidences, weak low-risk coverage, and poor generalization of selective prediction.

We propose to train confidence as a cross-question signal for which each per-completion target is conditioned on the other answers given by the model to the same prompt and other prompts, rather than only on its own correctness label. Selective prediction evaluates confidence over a collection of answers: for any chosen risk tolerance, a threshold determines which answers would be accepted and which would be abstained. We therefore reward each confidence by the selection behavior it would induce across the set, rather than by a fixed correctness target. Given a set of recent question-answer pairs with their confidence scores and correctness labels, we sort the set by confidence and identify, at a chosen risk tolerance, the largest subset of top-confidence answers whose error rate stays within tolerance. The confidence at the boundary of this acceptable subset defines the abstention threshold for that risk level, and each completion is then rewarded according to where its own confidence sits relative to this threshold: lying above is reinforced for correct answers, and lying below is reinforced for incorrect ones. Each risk tolerance induces its own threshold, so when reinforcing abstention at different risk levels, the same confidence value receives different rewards per risk level. Because every threshold depends on the set, the supervision a model gets on any one answer reflects how that answer compares to its peers rather than any fixed correctness target. Furthermore, we find that encouraging the model to predict diverse confidence scores, rather than collapsing around round numbers (e.g. single-decimal scores such as 0.8 or 0.9, or centesimals ending only in 0 or 5), improves coverage at low risk tolerances by preserving higher confidence-score resolution. papers.title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

papers.intro:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into effective actions across a wide range of robotic manipulation and embodied control tasks [17, 3, 5, 4, 21, 7]. In dynamic environments, agents must reason over long spatiotemporal horizons and adapt their actions as conditions change. Most VLA models rely on large-scale offline pretraining [13, 23, 29, 16, 22]. They perform well on in-distribution tasks but struggle in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, where they encounter tasks and environmental variations that pretraining data rarely cover [3, 13, 36].

Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a way for VLA models to respond to distribution shifts during deployment [33, 1, 30, 24]. As a robot acts, incoming visual observations and the resulting environmental feedback provide supervision without expert action labels [14]. These signals can help the model adapt its perceptual representations and action decisions while retaining knowledge acquired during pretraining. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization reduces the memory cost of TTA by estimating gradients from forward evaluations under perturbations [2, 38, 41, 42]. MeZO uses this approach to fine-tune large language models with near-inference memory usage and achieves performance comparable to first-order fine-tuning on several downstream tasks [27]. Dust, a state-of-the-art ZO optimizer, uses activation-space perturbations and parallel evaluations to match or exceed the performance of backpropagation at large perturbation population sizes [8]. In our preliminary VLA-TTA experiment (Figure 1), Dust quickly approaches AdamW’s task success rate [19, 26]. After 6,000 steps, Dust’s success rate plateaus and then drops substantially, eventually reaching a level comparable to that of SignSGD. We refer to this pattern of stagnation followed by decline during long-horizon ZO adaptation as the performance plateau problem.

The performance plateau problem motivates Dune (Dust Using Nodewise Error-feedback), a memory-efficient ZO optimizer that uses regression over historical statistics to recover reliable update directions when perturbation noise overwhelms the dominant error signal. At each step, Dune constructs regression features from model output residuals and time buckets that encode the stage of adaptation. It uses historical statistics with decaying weights to predict layerwise error signals from these features. Dune then forms a weighted combination of these predictions and the current ZO perturbation observations to preserve the dominant direction of the error signal and suppress high-frequency perturbation noise. Finally, it updates the historical statistics with the raw perturbation observations from the current batch, allowing the regression to track changes as adaptation proceeds. This mechanism stabilizes long-horizon VLA-TTA while retaining the memory efficiency of ZO optimization. Our paper mainly makes the following contributions: • Dune Paradigm. To overcome performance plateaus in VLA-TTA, Dune predicts layer-wise error signals via online ridge regression over output residuals and flow-matching time buckets, fusing them with current perturbation observations for stable updates without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Performance Plateau Theory. Under Gaussian perturbation and convex quadratic objectives, we establish a loss recursion showing how estimation variance limits convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, theoretically motivating historical error regression. Extensive Experiments. Across LIBERO benchmarks and real-world robots, Dune substantially boosts long-horizon task success rates with a significantly reduced memory footprint, while ablations confirm improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

papers.title: The compressible-incompressible CAO problem introduced by Lions, Temam and Wang
papers.abstract: We study the (CAO) system of Lions-Temam-Wang, describing a compressible atmosphere coupled to an incompressible ocean through a fully nonlinear boundary condition representing wind stress at the interface. In their foundational work, the system is reformulated in pressure coordinates under the assumption that the pressure is constant at the interface, leading to a purely incompressible system. In this article, we prove for the first time the strong well-posedness of the coupled compressible-incompressible system both locally and globally for small initial data.

papers.intro:
The interaction between the atmosphere and the ocean has become a central focus in both the field of theoretical research and operational weather prediction. In this context, Lions, Temam, and Wang [27, 28] developed a comprehensive model for atmosphere-ocean dynamics (CAO) that accounts for the effects of boundary layers near the interface. The model is based on a system of two coupled primitive equations. One describing atmospheric motion and the other governing oceanic dynamics, see also their earlier works [25, 26]. More specifically, the atmosphere is described by the compressible primitive equations, which serve as a framework for large scale atmospheric behavior and the ocean is modeled using the incompressible primitive equations, widely employed for understanding large-scale ocean currents. At the interface, the mechanical coupling process is realized via a fully nonlinear boundary condition that models the drag force exerted by the wind on the ocean surface. This interface condition plays a critical role in capturing the exchange of momentum between the two fluid domains and introduces significant mathematical challenges due to its nonlinearity. For a detailed description of the full model we refer to Section 2.

The primitive equations are widely considered a core model for representing geophysical flows, such as those in the ocean and atmosphere. They are derived from the Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq equations by simplifying the vertical component of motion under the assumption of hydrostatic balance. Since vertical velocity is difficult to observe directly, the hydrostatic approximation is commonly used.

papers.title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
papers.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps the activations of large language models (LLMs) in a higher-precision format, pushing the on-chip inference cost to the activation arithmetic. Bit-serial, variable-length accelerators offer a promising path to reduce this cost by lowering activation precision while preserving model quality. They process only the mantissa bits that each layer needs. The length has to be chosen per layer and operator, and today it is chosen by offline calibration: a search driven by the perplexity of the full model on a representative dataset. The search is repeated for every model and workload, and its result degrades silently on other data. This paper presents Kameleo, an accelerator that selects the activation precision at runtime, on the accelerator, from the data it is processing. Kameleo replaces the global perplexity by a local proxy that compares the output of each GEMM at reduced and at full precision. It exploits the fact that a bit-serial datapath produces this comparison almost for free, because the reduced-precision result is an intermediate state of the full-precision computation. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload set the precision of every GEMM. On four LLMs and seven datasets, Kameleo stays within a 1% perplexity budget at a 2.11-2.34x reduction of prefill cycles on the matrix multiplication unit (MXU), close to the reduction of configurations calibrated offline on the evaluation data itself. Calibrated configurations transferred to other data, in contrast, often violate the budget. The selection hardware adds only 3.7% to the accelerator area. Kameleo thereby makes variable-length mantissas feasible in real deployments, where offline calibration for every model and workload is not.
papers.intro:
The predominant quantization strategy for today’s large language models (LLMs) is weight-only quantization. Low-bit integer weights proportionally increase the throughput of the memory-bound decode stage, while keeping the activations in a higher-precision format (e.g., FP16) leaves the task accuracy intact [1, 2, 3, 4]. The higher-precision activation arithmetic is, however, far more complex than the integer weight arithmetic, so the on-chip bottleneck for energy and throughput shifts to the activations (Fig. 1a). Recent accelerators push the Pareto front further by pairing the low-precision weights with outlier-aware activation data types [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], and variable-length formats [5, 6] give each general matrix multiplication (GEMM) only as many activation bits as it needs. On a bit-serial datapath the mantissa length translates directly into cycles, so every bit that a layer can do without is a proportional throughput gain in the compute-bound prefill phase (Fig. 1b).

The predominant quantization strategy for today’s large language models (LLMs) is weight-only quantization. Low-bit integer weights proportionally increase the throughput of the memory-bound decode stage, while keeping the activations in a higher-precision format (e.g., FP16) leaves the task accuracy intact [1, 2, 3, 4]. The higher-precision activation arithmetic is, however, far more complex than the integer weight arithmetic, so the on-chip bottleneck for energy and throughput shifts to the activations (Fig. 1a). Recent accelerators push the Pareto front further by pairing the low-precision weights with outlier-aware activation data types [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], and variable-length formats [5, 6] give each general matrix multiplication (GEMM) only as many activation bits as it needs. On a bit-serial datapath the mantissa length translates directly into cycles, so every bit that a layer can do without is a proportional throughput gain in the compute-bound prefill phase (Fig. 1b).

The difficulty of a variable format is that its length has to be chosen, and existing work selects the precision through extensive offline calibration. The greedy search of ANDA [5], for instance, tries candidate lengths for every GEMM type and evaluates the perplexity (PPL) of the full model on a representative calibration dataset after every step. This regime has two shortcomings. First, calibration is compute-intensive, since every search step is a full-model evaluation, and ANDA needs 13 to 25 evaluations per model and dataset. Second, the result is data-dependent. The search has to be redone for every model and every workload, and the accuracy degrades silently when the deployment data drifts away from the calibration data, as Sec. IV-D shows. Both make variable-length activation precision impractical in deployment (Fig. 1c).

Online precision selection requires a quality signal that is local and label-free, in contrast to the global PPL used in offline calibration. Kameleo uses the deviation between the output of a GEMM at a reduced mantissa and the same output at full precision. II). • A lightweight extension of a bit-serial processing element (PE) that captures the candidate results during the ordinary full-precision pass. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload then set every GEMM’s precision in situ (Sec. III). • An evaluation on four LLMs and seven datasets, in which Kameleo reaches 80–97% of the cycle reduction of configurations calibrated on the evaluation data itself and maintains model quality on data where offline calibrations fail (Sec. IV).

papers.title: A Task-Level Bias Taxonomy for Historical Image Retrieval
papers.abstract: In recent decades, galleries, libraries, archives, and museums (GLAM institutions) have digitised vast amounts of cultural heritage material, including historical imagery. A major challenge in making these collections publicly accessible is enabling effective search and discovery. Many historical images contain incomplete, sparse, or no descriptive metadata. Consequently, machine learning (ML) methods are increasingly being used to generate or enrich metadata to improve the searchability of such collections. However, artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems can reproduce or amplify existing biases, particularly when applied to historical imagery. Factors such as differences between the data used to train the models and the historical images on which they are applied, degraded image quality, monochrome photographs, and historically biased or incomplete descriptions can reduce model performance and introduce bias into search and retrieval results. In this paper, we examine different forms of bias in historical image collections and review current methods to mitigate them. We investigate how these biases arise and how they influence AI-supported search and retrieval systems.

papers.intro:
Historical image collections are not neutral: the categories used to describe them, and the omissions of what was documented, reflect the priorities and power relations of the period and institutions that produced them [9, 7, 20]. These issues are particularly evident in colonial collections, which were shaped by unequal power relations and colonial perspectives. When such collections are made searchable, particularly where retrieval is supported with modern machine learning (ML) methods, these embedded assumptions are not simply preserved but risk being actively reproduced or reinforced, shaping how present-day users access and understand the past [13, 8].

papers.title: I See You: Initial Multi-Robot LiDAR Registration with Mutual-Observation Checks
papers.abstract: Compared to single-robot deployments, multi-robot teams can significantly improve search-and-rescue (SAR) mission success by covering large areas in parallel. To collaborate effectively, these robots must be registered in a common reference frame. Standard registration methods typically rely on external infrastructure or significant map overlap, but real deployments require infrastructure-free, stationary initial alignment for immediate operation. While global LiDAR point cloud registration addresses this, existing single-scan methods often fail silently in aliased or degenerate environments. Approaches scaling beyond two agents also remain rarely evaluated in real-world scenarios. We propose a centralized, deployment-ready framework for pre-mission multi-robot registration. Our system performs pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment and actively rejects impossible pose hypotheses via deterministic plausibility checks. We validate the framework on a real-world custom dataset of four synchronized robots in various environments with ground truth. The checks reject more than a third of the incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting less than 1% of the correct ones, and reduce the number of team registrations with a wrong robot pose by 38%. Dataset and code are publicly available.

Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) accelerate search and rescue (SAR) operations by covering large disaster sites in parallel [1, 2]. To coordinate safely, these robots rely on multi-robot simultaneous localization and mapping (MR-SLAM). While MR-SLAM is a rapidly advancing field, unconditionally deploying these systems in unstructured, ad-hoc disaster zones remains a severe practical challenge. A fundamental prerequisite for such missions is initial inter-robot registration: before any collaborative mapping can begin, every robot must establish its pose within a shared reference frame (Fig. 1).

To coordinate safely, these robots rely on multi-robot simultaneous localization and mapping (MR-SLAM). While MR-SLAM is a rapidly advancing field, unconditionally deploying these systems in unstructured, ad-hoc disaster zones remains a severe practical challenge. A fundamental prerequisite for such missions is initial inter-robot registration: before any collaborative mapping can begin, every robot must establish its pose within a shared reference frame (Fig. 1).

Some MR-SLAM frameworks require a coarse initial relative pose [2]. Others attempt to build the shared frame as the robots cross paths during exploration [3, 4, 5]. Yet, immediate alignment is an important requirement for field deployments. Operators need a unified view to safely coordinate the initial rollout, and downstream SLAM algorithms benefit from a solid starting estimate to prevent early divergence. Standard workarounds bridge this gap using manual calibration, external infrastructure, or GNSS. In ad-hoc, unstructured environments, these dependencies introduce critical single points of failure.

papers.title: LocoMuJoCo: A Comprehensive Imitation Learning Benchmark for Whole-Body Control
papers.abstract: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.

papers.intro:
Humanoid robots have advanced rapidly in recent years, and improvements in hardware have made the sim-to-real transfer of learned controllers increasingly practical. Because humans and humanoid robots share broadly similar embodiments, human motion data provide an abundant source of training demonstrations. Despite this progress, the imitation learning (IL)/reinforcement learning (RL)benchmarking landscape remains fragmented across single-robot codebases, manipulation-only suites, and toy locomotion tasks, forcing researchers to re-implement data pipelines, retargeting methods, simulators, and evaluation metrics whenever they change embodiments.

papers.title: DUV (257 nm) LIDT of Anti-Reflective Coatings
papers.abstract: Laser-induced damage threshold in the deep ultraviolet (DUV) was used to perform tests on AR coated windows intended for industrial processes. The 257 nm wavelength was generated from Yb:YAG fundamental (1030 nm) and the long-term LIDT stability (up to 100000 shots) was selected as representative for minimal industrial qualification. Selected setup for the fourth harmonics generation consists of two stages, generation of second harmonic and subsequently the fourth harmonic with 13,4% conversation efficiency. In both 1-on-1 and S-on-1 experiments, the optics coated with Al2O3/SiO2 by ion beam sputtering technique demonstrated the highest LIDT value of 0.73 and 0.5 J/cm2 respectively. Various damage morphologies, color centers, ballistic damage, delamination, and blistering were observed across the samples with respect to the 1-on-1 and S-on-1.

papers.title: Twisted Verlinde formulas for cyclic orbifolds and the order-two simple current of a vertex operator superalgebra
papers.abstract:
Let $V=\Vev\oplus J$ be a simple vertex operator superalgebra with $\Vev$ simple, rational and $C_2$-cofinite, and let $G$ be a finite cyclic group acting faithfully on $\Vev$. For arbitrary twisted $V$-modules we prove: (1) for $G$ of arbitrary order, a twisted Verlinde formula for $\Vev$; (2) unitarity of the orbifold $S$-matrix block in generating sectors; (3) as a consequence, a formula for $N^{X_3}_{X_1,X_2}\pm N^{J\boxtimes X_3}_{X_1,X_2}$ as sums over $J$-orbits of $G$-stable untwisted modules, in which $J$-fixed points enter with weight two and in the minus sign, with a parity selection rule (read in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$) and a dimension sum rule; (4) simplicity of $V^G$. These results concern the $G$-graded fusion category of $\Vev$ together with the order two invertible object $J$ with $\theta_J=-\dim_qJ$.
  The statements are tested numerically on six
  examples (odd and even orders up to $15$, both signs of $\dim_qJ$, $J$-fixed modules).

papers.title: A novel pathway to stellar-mass black hole growth: Re-accretion of gas from stellar wind bubbles
papers.abstract: The formation of high-mass stellar black holes (BHs) observed in mergers by gravitational wave observatories remains difficult to explain using standard models of stellar evolution. We investigate whether newly formed stellar-mass BHs in dense molecular clouds can significantly increase their final mass by accreting gas from pre-existing, wind-blown interstellar bubbles produced by their progenitor stars. We performed 1D and 3D hydrodynamic simulations of interstellar bubbles driven by stellar feedback, incorporating thermal conduction, radiative cooling, gravity, ionizing radiation, stellar winds, and supernova (SN) explosions. We modeled the subsequent accretion onto the central BH for two formation scenarios: core-collapse SN and direct collapse. Our parameter space study encompasses over 500 1D simulations, varying initial cloud densities, gravitational binding energies, progenitor masses ($40-257\,M_\odot$), and metallicities ($0.66\,Z_\odot$ and $0.016\,Z_\odot$), and tracks the bubble evolution for millions of years post-BH formation. Scenarios exhibiting significant re-accretion were further validated using high-resolution 3D simulations. Our simulations show that BHs formed via direct collapse from low-metallicity progenitors can accrete up to $6.9\,M_\odot$ of gas from massive inner shells formed by late-stage slow winds, resulting in final BH masses of up to $93\,M_\odot$. Conversely, we find no significant re-accretion in scenarios involving an SN explosion or high-metallicity progenitors; in these cases, fast winds or SN ejecta efficiently evacuate dense structures from the bubble interior, leaving behind a hot, low-density medium. [abridged] This mechanism may help explain the unexpectedly high masses of BHs observed in gravitational wave events.

papers.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.

papers.intro:
Video generators are increasingly evaluated as world models that predict how objects move, collide and interact [34, 37, 53]. Yet few-step sampling exposes a striking leaderboard puzzle. PhaseLock [19] observed that CogVideoX [57] scores higher on Physics-IQ [34] after 2 denoising steps than after 50. Measuring reduced low-frequency phase coherence across those steps, PhaseLock guided sampling with a two-step prior to raise official scores across three models. In the generated videos themselves, however, two-step outputs blur moving objects, agree across seeds and stop moving early (a, Fig. 2). Judge-based evaluation points the opposite way: on PhyWorldBench [17], which rates physical realism without a reference recording, Open-Sora improves with more denoising steps.

Why can visibly degraded videos score higher on a reference-based physics benchmark? Film the same experiment twice, and small unseen differences send the two takes down distinct trajectories (a). A calibrated world model represents this distribution of possible futures, drawing one plausible branch per seed instead of aiming at a single outcome. Physics video benchmarks, however, usually compare one generated video with one real recording [34, 42]: Physics-IQ releases two takes of each scene, yet scores every sample against take 1 alone and uses take 2 only for normalization. When nature takes another branch, a faithful draw lands far away, while a middle-ground prediction stays closer on average. Weather models trained with MSE likewise “hedge their bets” by predicting a blurry mean state with low RMSE [44]. Meanwhile, a large human study asks whether metrics should target “a specific observed outcome” or “the broader space of physically plausible outcomes” [43]. A basic question remains open for reference benchmarks: how much of the few-step gain reflects a closer predictive distribution, and how much comes from score-induced hedging?

Our key insight is that single-sample distance splits exactly. Consider any negative-type distance, meaning one embeddable as squared Euclidean distance in a feature space [49]. For any such distance, the expected distance between one sample and one recording equals a proper kernel score plus half the model’s self-dispersion, an identity from forecast verification [13, 10]. We show that every Physics-IQ component belongs to this class, namely pixel MSE and the three thresholded motion-mask IoUs with their empty-mask convention, as does PhaseLock’s phase-coherence diagnostic on a fixed frequency support. Because half self-dispersion depends only on pairs of model outputs and never sees the recording, shrinking dispersion improves the single-sample score whenever it saves more than the kernel score loses. We call the gain bought this way the dispersion premium. A branching pendulum gives this premium physical geometry. When two valid futures swing left and right, their mean position sits on the chord midpoint inside the arc like a shorter pendulum, saving under squared distance exactly the drop in squared length; in pixels it is a double exposure. On binary masks, where superimposing paths fails, uncertain motion rewards standing still.

The identity and kernel-score properness are classical; our contribution is to make them operational for a physics benchmark built from thresholded masks and an empty-mask convention, and to show that this changes conclusions about real world models (). First, we show that any official Physics-IQ difference on a fixed scene set splits with the official weights into a kernel part and a dispersion premium. Second, we introduce Kernel Physics-IQ, an unbiased two-sample score normalized by 52 non-duplicate take pairs that replaces pixel MSE (whose kernel sees only the pixel mean) with full-video RMS. Third, across five image-to-video world models, we show that default two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ for every model (b). On CogVideoX, its +0.055+0.055 official gain reflects a 0.200 dispersion premium hiding a 0.145 kernel loss, as cross-seed overlap jumps far faster than overlap with the recording. At fixed weights across CogVideoX, Cosmos and Wan2.1, shifting only the two-step node raises Kernel Physics-IQ with no detected official difference (Fig. 5a). Finally, in synthetic worlds with known distributions, official scoring ties faithful sampling with one-outcome predictors and mixtures with wrong probabilities, whereas Kernel Physics-IQ ranks the true distribution highest. Adding one sample per condition removes the incentive to hedge in expectation, so we recommend reporting Kernel Physics-IQ alongside sample dispersion.

papers.title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge
papers.abstract: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.
papers.intro:
I trust the computational devices that surround me almost blindly. I trust my smartphone for GPS navigation, I trust my laptop to recognize my thumb for unlocking and so on. Yet, sometimes these devices fail in various ways: an incorrect route might be calculated, a thumbprint might not be recognized, etc. These acts of failure, as long as there are not too many of them, however, generally do not erode my trust in these devices. I keep on using them and view them rather as just exceptions that we might keep an eye out for. Of course, it might lead to smaller or larger inconveniences from time to time but that is part of the deal: to trust is to open oneself to potential risks and vulnerabilities. I am fairly confident I am not alone in this and that many other people, or even institutions, conduct themselves daily in a similar manner.

The notion of computational trust at play here is not a new concept but its importance is felt much more keenly in recent years with the latest advent of AI chatbots, LLMs, and blackboxed algorithmically guided decision procedures in general. There is already a large number of formal models of computational trust on the market [12, 6], however, they often seem to lack certain philosophical and logical simplicity one might expect for a notion as basic as trust [17]. Or perhaps, “basic” is not the right word, but trust definitely does not seem much more complex notion than notions such as knowledge or belief, which have been stable topics in western philosophy from very early on and we have simple yet powerful models for them based on epistemic interpretation of modal logic, initiated in modern era by von Wright [40] and Hintikka [27] in the 50s and 60s.

papers.title: Large transformation strain of $\mathrm{Ni}_{50}\mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Ga}_{27}$ microwires produced by the Taylor-Ulitovsky method
papers.abstract: The martensitic transformation and associated tensile strain of $\mathrm{Ni}_{50}\mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Ga}_{27}$ microwires produced by the Taylor--Ulitovsky method were investigated using thermomechanical analysis, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and in-situ tensile X-ray diffraction (XRD). EBSD mapping at room temperature reveals cubic austenite in a nonstrained part of the microwire and tetragonal martensite in the strained part. Both EBSD and XRD show that both austenite and martensite have $[001]$ directions approximately parallel to the wire axis. The axial transformation strain calculated from the measured lattice parameters is approximately $15.4\%$. Thermal cycling under constant stresses of $20\text{--}100~\mathrm{MPa}$ reveals experimental transformation strains of $13.2\text{--}14.0\%$. Increasing tensile stress raises the transformation temperatures, with a stress--temperature slope of approximately $1.52~\mathrm{MPa}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$, comparable to that reported for $[001]$-oriented $\mathrm{Ni\text{--}Fe\text{--}Ga}$ single crystals. Overall, the observations confirm that the large macroscopic strain of up to $14.0\%$ relates to the nearly complete martensitic transformation in the microwire.
