papers.intro:
Taylor-Ulitovsky glass-coated microwires represent a unique class of metallic materials produced through the simultaneous drawing of a molten metallic core enclosed within a softened glass capillary [18, 21]. This technique enables the fabrication of continuous composite microwires with metallic core diameters ranging from submicrometer dimensions to several tens of micrometers while maintaining excellent geometric control and reproducibility [2]. Microwires from the Taylor-Ulitovsky method exhibit microstructures that can differ significantly from those obtained by conventional bulk casting routes [4, 6, 17]. The method allows continuous production of wire lengths extending to several kilometers, making it attractive for large-scale manufacturing [2]. These advantages have stimulated increasing interest in Taylor-Ulitovsky microwires for sensing, actuation, magnetic, and shape-memory applications, where miniaturization and high functional performance are essential [2, 5, 8, 12].

This technique enables the fabrication of continuous composite microwires with metallic core diameters ranging from submicrometer dimensions to several tens of micrometers while maintaining excellent geometric control and reproducibility [2]. Microwires from the Taylor-Ulitovsky method exhibit microstructures that can differ significantly from those obtained by conventional bulk casting routes [4, 6, 17]. The method allows continuous production of wire lengths extending to several kilometers, making it attractive for large-scale manufacturing [2]. These advantages have stimulated increasing interest in Taylor-Ulitovsky microwires for sensing, actuation, magnetic, and shape-memory applications, where miniaturization and high functional performance are essential [2, 5, 8, 12].

Reversible transformations between the ordered cubic L21 austenitic phase and modulated martensitic structures provide the basis for their shape-memory behavior [9, 8], while their magnetic coupling enables additional functionalities such as magnetocaloric effects [20, 12].

papers.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
papers.abstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD

papers.title: Post-Hopf structures on $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and post-Lie bialgebras
papers.abstract: We classify post-Hopf structures on the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, for $q\in\mathbb{C}^\times$ not a root of unity, proving that there are exactly three isomorphism classes. We then investigate the semiclassical limits of post-Hopf quantized universal enveloping algebras and derive a compatibility condition between the induced post-Lie product and Lie cobracket. This leads to the notion of a post-Lie bialgebra. We construct a nontrivial topological post-Hopf structure on $U_\hbar(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and determine its semiclassical limit. For the standard Lie bialgebra structure on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, we classify all compatible post-Lie products up to isomorphism and show that the nontrivial class admits a quantization. Finally, we formulate the general quantization problem for post-Lie bialgebras.

papers.intro:
Quantum groups originated in the study of quantum integrable systems and have since become fundamental objects in several areas of mathematics and mathematical physics. One of the first examples appearing in the literature was the quantum deformation of the universal enveloping algebra U⁡(𝔰​𝔩2)U(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}) introduced by Kulish and Reshetikhin [11]. This construction was subsequently generalized by Drinfeld and Jimbo to quantum enveloping algebras Uq​(𝔤)U_{q}(\mathfrak{g}) associated with semisimple Lie algebras 𝔤\mathfrak{g} [5, 9]. The passage to the semiclassical limit revealed the underlying structure of a Lie bialgebra, namely a Lie algebra equipped with a compatible Lie cobracket, and naturally led to the converse question of whether every Lie bialgebra admits a quantization [4]. This problem was solved by Etingof and Kazhdan, who constructed a quantization functor from Lie bialgebras to quantized universal enveloping algebras (QUEAs) [6]. Moreover, in the sixth paper of their series, they proved that their quantization of a Kac–Moody Lie bialgebra with its standard quasitriangular structure is isomorphic to the corresponding Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum group [7].

papers.title: Thinflow: Organizing HPC Benchmarking Campaigns as Rerunnable Directory Trees
papers.abstract: A benchmarking campaign provides the measurements behind an HPC performance study: code variants are built, swept over core or node counts, and measured repeatedly. Moving such a campaign to another supercomputer or rerunning it months later requires work that is not part of the study itself. Job scripts are adapted to each supercomputer, and what exactly ran is often reconstructed afterwards. We present Thinflow, a small Bash engine for organizing HPC benchmarking campaigns as rerunnable directory trees of tasks and runs. A task is a directory with a short shell script next to the code. For each sweep, one command builds the code, runs the benchmarks, and plots the results. Thinflow derives the execution order from declared dependencies and writes it to a plain-text manifest. Per-supercomputer profiles submit the runs to a workload manager such as Slurm. Each run writes a provenance record of its environment, hardware, and parameters. The engine ships inside the campaign directory, so a campaign stays rerunnable without installing a separate tool and, once completed, may serve as a paper artifact. In a case study, we ran one campaign with identical task files on three Slurm partitions of two supercomputers, on up to 16 nodes. This strong-scaling study of matrix multiplication in C/OpenMP, C/MPI, and Julia/MPI comprises 37 task files with 217 non-comment lines. Its 455 benchmark runs recorded what differed per partition, chiefly profiles and command-line parameters. This suggests that such a campaign needs little structure beyond plain shell files.

papers.intro:
Performance studies in HPC rest on benchmarking campaigns: several variants of a code are built, each variant is swept over core counts, node counts, or problem sizes, every point is repeated to quantify variability, and the measurements end up in the figures of a paper. Moving such a campaign to another supercomputer, rerunning it months later, or handing it to a coauthor, reviewer, or reader requires work that is not part of the study itself. Job scripts are adapted to each supercomputer, failed runs are found and resubmitted, and what exactly ran is often reconstructed afterwards.

They differ in scope: JUBE targets systematic benchmark studies of any size, ReFrame targets regression and performance testing across supercomputers, and Benchpark shares benchmark and system specifications across sites. We explore one small corner of the same design space: a single, paper-sized campaign that its authors write, run on a few supercomputers, and publish together with the engine that runs it. We ask whether a few conventions on top of plain shell files suffice to move such a campaign between supercomputers and to record what ran.

In this paper, we present Thinflow 11 1 https://github.com/ums-cpl/task-driven-experimentation, a small Bash engine that organizes such a campaign as a directory tree of tasks and runs. A task is a unit of work, such as compiling a code variant, running a benchmark, or plotting results. A run is one execution of a task, for example one repetition of one point of a parameter sweep. Thinflow has the following five properties: P1 A task is a directory with a short shell script and optional KEY=VALUE settings, settings are inherited along the tree, and each run has its own output directory. Thinflow derives the execution order from declared dependencies and writes it to a plain-text manifest before anything is submitted. P2 Job submission is confined to per-supercomputer profiles, so the engine is workload-manager agnostic. Once a campaign’s tasks avoid values specific to one supercomputer, moving it to another means writing profiles and setting parameters, not editing tasks. P3 Every run writes a provenance record next to its output (environment, hardware, parameters, git state) and marks its outcome, so failed runs can be listed and rerun on their own. P4 The engine is a set of Bash scripts that is copied into each campaign and needs no installation. P5 Tasks can call anything, such as compilers, MPI launchers, Julia, gnuplot, or Python.

papers.title: A joint framework for SPX, VIX and VXX
papers.abstract: Options on VXX bring the dynamics of the VIX futures curve into the joint SPX-VIX calibration problem. We construct a common model by specifying the VIX and then recovering instantaneous SPX variance from the requirement that its risk-neutral conditional expected average over the next thirty days equals the squared VIX. With truncated signatures of time-extended polynomial diffusions, this recovery reduces to finite-dimensional linear algebra and gives explicit access to the futures underlying VXX. The same specification therefore governs equity variance and rolling volatility exposure. To accommodate flexible specifications while respecting variance nonnegativity, we develop a regularized model and quantify the pricing errors of its tractable VIX and VXX proxies. Applications to short-dated option smiles illustrate joint calibration across the three markets, with Monte Carlo estimates of the proxy error bounds well below quoted bid-ask spreads.

papers.intro:
Options on the S&P 500 index (SPX\mathrm{SPX}), the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX\mathrm{VIX}), and the iPath S&P 500 VIX Short-Term Futures ETN (VXX\mathrm{VXX}) price different aspects of the same volatility risk. The VIX links equity options to risk-neutral expected future variance, while VXX turns exposure to the volatility futures curve into a traded investment product. Their option markets therefore impose distinct constraints on a common set of dynamics. A joint model must accommodate these constraints while preserving the relations that connect the equity index, the volatility index, and the rolling futures strategy.

The additional modeling content of VXX comes from the roll. The note tracks a strategy in the first two VIX futures contracts, with weights adjusted to maintain short-term exposure; see Barclays Bank PLC (2018). Its evolution depends on the level and shape of the futures curve and on the joint dynamics of the contracts entering the strategy. Consequently, the information relevant to VXX options extends beyond the marginal VIX distributions at individual maturities. The empirical findings of Lu (2023), who documents that VXX option information is not fully spanned by VIX options, support this distinction. Incorporating VXX into a joint calibration thus makes the dynamics of rolling volatility exposure an additional part of the modeling problem.

The joint SPX–VIX calibration problem has generated a broad range of models, motivated in particular by the need to reconcile the pronounced downside skew of SPX options with the increasing implied-volatility smile of VIX options. Affine and jump specifications have been studied in Cont and Kokholm (2013); Baldeaux and Badran (2014), while Papanicolaou and Sircar (2014) and Fouque and Saporito (2018) develop regime-switching and stochastic vol-of-vol models, respectively. Continuous models include quadratic rough Heston in Gatheral et al. (2020), the quintic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model in Abi Jaber et al. (2023), and the path-dependent specifications in Guyon and Lekeufack (2023); Guyon and Mustapha (2023) study neural calibration. A complementary line of work formulates calibration directly under consistency constraints, using optimal transport in Guo et al. (2022) and dispersion-constrained martingale Schrödinger problems in Guyon (2024). These contributions provide different ways of matching the two option markets while respecting the relation between equity returns and future variance.

The literature on VIX derivatives and volatility-linked notes addresses a further part of this structure. Direct models for VIX futures and options provide tractable descriptions of the volatility-index market; see Lin and Chang (2010); Mencía and Sentana (2013). The investment and trading properties of volatility exchange-traded products are studied in Alexander and Korovilas (2013); Avellaneda and Papanicolaou (2019). Grasselli and Wagalath (2020) derive an analytical link between VIX and VXX, and Grasselli et al. (2024) develop a framework for their joint option calibration. More recently, Lu (2023) examines the role of volatility clustering, and Lu (2025) uses a discrete-time analytical framework to incorporate information from high-frequency VIX data. These works show how the futures curve and the rolling rule shape VXX dynamics. The present paper embeds this relationship in a model that also retains the connection to SPX variance and options.

Recovering equity variance from prescribed volatility-index dynamics is itself a consistency problem. Badran and Goldys (2015) derive restrictions for jointly modeling VIX futures and equity derivatives, and Papanicolaou (2022) formulates and studies the inverse problem of recovering stochastic volatility from a VIX market model. The latter work identifies both solvability and nonnegativity of the recovered variance as central requirements. Our contribution is a finite-dimensional signature realization of this inverse construction, coupled with the VXX rolling strategy and quantitative control of the approximations used in calibration.

The mathematical structure comes from combining polynomial processes with path signatures. Affine models and their polynomial extensions offer tractable conditional moments and, in the affine case, transform methods; see Duffie et al. (2003); Cuchiero et al. (2012); Filipović and Larsson (2016). Signatures, rooted in Chen’s work on iterated integrals Chen (1954) and subsequently developed within rough-path theory Lyons (1998); Lyons et al. (2007); Friz and Victoir (2010), encode a path through its iterated integrals and provide a systematic family of coordinates for path-dependent models. Their financial applications include pricing and hedging in Lyons et al. (2020), optimal stopping in Bayer et al. (2023), and model calibration in Cuchiero et al. (2023). The affine and polynomial structure of signature dynamics is developed in Cuchiero et al. (2026). For polynomial primary diffusions, truncated signatures retain a finite-dimensional polynomial structure, and their conditional expectations can be computed by matrix exponentials.

papers.title: Exploring Semantic Table Search in Data Lakes
papers.abstract: Discovery of relevant datasets within data lakes remains a key challenge. Union and join search are effective techniques for discovering data when augmenting an existing table. In exploratory search, instead, keyword search is commonly adopted to find a relatively small set of highly relevant tables matching some search terms. In this context, semantic search is a new technique that exploits the presence of named entities in exemplar tuples used as queries and in target tables. Hence, keyword search and entity search are able to find a diverse set of tables. In this work, we propose \texttt{Thetis++}, which combines keyword and semantic table search to discover relevant tables that combine the semantic signal with the presence of exact keyword matches. Incorporating multiple paradigms and sources of information allow us to combine the best of multiple worlds. Therefore, we study many alternative techniques for combining rankings and evaluate these for the table search task in data lakes. We explore both unsupervised and supervised techniques, including TOPSIS. Finally, alternative to Thetis++ combining keyword and semantic relevance signals, we study a variant of learning-to-rank for the table search task in data lakes. Our evaluation highlights both the limitations of many standard approaches along with some promising directions offered by learned approaches. Furthermore, while indexes for keyword search are quite efficient, here we provide insights into how to improve the scalability of prefiltering techniques for semantic search, comparing LSH indexes with Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds. Our experiments show that HNSW drastically improves the runtime of semantic table search by 4.7X on average whilst retaining the high-quality tables. Together, our findings plot the line for effective and efficient data discovery techniques for semantic data lakes.

papers.intro:
In recent years, data lakes have become a primary choice for storing heterogeneous data within organizations Esmailoghli et al. (2026); Schmid et al. (2019); Dibowski and Schmid (2021). The high flexibility of data lakes allows, among others, to ingest data independently from the source, the domain, and the application for which it has been produced. As a result, data lakes contain an increasing number of distinct, heterogeneous datasets with varying structures, leading to a high level of complexity and diversity in both data formats and content Schmid et al. (2019). This also presents unmatched challenges for organizations in terms of data integration and data exploration workflows Chapman et al. (2020); Miller (2018).

In this work, we focus specifically on the task of data discovery, where the main challenge is to find the right data to solve a given data science problem Miller (2018); Chai et al. (2022). This is also important in RAG systems, where finding the right data enables the system to produce high-quality answers to a user query Wei et al. (2025). For example, a data scientist aiming to understand a given phenomenon is frequently aware of some data describing it and still needs to search and retrieve all the other tables in the data lake with additional relevant data 11 1 Although data lakes can store any data format, in this work, we focus specifically on CSV tables and in JSON data flattened in the form of a table.. However, in large-scale setups, we cannot expect data scientists to be aware of all available datasets. Instead, data scientists may more easily be aware of entity names describing relevant items or concepts. When a user is able to list relevant entities, they can employ an entity-centric approach, where user queries are composed of example entities of interest Mottin et al. (2016); Lissandrini et al. (2018). This type of data discovery requires that entities, their relationships, and concepts of interest are tracked across the entire data lake. Knowledge graphs (KGs) Schmid et al. (2019); Sequeda et al. (2019); Noy et al. (2019) are a key data model for modeling entities, relationships, and their occurrences in different datasets. KGs form a heterogeneous network of entities, their attributes, and relationships among them - usually stored as RDF graphs Manola and Miller (2004). Hence, KGs can be employed to tackle the problem of tracking the tables connected to the entities of interest (see the example in Figure 1a). In this context, a natural question arises w.r.t. information discovery and dataset search: How to find the most relevant tables for a given set of entities of interest?

Semantic relevance search Christensen et al. (2025) is an alternative to existing table search methods and has a different goal from other search methods (see Figure 2): it consists of ranking tables by their semantic relevance to a set of example entity tuples as input query Christensen et al. (2025). This differs from keyword search, where tables are retrieved based on syntactic similarity to a set of input keywords; thus, retrieving a smaller set of relevant tables (i.e., only tables T​3T3 and T​5T5 are retrievable in Figure 1b). Furthermore, semantic relevance search results should be ranked based on the semantics behind the user intent instead of implicit relevance derived from the frequencies of the token matches. To overcome these limitations, we exploit the semantic relatedness of the contents of a table through the links to the KG (as in Figure 1a), enabling semantic similarity between table entities22 2 We consider entities to be within cells; thus, each row can contain multiple entities.. In the past, semantic data lakes have been limited to direct mappings between the schema of each table and the schema of a KG, i.e., making the KG a global view integrating the data of each table Endris et al. (2019); Mami et al. (2019); Hai et al. (2016). This approach requires a prohibitive amount of manual annotations to reconcile dataset schemas to match the reference KG Sequeda et al. (2019); Ilyas et al. (2022). A different approach is instead to identify entity mentions in the datasets and link only those mentions to the entities in the KG. This entity linking process can be easily automated with little human supervision Ritze and Bizer (2017); Bhagavatula et al. (2015); Tyagi and Jimenez-Ruiz (2020). Hence, we remove the limiting requirement of aligning all datasets to a KG, and we directly exploit entity linking annotations. Importantly, our approach can work even in the common case that the KGs have only partial coverage over the data lake, i.e., not all data lake entity mentions need to be linked to the reference KG. Finally, given entity linking annotations, we can exploit any information encoded in a KG to accommodate any semantic entity similarity.

papers.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
papers.abstract: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.

papers.intro:
Obtaining a class label may require a human annotator, expert assessment, diagnostic procedure, or user interaction. A query does not always produce a label: an annotator may decline an ambiguous case, an expert may find the available information insufficient, or a user may not respond. This raises two questions for active learning: which observations should be queried, and how should the possibility and the observed pattern of response affect query selection?

Classical active learning allocates a limited labeling budget by selectively requesting labels (Lewis and Gale, 1994; Lewis and Catlett, 1994; Settles, 2009). papers.title: Iterative constructions of semifields 2-dimensional over a nucleus
papers.abstract: The construction of finite semifields dates back to Dickson's work in 1906. To the best of our knowledge, only two iterative constructions were previously known: those of Hiramine, Matsumoto and Oyama in 1987, and of Kantor and Williams in 2004. The latter yields, for suitable even orders, superpolynomially many pairwise non-isotopic semifields. In this paper, we use skew-polynomial rings to give a new iterative construction of finite semifields. This construction produces large families of pairwise non-isotopic semifields, each of which is $2$-dimensional over one of its nuclei. In particular, we show that this construction method yields semifields not contained in any family of semifields known so far.

papers.intro:
Finite semifields are finite not-necessarily associative unital division algebras. Semifields have received a lot of attention in the last around 100 years, starting with the work of Dickson [6] who constructed the first finite semifield that is not a field. Dickson’s motivation to study semifields was purely of algebraic nature. Subsequent inquiries into constructions and properties of semifields were often motivated by applications in both pure and applied mathematics, with semifields for instance exhibiting an intimate relation to non-Desarguesian projective planes in finite geometry [17] as well as optimal rank-metric codes [33].

The probably most fundamental question on finite semifields is about their ubiquity. Kantor [15] asks if the number of non-isotopic semifields grows superpolynomially in the order of the semifield, providing an affirmative answer in the case of even order semifields [16]. In the odd order case, this question is still wide open. Indeed, the current best known bound is not even linear in the order of the semifield [9]. This suggests that current constructions of odd order semifields are severely lacking. In particular, mimicking the approach of [16] that led to the superpolynomial count for even order semifields seems instructive. One key reason why Kantor and Williams [16] were able to achieve these counts was that their construction relied on an iterative approach, starting with a known semifield.

In this paper, we attempt a similar approach, realizing an iterative construction of semifields starting from a known family of semifields. We are however unable to achieve the superpolynomial count using our construction. However, our new construction still yields some very interesting results: Firstly, outside of the Kantor-Williams construction and the Hiramine-Matsumoto-Oyama (HMO) construction [10], our construction is the only iterative construction of semifields, opening the door to future refinements to attack Kantor’s question on the number of odd order non-isotopic semifields. We expect that the techniques we develop here can yield crucial tools for a potential resolution of this question. While that is also probably a reason why the number of non-isotopic members in this family is not large enough to resolve Kantor’s conjecture, the counts we do achieve show that the number of such semifields is still surprisingly large. Since nuclei lead for instance immediately to large autotopism groups (as well as collineation groups for the related projective planes), our construction thus yields many non-isotopic examples of highly symmetric semifields and semifield planes.

papers.title: Distortion in Online Voting
papers.abstract:
We initiate the study of distortion in online voting, a framework that bridges computational social choice and online algorithms. In contrast to the classical offline setting, where the full election instance is known in advance, we consider a dynamic environment where a fixed set of voters is present from the beginning, but alternatives arrive sequentially over time. Upon each arrival, a mechanism must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to retain the currently selected candidate or switch to the newly arriving one, operating solely on the partial ordinal rankings induced by the underlying cardinal preferences.
  We provide upper and lower bounds for deterministic and randomized mechanisms under two standard cardinal preference frameworks.
  Utilitarian framework: For deterministic mechanisms under adversarial arrival order, we establish an $\Omega(mn)$ lower bound and give an matching online algorithm with distortion at most $\frac{2}{3}m(n+\frac{1}{4})$. For randomized rules, we introduce regularity, which allows any regular, order-independent offline randomized rule to be converted into an online rule with the same expected distortion. The Harmonic voting rule satisfies this property, yielding online distortion $O(\sqrt{m\log m})$.
  Metric framework: For deterministic mechanisms, maintaining an alternative within a $\varphi$-weighted uncovered set guarantees distortion $2+\sqrt{5}$. We show that matching-based offline rules achieving distortion $3$ cannot be directly implemented online. We establish a lower bound of $\sqrt{13}$, even with three alternatives, and a matching upper bound for three alternatives and any number of voters. For randomized mechanisms, regularity gives an online distortion of $3-\frac{2}{n}$ via Random Dictatorship.

Following classical decision-theoretic models [30], each agent assigns a cardinal value to every alternative, representing either its cost or its utility. Since ordinal rankings retain only the relative order of alternatives and discard cardinal information, voting rules based solely on rankings may select outcomes that are far from optimal under the underlying cardinal preferences. This inefficiency is captured by the notion of distortion. Online algorithms are among the most extensively studied areas of algorithm design. In this setting, the input is revealed over time rather than given in advance. As new information arrives, the algorithm must make decisions immediately and irrevocably, without knowledge of future inputs. This framework naturally models many real-world scenarios where waiting to observe the full input is impossible or undesirable.

In contrast, most work in voting theory assumes an offline setting, where the full election—both the set of candidates and the preferences of all voters—is known in advance. This assumption is appropriate for traditional elections, where the set of candidates is fixed before voting begins. However, many modern applications of voting are inherently online. For example, in recommendation systems, new items arrive continuously, and the system must repeatedly decide which item to promote based on current user feedback, without knowing future items. Similarly, in hiring or admission processes, candidates may apply over time, and decisions or rankings may need to be updated as new applications arrive rather than after all applications are received. In crowdsourcing platforms, proposals or tasks can appear sequentially, and a selection must be made without access to all future submissions.

This decision is irrevocable: once an alternative is rejected, it cannot be reconsidered later. At each time step, each voter reports a ranking over the set of currently revealed alternatives, and the decision is made based only on these partial rankings. This replacement mechanism follows the established online model with preemption, also called free disposal, studied in online optimization [6, 11]; here the maintained solution consists of a single candidate.

papers.title: Reading Across Space, Time and Frequencies: Tensor Decomposition of SEEG Signals to Support Epileptogenic Zone Definition
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) is an invasive technique used in the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy to support the localization of the Epileptogenic Zone (EZ). SEEG data are particularly complex to analyze, as they include hundreds of components, named channels, each associated with a different brain site, with interactions varying in both time and frequency. In this study, we propose a new framework for SEEG analysis, based on the Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition, to extract the latent modes underlying seizure generation. We model SEEG signals as a third-order tensor (channel x time x frequency), and factorize the tensor into rank-1 factors. We then exploit the channel-specific factor as an unsupervised feature set for identifying the EZ. The framework is validated on SEEG-recorded seizures from 35 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. The results show that the joint combination of multiple frequency bands significantly enhances classification performance.

papers.title: GraphEP: A Calibrated Data System and Benchmark for Learning Cardiac Electrophysiology
papers.abstract: High-fidelity simulations generate spatiotemporal data that are difficult to obtain experimentally, yet their outputs are rarely ready for scientific machine learning. Cardiac electrophysiology (EP) exemplifies this challenge: data reside on anatomy-dependent volumetric meshes, propagation follows anisotropic material fields, and relevant events span multiple temporal scales. We introduce GraphEP, a calibrated data system that converts cardiac meshes and simulation protocols into compact, graph-native trajectories of full-field transmembrane potential. GraphEP includes 732 left-ventricular simulations across 20 anatomies, with healthy and scarred substrates of varying severity and multiple pacing configurations. Each sample provides geometry, tissue and material features, stimulation, connectivity, derived activation targets, and provenance in PyTorch Geometric format. We benchmark four inductive biases for predicting transmembrane potential Vm(t): local message passing, global neural operators, multi-scale hierarchical graph transformers (HGT), and physiology-informed models. The latter include HGT-Lag, which separates activation timing from action-potential morphology, and the stateful Graph Aliev-Panfilov Action-Potential ODE (GAP2ODE), which evolves excitation and recovery autoregressively with frame-wise stimulation and graph diffusion. Results show that wider spatial communication improves on local message passing, while physiological structure provides the strongest inductive bias: HGT-Lag and GAP2ODE lead on complementary metrics by explicitly modeling propagation, recovery, and temporal state. GraphEP offers a reproducible pathway from mechanistic cardiac EP simulations to analysis-ready data and a controlled benchmark for learning on irregular anatomical geometries.

papers.intro:
Cardiac electrophysiology (EP) couples fast, nonlinear cellular dynamics with anisotropic propagation through a three-dimensional myocardium. A simulation is therefore neither a conventional image nor a fixed-sensor time series: every anatomy is represented by a different unstructured volumetric mesh, and every vertex carries a signal characterised by a sharp depolarisation front followed by substantially slower recovery. Moreover, the domain is geometric rather than merely discrete, as conduction depends on local material properties such as fibre, sheet, and sheet-normal directions. Cardiac EP, therefore, offers a useful test bed to learn multi-scale spatiotemporal dynamics on irregular geometries.

Cardiac EP, therefore, offers a useful test bed to learn multi-scale spatiotemporal dynamics on irregular geometries.

The challenge for scientific machine learning (SciML) is not only to solve or approximate the underlying cardiac forward model, but also to transform simulation outputs into a reproducible and analysis-ready data representation. High-fidelity EP cohorts remain expensive to generate and difficult to compare. Therefore, neural surrogates commonly use a fixed or simplified geometry, and simulation outputs are rarely released with reusable graph features Gsell et al. (2024). A cross-anatomy dataset requires consistent geometry processing, physiological calibration, tissue labelling, stimulation protocols, graph construction, feature semantics, target extraction, normalisation, dataset splits, and provenance. Existing components such as openCARP Plank et al. (2021), the ForCEPSS calibration protocol Gsell et al. (2024), and public four-chamber human heart geometries Strocchi et al. (2020) make high-fidelity simulation possible, but are not, on their own, sufficient to define a reusable SciML corpus or benchmark. The quantitative benchmark in this first release is restricted to LV samples. Its split is sample-disjoint but not anatomy-disjoint: all 20 anatomies occur across train, validation, and test, while pacing configurations and pathological manifestations vary between samples. The benchmark, therefore, evaluates the learning of propagation rules across unseen samples on known anatomical identities. In this contribution, we also show biventricular and whole-heart simulations to demonstrate the scope of the generation pipeline as a system ready for SciML data preparation.

papers.title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images
papers.abstract: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.

Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA elements: text, shapes, cutouts, and photographs over a background. Blending these layers produces an alpha-composited image. Keeping these elements separate enables selection, movement, and reuse after generation. Standard text-to-image diffusion [24] instead produces a flattened raster, in which those editing units are entangled.

Keeping these elements separate enables selection, movement, and reuse after generation. Layered models already generate coherent transparent elements, but they share two constraints. First, every layer has its own spatial latent: a full-canvas grid in Qwen-Image-Layered (QIL) [34] and a region grid in MRT [27]. The sequence processed by the denoiser, and with it compute and memory, therefore grows with the number and extent of layers (Section 4.5). Second, structure is decided before content: QIL takes a requested layer count, and MRT a layout that is supplied or estimated beforehand, so the number of layers, and in MRT their placement, is fixed before denoising begins. The two are linked: deciding structure jointly with content means denoising many candidate layers, which is costly when each one is a spatial grid.

The use of a prior layout is analogous to two-stage instance segmentation (e.g., Mask R-CNN [7]): propose regions, then predict instances. As in that setting, the second stage cannot revise what the first provides: a missing or misplaced region is not corrected during layer generation, and the layout must come from a separate model or the user. Inspired by the shared prototype masks and per-instance coefficients in YOLACT [2], we instead factorize a design into a shared spatial grid and layer-specific candidates, extending the idea to joint generation and nonlinear decoding of RGBA layers. We propose a token-per-layer representation. ProtoVAE jointly encodes the layer stack into a shared spatial grid (the prototype) and one candidate vector per layer, including the background. Each candidate summarizes its layer in the context of the full composition and conditions the decoder to reconstruct the corresponding RGBA layer from the shared grid (Figure 2).

papers.title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
papers.abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.

An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) searching for a regional target must decide where to move, when to observe and which predictions to compute. Overhead imagery narrows the search region; current camera observations establish local target evidence. Cross-view benchmarks connect these perspectives (Dai et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2023). Closing the sensing loop adds an operational question: which prediction is worth computing before the vehicle commits its next movement?

Two uncertainties shape that decision. Positive and negative observations update an uncertain overhead prior. Future-view scores are uncertain too. A move may leave the target occluded but enable a useful view one step later. We score reachable views over a short horizon, execute the first move, and replan. A cheap proposer scores candidates before selective WM queries. Several paths may start north. Once north is verified as the best first action, their ranking cannot change it.

papers.title: A variational theory for von K\'arm\'an vortex streets
papers.abstract: We construct von K\'arm\'an vortex streets as global kinetic energy maximizers for the 2D Euler flow in an infinite periodic channel: our variational framework imposes no a prior symmetry, support constraints, or sign conditions on the admissible class. More specifically, under $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ constraint of the absolute vorticity maximum with other natural constraints, we show that the maximizers are traveling pairs of simply connected vortex patches of support radius $O(\varepsilon)$, converging to the von K\'arm\'an point-vortex configuration satisfying glide reflection symmetry as $\varepsilon \to 0$. We prove nonlinear stability of the von K\'arm\'an streets under a bound on the vertical support, using a compactness result valid for more general assumptions. Furthermore, we construct slightly tilted asymmetric von K\'arm\'an vortex streets as energy maximizers under a tilted moment constraint.

papers.title: SGAR: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction via Sparse Geometry-Guided Attention
papers.abstract: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.
papers.intro:
Multi-view scene reconstruction is a long-standing problem in computer vision. Classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) solutions treat this as a geometric estimation problem and solve it with a multi-stage pipeline built on projective geometry and robust optimization. Although effective, SfM methods are based on complex pipelines and produce only sparse reconstructions [36, 34, 53, 38, 46, 37]. Recent feed-forward models such as VGGT [60] and DejaView [8] replace it by a single network that predicts cameras and geometry for all views in a single forward pass, matching or even surpassing the earlier methods in a fraction of the time when the views overlap substantially. At the core of these methods is global attention: The tokens of all views are processed jointly, so that every view is interpreted in the context of every other. This is what makes these approaches so powerful, but also what makes them expensive as the cost of global attention grows quadratically with the total number of views. For example, in DejaView [8], the time cost grows from a few seconds in 100100 views to more than 300300 s in 1,0001{,}000 views on one Nvidia A100 GPU. This severely restricts the applicability of feed-forward models to time-sensitive applications, such as robot navigation, and to providing a fast initialization for optimization-based reconstruction pipelines.

A lightweight projection, trained with a contrastive loss on ground-truth geometry, maps patch tokens into an embedding space in which tokens observing the same surface lie close together. papers.title: Contactless Estimation of Respiratory Frequency Using 3D-CNN on Thermal Images
papers.abstract: Monitoring physiological parameters such as respiratory rate ($f_R$) is essential for diagnosing and managing various pathological conditions. Thermal imaging offers a promising contactless alternative to traditional methods, which often rely on partially invasive sensors or obtrusive wearable systems. However, existing approaches for $f_R$ estimation from thermal signals typically require extensive pre-processing and manual or semi-automatic region-of-interest (ROI) tracking, limiting their practical applicability. This study proposes a deep learning-based method for estimating $f_R$ directly from thermal videos, eliminating the need for complex pre-processing and ROI tracking. A 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) is developed to operate on raw thermal video data. To address challenges related to small datasets, the model is trained using data augmentation and transfer learning from synthetic datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a validation $R^2$ score of approximately 0.61 on both pre-processed and raw thermal videos. By simplifying the workflow, this method holds promise for enhancing the feasibility of thermal imaging in real-world applications, such as remote healthcare and driver monitoring in automotive applications.

papers.intro:
Respiratory rate, also known as respiratory frequency (fRf_{\mathrm{R}}), is a vital sign of significant importance sensitive to different pathological conditions and stressors. Within the healthcare field, it is used for diagnosing, prognosing, and managing pneumonia [1]. Moreover, there is significant evidence indicating that fRf_{\mathrm{R}} serves as a crucial predictor for clinical deterioration and cardiac arrest [2, 3]. In addition, the fRf_{\mathrm{R}} is an indicator in neonatal intensive care units [4, 5]. Indeed, respiratory diseases stand out as a primary cause of morbidity among neonates, with a higher prevalence among preterm infants [6]. Monitoring respiration, specifically fRf_{\mathrm{R}}, aids in detecting sudden infant death syndrome, one of the major causes of death in infants [7, 8]. In the field of psychophysiology, fRf_{\mathrm{R}} serves as a reliable indicator of mental stress and cognitive load. It proves valuable for assessing stress levels not only in workplace and computer-related tasks but also in the contexts of aviation and automotive to assess stress levels or drowsiness in pilots and drivers [2, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Finally, fRf_{\mathrm{R}} is a reliable indicator of physical effort and fatigue [13, 14].

Within the healthcare field, it is used for diagnosing, prognosing, and managing pneumonia [1]. In addition, the fRf_{\mathrm{R}} is an indicator in neonatal intensive care units [4, 5]. Indeed, respiratory diseases stand out as a primary cause of morbidity among neonates, with a higher prevalence among preterm infants [6]. In the field of psychophysiology, fRf_{\mathrm{R}} serves as a reliable indicator of mental stress and cognitive load. It proves valuable for assessing stress levels not only in workplace and computer-related tasks but also in the contexts of aviation and automotive to assess stress levels or drowsiness in pilots and drivers [2, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Finally, fRf_{\mathrm{R}} is a reliable indicator of physical effort and fatigue [13, 14].

Nonetheless, fRf_{\mathrm{R}} remains one of the least documented and underestimated vital signs in clinical practice, mainly due to limitations in current clinical monitoring techniques [15, 14, 16, 17, 3]. Indeed, manual counting of respiratory cycles is still performed in cardio-respiratory resuscitation, posing a challenging task even for trained professionals, and yielding subjective outcomes [3]. Other modalities rely on the attachment of sensors to the patient’s body, which induces stress and discomfort. Indeed, sensor placement in psychophysiology has the limitation of potentially altering the natural psychophysiological behavior of the subject monitored. Furthermore, the removal of adhesive electrodes often leads to epidermal stripping and skin disruption in neonatal intensive care [18]. To overcome these limitations, contactless methods have been proposed to monitor respiration [2]. In particular, InfraRed Thermography (IRT) has been taking hold because of the great advantage of remotely monitoring the infrared radiation emitted by objects, enabling passive and non-intrusive monitoring of skin temperature. Unlike visible recordings, IRT remains unaffected by lighting conditions and can function in the darkness, making it well-suited for monitoring drivers or conducting sleep studies. Notably, respiratory cycles are visible to the naked eye in IRT, as exhaled air, being warmer than inhaled air, generates observable variations in radiation intensity or temperature within the nasal/nostrils region of interest (ROI).

Therefore, most imaging methods for fRf_{\mathrm{R}} monitoring involve identifying and tracking specific features or anatomic landmarks to extract the respiration signal by averaging the temperature of the pixels within a chosen ROI, such as the nose or nostrils, over time. For instance, [19] introduced a network of probabilistic trackers to segment the nostril region and exploited wavelet analysis to reconstruct the breathing information. A related approach was followed in Abbas et al. [20] for neonatal non-contact monitoring of the respiratory activity. The ROI was defined in the first frame and no tracking algorithm was used. Building on this, Pereira et al. [8] manually selected the nose region in the first frame and applied a tracking algorithm to compensate for the motion in the following frames. In [21], the authors proposed a method to automatically detect the respiration region using Canny edge detector. The contribution outlined in [22] consists of a real-time tracking of human nostrils using an ensemble of regression trees. The authors demonstrate its robustness in scenarios involving head motion and object occlusion. Other studies suggested to consider not only temperature modulation around the mouth and nostrils but also the body movements, detecting respiration by blending the temperature change of ROIs and breathing motion [23, 24]. A multi-sensor approach, using both visible and infrared technologies, to increase the robustness and reliability of region detection and tracking has been used in [24, 25]. Similarly, Scebba et al. fused the information obtained in the near-IR and far-IR spectra from the nostril and chest [26]. They extracted multiple streams of respiratory information from independent video modalities and then applied two dedicated data fusion models to determine whether the subject was breathing, and at which frequency. Yet, a noteworthy limitation of these studies lies in the demand for sophisticated algorithms not only to detect and track specific regions of interest but also to accomplish frame registration across diverse modalities. ROI detection to identify the nose in IR videos in order to extract breathing-relevant pixels can be particularly challenging if the videos have low contrast or suffer from suboptimal focusing. These conditions may compromise the overall robustness of the approach, making accurate ROI detection more challenging and potentially affecting the reliability of breathing signal extraction. To skip the region selection and tracking procedure, Scebba et al. [27] extracted respiration signals based on pixel time series, avoiding image segmentation. However, they cropped the frames around the nose, making the algorithm still region-based. A grid-based approach, which does not use any anatomical region selection, was proposed in [18] to estimate fRf_{\mathrm{R}}. A signal quality index was empirically developed to automatically distinguish ROI in the video containing the respiratory signal from those containing only noise. They used Bayesian fusion of the selected ROIs to get robust estimations for fRf_{\mathrm{R}}. The major drawback of the proposed algorithm is the sensitivity to motion artifacts. Moreover, both ROI-based and grid-based approaches require adequate pre-processing of the recordings to ensure a reasonable signal to noise ratio of the extracted breathing signal.

papers.title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

papers.intro:
Sequential training can severely degrade neural network performance on previously learned tasks, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989). Continual learning (CL) aims to adapt to changing tasks while retaining acquired knowledge. Evaluation typically relies on task-boundary measures such as final performance, forgetting, and backward transfer, which can overlook temporary failures during adaptation. In supervised CL, De Lange et al. De Lange et al. (2023) identified the stability gap: a sharp drop in previous-task performance after a task transition, followed by partial or complete recovery. This gap can occur even when all past-task data remain available (Hess et al., 2024), a setting referred to as incremental joint-training.

In supervised CL, De Lange et al. De Lange et al. (2023) identified the stability gap: a sharp drop in previous-task performance after a task transition, followed by partial or complete recovery. This gap can occur even when all past-task data remain available (Hess et al., 2024), a setting referred to as incremental joint-training.

Whether a stability gap also occurs in continual reinforcement learning (CRL) remains unexplored. Existing CRL evaluations emphasize final performance, or they look at transfer and forgetting measured only at task boundaries or after convergence (Wołczyk et al., 2021). Temporary performance drops may therefore have remained hidden. To isolate these dynamics, we introduce a lightweight transformed-state benchmark inspired by Permuted-MNIST (Goodfellow et al., 2013). Tasks share environment dynamics, rewards, and action spaces but apply different orthogonal transformations to the state representation. We compare value-based and actor-critic algorithms across discrete and continuous action spaces, using frequent evaluation of past tasks to test whether a stability gap arises in CRL.

papers.title: What Places an Action Boundary? Structure-Aware Attribution for Temporal Action Localization
papers.abstract: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.

papers.intro:
Temporal action localization (TAL) is a fundamental task in video understanding, with many downstream applications [48]. For each action instance in an untrimmed video, a TAL detector predicts its class label together with its start and end times. Of these outputs, the start and end times are the bottleneck: localization error was found to be the most significant error, and predictions with localization errors can still be among the highest-scored [2, 54]. Detector designs attribute this to the classifier relying on discriminative content that is less informative about boundary placement [58, 31, 16]. However, to our knowledge, this explanation has not been examined at the level of input evidence. Even with continued advances in TAL detector design, changes to temporal aggregation often yield only modest gains under controlled comparisons [30]. These findings motivate a closer examination of how temporal evidence contributes to classification and, in particular, boundary placement, calling for attribution methods that faithfully explain both outputs while respecting the temporal structure of video inputs and TAL detectors.

These findings motivate a closer examination of how temporal evidence contributes to classification and, in particular, boundary placement, calling for attribution methods that faithfully explain both outputs while respecting the temporal structure of video inputs and TAL detectors.

Simplifying a bit, TAL can be seen as the temporal counterpart of object detection. In object detection, attribution methods explain individual predictions through their class scores and bounding-box coordinates [56, 52]. We study a similar attribution task in TAL, attributing an action instance’s class score and temporal boundaries to the input snippet embeddings.

Explaining TAL detections faces one challenge and one gap. The challenge is that a snippet’s contribution depends on its temporal context. First, neighboring snippets are temporally redundant: they carry overlapping evidence, so masking one can leave its information available in the others [27, 18]. Second, TAL detectors draw on temporal context beyond the action itself, from the surroundings of a proposal and its boundaries [58, 8, 29] to background and video-level semantics [53, 50], and this context improves their mean average precision (mAP). Because of these dependencies, a snippet may contribute little when redundant evidence is present but become important when that evidence is absent. Straight-line integrated gradients (IG) [46] restores all snippets simultaneously along a single path, limiting its ability to capture such context-dependent contributions.

The mentioned gap concerns boundary attribution. Although existing detector attribution methods explain both classification and localization outputs, they largely apply the same attribution design to both [25, 33, 52, 35, 51]. However, boundary localization is a distinct task. Unlike a class score, a boundary position is a continuous output that can shift in either temporal direction and whose explanation depends on the reference it is compared against [26], calling for attribution designs tailored to boundary placement. Faithfulness evaluation faces a related gap. Existing detection attribution tests evaluate localization using unsigned measures, such as absolute boundary displacement [33], which cannot distinguish evidence that moves a boundary earlier from evidence that moves it later. To address them, we introduce a structure-aware attribution framework for TAL. Instead of attributing temporal evidence along a single path, we average contributions over different restoration orders to capture their dependence on temporal context, while exploiting the detector’s structure to keep computation tractable. Combining attribution analysis with controlled interventions, we show that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement.

papers.title: Tracing Magnetic Helicity in Interplanetary Space. A Multi-Spacecraft Analysis of the 2024 March 23 ICME
papers.abstract: We study the evolution of the magnetic helicity content of an ICME event by inferring its magnetic-field-related quantities at different stages between the Sun and Earth using remote sensing and in-situ observations. We study an eruptive X1.1 flare/CME event and its associated ICME originating from NOAA active region (AR) 13614 on 2024 March 23 00:58 UT. Using magnetogram data of the AR during the flaring event, along with non-linear force-free (NLFF) magnetic field modeling, we reconstruct the magnetic field in the solar corona and analyze its magnetic helicity budget. The helicity is also tracked in-situ in the heliosphere using four well radially-aligned spacecraft (Solar Orbiter at 0.39 AU, BepiColombo at 0.58 AU, STEREO-A at 0.96 AU and Wind at 0.99 AU) measuring the ICME magnetic field signature. We use different force-free magnetic field models (Lundquist, Gold-Hoyle) to evaluate the helicity values at each spacecraft. With the Gold-Hoyle-based model (expansion-modified force-free model, 3DCORE), we also reconstruct the ICME and its propagation in the heliosphere. We ultimately compare the results obtained for each model and spacecraft to the values computed in the corona to give a general understanding of how the event's magnetic field evolved. The NLFF modeling of the AR indicates a left-handed (negative helicity) flux rope (FR) positioned along a slightly northeast-southwest axis, in agreement with chromospheric and coronal observations (H-alpha, SDO/AIA), and yields a helicity budget computed of $-2.16\pm1.32\times10^{41}~\text{Mx}^2$. The helicity inferred from in-situ modeling methods reveals values in a similar range ($-2.0\pm1.0\times10^{41}~\text{Mx}^2$), but is highly sensitive to the spacecraft crossing position through the ICME. It appears that the results given by 3DCORE are more consistent between all spacecraft, as well as with the values inferred at the AR.

papers.intro: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are powerful expulsions of magnetized coronal plasma from the solar atmosphere with speeds of hundreds to thousands of kilometers per second. Their large-scale propagation and expansion into the heliosphere are known as interplanetary CMEs (Kilpua et al., 2017, ICMEs;) and are distinct from the solar wind because of their magnetic field strength, declining velocity profile, low plasma β\beta and other features (Bothmer and Schwenn, 1998; Zurbuchen and Richardson, 2006). An Earth-directed ICME can severely affect our space weather and thus our technology on ground and in space (Schwenn, 2006; Temmer, 2021; Cliver et al., 2022, e.g.). ICME properties such as magnetic field orientation are often measured in-situ by spacecraft at different positions in the heliosphere. These measurements helped develop a representation of ICMEs where the front shock is often followed by a sheath region characterized by a turbulent and compressed magnetic field. The core of the ICME is located in the following part where the magnetic field is enhanced and smoothly rotating, indicative of a magnetic flux rope (MFR), defined by helical field lines coiled around a common central axis. ICME magnetic field structures with clear flux rope features are often described as magnetic clouds (MCs; Burlaga et al. (1981)). Previous studies have depicted a classical axi-symmetric geometry (Zurbuchen and Richardson, 2006; Wang et al., 2018) and a self-similar expansion in the radial direction (Démoulin and Dasso, 2009; Vršnak et al., 2019) that a large part of observed ICMEs exhibit (Nieves-Chinchilla et al., 2019; Cane and Richardson, 2003). More recently, this understanding is evolving towards a truly 3-dimensional structure with non-uniform cross-section and twist (Al-Haddad and Lugaz, 2025). Their expansion is also believed to be significantly impacted by the background solar wind velocity and the magnetic pressure difference (Zhang et al., 2025). ICMEs increase in size and decrease in magnetic field strength during their propagation can be modeled as power-law functions (Davies et al., 2024; Salman et al., 2024; Leitner et al., 2007, e.g.). The magnetic field decay index (nbn_{b}) best fit was shown to be of the order of nb=1.6±0.2n_{b}=1.6\pm 0.2 by Patsourakos and Georgoulis (2016) and more recently by Möstl et al. (2026), whereas the expansion factor was constrained to 0.45<na<1.140.45<n_{a}<1.14 (Gulisano et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2022). Several phenomena can impact ICME propagation in the heliosphere and explain the observed differences in in-situ magnetic field measurements, even with low spacecraft separation (Lugaz et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2020; Regnault et al., 2024). Different sources may cause these differences, such as magnetic configuration, solar wind drag, as well as reconnection processes between the flux rope and the sheath region (Luhmann et al., 2020). The magnetic reconnection between the ejecta and sheath region has been interpreted as an “erosion” of the flux rope (Ruffenach et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018), changing its geoeffectiveness. Moreover, CMEs that occur in close succession can interact with each other if the following one is faster than the first one, causing great changes in the CME in-situ profile between the Sun and Earth. Their interaction is a complex phenomenon (depending on their respective direction of propagation, speed, magnetic field orientation and timing) which is not yet fully understood (Sabri and Poedts, 2026; Manchester et al., 2017). Additionally, the flux rope shape is evolving during its propagation in the heliosphere, leading to a flattening of the cross section referred to as “pancaking effect” (Riley and Crooker, 2004; Davies et al., 2021). Most of the CME/ICME events originate from solar active regions and are associated with solar flares (Webb and Howard, 2012). Energetic flares, especially X-class flares, have a CME-association rate of about 90% (Yashiro et al., 2006). A large eruptive flare also unveils growing magnetic field arcades (visible in soft X-ray (SXR) and extreme ultra-violet (EUV) imaging) exhibiting their footprint in the lower solar atmosphere, often in the form of two bands of bright emission (so-called flare ribbons) on either side of the polarity inversion line (Fletcher et al., 2011; Benz, 2017). CMEs erupting from a flaring active region are also often associated with coronal dimmings, i.e. a sudden decrease of coronal emission in EUV and SXR. They are interpreted as "footprints" of the erupting flux rope and are directly linked to the mass loss. For details on flaring ARs and coronal dimmings, we refer to the reviews by Toriumi and Wang (2019) and Veronig et al. (2025). A common way to investigate the solar counterpart of an ICME is to study the magnetic helicity of the source active region, which is a measure of the shear or twist of the magnetic field. An important property of helicity is its conservation (quasi-conservation) in ideal (resistive) magnetohydrodynamics (Berger and Field, 1984), because its dissipation time is longer than the energy dissipation time. This conservation suggests that the helicity budget of a pre-eruptive active region should be related to the helicity content in the MC ejected from the flaring AR, provided that the magnetic complexity of the ejected structure is not altered by processes during its travel in interplanetary space (Lugaz et al., 2013). Such a comparison can be done by evaluating helicity using ICME magnetic field signatures measured by different spacecraft in the heliosphere (Zhang et al., 2025). By fitting these signatures with a model assuming a basic structure of the field and topology, it is possible to infer the magnetic helicity content of the flux rope and then compare it to the helicity budget of the source active region. A few studies have attempted such comparisons (Dumbović et al., 2021; Thalmann et al., 2023; Al-Haddad and Lugaz, 2025), and advocate for comparisons to in-situ measurements with spacecraft closer to the Sun, to reduce the changes that may happen during the ICME propagation in interplanetary space. The increasing number of spacecraft in the inner heliosphere, notably with the addition of Solar Orbiter (SolO) and Parker Solar Probe (PSP), may provide this needed data. Combining them with L1 measurements allows multiple spacecraft to probe the same MC. This multi-regime (from Sun to Earth) approach can also show evidence of different processes altering the ICME helicity content. We present here the analysis of an ICME detected by a constellation of four spacecraft (i.e., Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, STEREO-A and Wind) between 2024 March 23 and 2024 March 26 at different radial distances from the Sun, from 0.39 AU up to ~1 AU. The ICMEs probed by these spacecraft are associated with this flare by the lineup catalog available online11 1 https://helioforecast.space/lineups (Möstl et al., 2022, see). This configuration enables the tracking of key physical parameters from the Sun to Solar Orbiter and onward to near-Earth orbit. The main objective of this study is to study the magnetic helicity evolution of this ICME, and to connect it to the helicity of the solar source region and the related X1.1 flare/CME event.

papers.title: One-to-Many: Diverse and Bidirectional Image-to-Image Translation via Rectified Flow
papers.abstract: Many paired image-to-image translation tasks admit multiple valid target appearances, while training provides only one target per source. We propose One-to-Many Flow (O2MFlow), a latent-conditioned Rectified Flow (RF) model for one-to-many generation and backward translation (target$\rightarrow$source) within a single transport framework. Conditioning the RF dynamics on an appearance latent turns transport into a family of latent-indexed bijections: a fixed latent gives a mapping that is inverted by time-reversed integration, and sampled latents produce diverse outputs for the same input. We formalize reusable appearance variations as Shared Latent Transport and show that Kullback--Leibler (KL) regularization directly controls the source--latent distribution gap between training and generation. Across three benchmarks, O2MFlow offers dataset-dependent forward diversity--fidelity trade-offs and the lowest backward LPIPS-Dist among evaluated methods, with the lowest backward FID on two benchmarks.

papers.intro:
In appearance-ambiguous tasks, paired image-to-image translation is one-to-many, yet each training source has only one observed target. The task maps a source-domain image to a target domain while preserving task-relevant structure, as in edge-to-photo synthesis and semantic label-to-image generation [13]. The input, however, constrains geometry but leaves appearance underdetermined [34]: the same edge map corresponds to many plausible photos with different colors, materials, or lighting. A useful translator must therefore produce diverse outputs that keep the input structure, and it must learn these variations without ever observing two valid targets for the same input.

The task maps a source-domain image to a target domain while preserving task-relevant structure, as in edge-to-photo synthesis and semantic label-to-image generation [13]. The input, however, constrains geometry but leaves appearance underdetermined [34]: the same edge map corresponds to many plausible photos with different colors, materials, or lighting. A useful translator must therefore produce diverse outputs that keep the input structure, and it must learn these variations without ever observing two valid targets for the same input.

Many applications also require backward translation (target→\rightarrowsource), e.g., extracting a structural representation from a real target-domain image for editing, verification, or analysis. A separately trained backward predictor is not the inverse of the forward mapping, so the two directions can disagree on the same image pair. Backward translation should therefore invert the forward model.

Fig. 1(a) shows conventional single-output models such as pix2pix [13], which learn non-invertible mappings and yield a single output per input. Fig. 1(b) illustrates invertible transport models based on Rectified Flow (RF) [21]. Because inversion is obtained by time-reversed integration of the same ordinary differential equation (ODE), these models naturally support backward translation; however, standard RF models a one-to-one mapping and cannot represent diverse outputs for the same input. In contrast, Fig. 1(c) represents latent-variable approaches such as BicycleGAN [34], which generate diverse outputs but map latents to outputs in a single feedforward pass and provide no inverse from target to source. Diffusion bridges [18, 14] draw diverse samples, even in both directions, but do not reverse the forward map using a shared appearance latent. Fig. 1(d) depicts the desired setting: a single framework that supports both one-to-many forward translation and backward translation.

Sampling different latents from a prior yields diverse outputs for the same input, while a fixed latent defines an invertible transport (Sec. 3), so backward translation is time-reversed integration of the same dynamics rather than a separate generator.

Target-encoded latents can convey appearance information, and the shared field allows them to be reused across inputs. We formalize valid, diverse outputs with cross-source consistency as Shared Latent Transport and examine this behavior empirically. Training uses target-encoded latents, whereas generation samples the prior. We show that Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization bounds the resulting source–latent distribution gap, equaling it under the empirical distribution with a unique target per source; this explains its role in aligning training and generation.
