papers.title: A Lightweight Hybrid Approach for Milling Force Reconstruction from Internal Machine Signals
papers.abstract: Data-driven monitoring based on milling force can enable advanced manufacturing services including process optimization and condition monitoring. However, industrial implementation is often hindered by costly and intrusive hardware and large training data requirements. This paper therefore presents a hybrid approach using machine-internal signals and machining metadata to enable force-based monitoring on brownfield machines without additional sensors. Commonly available machine signals have relatively low sampling rates and cannot directly represent high-frequency milling-force variations, especially at higher spindle speeds. Instead of learning the complete force signal, which would increase model complexity, data requirements, and overfitting risk, a supervised machine-learning model predicts only the average milling force from selected machine-signal features and machining parameters. This low-frequency estimation parameterizes a static milling force model that reconstructs the force behavior over one spindle revolution. Although the static model does not reproduce all dynamic effects, it captures the force distribution, load levels, and angular regions of highest tool engagement. The approach is evaluated on one milling machine across varying process parameters, engagement conditions, cutting tools, and two workpiece materials. Dynamometer measurements are required only for development and validation. Ridge regression achieves an $R^2$ of $0.984$ and $0.991$ for average-force prediction on the test data ($\bar{F}_x$ and $\bar{F}_y$). The reconstructed force behavior over one spindle revolution achieves an $R^2$ of $0.962$ and $0.982$ ($F_x$ and $F_y$) compared with the reconstruction based on measured force features. The method provides a cost and computationally efficient basis for process monitoring, tool condition assessment, and process optimization on existing machines.

papers.intro:
Cutting forces reflect the tool–workpiece interaction and provide valuable information for process monitoring and optimization [1, 2]. Their magnitude and progression depend on process conditions, machining system dynamics, and tool state. Process conditions determine the nominal chip thickness, while relative motion between the tool and workpiece modifies it. The tool state influences how this chip thickness translates into force. These forces, in turn, cause deflections and vibrations that further change the chip thickness. This feedback makes force prediction across operating conditions challenging.

Spindle signals provide an alternative representation of the cutting load. During milling, the spindle drive compensates for the cutting torque to maintain the commanded rotational speed. This work therefore investigates a lightweight cascade combining selected spindle and feed drive signals with machining metadata. Rather than learning the instantaneous force progression, classical regression estimates mean in-plane forces. These parameterize a static milling force model that reconstructs the angular force progression over one spindle revolution. The main contributions are:

1. Lightweight data-driven estimation of mean in-plane cutting forces from spindle signals, feed drive signals and machining metadata. 2. Hybrid reconstruction of the force progression using a data-driven approach and a static milling model. 3. Experimental validation across varying process conditions, tools, and workpiece materials, with force sensing required only for development and validation.

papers.title: ZoionNET: Low-Power Animal Intrusion Detection Using an Acoustic Deep-Learning Classifier for a Cellular Remote-Sensing System
papers.abstract: Crop raiding and village intrusion by elephants and large felids impose a recurring cost on communities along forest boundaries in southern India, and existing camera-based monitoring has proven difficult to sustain on the power budgets available at such sites. We present ZoionNET, a battery-powered sensing node that detects animal intrusion acoustically rather than visually. Audio from an onboard PDM microphone is sampled at 8 kHz, converted to mel-spectrograms on-device, and classified on an Arm Ethos-U55 microNPU by two int8-quantised YOLOv8 models arranged as a two-state machine: a lightweight always-on model runs in a dormant state and gates a four-class species classifier through exponential-moving-average thresholds, so the heavier model runs only when an intrusion is likely. A digital vibration sensor supplies a complementary seismic channel. Inferences leave the node as JSON over a cellular Notecard, reaching a web dashboard and SMS alerts to forest rangers without any local gateway. The two models reach reported accuracies of 0.974 and 0.946 on held-out audio, and a complete node costs USD 133.57 in parts. We report the system as built and deployed, and identify explicitly what has not yet been measured, most notably the energy behaviour that motivates the two-state design.

papers.title: Large-scale regularity theory for optimal $p-$transport maps and application to concentration in the matching problem
papers.abstract: We consider the random bipartite matching problem between two independent families of uniformly distributed points in dimension three and higher, for the cost given by the $p$-th power of the distance. We show that, up to logarithmic factors, every moment of the displacement of the optimal matching is of the order of the typical interparticle distance. This is a higher integrability, or Calder\'on--Zygmund type, estimate for optimal transport, and it settles, on the torus and up to logarithmic factors, a recent conjecture of D'Achille, Mattesini and the third author. As a consequence, we obtain concentration of the matching cost around its mean for every $p\ge2$. The proof combines a deterministic large-scale regularity theory for optimal transport with $p$-costs, based on a harmonic approximation by a non-linear elliptic equation of $p$-Laplacian type, with tail bounds on local matching costs.

papers.title: Posterior Matching Distillation
papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

Diffusion and Flow models [19, 53, 31, 30, 2] have emerged as a powerful approach to generative modeling, particularly for images [45, 10, 57, 58, 26, 27] and video [55, 3, 25, 60, 39, 1], with growing applications to text [43]. Their sampling process progressively transforms noise into a data sample through a sequence of denoising steps, typically requiring many neural network evaluations. Diffusion distillation aims to reduce this computational burden by training a student to generate samples in one or a few steps [48, 54, 62, 61, 49, 47, 4]. However, a noisy state can correspond to many plausible clean samples, while a conventional denoiser provides only a single estimate. This raises a fundamental question: what information about the teacher’s generative distribution should a few-step student preserve?

Diffusion and Flow models [19, 53, 31, 30, 2] have emerged as a powerful approach to generative modeling, particularly for images [45, 10, 57, 58, 26, 27] and video [55, 3, 25, 60, 39, 1], with growing applications to text [43]. Their sampling process progressively transforms noise into a data sample through a sequence of denoising steps, typically requiring many neural network evaluations. Diffusion distillation aims to reduce this computational burden by training a student to generate samples in one or a few steps [48, 54, 62, 61, 49, 47, 4]. However, a noisy state can correspond to many plausible clean samples, while a conventional denoiser provides only a single estimate. This raises a fundamental question: what information about the teacher’s generative distribution should a few-step student preserve?

Existing diffusion distillation methods differ in what they seek to preserve from the teacher. Trajectory-based approaches aim to preserve the teacher’s sampling process with fewer evaluations. These include progressive distillation [48], which compresses successive denoising steps, consistency distillation [54], which learns mappings to trajectory endpoints, and flow-map distillation [4, 47], which learns transitions between noise levels. Distribution-based approaches, in contrast, seek to preserve the teacher’s generated distribution without requiring the student to follow the same sampling trajectories. A student may reproduce the teacher’s overall output distribution while learning a different conditional distribution at each noise level [62, 61]. This limitation is particularly relevant to Distribution Matching Distillation, which uses an approximate reverse-KL objective to align noise-perturbed student and teacher distributions. The mode-seeking nature of reverse KL can favor dominant modes at the expense of less frequent outcomes, potentially reducing sample diversity [59, 32]. PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. In practice, stochasticity is introduced by simply doubling the first layer’s input features, and each tilted mean is estimated using as few as four student evaluations per noisy state. The choice of exponential weights is deliberate: under Gaussian corruption, exponentially reweighting the posterior is equivalent to shifting the noisy input at the same noise level [40, 20, 41, 42, 38], an elementary identity we call the Tilt=Shift Identity. As illustrated in Fig. 2, this identity allows each target mean to be obtained through a single evaluation of the frozen teacher at the shifted input, rather than through computationally expensive Monte Carlo estimation requiring multiple teacher posterior samples. papers.title: Wearable Logo, Silent Hijack: Stealthy Cross-Modal Semantic Attacks on Visible--Infrared Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Logos appear naturally on clothing and daily necessities, where their recognizable shapes and semantic associations make them familiar visual cues. This familiarity helps them blend into real-world environments and remain visually inconspicuous. We ask whether an existing logo can serve as a carrier for coordinated targeted semantic attacks on visible-infrared (VIS-IR) vision-language models (VLMs) without changing its original outline. This setting requires expressive adversarial variation within a fixed shape while accounting for different appearance characteristics and model responses across modalities. We propose Logo-guided Semantic Attack (LoSA), a score-based black-box framework that optimizes a logo's interior appearance and placement while preserving its silhouette. LoSA uses a contour field and low-frequency graph spectral modes to structure the interior color layout, a frozen appearance adapter to couple VIS and IR appearances, and particle swarm optimization to jointly optimize shared design parameters. Experiments across four datasets demonstrate that LoSA consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines in simultaneous Top-1 targeted success. Cross-architecture experiments, visual naturalness ratings, and captioning/VQA transfer analyses further characterize its effectiveness and limitations. These findings reveal that familiar visual symbols from real-world environments can serve as shape-preserving carriers for coordinated targeted semantic attacks across imaging modalities.

papers.title: Decomposition of trilinear forme
papers.abstract: In this work, we are interested in the decomposition of trilinear forms. We associate this decomposition with the decomposition into irreducible subspaces of the group algebra associated with the symmetric group. We have a correspondence between a ternary form and a symmetric trilinear form, in the same way that we have the correspondence between a quadratic form and a symmetric quadratic form. We are then interested in the decomposition of ternary forms into a sum of cubes of linear forms and as an application we find the Tartaglia formulae on the expression of the roots of equations of degree 3.

papers.title: The sharp constant in a theorem of \v{S}emrl on approximate isometries of Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: Let $H,K$ be real Hilbert spaces and $f:H\to K$ an $\epsilon$-isometry with $f(0)=0$. \v{S}emrl proved that there is a linear isometry $U:H\to K$ such that, with $P$ the orthogonal projection onto $\text{Im}\, U$, one has $\|Pf(x)-Ux\|\leq2\epsilon$ and $\|(I-P)f(x)\|\leq\sqrt{6\epsilon\|x\|+\epsilon^2}$ for all $x\in H$, and asked for the optimal constant $A\in[2\epsilon,6\epsilon]$ in a bound of the form $\sqrt{A\|x\|+B}$. We prove that $A=6\epsilon$, so that \v{S}emrl's theorem is best possible. More precisely, $\|(I-P)f(x)\|\leq\sqrt{6\epsilon\|x\|-3\epsilon^2}$ for $\|x\|\geq2\epsilon$, and this bound is attained, for every value of $\|x\|\geq2\epsilon$, by an explicit $\epsilon$-isometry $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$.

papers.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
papers.abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

Split federated learning (SFL) enables collaborative training by partitioning models across clients and servers (Thapa et al., 2022). However, removing learned information becomes challenging when knowledge is distributed across coupled model partitions. Split federated unlearning (SFU) (Chen et al., 2026) further considers restricted update modes, where only client-side, server-side, or both partitions can be modified, complicating the balance between effective forgetting and retained utility.

Existing machine unlearning (Fan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a) and federated unlearning methods (Zhao et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025) primarily rely on parameter-level or gradient-based interventions. SURE (Chen et al., 2026), the first dedicated SFU approach, addresses partition-constrained unlearning through importance-guided perturbation and retained-data recovery. Nevertheless, such parameter-level interventions do not coordinate how forgotten representations evolve across the split. This limitation is particularly relevant as reduced target predictions do not necessarily imply the removal of discriminative information from internal representations (Gao et al., 2026).

Beyond these limitations, SFU presents a fundamental challenge: representation changes are asymmetric across model partitions. Client-side updates affect both representation endpoints, whereas server-side updates leave cut-layer features unchanged. Moreover, the two endpoints occupy distinct representation spaces, making consistent semantic realignment difficult, particularly when one partition is frozen. This raises a central question: How can forgotten representations be coherently realigned under partition-specific update constraints while preserving retained-data utility?

papers.title: Minimization of free energy in a Poisson--Boltzmann problem
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study a mathematical model in which an ionic solution composed of several types of spherical ions is confined between two uniformly charged parallel planes. The ion concentrations at equilibrium, determined by the interplay between thermal and electrostatic effects, are obtained by minimizing the free energy of the system. The resulting minimization problem is infinite-dimensional, and we prove the existence and uniqueness of its solution by means of a norm-convergence direct method based on the Banach--Saks property of the space in which the problem is posed. The existence proof is technically challenging because the functional to be minimized is not coercive in general. Three illustrative problems are considered and solved numerically.

The study of electrostatic interactions between charged structures and ions is crucial for understanding the behavior of soft matter, particularly living matter (see [18]). Biological systems typically contain a multitude of charged structures. Membranes, cellular components, globular proteins, polyelectrolytes, and DNA are examples of biological structures carrying electric charges and, consequently, exhibiting electrostatic behavior (see [3, 10]). These charged structures are immersed in biological media, such as blood, containing free ions in addition to water molecules. Understanding the physical processes occurring between two negatively or positively charged structures is important from the biological point of view (see [18]).

The aim of this paper is to present such a model for the case of spherical ions and to prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the PB problem, i.e., the existence and uniqueness of the ion concentrations minimizing the free energy. The existence proof is based on a direct method, but it does not employ standard weak-compactness arguments, such as those based on dual spaces and the Banach–Alaoglu theorem. Instead, it relies on the Banach–Saks property of the infinite-dimensional space in which the PB problem is formulated and uses norm convergence. Moreover, because the functional to be minimized may fail to be coercive, the proof requires nonstandard and technically challenging arguments, which also yield an essential boundedness result. Existence and uniqueness results for free-energy minimization in PB problems different from the one considered in the present paper, and based on different approaches, can be found in [15] and [13].

By means of a variational procedure based on the Euler–Lagrange equations, the free-energy minimization problem can be reformulated as a boundary value problem with Neumann conditions for a second-order differential equation whose solution is the electrostatic potential (see [1]). This potential determines the ion concentrations minimizing the free energy. When the ions are modeled as point particles, the resulting differential equation is an ordinary differential equation. More realistic models can be obtained by considering ions with a geometrical structure, such as rod-like or spherical ions. In these cases, the resulting differential equation is an integro-differential equation. Such integro-differential equations, and their numerical treatments, are presented in [16, 17, 12] for rod-like ions and in [5, 22, 23, 6] for spherical ions. These papers do not address the question of existence and uniqueness of the solution of the boundary value problem for the second-order integro-differential equation.

The present paper includes three illustrative examples of PB problems for the spherical ions model considered here, in which the ion concentrations minimizing the free energy are computed numerically. Unlike the approaches adopted in the papers cited above, these concentrations are not obtained by reformulating the minimization problem as a boundary value problem for the potential. Instead, they are computed directly by minimizing the free energy. This approach avoids the lengthy mathematical calculations required by the variational procedure used to derive the boundary value problem. Since the minimization problem is infinite-dimensional, it must first be discretized into a finite-dimensional minimization problem, after which a standard optimization solver can be used to compute its minimum. The description and analysis of the discretization of the infinite-dimensional minimization problem are not included here and will be the subject of a companion paper.

papers.title: Intra-day variability of the gamma-ray/optical emission of 3C 454.3: the complexity beyond the long-term correlation
papers.abstract:
Simultaneous $\gamma$-ray/optical observations probe particle acceleration and radiative processes in blazar jets. The blazar 3C 454.3 shows a significant long-term correlation between these bands, often interpreted as support for the canonical one-zone leptonic emission model. However, both bands show strong intra-day variability, and whether the correlation persists during individual flares remains unclear.
  We study the $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation and intra-day variability of 3C 454.3 over 17 years (2007--2024), on timescales $\leq 24$ h.
  We analyse AGILE and Fermi-LAT observations using light curves binned from 3 to 48 h, together with simultaneous $R$-band photometry from WEBT and public optical data sets. We examine the flux and spectral evolution of individual flares, estimate time-dependent correlation properties, and derive Compton dominance from optical and $\gamma$-ray luminosities.
  We confirm the long-term correlation, but find large intrinsic dispersion and a slope of $\eta \simeq 1.6$--$1.7$, inconsistent with a single canonical one-zone scenario. On shorter timescales, correlation strengths range from weak to strong, with slopes spanning $\eta \simeq 0.4$--$2.0$. We also find orphan flares in both bands, diverse flare morphologies, distinct Compton-dominance patterns with rapid excursions from $\sim 10$ to 120, and heterogeneous spectral trends. The shortest resolved variability timescales ($t_{\rm var} \lesssim 3$ h) indicate that localized emission regions are required by causality.
  The $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation in 3C 454.3 thus arises not from a single emission regime, but from multiple epoch-dependent physical states. Increasing temporal resolution reveals richer variability, highlighting the importance of systematic intra-day, multi-epoch studies of bright FSRQs.

Blazars are Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) with relativistic plasma jets oriented close to the observer’s line of sight (Urry and Padovani, 1995; Padovani et al., 2017). Their broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) features two distinct peaks. In flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), these occur in the millimetre/near-infrared and MeV-GeV bands, respectively, whereas in BL Lacertae objects (BL Lacs) they span from infrared to X-rays and from X-rays up to TeV energies (Ghisellini, 2016; Prandini and Ghisellini, 2022). The low-energy peak originates from synchrotron radiation of relativistic electrons. The high-energy peak is attributed either to leptonic processes via inverse Compton (IC) scattering of synchrotron photons (Maraschi et al., 1992; Bloom and Marscher, 1996, synchrotron self-Compton, SSC;) or external fields like the accretion disc, broad-line region (BLR), or dusty torus (Dermer and Schlickeiser, 1993; Sikora et al., 1994; Ghisellini and Tavecchio, 2009, external Compton, EC;), or to hadronic processes such as proton synchrotron radiation and secondary cascades (Mücke and Protheroe, 2001; Dimitrakoudis et al., 2012; Cerruti, 2020). Structurally, emission models are divided into one-zone scenarios, where emission is localized in a single compact region (Celotti and Ghisellini, 2008), and multi-zone, which distribute emitting particles along the jet or in moving plasmoids (Villata and Raiteri, 1999; Chen et al., 2011; Marscher, 2014; Raiteri et al., 2017; Shukla and Mannheim, 2020).

Blazar emission varies across all wavelengths on timescales from minutes to years (Rieger, 2019; Raiteri, 2025; Andruchow et al., 2026), and variability studies can provide constraints complementary to SED fitting. In one-zone leptonic models, variations of the low- and high-energy components should be simultaneous in the EC case since they arise from the same electron population, or delayed by ∼r/(c​δ)\sim r/(c\,\delta) at most in the SSC case due to the size rr of the emission region (Maraschi et al., 1992, c is the speed of light, δ\delta the Doppler factor, see). The correlation slope depends on the variability driver: electron density changes yield a quadratic relationship in SSC and a linear one in EC, whereas magnetic field variations produce a linear correlation in SSC but leave EC emission unaffected, potentially generating flares only in the low-energy band (Dermer et al., 1997; Böttcher and Chiang, 2002). Single-band events are usually referred to as ‘orphan’ flares (Liodakis et al., 2019, e.g. ). Multi-zone models introduce delays or additional orphan events; for example, mirror models (Vittorini et al., 2009; Vittorini et al., 2014; Tavani et al., 2015; Vittorini et al., 2017; Böttcher, 2021) predict that flare photons photo-ionize nearby BLR clouds or other plasmoids in the jet, creating delayed EC seed photons and causing γ\gamma-rays to decouple from the optical emission. Alternatively, they could also indicate hadronic processes (Böttcher, 2005; Cerruti, 2020).

papers.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.

authors.institution: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Trieste

papers.intro:
Small vision-language models (VLMs) now think before they answer, and on image tasks the thinking often does not end. The model card of Qwen3.5 [41] warns that its smallest models are more prone to entering thinking loops, and on image benchmarks the warning describes a major failure: with the card’s own sampling settings, a large share of the thinking model’s answers never leave the thinking phase, and most of those end in text that repeats itself until the tokens run out (Figs. 1 and 3). Each such answer spends the whole token budget and is lost, however good the reasoning before the loop was, while the answers that do finish are mostly correct (Sec. 2). Loops are most frequent on the vision-only problems of MathVerse and on GUI grounding, the step on which visual agents act (Sec. 3.2).

The remedies in use act on the decoding and leave the model that loops as it was. Loops, however, arise from errors in what the model has learned, and sampling differently reduces them without removing that cause [40]. Penalising repeated tokens and banning reflection words change which words the model may write, not what drives it into a loop. Budget forcing asks for an answer at a budget but does not keep the model from running to it: about as many answers reach the budget as the thinking model loses at the token limit (Sec. D.7). Directional ablation [1] edits the weights, but by a fixed recipe, and on the larger model no edit it finds passes its own accuracy check. What is missing is a way to find the cause in the network and remove it there.

Keel repairs the model itself, the way an engineer repairs code: the editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, reads the VLM’s weights, rewrites the faulty part and tests the fix, without gradients or training. The result is plain weights of unchanged size and per-token cost, and the repair also applies to already-edited weights. Interpretable weight-editing methods [36, 1, 44] must be told in advance what to change, a fact to rewrite or a contrast that defines the direction to remove; Keel names only the symptom and leaves finding the mechanism, choosing where to act and writing the fix to the editor. A recent blog post had the same frontier model, shown no images, remove a loop direction from the language model of Qwen3.5-0.8B on text-only mathematics [45]; Keel is the first to bring such agentic editing to VLMs on image tasks, with editors that see the images and edits selected on questions no editor saw.

papers.title: VidToC: Rethinking Video Token Compression for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.

papers.intro:
Developing general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) Comanici et al. (2025); Achiam et al. (2023) for video understanding has attracted increasing attention, enabling applications ranging from video platform services Yang et al. (2023a) to embodied agents Black et al. (2024). Scaling these models to long videos exposes a fundamental bottleneck: even a one-minute short video sampled at 1 frame per second can produce over ten thousand visual tokens when encoded by a standard vision encoder Zhai et al. (2023). Such explosive token growth significantly increases the memory footprint for KV-cache storage and inference latency caused by the quadratic attention complexity in transformer-based MLLMs. Recent studies address this issue through two complementary directions: 1) visual token compression methods that reduce the number of tokens passed to the language model Chen et al. (2024a); Zhang et al. (2025b); Alvar et al. (2025); Wen et al. (2025), and 2) efficient backbone architectures that reduce the cost of processing long sequences Gu and Dao (2024); Dao and Gu (2024); Basant et al. (2025).

Our evaluation covers training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary tasks, namely general QA, temporal grounding, and detailed captioning.

Our findings can be distilled into three insights. (1) In training-free settings, simple methods are competitive for general QA and detailed captioning, while temporal grounding benefits from suitable importance-based selection and preserving original position indices. (2) Under matched token budgets, projector-level compression is a strong training-free default, while multi-stage combinations can balance performance across tasks. (3) Relative method strengths broadly transfer across the two backbones, but the evaluated hybrid model exhibits greater output stability under aggressive merging and greater sensitivity to training-free compression on temporal grounding.

papers.title: Determinant Massey products
papers.abstract: We introduce the determinant Massey product, a secondary operation on the cohomology of commutative dg algebras which is reminiscent of the classical Massey product. We prove some of the elementary properties of this product, compute several examples, and relate them to classical and matric Massey products. When 2 is invertible, a determinant Massey product is a matric Massey product, but over $\mathbb F_2$, it is not. In this case, we produce a finite-dimensional cdga whose Harrison cohomology does not inject into its Hochschild cohomology, and a divided powers algebra which is formal as an associative dg algebra, but not as a commutative one, with an explicit determinant Massey product witnessing the failure. Over $\mathbb Q$, we use determinant Massey products to construct a simply-connected coformal space with Koszul cohomology ring and vanishing ordinary Massey products of all orders, which is not formal.

papers.intro:
Ever since W. S. Massey introduced what nowadays are called Massey products [38, 27], a secondary operation on the (co)homology of differential graded associative algebras, these have come to play a major role in algebraic topology and spread to many other seemingly unrelated areas. The existence of these and related higher-order products is due to the vanishing of certain equations that follow from associativity, commutativity, and more complex operadic operations [34, 11]. Their first application was the Jacobi identity for Whitehead products [38], and they detect that the Borromean rings are non-trivially linked [28, 29]. Subsequent applications to algebraic topology abound. For example, Longoni and Salvatore used them to show that configuration spaces do not reflect homotopy equivalences [25], and Livernet to show that the Swiss cheese operad is not formal [24]. They have also been extensively studied in the context of the Adams spectral sequence and the computation of the stable homotopy groups of spheres [21, 23]. Recently, their behaviour in the Galois cohomology of number fields has become of major interest in arithmetic geometry [9, 20, 18, 19, 32, 33], including playing a role in constructions of integral points on elliptic curves [22]. They have appeared as far afield as in the analysis of differential equations [26] and mathematical physics [4]. Despite the recent interest in ∞\infty-algebras, which are marvellous theoretical tools, they are not exactly the same thing as Massey products [5, 11], which are better suited to practical computations and the construction of counterexamples.

A significant limitation of classical Massey products is that they rely on initial monomial vanishing conditions in cohomology, such as a​b=0ab=0. In [6], Campos, Petersen, Robert-Nicoud and Wierstra show that two commutative dg algebras over a field of characteristic zero that are quasi-isomorphic as associative dg algebras are also quasi-isomorphic as commutative dg algebras. The first author showed, using Frobenius-type obstructions, that this fails in positive characteristic [12]. Determinant Massey products cannot detect this failure when 22 is invertible, as matric Massey products are invariants of the associative homotopy type. Over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} they can detect this failure at the level of deformation complexes. We give examples of a graded commutative algebra whose Harrison cohomology does not inject into its Hochschild cohomology (Proposition 4.1), and a divided powers algebra that is formal as an associative dg algebra but not as a commutative one (Proposition 4.2), significantly strengthening the results of [12]. Over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the simplest possible algebra with a non-vanishing determinant Massey product is also intrinsically interesting. papers.title: A Matter of Representation: Evolving Partial Spreads for Bent Functions
papers.abstract: Partial spread ($\mathcal{PS}$) bent functions are Boolean functions of maximum nonlinearity built from families of subspaces that pairwise intersect only in the null vector. We design an Evolution Strategy (ES) to construct such partial spread families, comparing two encodings: one based on generator matrices of the subspaces, and one based on spread sets. With the latter, combined with a ruin-and-rebuild operator, the ES finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions up to $n=10$ variables. An ablation study shows that mutation is necessary, while the population size is not, and that a restarted look-ahead greedy heuristic outperforms the ES on the hardest instance. We investigate this finding with a landscape analysis of the stagnation points, and we also introduce a quality-diversity variant of the ES which finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions of low algebraic degree for 8 variables. Interestingly, the bent functions evolved by the ES have higher 2-ranks and mostly higher degrees than those obtained by a baseline Genetic Programming optimizer.

papers.intro:
In the mid-19th century, Reverend Thomas Kirkman posed the following combinatorial puzzle in The Lady’s and Gentleman’s Diary [19]: given fifteen young ladies in a school, how can they walk out three abreast for seven days in such a way that no two of them walk twice in the same row? This puzzle later became known as Kirkman’s Schoolgirl Problem [11]. An elegant solution, which goes back at least to Rao [31], identifies the fifteen schoolgirls with the nonzero strings of four bits, and lets any three girls walk in a row only if the XOR of their strings is the all-zero string. Each day then partitions the fifteen girls into five such rows, and seven days with no rows in common provide a solution to the riddle [3].

An elegant solution, which goes back at least to Rao [31], identifies the fifteen schoolgirls with the nonzero strings of four bits, and lets any three girls walk in a row only if the XOR of their strings is the all-zero string. Each day then partitions the fifteen girls into five such rows, and seven days with no rows in common provide a solution to the riddle [3].

From a geometric standpoint, each row (augmented with the all-zero string) is closed under XOR, and it is thus a 2-dimensional subspace of 𝔽24\mathbb{F}_{2}^{4}. Any subset of rows on a given day is a family of subspaces that intersect only in the null vector, which is called a partial spread. This construction yields another interesting combinatorial object: the six girls (or more precisely, their 4-bit strings) in any two rows on a single day define the support of a bent function.

This construction yields another interesting combinatorial object: the six girls (or more precisely, their 4-bit strings) in any two rows on a single day define the support of a bent function.

Bent functions are those Boolean functions that are as far as possible from linear ones, and they have several applications in cryptography, coding theory, and sequence design [9]. The example above is the smallest instance of a general construction introduced by Dillon [12], namely the partial spread class 𝒫​𝒮−\mathcal{PS}^{-}: for n=2​mn=2m variables, the union of 2m−12^{m-1} mm-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} with trivial pairwise intersection gives the support of a bent function, once the null vector is removed. The class 𝒫​𝒮+\mathcal{PS}^{+} instead takes 2m−1+12^{m-1}+1 subspaces and keeps the null vector in the support. The union of 𝒫​𝒮−\mathcal{PS}^{-} and 𝒫​𝒮+\mathcal{PS}^{+} gives the partial spread bent functions class 𝒫​𝒮\mathcal{PS}. To obtain a function in this class, one must first find an appropriate partial spread, and exhaustive search quickly becomes infeasible even for small numbers of variables. For instance, with n=10n=10 one has to choose 16 subspaces among more than 10810^{8} candidates for a 𝒫​𝒮−\mathcal{PS}^{-} function, turning what is a brain teaser for fifteen schoolgirls into a hard combinatorial search problem.

So far, the main approaches in the literature to design bent functions—whether in the partial spread class or not—rely on algebraic constructions [9] or metaheuristic optimization algorithms [13]. The former give complete control over the class of bent functions that can be obtained, but less variability. The latter provide, in principle, more diversity, since they blindly search the space of truth tables (or equivalent representations of Boolean functions, like syntactic trees), guided only by a fitness function that usually measures the nonlinearity. On the other hand, with metaheuristics it is more difficult to enforce certain properties on the resulting bent functions, such as being defined by a partial spread. A third option is to constrain the metaheuristic to search for the combinatorial object underlying a construction, rather than for the function itself.

The aim of this paper is to investigate to what extent Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) can be used to evolve bent functions in the partial spread class. Since a subspace can be encoded by a generator matrix—like a linear code—our idea starts from the Evolution Strategy (ES) of [7] to evolve binary linear codes. However, a direct adaptation of this approach to optimize families of m×2​mm\times 2m matrices with trivial pairwise intersection already fails at n=10n=10 variables. We therefore introduce a spread-set encoding, where two fixed subspaces (denoted as E0E_{0} and E∞E_{\infty}) always belong to the family. Every remaining member of the family is then the graph of a linear map described by an m×mm\times m matrix, and two such subspaces have trivial intersection if and only if the difference of their matrices is invertible. Since each column of the difference depends only on the same column of the two matrices, a conflicting subspace can be removed and rebuilt in an exact way, instead of being modified one vector at a time as in [7].

The contributions of this paper are as follows: • Representation. We compare the performance of the ES with the subspace and spread-set encodings. With n=8n=8 variables, the ES always converges under both encodings. For n=10n=10, the subspace encoding always fails, while the spread-set encoding combined with the exact ruin-and-rebuild operator achieves a full success rate for the 𝒫​𝒮−\mathcal{PS}^{-} target and a 74% success rate for 𝒫​𝒮+\mathcal{PS}^{+}. Mutation turns out to be crucial, while the population size has no significant effect. Moreover, a restarted greedy heuristic with look-ahead on the same encoding has a higher success rate than any ES variant on the hardest instance (n=10n=10 with the 𝒫​𝒮+\mathcal{PS}^{+} target). • Landscape Analysis. We measure the number of matrices that need to be replaced to reach a partial spread from the points where the ES stagnates. For n=10n=10, this number is mostly 4 for the 𝒫​𝒮−\mathcal{PS}^{-} target and mostly 7 for 𝒫​𝒮+\mathcal{PS}^{+}, consistent with the performance of the ES. Conversely, the 2-ranks of bent functions evolved by Genetic Programming [28] all lie within the Maiorana–McFarland bound.

papers.title: Variational Trajectory Flow Matching with a Non-Linear Interpolant
papers.abstract: Simulation-free methods such as Trajectory Flow Matching learn dynamics by regressing the time derivative of a local interpolant placed between consecutive observations. The interpolant defines the regression target, and under sparse, irregular sampling, it underrepresents the dynamics and bounds what can be learned. We show that no fixed interpolant dominates: the best of linear, quadratic, spline and quintic changes with the system and with the sampling density. We propose to learn the interpolant instead. An amortized implicit neural representation (INR) is fitted to the training trajectories and frozen as a teacher supplying the target velocity to a learnable velocity field. We further frame the velocity field within a variational framework, yielding a probabilistic forecaster that, at inference, requires only the velocity field and no SDE solver. We evaluate our method on a range of dynamical systems: it consistently achieves high accuracy and more stable long-horizon rollouts under sparser observations, at matched velocity-field capacity.

papers.intro:
Modelling dynamical systems is challenging across scientific domains, particularly when states evolve in high-dimensional spaces, as in fluid dynamics, climate science, biology, neuroscience, and engineering. Flow Matching-based methods (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024) are continuous-time generative models with the ability to capture complex data distributions. They bypass the need for a numerical solver during training and avoid differentiating through it, which improves memory scalability and makes high-dimensional settings more tractable, whereas simulation-based approaches (Chen et al., 2018; Kidger et al., 2020; Dupont et al., 2019) can be more constrained. Recent simulation-free extensions include Trajectory Flow Matching (Zhang et al., 2024, TFM), proposed for dynamics learning and time-series forecasting.

Recent simulation-free extensions include Trajectory Flow Matching (Zhang et al., 2024, TFM), proposed for dynamics learning and time-series forecasting.

Unlike standard Flow Matching, TFM learns state-to-state dynamics rather than a noise-to-state or noise-to-trajectory transformation (Fu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). State-to-state dynamics preserves temporal causality: the velocity at a query time describes the physics of the real system, not an unrelated velocity artifact induced by a Gaussian probability path from noise to data. This makes TFM a natural framework for non-linear, high-dimensional continuous-time dynamics.

This makes TFM a natural framework for non-linear, high-dimensional continuous-time dynamics.

However, real-world observations are often sparse and irregular in time: a sensor collects measurements at various time points and under diverse conditions when possible, and numerical solvers are run at different step sizes for compute cost. In this regime, trajectory-matching methods rely on an often implicit modelling decision: they construct a probability path between observations and regress its analytical time derivative. The chosen interpolant is not merely a numerical detail: it determines the target velocity used for training and constrains which dynamics can be represented. In particular, the linear interpolant used in TFM provides a first-order approximation of the trajectory between consecutive observations. It is accurate only when the interval is short relative to the curvature of the dynamics. Such an assumption is often violated by real systems that are curved and their velocity may change between samples. The resulting velocity of TFM is then constant over the interval, whereas the true velocity is not.

This limitation has motivated several variants of TFM for sparse or irregularly sampled data. In this work, we review these methods within a unified framework and investigate how their interpolant assumptions affect the learned dynamics. TFM relies on linear interpolation; later methods replace it with quadratic (Islam et al., 2026, LFM), cubic spline (Rohbeck et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025, MMFM), or quintic spline (Hou et al., 2026, CFO). These methods can provide more flexible local approximations, but they keep the same underlying assumption: the interpolant is fixed in advance and fitted locally from only a few neighbouring observations. As a result, the learning targets vary with the sampling times, and this dependence can be significant when observations are sparse. Figure 1 illustrates this failure mode.

A complementary line of work incorporates known physical expressions. Physics-informed generative models impose differential-equation constraints as soft regularizers (Sholokhov et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Baldan et al., 2026) for learning forward models, while hybrid models embed known dynamics into the model architecture for forecasting tasks (Takeishi and Kalousis, 2021; Qian et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2021; Takeishi and Kalousis, 2023; Wehenkel et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2026). These approaches operate in a distinct setting: they assume access to, or exploit, explicit physical information. Other relevant work focuses on large-scale PDEs with varying geometries using spatial mesh-free methods, such as Neural Operators (Lu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022; Serrano et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023), which learn mappings between functional spaces rather than on discrete fixed grids. In this paper, we study the limitations introduced by fixed interpolation targets in simulation-free methods and propose a solution for learning dynamics from irregularly sampled trajectories.

papers.title: Collineations of the diamond lattice in a Hilbert space
papers.abstract: Let $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ be non-trivial closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}=\{0\}$ and $\mathscr{M}+\mathscr{N}$ is dense in $\mathscr{H}$. We characterize when there exists an invertible operator on $\mathscr{H}$ which maps $\mathscr{M}$ onto $\mathscr{N}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ onto $\mathscr{M}$. We prove that such an operator exists if and only if $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ have a common algebraic complement. This happens if and only if either neither of the operators $(I-P)Q$ and $(I-Q)P$ is compact, or $P-Q$ is compact and $\dim(\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}^\perp)=\dim(\mathscr{M}^\perp\cap\mathscr{N})$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the orthogonal projections onto $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$. Moreover, the operator can be chosen to be an involution. Consequently, the group of collineations of the diamond lattice $\{\{0\},\mathscr{M},\mathscr{N},\mathscr{H}\}$ which fix $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ is always complemented in the group of all its collineations.

papers.title: Spectral asymptotics for vector-valued magnetic Schr\"odinger operators
papers.abstract: We consider vector-valued magnetic Schr\"odinger operators $-\Delta_{a} +V$ with magnetic potential ${a}\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ and electric potential $V$ given by a symmetric and positive semidefinite $m\times m$ matrix-valued function whose entries belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Assuming that $\|\operatorname{curl} {a}(\cdot)\|\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^m} + V$ belongs to a certain matrix reverse H\"older class, we characterize necessary and sufficient conditions under which the spectrum of $-\Delta_{a} +V$ is discrete, and study the eigenvalue asymptotics and exponential decay of eigenfunctions.

papers.title: AGE-Capture: Autonomous, General, and Efficient UAV Capture for High-Fidelity Scene Reconstruction
papers.abstract: High-fidelity scene reconstruction with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) requires more than identifying valuable viewpoints: the system must autonomously acquire informative observations and determine task completion under different sensing configurations and limited flight resources. We present AGE-Capture, an autonomous, sensor-adaptive, and efficient active-capture framework for real UAVs. Building on renderability, the framework uses a lightweight online state to evaluate the utility of candidate views, assess task progress, and guide flight execution. By decoupling geometric exploration from reconstruction observations and establishing a unified camera-ray interface, the framework allows different range sensors and RGB camera models to share a reconstruction-driven acquisition pipeline. Reconstruction-frontier viewpoints characterize residual acquisition value for region screening and autonomous termination; dynamics-aware hierarchical planning combined with asynchronous event-driven capture reduces unnecessary inter-region motion, time spent waiting for plans, and repeated observations. Across ten indoor and outdoor simulation scenes, AGE-Capture achieves a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) $3.30$--$3.53\,\mathrm{dB}$ higher than that of the online baselines while using $58.2\%$ of the common mission-time budget on average. Its mean peak GPU memory usage is $91.0\%$--$93.3\%$ lower than that of the same baselines. Experiments with different sensor configurations validate the adaptability of the shared acquisition pipeline, while flights in nine real-world scenes further demonstrate onboard closed-loop operation under practical computational and motion constraints.

Yet reconstruction quality remains strongly dependent on the spatial and angular coverage of the acquired observations. Active reconstruction addresses this dependence by selecting observation positions and viewing directions that improve the current scene representation under limited acquisition resources. For large-scale real-world scenes, UAVs provide a practical platform because they can reach viewpoints at different elevations and headings (Fig. ).

Existing active-capture methods primarily address where to observe next. Traditional next-best-view (NBV) methods evaluate candidate viewpoints using geometric uncertainty, information gain, coverage, or visibility [3]. Identifying valuable candidate viewpoints, however, is only one part of a deployable UAV active-reconstruction system. The system must also accommodate heterogeneous sensing configurations and coordinate acquisition decisions with execution under limited flight resources. Existing methods commonly evaluate reconstruction under a fixed view count or time budget. These limits constrain capture but do not indicate whether further observations would improve the reconstruction. The system must therefore assess residual reconstruction value online and terminate capture when further acquisition is no longer warranted.

Renderability-based reconstruction gain provides a state representation suitable for this online decision process. R3CON represents the value of candidate observations through a lightweight renderability state that is decoupled from a particular reconstruction backend, avoiding repeated optimization of a complete neural radiance field during planning [7]. Its computation and storage requirements support frequent online queries and updates. We build a closed-loop UAV capture process around this state: heterogeneous RGB observations are converted to a common camera-ray representation and update the state; the state guides region scheduling and local NBV selection; and the UAV acquires the next observation at the selected viewpoint.

We decouple geometric sensing from reconstruction observations and construct a common observation interface using camera rays, allowing RGB camera models with calibrated ray mappings to share the same reconstruction-aware active capture pipeline, while the geometric exploration module handles depth-map and LiDAR inputs. • A reconstruction-frontier mechanism for autonomous task completion. papers.title: Ties at the Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison of CVSS and EPSS at a Fixed Budget
papers.abstract: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.

Organizations face a large and continually changing set of vulnerabilities that may expose their systems to attack. Deciding where to intervene requires analytical work to assess relevance, investigate exploitation evidence, and identify appropriate protective measures. Limited analyst time and supporting resources constrain the number of vulnerabilities that can receive this attention, making prioritization a resource-allocation problem.

We present a methodology for evaluating alternative prioritization strategies within an explicit analytical budget. In this study, we represent that budget as a fixed number of CVEs selected for further assessment, providing a common basis for comparing strategies using information available at a defined decision time. This approach makes it possible to examine how score availability, provenance, and tie-breaking affect which CVEs are selected.

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) describes vulnerability characteristics and severity (FIRST, 2019). The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates near-term exploitation probability (FIRST, 0000b). We compare their rankings against subsequent listing in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Our question is: At a fixed decision horizon and selection budget, how do CVSS and EPSS compare in capturing subsequent KEV listings, and how do score provenance and cutoff ties affect that comparison?

When more CVEs share the cutoff score than the remaining places can accommodate, the score alone cannot determine which of them are selected. We call this group the cutoff tie block. The tie-breaking rule then becomes part of the resource-allocation policy, and its effect must be included in the comparison. We report capture under the fixed rule and its minimum and maximum across alternative selections within this block. The 2025 EPSS advantage survives all these CVSS alternatives, whereas the Q1 ordering can reverse.

(3) We document score provenance and compare NVD-vector availability by subsequent KEV outcome, with supporting records for individual positive CVEs.

papers.title: Global-in-Time Nonrelativistic Limit and KAM Tori for the Complex Klein-Gordon Equation on the Circle
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a global-in-time nonrelativistic limit for families of small-amplitude quasi-periodic solutions of the cubic complex Klein-Gordon equation on the circle. Firstly, we construct by a KAM block scheme, small-amplitude two-frequency invariant tori and show that their linear stability depends on whether the two excited Fourier indices coincide or are distinct: coincident indices yield linearly stable tori, whereas distinct indices yield partially hyperbolic tori. Moreover, controlling the dependence of the KAM scheme on the speed of light, we construct quasi-periodic solutions whose frequencies, after a gauge transformation, coincide exactly with those of quasi-periodic solutions of the limiting coupled NLS system, obtaining an approximation uniform for all times in the nonrelativistic regime. By this result, we further show that there exists a positive-measure set of frequencies such that, for each frequency, we can fix a quasi-periodic solution of the coupled NLS system and a suitable subsequence of Klein-Gordon solutions converging globally in time to the fixed NLS solution.

papers.title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
papers.abstract: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using four representations trained on WikiText-103: two count-based PPMI configurations and two Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings reveal systematic linguistic organisation at multiple geometric scales and its sensitivity to representation choices.

papers.title: Dynamic Human-Robot Role Allocation through Entropy-Based Monitoring and LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.
papers.intro:
Role allocation in human-robot collaboration (HRC) originally relied on fixed, predefined strategies derived from the inherent capabilities of humans and robots. In line with Fitts’ List of “Men Are Better At/Machines Are Better At” [1], humans were typically assigned tasks demanding reasoning, adaptability, or creativity, whereas robots were responsible for operations that were repetitive, precise, or hazardous. As technology advances and increasingly powerful AI models emerge, the traditional separation between human and robot capacities is becoming less distinct, calling for adaptive and context-sensitive role assignment strategies [2]. By monitoring online the state of the human, the robot, and the surrounding environment, roles can be dynamically adjusted during task execution, optimizing the team performance and fostering fluid collaboration [3, 4].

In line with Fitts’ List of “Men Are Better At/Machines Are Better At” [1], humans were typically assigned tasks demanding reasoning, adaptability, or creativity, whereas robots were responsible for operations that were repetitive, precise, or hazardous. As technology advances and increasingly powerful AI models emerge, the traditional separation between human and robot capacities is becoming less distinct, calling for adaptive and context-sensitive role assignment strategies [2]. By monitoring online the state of the human, the robot, and the surrounding environment, roles can be dynamically adjusted during task execution, optimizing the team performance and fostering fluid collaboration [3, 4].

In industry and healthcare, repetitive tasks and heavy lifting can lead to musculoskeletal injuries and reduced productivity. Embedding physical condition and ergonomic assessments within role allocation strategies facilitates optimized load sharing, promoting both human well-being and system efficiency. Classical approaches rely on explicit ergonomic thresholds or rule-based criteria. For example, Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA)-based systems [5] reassigned tasks to the robot when human posture becomes unsafe, while other methods combined initial offline allocation with online fatigue estimation from motion tracking [6]. To manage more complex constraints, several works use optimization-based role allocation. Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) formulations [7, 8] balanced makespan, precedence, and ergonomic load from estimated worker’s posture, updating task assignments online as human performance evolves. In [9], authors proposed an AO⋆ search over an AND/OR Graph (AOG) of feasible assembly sequences and agent assignments, with nodes as subassemblies and agent-specific edges as actions. Task costs reflect agent suitability: robots have fixed costs and penalized infeasible tasks, while human costs depend on KWear, derived from Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) scores and posture duration. When KWear exceeds safe limits, tasks shift to the robot until recovery. Alternatively, data-driven approaches can estimate fatigue through learned biomechanical models [10], assigning demanding tasks to the robot. When tasks cannot be decomposed, allocation shift to the control level, with robots adapting assistance policies based on human fatigue measured via EMG [11] or switching control modes dynamically [12]: a strategy that is effective but often task-specific and difficult to generalize. However, although these strategies reduce musculoskeletal strain, when tasks have similar ergonomic risk scores, the resulting role assignment may become non-intuitive. While users readily accept not being assigned to clearly high-risk tasks like heavy lifting, being asked to perform a task with comparable risk but against their intentions can also feel frustrating.

Other approaches exploit cognitive load measures or user preferences to improve both performance and user satisfaction. Early approaches relied on rule-based strategies: the robot adjusts its autonomy level or reassigns subtasks when cognitive load, stress, or trust estimates cross predefined thresholds [13, 14]. A second family of methods formulated allocation as an optimization problem, selecting roles that balanced productivity with human well-being, keeping mental or physiological stress within safe limits [15, 16]. More recent work has shifted toward learning-based personalization. Robots learn human capabilities or trustworthiness from task outcomes and allocate roles accordingly [17], or model collaboration as a two-player game in which both partners negotiate roles that satisfy productivity and stress objectives, approaching equilibrium through experience [18]. In this context, estimates of trust or stress are not intentional inputs provided by the user, so the resulting allocations may confuse an operator who still wishes to retain some freedom in choosing what to do. More recently, Large Language Models (LLM)s have been used to process explicit user requests, which represents a step toward more intuitive collaboration thanks to the naturalness of verbal communication. For instance, [19] allowed users to express states or preferences directly (e.g., “I have a back pain”), which an LLM translated into allocation costs, reducing the likelihood of assigning to the user tasks that strain their back.

While the above-mentioned approaches typically prioritized a single optimization objective, the following combine multiple factors simultaneously. [20] introduced a capability-based framework scoring agent-task pairs by task complexity, dexterity, and physical effort. [21] formulated allocation as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem that accounts for makespan, workload, quality, preferences, and spatiotemporal constraints, with dynamic re-allocation during execution, but its computational burden limits online use. To address this, [22] leveraged Behavior Trees (BT)s to decompose jobs into smaller subproblems, solving a MILP only for currently unlocked tasks. Allocation considered capabilities, ergonomics, and availability. However, having many factors influencing the allocation decision, it becomes even harder for the user to understand why certain tasks are assigned to them. In [23], an augmented reality interface was used for negotiation: the user could explicitly accept or reject proposed allocations, updating preference-based costs that influenced future algorithm decisions. In this way, the user became part of the decision-making process, recognizing that their intentions were taken into account. However, continuously requiring the user to confirm allocations can negatively affect the fluency of the interaction, interrupting task execution and eventually becoming tedious and unnatural [24]. Moreover, the human freedom of action remains limited, as the user can only accept or reject the proposed allocation without actively taking initiative within the collaboration. Allowing users to choose actions on the fly, rather than following imposed allocations, remains relatively underexplored despite its relevance for tasks admitting multiple valid execution sequences, such as lightweight assembly. To include human decision-making authority in a role allocation framework, [25] used wearable devices to recognize gestures, informing an AOG-based task manager of the human’s ongoing activity and triggering compatible robot actions. However, their approach required task-specific gesture training and did not assess activity completion and correctness.

papers.title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
papers.abstract: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.

OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language introduced by Aït-Kaci Aït-Kaci (1984); Aït-Kaci and Podelski (1993). It is based on sorts, which represent classes of objects, and features, which represent functional attributes. Sorts are organized in a subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities and their constraints. Reasoning with OSF logic is based on the normalization (or unification) of OSF terms, a procedure that aims to combine the constraints expressed by one or more terms while taking the sort hierarchy into account. OSF logic is at the basis of CEDAR Amir and Aït-Kaci (2017), a Semantic Web reasoner that normalizes and optimizes queries expressed as OSF terms before translating them into SPARQL, possibly leading to more efficient retrieval.

papers.title: Fast electrons and high energy photons produced in strong-field ionization of atoms as diagnostics of multi-petawatt laser beams
papers.abstract: We calculate numerically energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons emitted in the process of tunnel photoionization of argon by a focused laser beam of multi-petawatt power. By scanning the beam power and varying the degree of focusing and the field polarization, we show these distributions to be sensitive both to the peak laser intensity and to the field configuration in the focal spot. Investigated parameters of the laser beam correspond to those of several recently commissioned lasers of multi-petawatt power. These findings, in line with the earlier reported proposals, provide a basis for the development of a reliable ionization diagnostics of extremely intense laser fields.

papers.intro:
The development of super-intense laser sources of electromagnetic radiation has demonstrated considerable progress over the past two decades. Several multi-petawatt laser facilities have been put into operation [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Even more ambitious projects of sub-exawatt sources are currently under development and construction [6, 7]. Among the multiple potential applications of petawatt (PW), multi-PW and exawatt sources of ultrashort laser pulses, studies of fundamental effects of the interaction of electromagnetic field with charged particles in nonlinear and non-perturbative regimes are of primary significance for fundamental physics. These include investigations of the radiation reaction force in classical and quantum regimes, relativistic ionization, effects of nonlinear quantum electrodynamics, various schemes of laser acceleration of electrons and ions, and more. The current status of this thriving research area is outlined in reviews [8, 9, 10, 11] and the literature quoted there. The precise knowledge of the peak intensity, which can be achieved in the focus of a super-intense laser beam, and of the intensity distribution and field configuration in the focal area is of key significance for the reliable analysis of experimental data as well as for the determination of principal requirements for the search of certain effects with the use of a given laser source.
