This raises a high demand for methods of direct diagnostics of extreme electromagnetic fields in the foci of multi-PW laser beams. To clarify terminology, note that we call diagnostics direct if it is based on measurements of effects, which take place in the laser focus in the full power mode of the beam. Several nonlinear effects, which can serve as sensitive tools for field diagnostics, have been examined in theory and, partially, experimentally. An incomplete list includes tunnel ionization of multielectron atoms [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], acceleration of electrons and ions created in the laser focus through ionization [18, 19, 20, 21], nonlinear Thomson and Compton scattering of photons of an intense laser pulse on a beam of fast electrons [22, 23, 24]. For further references, we direct the reader to review [11]. Among these effects, tunnel ionization of heavy atoms and ions possesses two significant advantages: it is highly nonlinear and local. Each of these features potentially allows us to probe the laser intensity and measure its peak value with good accuracy [15, 16]. However, the method has also certain shortcomings: (a) the tunnel ionization diagnostics appears most sensitive to the value of the laser intensity only when the latter is close to the ionization threshold of s-electrons [17] and (b) in the non-relativistic domain, which for tunnel ionization spreads up to ≃1024−1025​W/cm2\simeq 10^{24}-10^{25}{\rm W/cm}^{2} the ionization probability is solely determined by the electric field amplitude so that the method probes intensity and not the electric and magnetic fields vectors. At the same time, in an experiment targeted at measurements of production of highly charged ions [12, 13, 14], one could register also fast electrons produced through nonlinear ionization [20, 21] and high-energy photons emitted by such electrons while they leave the focus. Such three-fold diagnostics realized in the frame of one experiment could essentially improve the accuracy of measurements, both for the intensity peak amplitude and also for the field distribution in the focal area.

We change the hitherto unknown parameters of the beam including its degree of focusing and the peak value of the field amplitude in the focus center to trace the evolution of electron and photon distributions triggered by this change. These trajectories are then used to find the spectra of emitted photons according to the method applied in our earlier work [25]. The MC code developed in this work allows greatly accelerating the calculations, compared to a particle-in-cell (PIC) code, because the statement of the problem excludes the necessity of calculation of the back reaction of charges on the electromagnetic field configuration.

papers.title: Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity
papers.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in expectation and with high probability.

papers.intro:
Many supervised machine learning tasks can be formulated as stochastic convex optimization (SCO) problems. In regression, e.g., a population risk ℒP​(θ):=𝔼⁡[ℒn​(θ)]:=𝔼⁡[1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(θ,(Yi,Xi))]\mathcal{L}_{P}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{L}_{n}(\theta)\right]:=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(\theta,(Y_{i},X_{i}))\right] is to be minimized, where XiX_{i} are i.i.d. observations from a prespecified distribution with true parameter ϑ∈Θ⊆ℝd\vartheta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} that shall be recovered. In times of big data, SCO is mostly solved using stochastic gradient-based optimization procedures where ℒP\mathcal{L}_{P} is approximated using the loss ℓ\ell evaluated on a subsample of the observations instead of the whole empirical risk ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}. For classical regression models, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can be shown to achieve statistically optimal performance when recovering ϑ\vartheta through an SCO with properly specified loss components ℓ\ell (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992; Bach and Moulines, 2013; Toulis et al., 2014). When data privacy guarantees like approximate, Gaussian or Renyi differential privacy (DP) (Dwork et al., 2006; Dong et al., 2022; Mironov, 2017) need to be enforced, the picture is less clear even in simple convex and strongly convex settings. This work focuses on the simplest possible case, regression problems that can be solved through SCO with strongly convex and smooth Lipschitz losses with a single pass of SGD.

Objective perturbation solves such problems by privatizing the empirical risk through noise and solving this new optimization problem using standard convex optimization methods. Similarly, output perturbation algorithms solve the non-private problem first, e.g., using SGD and afterwards privatize the estimate by adding noise. Both approaches are known to be optimal for recovering the empirical/population risk minimizer for strongly convex and smooth problems (See Chaudhuri et al., 2011; Kifer et al., 2012; Talwar et al., 2014 for objective and Zhang et al., 2017; Lowy and Razaviyayn, 2021 for output perturbation).

Noisy SGD-type algorithms follow another approach and privatize every single gradient within the iterations of SGD via additive Gaussian noise. This approach was introduced by Song et al., 2013 and later popularized under the name of DP-SGD by Abadi et al., 2016. Initially, the privacy of such algorithms was shown through composition theorems or privacy amplification by subsampling. Privacy guarantees based on amplification by subsampling analyze Noisy SGD’s privacy when mini-batches are sampled uniformly at random, with or without replacement or using Poisson sampling (Abadi et al., 2016; Mironov et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2022; Bu et al., 2020). In a concurrent line of work, the privacy amplification by iteration guarantees in Feldman et al., 2018; Feldman et al., 2020 tighten privacy bounds by analyzing the Renyi DP leakage when only releasing the last iterate after one pass of Noisy SGD over the data, with fixed disjoint batches. Most recently, works by Chourasia et al., 2021; Altschuler and Talwar, 2022; Ye and Shokri, 2022 introduced convergent Renyi DP bounds, for full-batch and mini-batch Noisy SGD, where the privacy loss on (strongly) convex and smooth losses eventually stops growing after a fixed number of iterations. Likewise, Bok et al., 2024 proved this phenomenon under Gaussian DP. Such convergent Renyi DP bounds extend to non-convex and also non-smooth losses (Asoodeh and Diaz, 2023; Altschuler et al., 2024; Kong and Ribero, 2024; Chien and Li, 2025; Liang et al., 2026). Unfortunately, the generic convergent privacy bounds seem to be too weak for optimal utility guarantees under strong convexity. For instance, the privacy bounds requiring strong convexity like Altschuler et al., 2024, Theorem 5.1 are stated for constant stepsizes, tie the privacy inducing noise to a lower bound on the batch size or introduce excess polylog⁡(n)\operatorname{polylog}(n) factors. Others like Bok et al., 2024, Theorem 4.2 and Ye and Shokri, 2022, Theorem 4.2 do not provide closed form expressions required for deriving precise guarantees. They also all impose strong convexity on the loss components ℓ\ell. However, in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with d>1d>1, the components ℓ\ell used for parameter estimation for important regression models -- like generalized linear models (GLMs)11 1 See, e.g., Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972 for an introduction. – are not strongly convex without regularization. papers.title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
papers.abstract: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.

Small bodies such as asteroids and comets, remnants of the early Solar System, preserve pristine materials and yield critical insights into the chemical and physical processes driving its formation [18, 28]. Beyond their scientific value, small bodies have also drawn attention for the risk they pose as impact hazards to Earth [6]. Consequently, increasing attention has been devoted to their exploration through spacecraft missions, including sample-return campaigns and technology demonstrations [8, 27, 22, 17, 13]. As more exploration missions emerge, accurately understanding the dynamical environment around these bodies becomes increasingly important, particularly because of the challenges posed by their irregular shapes, weak gravitational forces, and complex physical characteristics [19].

The irregular geometry of small bodies strongly affects their local dynamical environment. Shape determines the gravitational field, constrains internal mass distribution, and influences orbital stability and spacecraft maneuvering. It also affects illumination and eclipse conditions, which modulate solar radiation pressure, a dominant perturbation in the weak-gravity regime of small bodies. Accurate shape estimation is therefore fundamental for mission design, guidance, navigation, control, and operational safety, as well as for optimizing scientific observation strategies.

Machine learning approaches, in particular, offer the potential to efficiently generate and refine 3D models from sparse or partial observations [5, 24, 3]. Among these, occupancy networks and other implicit surface representations are especially promising for small-body missions, as they can represent complex geometries and be updated incrementally with new measurements. However, existing learning-based methods typically require RGB imagery or depth data and assume sufficient downlink capacity for ground processing. In this work, we leverage EclipseNets [1, 4], pre-trained on rough a priori knowledge of the asteroid’s shape, to bootstrap the reconstruction process. As the spacecraft orbits the target and collects additional silhouette information (derived, for instance, from points of entrance and exit in eclipse regions detected with a simple Sun sensor), this data is used to iteratively train an occupancy network. The resulting workflow produces a continuously improving 3D representation of the asteroid, enabling real-time, onboard shape reconstruction. This approach is particularly suited to the challenges of modern small-body exploration, supporting autonomous navigation, hazard assessment, and efficient scientific operations on missions with limited computational and communication resources.

During the mission, Sun sensor eclipse entry and exit events are collected and used to refine this model in situ. The refined EclipseNet generates silhouettes for arbitrary viewpoints, which are then converted into orthographic rays and used to train a neural signed-distance field representation of the asteroid. This final representation produces a continuously improving 3D model suitable for onboard navigation and scientific analysis.

papers.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
papers.abstract:
The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way.
  The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

papers.intro:
Learning has two complementary aspects: generalization and simplification. A scientist who observes the outcomes of many experiments may seek to predict the outcome of a new one; this is generalization. The same scientist may also seek to explain the observed outcomes in terms of a small number of informative experiments, from which the remaining observations can be recovered by reasoning; this is simplification. These perspectives are connected by a classical guiding principle: Occam’s razor suggests favoring simpler explanations among those consistent with the observations. In learning, this principle motivates the intuition that a concise explanation of observed data may also generalize well to new examples. Understanding when and how this intuition can be made precise is a fundamental question about learning. Simplification is also of particular interest in modern machine learning, where models that generalize well are often difficult to interpret.

In many geometric problems, the concept returned by a learning algorithm is determined by only a few examples. For instance, the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing all positive examples in the plane is determined by at most four of them: one for each of its sides. This observation suggests a way to understand generalization through the amount of data needed to specify the learner’s output. Indeed, and as discussed in more detail below, Littlestone and Warmuth showed that such algorithms generalize in Valiant’s PAC setting.

Such a scheme can be viewed as a protocol between two players: a compressor and a reconstructor. The compressor receives a labeled dataset and sends the reconstructor a small subset of its examples, possibly accompanied by a short string of side-information bits. From this message alone, the reconstructor must produce a concept consistent with every example in the original dataset, including those it never received.

papers.title: Influence of variable IMF on the dynamical black hole mass estimates in massive ETGs
papers.abstract: Several studies have shown that the stellar initial mass function (IMF) in massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) is not universal. Recent results from stellar population synthesis models, based on integral-field unit (IFU) observations, indicate that the IMF varies radially, becoming increasingly bottom-heavy towards galaxy centres. This radial variation alters the stellar mass-to-light ratio ($\rm M_{*}/L$) and can significantly affect dynamical black hole (BH) mass estimates in massive ETGs. In this study, we investigate the impact of a radially varying IMF on BH mass estimates for five massive galaxies: NGC3923, NGC4261, NGC4636, IC4296, and IC4329. Using DYNAMITE, a triaxial Schwarzschild orbit-based modelling code, we perform mass modelling of these galaxies based on MUSE and SINFONI IFU observations. Our models incorporate radially varying stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$ profiles derived from spatially resolved stellar population modelling with a free IMF, and we compare the resulting BH masses with those obtained from dynamical models assuming a constant stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$. All galaxies in our sample show bottom-heavy IMFs in their central regions, with the IMF generally becoming lighter towards larger radii. We obtain constrained BH masses for NGC3923 and IC4329, while only upper limits are obtained for NGC4261, NGC4636, and IC4296. Compared with the constant-$\rm M_{*}/L$ models, the variable-$\rm M_{*}/L$ models yield BH masses lower by approximately 83% and 11% for NGC3923 and IC4329, respectively, while the BH mass upper limits for the other galaxies can increase or decrease. Our results demonstrate that spatial variations in the IMF and stellar $\rm M_{*}/L$ can have a non-negligible but strongly galaxy-dependent impact on dynamical BH mass measurements. These results highlight the importance of accounting for such variations in future dynamical modelling efforts.

papers.intro:
Measurements of the different mass components in massive early-type galaxies (ETGs)—notably black hole (BH), stellar component, and dark matter (DM) —provide critical constraints on galaxy formation models. These components exhibit tight scaling relationships with one another, indicating that they co-evolve alongside the growth and evolution of the galaxy. The BH mass strongly correlates with various galaxy properties such as velocity dispersion, bulge mass, and luminosity, suggesting a close link between the evolution of BHs and galaxies (Ferrarese and Ford, 2005; Kormendy and Ho, 2013; van den Bosch, 2016; Saglia et al., 2016). Accurate measurements of these components are crucial for understanding these relationships, and by extension, for refining galaxy formation models. However, a major challenge arises from the degeneracy of these components in their contribution to the total mass, making it difficult to disentangle and accurately decompose the total mass into its individual components.

The knowledge about the stellar mass and other stellar properties of ETGs can be derived with the stellar population models (Tinsley, 1980; Trager et al., 2000; Thomas et al., 2005; Conroy and van Dokkum, 2012) whereas the BH mass and total mass can be derived from the dynamical modelling studies. Multiple studies of massive galaxies based on stellar population modelling either using the line strength or the full spectrum fitting techniques, have shown spatial variations in properties such as the mass-to-light ratio (M/L), color, metallicity, age, alpha-element abundance ratio, and the initial mass function (IMF) (Worthey et al., 1992; Mehlert et al., 2003; Sánchez-Blázquez et al., 2006a; Spolaor et al., 2009; Kuntschner et al., 2010; Conroy and van Dokkum, 2012; Sánchez-Blázquez et al., 2014; González Delgado et al., 2015; Smith, 2020). These variations in stellar properties essentially reflect the formation and evolutionary histories of massive galaxies. Massive galaxies are believed to be evolved in two evolutionary phases: first in-situ formation with an intense burst of star formation and second ex-situ with the growth in outer envelopes resulting from the infall or merger events of low mass galaxies (Oser et al., 2010; van Dokkum and Conroy, 2010a).

One of the key, yet debated, findings from stellar population models of massive galaxies is the existence of a variable initial mass function (IMF) in ETGs (van Dokkum and Conroy, 2010b; Spiniello et al., 2011; van Dokkum and Conroy, 2012; Ferreras et al., 2013; La Barbera et al., 2013; Martín-Navarro et al., 2015b; Spiniello et al., 2014; Conroy et al., 2014; Parikh et al., 2018, see also Cappellari et al. 2012 for IMF variation from a dynamical modelling perspective). Although the IMF was previously thought to be invariant based on studies of the Milky Way, most stellar population studies of ETGs have found a Salpeter-like or even steeper IMF slope in their central regions, suggesting an excess of low-mass dwarf stars in the cores of massive galaxies. With advances in IFU data and techniques, recent studies such as Martín-Navarro et al. (2019); Martín-Navarro et al. (2021); Martín-Navarro et al. (2024) have demonstrated that this IMF variability is confined to the inner few kiloparsecs and may be correlated with the metallicity of the galaxies. More recently, Parikh et al. (2024) have confirmed IMF variability using a sample of seven massive galaxies based on MUSE IFU data.

Most BH mass estimates have been derived using dynamical modelling of stellar or gas kinematics. Although an indirect approach, dynamical modelling can also be used to infer the IMF of galaxies. If the DM halo contributions are properly accounted for and subtracted from the total mass, then the dynamical stellar M/L ratio can be determined. papers.title: Finite groups with a fixed-point-free automorphism satisfying an irreducible identity
papers.abstract:
For any given irreducible polynomial $f(x)=a_0+a_1\cdot x+\cdots+a_d\cdot x^d\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, we study the structure of finite groups $(G,\cdot)$ that have a fixed-point-free-automorphism $\alpha$ satisfying the condition \[
  \{g^{a_0}\cdot\alpha(g)^{a_1}\cdots\alpha^d(g)^{a_d}\mid g\in G\}=\{1\}. \] We show that such a group $G$ is nilpotent of class at most $d^{2^d}$, provided that $|G|$ is coprime to an explicit, non-zero, integer invariant $\iota(f(x))$ of $f(x)$. We do this by extending the solutions of the Frobenius conjecture. We also extend the solution of the restricted Burnside problem in prime exponent and the classification of the $n$-abelian groups.

papers.title: momipy: A time-resolved momentum microscopy data analysis workflow
papers.abstract: Photoemission momentum microscopy is an emerging approach to photoelectron spectroscopy that is transforming electronic band structure mapping at both laboratory-based and large-scale facilities. Its extension to time-resolved measurements has recently enabled major advances, ranging from the femtosecond imaging of exciton wavefunctions to dark-field photoelectron microscopy of light-induced dynamics and strong light-matter interactions. However, the rapid acquisition of high-dimensional data sets (including electron in-plane momenta $k_x$ and $k_y$, kinetic energy $E_\mathrm{kin}$, time $\Delta t$, and more) poses substantial challenges for data handling and analysis. A typical workflow encompasses data acquisition, exploratory visualization, calibration and targeted feature extraction, with data management ideally guided by FAIR principles. Here, we present momipy, a Python package that streamlines the momentum microscopy data analysis workflow efficiently and at low computational cost. Among other features, momipy provides interactive 4D data visualization, energy and momentum calibration, space-charge correction, and a broad selection of multidimensional data analysis routines, including binning, momentum-map extraction and time-, energy- and momentum-resolved model fitting. momipy is accompanied by a selection of interactive example scripts, supporting adoption of momipy by both experienced researchers and users new to momentum microscopy.

papers.intro:
Time- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (tr-ARPES) provides unrivaled access to the electronic structure of materials, combining full momentum information with the ability to map ultrafast dynamics with femtosecond time resolution [7]. Recently, the extension of this technique by so-called momentum microscopes in combination with short-pulse extreme ultraviolet light sources has enabled a series of landmark discoveries, ranging from the tracing of exciton dynamics in 2D semiconductors [30, 41, 28] and organic semiconductors [34, 56, 6, 5, 3] to the observation of Floquet-Bloch states [33] and Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene [11]. The driving force behind these discoveries was the development of dedicated ultrafast time of flight momentum microscopy setups at several laboratories [24, 4, 31, 14, 56, 19, 1, 23, 40, 17], including ours, that combine momentum microscopy with high-repetition-rate high-harmonic-generation light sources [9, 39, 12, 8]. Time-resolved momentum microscopy is also becoming increasingly available at facility beamlines, including free-electron lasers [13, 29, 10, 15, 49]. By joining an electron microscope lens column with momentum-resolved detection and time of flight energy resolution, momentum microscopy can measure multidimensional datasets spanning in-plane momentum coordinates, kinetic energy, pump-probe delay and additional parameters such as temperature, photon energy, polarization, spin, or geometry with unprecedented efficiency [32, 27, 45, 53]. While conventional ARPES can in principle access similar multidimensional information, momentum microscopy achieves this with vastly superior data collection rates due to its non-scanning measurement principle, enabling measurements that would be prohibitively time-consuming or impractical with traditional ARPES setups.

Momentum microscopy at its core measures the photoemission intensity II depending on both in-plane momenta kx,kyk_{x},k_{y} and kinetic energy EkinE_{\text{kin}} of the photoemitted electrons. Thus, a single static measurement produces an (at least) three-dimensional dataset containing I⁡(kx,ky,Ekin)I(k_{x},k_{y},E_{\text{kin}}) data. This might be recorded and stored directly in histogram form. Alternatively, a data stream might be recorded where a list of detected electrons is stored along with their in-plane momenta, kinetic energy and detection timestamps as an event list (see Figure 1a). While the latter approach enables further data preprocessing opportunities, the starting point for data analysis is in almost all cases a three- (or higher) dimensional histogram. With pump-probe delay Δ​t\Delta t introducing an additional temporal axis, time-resolved momentum microscopy inherently possesses a high data complexity. Further experimental degrees of freedom such as temperature, pump/probe polarization, photon energy or spin dependence add yet more axes to the multidimensional dataset. If not handled carefully, this can rapidly increase the data file sizes and cause the evaluation procedure to exceed the computational resources available. Hence, a crucial challenge is the distillation of key information from the collected raw data in a systematic, time- and resource-efficient manner.

Beyond the handling of large multidimensional datasets, a second challenge lies in disentangling relevant features of the photoemission spectrum from instrumental measurement artifacts. Despite its power, momentum microscopy is prone to instrument-induced distortions, mainly from space charge and the lens system, that are significantly more pronounced than in conventional time-resolved ARPES experiments [31]. Aberrations of the electrostatic lenses can lead to anisotropic and energy-dependent momentum scaling [51, 52, 50, 61], which, if neglected, results in incorrectly assigned momentum axes that propagate into all subsequent analysis steps. Additionally, the Coulomb interaction between the photoemitted electrons in the lens column of the microscope can cause momentum-dependent energy shifts and broadening of spectral features [43, 37, 36, 20]. These so-called space-charge effects can lead to an incorrect energy assignment of spectral features, and, more critically, could be misinterpreted as a material response rather than an artifact. These two examples highlight the importance of detecting such distortions and properly accounting for them before interpreting the data.

Despite the ongoing establishment of momentum microscopy in labs worldwide, adequate software infrastructure for data handling and analysis is still lacking. While several tools exist that have been developed for conventional 2D ARPES workflows [47, 38, 21, 25], these are poorly suited to the demands of time-resolved momentum microscopy data. They lack automation features for reproducible data evaluation or momentum-microscopy-specific tooling. This applies specifically to the identification and handling of instrument-induced distortion. Several correction methods have been proposed [44, 61, 52, 60, 43], but significant improvements are still needed regarding development, sophistication, ease of use, and the quantification of how these corrections impact the data. Consequently, practitioners typically develop their own custom analysis code: a time-consuming process that could hinder reproducibility and complicate the adoption of FAIR-compliant data management practices, i.e. Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable data sets, for example built using the NeXus data format [26]. A notable contribution is the MPES package [60], which combines the processing of event-based momentum microscopy data with analysis and visualization capabilities. However, the workflow of MPES is specifically tailored to event-based collection schemes, focusing on the transition from event data to evaluation-ready histogram datasets, which are subsequently analyzed by custom evaluation procedures.

papers.title: Quasi-orthogonality is a geometric property
papers.abstract: Quasi-orthogonality is one of the key ingredients for proofs of optimal convergence rates for adaptive mesh refinement methods (Carstensen, Feischl, Page, and Praetorius, arXiv:1312.1171). The work of Feischl (arXiv:2008.12198) proposed a relaxed quasi-orthogonality that follows directly from the inf-sup stability of the underlying problem discretization. The proof uses an intricate connection to the stability of $LU$-factorization of matrices. Recently, Gantumur (arXiv:2609.16265) presented a vastly simplified argument based solely on Hilbert space arguments. Building on this idea, we show that quasi-orthogonality is a purely geometric property of a set of points. This property is checked for a large class of Petrov-Galerkin methods for monotone, non-linear equations.

papers.title: Optimal Beurling-H\"ormander-type uncertainty principles and nontriviality of Gelfand-Shilov spaces
papers.abstract:
We study how rapidly a nonzero function $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and its Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ can simultaneously decay. For each suitable weight function $\omega$, we construct a convex weight function $\varpi$ and establish the existence of a threshold $\Phi_{(\omega,\varpi^*)} \in (0, \infty)$, where $\varpi^*$ denotes the convex conjugate of $\varpi$. For $a,b > 0$, the conditions \[
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty |f(x)| e^{\omega(a|x|)} \, \mathrm{d}x < \infty
  \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty |\widehat{f}(\xi)| e^{\varpi^*(b|\xi|)} \, \mathrm{d}\xi
  < \infty \] force $f = 0$ when $ab > \Phi_{(\omega,\varpi^*)}$, whereas the functions satisfying both conditions form a dense subspace of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ when $ab < \Phi_{(\omega,\varpi^*)}$. Similar results are also established in higher dimensions. We characterize the weights $\omega$ for which $\varpi$ is equivalent to $\omega$ and use this to determine when the Beurling-H\"ormander uncertainty principle is optimal. A discrete form of the same construction yields a characterization of the nontriviality of Gelfand-Shilov spaces $\mathcal{S}^{M}_{A}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $\Sigma^{M}_{A}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ in terms of their defining weight sequences $M$ and $A$, under suitable regularity assumptions.

papers.title: On the feasibility of using [Eu/$\alpha$] to identify accreted and in-situ extragalactic globular clusters
papers.abstract: The chemical abundance ratio [Eu/$\alpha$] has been proposed as a discriminator between ex-situ and in-situ stellar populations in the Milky Way and external galaxies. Here we show with a high-quality, homogeneous dataset of integrated-light abundances for 28 globular clusters (GCs), where 21 are extragalactic and 7 galactic, that this behaviour holds in other Local Group galaxies. In particular, we find metal-rich ([Fe/H] > --0.7) M31 GCs have uniformly low [Eu/Si]$\sim-0.4$, indicating they represent an in-situ population. Lower metallicity GCs in M31 generally show high [Eu/Si] $\sim+0.4$, suggesting they originated in accreted progenitors, and these GCs lie at larger projected radii from the M31 centre. Furthermore, we compare the M31 GC abundances with similar determinations for the M31 bulge for Na, Mg, Si, Ti, Ca, Eu, Cr, Mn, Ba, Ni, and Cu. The in-situ M31 GCs and M31 bulge exhibit similar abundance trends, excepting Ba -- and possibly Cr and Ti, suggesting similar star formation processes. [Eu/Si] in the M31 bulge is consistent with in-situ Milky Way stars, but is higher than the M31 in-situ GCs. For M33 and intermediate-mass dwarf galaxies, we identify a mixture of in-situ and ex-situ GCs, while for lower-mass dwarfs, we identify primarily in-situ GCs. These results suggest that accreted GCs in massive galaxies originated, at least in part, from intermediate-mass, intermediate-metallicity progenitors. We support earlier suggestions that [Eu/$\alpha$] is a powerful in-/ex-situ separator for extragalactic GCs, demonstrating the potential of high-resolution integrated-light abundances for extragalactic archaeology.

papers.intro:
The assembly history of galaxies can be traced by the processes through which they accumulate their stellar populations. In particular, since star formation timescales and chemical enrichment are a function of host galaxy mass, the stellar population properties of the progenitor (in-situ) and accreted (ex-situ) components of galaxies are expected to differ (e.g., Tinsley 1979; Matteucci and Greggio 1986; Wheeler et al. 1989; Freeman and Bland-Hawthorn 2002). Globular clusters (GCs) have long been used as bright, surviving tracers of these accretion events.

In particular, since star formation timescales and chemical enrichment are a function of host galaxy mass, the stellar population properties of the progenitor (in-situ) and accreted (ex-situ) components of galaxies are expected to differ (e.g., Tinsley 1979; Matteucci and Greggio 1986; Wheeler et al. 1989; Freeman and Bland-Hawthorn 2002). Globular clusters (GCs) have long been used as bright, surviving tracers of these accretion events.

In the Milky Way (MW), kinematic and chemical tagging of stars and GCs has revealed common orbital and abundance signatures that link them to accreted dwarf galaxies (e.g., Nissen and Schuster 2010; Buder et al. 2021; Dodd et al. 2023). These accreted populations often exhibit specific dynamical and chemical characteristics that stand out against stars formed within the in situ population (Recio-Blanco et al., 2021). Specifically, it has been shown that accreted halo stars at high orbital energy exhibit elevated ratios of r-process to α\alpha-elements, e.g. [Eu/Si] (or sometimes [Eu/Ca]), whereas for in-situ stars at lower orbital energies these abundance ratios are lower (Monty et al., 2024). The general interpretation of the behaviour of [Eu/Si] is that α\alpha-elements are primarily produced in core-collapse supernovae on short timescales, while a major site for the production of r-process elements is thought to be neutron-star mergers, which presumably operate on much longer timescales. Furthermore, Kobayashi et al. (2023) indicate that Eu enrichment cannot be explained by neutron-star mergers alone, but instead requires contributions from both prompt and delayed r-process sources. Consequently, elevated [Eu/α\alpha] ratios are expected in systems that experienced more extended star formation histories compared to those formed through rapid, short-duration bursts. Therefore, the ratio between these two classes of elements can act as a "cosmic clock". In this picture, a high r-process/α\alpha-element ratio reflects the longer star formation timescales expected in the progenitors of accreted populations, which are typically lower-mass systems that were subsequently incorporated into more massive host galaxies (e.g., Hirai et al. 2025).

By compiling a comprehensive dataset of abundances for 54 MW GCs, Monty et al. (2024) found that the systematic differences in [Eu/Si] observed in field stars extend consistently to GC populations. Furthermore, the utility of [Eu/Si] as a chemical tag for linking GCs to their progenitor galaxies may extend beyond the MW and Local Group.

papers.title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
papers.abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.

papers.intro:
Neural networks are the least reliable when training data is scarce. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a principled way to deal with the fundamental uncertainty of this data regime (Mitros and Mac Namee, 2019; Kristiadi et al., 2020). They quantify both epistemic uncertainty, which arises from limited knowledge of the model, and aleatoric uncertainty, which is due to the inherent randomness of the data-generating process. They excel in high-stakes, safety-critical applications (Ghoshal et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2021), perform well with limited data, prevent overfitting (Depeweg et al., 2018), and can increase fairness and reduce bias (Doherty et al., 2023).

They excel in high-stakes, safety-critical applications (Ghoshal et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2021), perform well with limited data, prevent overfitting (Depeweg et al., 2018), and can increase fairness and reduce bias (Doherty et al., 2023).

BNNs quantify epistemic uncertainty by introducing a posterior distribution p⁡(𝜽∣𝒟)p(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathcal{D}) over the model parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}, given training data 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Propagating this uncertainty to the output η\eta is required for training and inference. Stochastic methods, such as Bayes by Backprop (Graves, 2011; Blundell et al., 2015), estimate it by sampling weights. Sampling-free methods, such as Deterministic Variational Inference (DVI) (Wu et al., 2019), CovProp (Wright et al., 2024), and Variational Bayesian Last Layers (VBLL) (Harrison et al., 2024), replace sampling with moment propagation, which removes noise at the cost of assuming a specific functional form for the pre-activations.

BNNs quantify epistemic uncertainty by introducing a posterior distribution p⁡(𝜽∣𝒟)p(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathcal{D}) over the model parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}, given training data 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Propagating this uncertainty to the output η\eta is required for training and inference. Stochastic methods, such as Bayes by Backprop (Graves, 2011; Blundell et al., 2015), estimate it by sampling weights. Sampling-free methods, such as Deterministic Variational Inference (DVI) (Wu et al., 2019), CovProp (Wright et al., 2024), and Variational Bayesian Last Layers (VBLL) (Harrison et al., 2024), replace sampling with moment propagation, which removes noise at the cost of assuming a specific functional form for the pre-activations.

We argue that these methods break down exactly where uncertainty quantification matters most. Indeed, DVI, CovProp and VBLL assume that the predictive distribution and the variational family are Gaussians. However, many applied problems require accurate estimates of tail probabilities—the probability of a 100-year flood or a multi-million-dollar insurance claim—for distributions that are often far from Gaussian. This Gaussian assumption shows up in two places in these methods: the likelihood, which captures aleatoric uncertainty, and the distribution of the network, which captures epistemic uncertainty. But in practice, the likelihood can be skewed, in Gamma regressions for claim sizes, for example. And the distribution of the network output also tends to be skewed in these cases, because tail predictions are often dominated by a few rarely active neurons. Hence, non-Gaussian variational families are required to properly handle these cases. Any propagation method that models either distribution as Gaussian can severely underestimate tail risk. In practice, the BNN literature uses many other variational families: spike-and-slab families for sparsification (Hubin and Storvik, 2019), scale mixtures for shrinkage (Louizos et al., 2017; Ghosh et al., 2019), and multimodal mixtures (Dusenberry et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2017)—though current sampling-free propagation methods are incompatible with these families.

We introduce CF-Prop, an exact and sampling-free method for uncertainty propagation in a single-layer Bayesian perceptron that uses characteristic functions (CF). The forward pass of the layer is expressed in the Fourier domain, making the predictive density tractable. We use this propagation algorithm as the backbone of a new method, Variational Inference via Characteristic Functions (CF-VI). CF-VI extends sampling-free variational inference beyond the Gaussian regime by expressing the predictive density of the Bayesian layer exactly and in closed form. It allows for both non-Gaussian predictive distributions and non-Gaussian variational families. It can accommodate any likelihood and any variational family with a tractable characteristic function.

The forward pass of the layer is expressed in the Fourier domain, making the predictive density tractable. We use this propagation algorithm as the backbone of a new method, Variational Inference via Characteristic Functions (CF-VI). CF-VI extends sampling-free variational inference beyond the Gaussian regime by expressing the predictive density of the Bayesian layer exactly and in closed form. It allows for both non-Gaussian predictive distributions and non-Gaussian variational families. It can accommodate any likelihood and any variational family with a tractable characteristic function.

CF-VI can be used to train a fully exact Bayesian perceptron or as an exact Bayesian last layer on a sampling-free or stochastic trunk. We show that CF-VI performs well on traditional benchmarks such as UCI regressions, and provides state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification on classification tasks with a large number of labels such as CIFAR-100. We also show that CF-VI performs exceptionally well in uncertainty quantification for neural GLMs commonly used in the actuarial sciences. In particular, we show that for a Gamma regression task on heavy-tailed data—predicting the size of insurance claims—other methods severely underestimate uncertainty in the tails of the distribution. In contrast, our method provides an exact description of the tail uncertainty. CF-VI is also computationally efficient: In many common cases, it adds only a modest overhead to the training of a fully deterministic neural network.

papers.title: Global existence versus blow-up for Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou lattices
papers.abstract:
This paper investigates the global behavior of infinite nonlinear lattices. In particular, for the Fermi--Pasta--Ulam--Tsingou-$\alpha$ lattice (FPUT-$\alpha$), we show global existence for small initial data via a region-based approach, and prove blow-up for negative energy and some positive energy, given appropriate conditions on the initial momentum and dispersion.
  Moreover, we extend these results to the nonlinear Klein-Gordon (DNKG) equation and nonlinear wave (DNW) equation. \

papers.intro:
The study of nonlinear lattices has both a rich history, including the pioneering work in numerics by Fermi, Pasta, Ulam and Tsingou [FPU55], as well as a wide range of applications in mechanics, optics or acoustics. Despite the vast amount of literature on FPUT lattices, there are still questions about the long-time behavior of certain models, such as the ones posed by Pankov in [Pan05]. In particular, the aim of the present paper is to provide a global existence result for the FPUT-α\alpha model with small positive energy, providing a solution of Problem 1.1 from Pankov [Pan05]. Moreover, we complement this result by establishing blow-up results for initial conditions with negative energy and certain initial conditions with positive energy. To this end we adapt a Levine–Glassey-type concavity argument from PDE-theory. We also provide examples of initial conditions satisfying our assumptions.

papers.title: On Romik's rationality conjectures for critical percolation
papers.abstract:
The completely packed $O(1)$ loop model can be viewed as an interface representation of critical bond percolation on the square lattice. We consider submatching events, which prescribe how these interfaces pair finitely many consecutive boundary points. Romik's rationality conjectures predict that the probabilities of these events on the semi-infinite cylinder are given by specific rational functions, which even become dyadic rationals in the half-plane limit.
  We derive explicit Pfaffian formulae for the probability of $k$ nested arches on the semi-infinite cylinder of circumference $2N$, valid for $k<N$. We deduce that these probabilities are rational functions of $N$ and, by taking the limit $N\to\infty$, that the corresponding half-plane probabilities remain rational. This establishes key aspects of Romik's conjectures.
  Our proof uses identities of Fonseca and Zinn-Justin, derived through the qKZ formalism, which express these probabilities as ratios of enumeration numbers for totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions (TSSCPPs). These plane partitions admit a dimer representation, allowing us to apply Kasteleyn theory. We evaluate the resulting hypergeometric sum using Zeilberger's and Gosper's algorithms and then take the half-plane limit $N\to\infty$. Along the way, we derive a somewhat simplified expression for the inverse Kasteleyn matrix entries (encoding correlations in TSSCPPs) of Ayyer and Chhita, which might be of independent interest.

A striking feature of many exactly solvable lattice models is that non-trivial finite-size observables can sometimes be described by explicit closed-form expressions. The completely packed O⁡(1)O(1) loop model provides a particularly clear instance of this phenomenon. On the semi-infinite cylinder and in the half-plane, the interfaces induce random noncrossing matchings of boundary points. Of particular interest are submatching events, which prescribe the pairing of a fixed number of consecutive boundary points. Motivated by earlier numerical observations and conjectures, Romik conjectured a specific rational-function form for the probabilities of these events on the cylinder, as well as dyadic rationality of the corresponding half-plane probabilities; see [19] and references therein.

The first step in this approach is provided by a result of Fonseca and Zinn-Justin [8]. Using integral formulae for a polynomial solution of the quantum Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (qKZ) equation, they relate certain components and partial sums of the ground-state vector of the O⁡(1)O(1) loop model to enumerations of families of non-intersecting lattice paths. These path ensembles admit a natural interpretation in terms of TSSCPPs. In particular, for the nested submatching events considered here, their results express the corresponding cylindrical probabilities as ratios of TSSCPP enumeration numbers, with the numerator counting configurations whose associated path ensemble has a prescribed number of initial horizontal paths.

papers.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. papers.intro:
Aerodynamic drag and lift are central quantities in car design and are usually estimated with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) [Elrefaie et al., 2024]. A high-fidelity simulation of a single design takes hours on a computing cluster, which limits the number of design variants that can be evaluated. Neural surrogates learn the map from the car geometry to the flow fields on its surface and predict the resulting forces in seconds [Lu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Pfaff et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024]. Their accuracy, however, depends on large training sets, typically thousands of car designs, each simulated with CFD. Car manufacturers and their suppliers hold many such simulations, but these data are proprietary and are not shared.

Aerodynamic drag and lift are central quantities in car design and are usually estimated with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) [Elrefaie et al., 2024]. A high-fidelity simulation of a single design takes hours on a computing cluster, which limits the number of design variants that can be evaluated. Neural surrogates learn the map from the car geometry to the flow fields on its surface and predict the resulting forces in seconds [Lu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Pfaff et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024]. Their accuracy, however, depends on large training sets, typically thousands of car designs, each simulated with CFD. Car manufacturers and their suppliers hold many such simulations, but these data are proprietary and are not shared.

Federated learning is designed for this setting. Clients train on their local data and send only model updates to a server, which aggregates them into a global model [Konečný et al., 2016a; Konečný et al., 2016b; McMahan et al., 2017; Kairouz et al., 2021]. It is used in practice, for example, for keyboard prediction on mobile devices [Hard et al., 2018] and for clinical models trained across hospitals [Sheller et al., 2020; Rieke et al., 2020; Dayan et al., 2021], among many other applications [Kairouz et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019]. A federation of car manufacturers faces two difficulties. First, the client data are heterogeneous, because each manufacturer produces its own range of body types, and data heterogeneity is a major obstacle in federated optimization [Zhao et al., 2018; Hsieh et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a]. Second, the learning problem is harder than the image classification tasks on which federated methods are usually evaluated. The surrogate predicts continuous fields at hundreds of thousands of surface points, and the drag is the integral of these fields over the surface. Since the forces on different parts of the body largely cancel in this integral, a small systematic error in one region leads to a large error in the predicted drag. To the best of our knowledge, federated training of aerodynamic surrogates has not been studied, and it is not known which federated optimizer is suited to it.

The optimizer is central to federated training because it determines how much local computation the clients can perform between communication rounds. More local epochs reduce the number of rounds but also let the client models drift apart [Stich, 2019; Wang and Joshi, 2021; Khaled et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021]. Standard federated optimizers such as FedAvg, SCAFFOLD and FedLion update each parameter independently [McMahan et al., 2017; Karimireddy et al., 2020; Tang and Chang, 2024]. Spectral optimizers instead update each weight matrix as a whole. The best-known example, Muon, replaces the momentum of a weight matrix with the nearest semi-orthogonal matrix [Jordan et al., 2024], which corresponds to steepest descent under the spectral norm [Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024]. Muon trains large language models efficiently [Liu et al., 2025a], and several federated variants have been proposed recently [Takezawa et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhang and Gao, 2025]. These methods have not been evaluated on simulation data, and it is unclear how many local epochs they tolerate when the client data differ.

In this paper, we study federated training of a car aerodynamics surrogate on DrivAerNet++ [Elrefaie et al., 2024]. The 6 857 cars we use amount to about 125 GB of surface data, nearly three orders of magnitude more than the MNIST and CIFAR benchmarks common in federated learning [LeCun et al., 1998; Krizhevsky, 2009]. The surrogate is a Transolver [Wu et al., 2024], a transformer for large meshes. Instead of computing attention among hundreds of thousands of points, Transolver groups the points into a small number of learned slices, computes attention among the slices, and maps the result back to the points, so that its cost grows linearly with the mesh size. We partition the training cars among six clients, either by body type, which gives the most heterogeneous split, or by Dirichlet sampling at three levels of heterogeneity. On these partitions, we tune three spectral and three non-spectral federated optimizers with one protocol and compare them with each other and with models trained on the pooled data. Our contributions are as follows. • We set up a federated benchmark for aerodynamic surrogates: a Transolver trained on DrivAerNet++ across six clients, with six federated optimizers tuned under one three-stage protocol. The code, the tuning records and the statistics of every run are public. • We propose two federated spectral optimizers: FedMARS-M, which adds the MARS variance-reduction term [Yuan et al., 2025] to the client momentum, and FedOLion, a federated version of OLion [Wang et al., 2026] (Section 3). • We show that FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized Muon with two to four local epochs per round, whereas the non-spectral methods require sixteen and remain 17 to 37% worse than FedMARS-M (Section 4). We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients (Section 5).

papers.title: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics
papers.abstract: This paper presents DARSY: a software tool for abstraction-based verification and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions. DARSY requires only a simulator of the system and a Lipschitz bound on its dynamics, and needs no knowledge of dynamics or noise distributions. The tool is fully automated and constructs a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions, whose probability intervals are obtained via statistical techniques and Lipschitz reasoning. Robust dynamic programming on this IMDP then yields a policy together with a lower bound on the probability that the unknown system satisfies a desired specification. This lower bound holds with a user-specified confidence; that is, it is probably approximately correct (PAC). The tool is implemented in Python and supports general Lipschitz-continuous system dynamics and specifications expressed in syntactically co-safe LTL (scLTL), which includes reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety specifications as special cases. Beyond standard IMDPs, DARSY implements a two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction that also bounds the probability of transitioning to aggregated state blocks, yielding smaller abstraction errors than IMDP abstractions and, as a result, tighter satisfaction guarantees. We demonstrate DARSY's broad applicability across a variety of benchmarks and specifications.

papers.intro:
The dynamics of many control systems, such as unmanned drones, mobile robots, and thermodynamic processes, are modeled by nonlinear stochastic difference equations (Söderström, 2002; Mesbah, 2016). These systems often must satisfy strict requirements despite their stochastic dynamics. For example, a mobile robot may need to visit a sequence of target locations while avoiding obstacles, despite random disturbances such as wind or wheel slip. Such requirements, called specifications, are expressed formally in temporal logics, such as syntactically co-safe linear temporal logic (scLTL) (Kupferman and Vardi, 2001; Belta et al., 2018), which includes the ubiquitous reach-while-avoid task as a special case (Fan et al., 2018; Summers and Lygeros, 2010). Because of the randomness in the system’s dynamics, such a specification generally cannot be satisfied with certainty. The goal of formal policy synthesis (Belta et al., 2018) is therefore to compute a control policy that achieves a high probability of satisfying the specification, together with guaranteed (and tight) bounds on this probability.

Because of the randomness in the system’s dynamics, such a specification generally cannot be satisfied with certainty. The goal of formal policy synthesis (Belta et al., 2018) is therefore to compute a control policy that achieves a high probability of satisfying the specification, together with guaranteed (and tight) bounds on this probability.

A well-established approach to formal policy synthesis is to abstract the system into a finite Markov decision process (MDP) or variant thereof (Lavaei et al., 2022; Lahijanian et al., 2015; Badings et al., 2023b; Haesaert and Soudjani, 2021; Gracia and Lahijanian, 2025). One can then synthesize an optimal strategy on this abstraction and refine it into a policy for the original system, such that guarantees on the abstraction carry over to the system (Abate et al., 2008; Tabuada, 2009; Mathiesen et al., 2025). A broad range of tools implement such approaches, including FAUST2 (Soudjani et al., 2015), StocHy (Cauchi and Abate, 2019), AMYTISS (Lavaei et al., 2020), SySCoRe (van Huijgevoort et al., 2023), and IMPaCT (Wooding and Lavaei, 2024). Several of these tools are compared in the ARCH-Competition on stochastic models (Abate et al., 2025). However, all of these tools are model-based: they require an explicit and exact model of the dynamics, often including the distribution of the stochastic noise. In practice, such a model is often unavailable because the dynamics may be too complex to model accurately, or the system may be accessible only through a simulator or experimental data.

Data-driven abstractions address this limitation by constructing abstractions from sampled transitions of the system, with guarantees that typically hold with a user-specified confidence (Makdesi et al., 2021; Coppola et al., 2023; Lavaei et al., 2023b; Kazemi et al., 2024; Hashimoto et al., 2022; Devonport et al., 2021; Banse et al., 2023; Peruffo and Mazo, 2023; Schön et al., 2024; Gracia et al., 2024a; Jackson et al., 2021; Badings et al., 2023b; Lavaei et al., 2023a; Ajeleye et al., 2023). papers.title: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM) serving frameworks accelerate inference by retaining previously computed states in a key-value (KV) cache. Paged serving frameworks such as vLLM organize this cache through block tables analogous to OS page tables, which map each request's logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, forming a software-managed address translation layer. Although fault attacks such as Rowhammer have exploited OS page tables to redirect memory accesses, prior fault attacks on LLMs have largely targeted the data plane, i.e., model weights or KV-cache contents, leaving KV-cache mapping unexplored.
  We present BlockJack (i.e., Block Hijack), the first KV cache address-translation fault attack in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries, BlockJack redirects a request's KV cache reads to blocks assigned to another tenant's request without modifying model parameters, prompts, or cached KV states. It achieves both confidentiality violation (victim information appears in attacker responses) and integrity violation (attacker-supplied context steers victim answers). We study paged KV cache mappings in vLLM and formally characterize when redirect targets are predictable. Across seven models spanning the Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Phi families, a faulted mapping exposes victim context. For the integrity attack, we examine how topic proximity, intra-topic divergence, and model behavior shape redirected responses. On a 248-scene medical benchmark, the integrity attack causes up to 41.1% of responses to recommend less urgent care, while still appearing consistent with the victim's question. We demonstrate physical feasibility of BlockJack with Rowhammer and subsequently evaluate assignment validation as a defense. Following responsible disclosure, vLLM and Sonar confirmed the vulnerability and proposed patches that we reviewed and validated.

papers.intro:
LLM are rapidly deployed in the real world for their exceptional generative capabilities in terms of language understanding and generation tasks. Recent systems use them for software development (e.g., OpenHands [1]), clinical reasoning (e.g., AMIE [2]), and scientific discovery (e.g., Co-Scientist [3]). Serving LLM models are increasingly expensive as model size, context length, and request concurrency grow. Autoregressive inference acceleration commonly uses the KV (KV) cache management that stores the attention keys and values of previously processed tokens, avoiding their recomputation at each decoding step. However, the cache grows with the number and length of requests, while variable request sizes can cause memory fragmentation and over-reservation. Serving frameworks therefore employ delicate KV cache management mechanisms to improve memory utilization and throughput. The mainstream framework/engine vLLM [4] uses PagedAttention [5] to manage the KV cache in fixed-size blocks. The vLLM-derived Sonar engine [6] follows the same block-based design. SGLang [7], in contrast, uses RadixAttention to organize and reuse cached prefixes.

papers.title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
papers.abstract: Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy -- the loss incurred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic groups of decision-subjects (DS) -- on static data, where reducing one often comes at the expense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder without increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never lowers any group's acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM's break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which may lower the advantaged group's acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group. Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs, allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.

papers.intro:
Algorithmic decision-making in consequential applications such as lending, hiring, and school admission imposes societal costs: decisions cost not only the decision-maker (DM) but also the decision-subjects (DS), and these costs can be unevenly distributed across demographic groups. This motivates a multi-objective perspective in which, alongside DM loss, we introduce the (un)fairness of decisions as a secondary objective, reflecting DS interests (Gupta et al., 2026). Since no single policy usually minimizes both objectives, we draw our attention to Pareto-optimal ones, where one objective cannot be improved without worsening the other. Such policies reveal the attainable trade-offs, i.e., how much DM loss increases to reach a given fairness level (Wei and Niethammer, 2022; Menon and Williamson, 2018), and allow stakeholders to discuss which policy to deploy. However, optimality is only defined on the static data on which policies are evaluated.

papers.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
papers.abstract: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

papers.title: Canted antiferromagnetism and spin-flop transition in honeycomb $\alpha$-Na$_2$PrO$_3$ revealed by angle-dependent torque magnetometry up to 35 T
papers.abstract: We report angle-dependent piezocantilever torque measurements on single crystals of the honeycomb magnet $\alpha$-Na$_2$PrO$_3$, proposed to display unconventional magnetism stabilized by anisotropic exchange interactions between spin-orbit entangled, pseudospin 1/2 Pr$^{4+}$ magnetic moments. Previous powder susceptibility observed signatures of a transition at low temperatures to antiferromagnetic order with a weak ferromagnetic moment. From the torque angular dependence in three orthogonal crystallographic planes, we infer a zero-field canted antiferromagnetic structure, with moments almost normal to the honeycomb layers, but weakly canted such as to give rise to a spontaneous magnetization along the in-plane monoclinic $a$-axis, with two magnetic domains related by time reversal. Sharp jumps in the torque angular dependence when the field projection along $a$ changes sign are interpreted as field-induced switching between the two degenerate domains with oppositely aligned ferromagnetic moments. We propose a minimal spin Hamiltonian including easy-axis exchange anisotropy and symmetry-allowed Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) couplings, for which mean-field calculations reproduce the main features of the observed angle-dependent torque. Torque measurements up to 35 T applied almost normal to the layers observe a strong anomaly attributed to proximity to the field-induced spin-flop transition predicted for the above Hamiltonian. We contrast the predicted magnetic phase diagrams for magnetic fields in different orthogonal crystallographic planes normal to the honeycomb layers and discuss how DM interactions convert some transitions into smooth crossovers and stabilize a phase boundary line connecting the spin-flop transition in field normal to the layers to magnetization saturation for in-plane field normal to $a$; such a phase boundary line does not exist in the absence of DM interactions.

This could provide the microscopic setting for realizing experimentally Kitaev [2] and in general, quantum spin compass models on honeycomb and related lattice geometries. Layered honeycomb iridates Na2IrO3 [3] and α\alpha-Li2IrO3 [4], α\alpha-RuCl3 [5], the three-dimensional hyperhoneycomb β\beta- [6, 7] and stripyhoneycomb γ\gamma-Li2IrO3 [8, 9], and more recently also hyperhoneycomb β\beta-Na2PrO3 [10] have been intensely investigated as candidate Kitaev materials in which frustrated anisotropic exchanges stabilize unconventional ordered states and/or spin dynamics.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II gives details of the experimental setup used for the magnetic torque measurements. The following Sec. III reports the torque angular dependence for field applied in three orthogonal crystallographic planes, from which we infer a model for the low-field magnetic structure in Sec. IV, described in terms of magnetic basis vectors compatible with the crystal structure symmetry in Sec. V. A minimal spin Hamiltonian with easy-axis XXZ exchange anisotropy accompanied by symmetry-allowed DM interactions (with an effective DM vector along the two-fold bb-axis) is proposed in Sec. VI, which also shows mean-field calculations compared with the measured torque data. The calculated magnetic phase diagrams for the minimal model for field applied in a plane normal to the honeycomb layers and containing the effective DM vector or normal to it are very different and the important role played by the DM interactions in changing the nature of the phases and/or phase transitions is discussed. papers.title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
papers.abstract: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.

papers.title: Sorting by block-reversals: closing the gap
papers.abstract:
In block-reversal sorting an elementary operation is to reverse the order of a contiguous block in a sequence, at cost proportional to the length of the block. In SODA 2004, Bender, Ge, He, Hu, Pinter, Skiena, and Swidan showed that every sequence of length $n$ can be sorted at cost $O(n\log^2{n})$ and some sequences can only be sorted at cost $\Omega(n\log{n})$.
  In block-partition sorting, an elementary operation is to partition the sequence into contiguous blocks, and simultaneously reverse all blocks. The model was introduced in SODA 2024 by Jel\'{i}nek, Opler, and Pek\'{a}rek, who showed that every sequence can be sorted in $O(\log^2{n})$ steps and some sequences require $\Omega(\log{n})$ steps.
  We close both gaps, showing that the upper bounds are tight, and the $\log^2{n}$ factors are unavoidable.

papers.title: Sequence-encoded amphiphilicity controls the interfacial tension of biomolecular condensates
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates exhibit surprisingly low surface tensions, despite forming dense, liquid-like phases. We propose that the low surface tension partially originates from the segmental amphiphilicity of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) that results in a surfactant-like behavior. We investigate this mechanism using a minimal coarse-grained IDP model containing only hydrophobic and polar residues, allowing us to systematically vary the polar fraction and, for selected cases, to probe the influence of sequence patterning of polar residues. To control for differences in thermodynamic phase behavior, we determine phase coexistence (binodals) for each sequence and compare systems at matched distances from the critical point. We find a disproportionately high fraction of polar residues at the condensate surface, which is closely correlated with the reduction in surface tension. For the sequences studied here, overall composition alone sets the phase behavior and establishes the overall trend in surface tension: increasing the polar fraction lowers the surface tension, with a polar fraction of one third reducing the surface tension by roughly twofold relative to a purely hydrophobic chain. In addition, sequence patterning enhances interfacial localization of polar residues and can lower surface tension beyond what composition alone achieves, revealing a sequence-dependent contribution to the surface tension that leaves the bulk phase behavior essentially unchanged.

papers.title: Information-Region MPC: Non-Iterative Distributed Control of Urban Traffic Signals
papers.abstract: Centralized model predictive control (MPC) exploits network-wide traffic information to obtain the optimal solution of the network-level control problem, but its computational burden grows rapidly with network size. Iterative distributed MPC reduces the size of local optimization problems, but requires repeated information exchange and coordination within each control update. To address these limitations, this paper proposes information-region MPC (IR-MPC), which approximates the first control input of centralized MPC using limited real-time data without iterative coordination. Based on historical traffic data, we quantify how perturbations at other intersections affect the centralized first control input of each intersection and use these couplings to construct a compact information region for every intersection. At each control update, each intersection then solves a local IR-MPC problem once using current data only from its information region. SUMO simulations on a real 28-intersection network show that IR-MPC with one processor per intersection computes its control inputs 9 times faster than centralized MPC and 15 times faster than a representative iterative decomposition-based distributed MPC method. IR-MPC reproduces 85% of the centralized control inputs exactly at the implemented one-second resolution, keeps 99.3% within 2s, and increases mean delay by only 0.03%.
