papers.title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
papers.abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.
papers.intro:
Diabetes mellitus currently affects more than 537 million adults worldwide; projections indicate a rise to 783 million by 2045 [1]. Beyond chronic microvascular and macrovascular sequelae, acute metabolic decompensations drive a high volume of emergency hospitalizations and unplanned 30-day readmissions. In the United States the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program financially penalizes facilities with excess readmission rates, thereby creating a pressing need for prospective, well-calibrated clinical decision-support systems that can guide post-discharge transitional care [2].

Diabetes mellitus currently affects more than 537 million adults worldwide; projections indicate a rise to 783 million by 2045 [1]. Beyond chronic microvascular and macrovascular sequelae, acute metabolic decompensations drive a high volume of emergency hospitalizations and unplanned 30-day readmissions. In the United States the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program financially penalizes facilities with excess readmission rates, thereby creating a pressing need for prospective, well-calibrated clinical decision-support systems that can guide post-discharge transitional care [2].

Two fundamental obstacles continue to limit the performance of contemporary readmission models. First, the majority of published risk tools rely almost exclusively on structured electronic health record (EHR) matrices—demographic attributes, laboratory values, diagnosis codes and medication counts [1, 3]. While these fields capture discrete physiological measurements, they systematically omit contextual information recorded in free-text clinical notes, including symptom trajectory, functional status and social determinants of health [4]. Second, clinical documentation in diverse healthcare environments frequently incorporates colloquial expressions, non-standard abbreviations and code-mixed phrasing (for example Hinglish) that standard English medical dictionaries fail to recognize [5, 6]. Concurrently, large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic reasoning yet, when deployed as end-to-end prognosticators, introduce risks of factual hallucination, poorly calibrated probability estimates and systematic failures in medical negation resolution [7, 8].

Two fundamental obstacles continue to limit the performance of contemporary readmission models. First, the majority of published risk tools rely almost exclusively on structured electronic health record (EHR) matrices—demographic attributes, laboratory values, diagnosis codes and medication counts [1, 3]. While these fields capture discrete physiological measurements, they systematically omit contextual information recorded in free-text clinical notes, including symptom trajectory, functional status and social determinants of health [4]. Second, clinical documentation in diverse healthcare environments frequently incorporates colloquial expressions, non-standard abbreviations and code-mixed phrasing (for example Hinglish) that standard English medical dictionaries fail to recognize [5, 6]. Concurrently, large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic reasoning yet, when deployed as end-to-end prognosticators, introduce risks of factual hallucination, poorly calibrated probability estimates and systematic failures in medical negation resolution [7, 8].

To address these limitations we present a neurosymbolic multimodal architecture (Fig. 1) that integrates three complementary information streams: (i) engineered structured EHR features, (ii) dense contextual representations obtained from Bio_ClinicalBERT and compressed by truncated singular-value decomposition (SVD), and (iii) discrete symbolic clinical entities extracted by an open-weight biomedical language model (Medictron-7B) operating inside a hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework [9, 10, 11, 12].

papers.title: Arithmetic Upper and Lower Bounds for the Denumerant Function II
papers.abstract: We apply the elementary arithmetic argument of the first paper of this series (arXiv:2204.13689) to binomial coefficients, and obtain upper and lower bounds for Sylvester's denumerant function for arbitrary positive integers $a_1,\dots,a_k$ that sharpen those of Agnarsson. The lower bound is a sum of binomial coefficients; it holds along the multiples of $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_k)$ without assuming that a solution exists, and it is greater than the polynomial lower bound of the first paper. In the upper bound the shift of Agnarsson's binomial coefficient is reduced.

papers.title: Arithmetic Upper and Lower Bounds for the Denumerant Function III
papers.abstract: We extend the denumerant to a weighted denumerant, the sum of a function $\mu$ over the solutions in non-negative integers of $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=n$. For the monomial weights $x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_k^{\alpha_k}$, with exponents $\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$, we prove upper and lower bounds of the kind of those of the first paper of this series (arXiv:2204.13689), with an explicit constant and explicit shifts. As an example of application, summing these bounds over all the numbers $a_1,\dots,a_k$ we find, by elementary means, the asymptotic main term of the sums $\sum_{y_1+\cdots+y_k=n}\sigma_{\alpha_1}(y_1)\cdots\sigma_{\alpha_k}(y_k)$ of products of divisor functions, for every $k$ and for real exponents $\alpha_i\neq0$ of either sign.

papers.title: Certified pandigital approximations of $\pi$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $e$
papers.abstract: In 2004 Erich Friedman asked for the best approximations of $\pi$, $e$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ and Feigenbaum's constant $\delta$ that use each of the digits $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, with addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, parentheses and the decimal point. We determine the optimal expressions for $\pi$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ for every $n \le 9$, with the digits in any order and in increasing order, and for $e$ when $n \le 6$. The optima are found by exhaustive search and certified by an independent algorithm that encloses every expression rigorously and decides each candidate with Arb and exact arithmetic; a second certified computation covers intermediate values of any size. Twenty-one entries improve the published records; for $\pi$ with the digits 1-9 the optimal error is $2.81\cdot 10^{-14}$. For $e$, whose records come from identities between power towers, we prove that Bamberger's formula is optimal within the natural family of such identities. All code and certificates are public.

papers.title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
papers.intro:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) have driven embodied learning toward larger and more heterogeneous model architectures. VLA models such as OpenVLA [21], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [18], and GR00T [40] integrate pretrained vision-language backbones with diverse action-generation modules, while world-action approaches such as Unified World Models [64], Cosmos Policy [22], and DreamZero [57] couple action prediction with video generation or future-state modeling. Meanwhile, large-scale multi-robot datasets [11, 20] have substantially expanded the volume and diversity of embodied training data. Together, these developments give rise to heterogeneous training workloads with distinct computation graphs, memory footprints, communication patterns, and data-processing requirements. Consequently, efficiently scaling embodied foundation models requires training infrastructure capable of accommodating such diversity while delivering high performance.

Together, these developments give rise to heterogeneous training workloads with distinct computation graphs, memory footprints, communication patterns, and data-processing requirements. Consequently, efficiently scaling embodied foundation models requires training infrastructure capable of accommodating such diversity while delivering high performance.

Efficient training of heterogeneous VLA and WAM models faces two closely related challenges. First, diverse model architectures and training objectives give rise to substantially different performance bottlenecks. Variations in attention structures, computation graphs, activation-memory requirements, and distributed execution patterns shift the dominant costs among computation, memory, execution overhead, data I/O, and communication. These bottlenecks also depend on hardware characteristics, making a fixed optimization strategy insufficient across models and hardware platforms. Second, the embodied learning ecosystem remains fragmented. Despite recent efforts toward unified robot learning frameworks [7, 12], many embodied foundation models still rely on independently developed training stacks, with customized distributed execution, data processing, and evaluation pipelines. Although broadly reusable system optimization mechanisms exist, including optimized attention [13, 15], graph compilation [3], CUDA Graphs [38], and communication optimization [52], their effective integration and configuration often depend on model architectures and hardware characteristics. Consequently, similar optimizations must be repeatedly integrated, tuned, and validated across separate training stacks, limiting cross-model optimization reuse and increasing engineering overhead. This raises a fundamental systems question: can heterogeneous embodied models share a common training infrastructure while still enabling model-specific, high-performance optimization?

We address this question with LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous VLA and WAM models. The key design principle is to separate model-specific computation from reusable training infrastructure. Although these models differ substantially in architecture, learning objectives, and execution patterns, they share common system-level functionalities, including training orchestration, distributed execution, data processing, optimization, checkpoint management, and evaluation. To capture this commonality without imposing a fixed computational structure, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a unified abstraction layer built around configuration-driven model registration, a lightweight model interface, and an extensible training engine. These abstractions allow heterogeneous models to reuse shared training infrastructure while preserving their individual computation graphs and training requirements. More importantly, this separation provides a foundation for cross-model optimization reuse: shared optimization mechanisms can be integrated once at the framework level, while architecture-specific and hardware-aware optimization choices remain customizable. In this way, LoongForge-Embodied combines the benefits of unified training infrastructure with the flexibility required for model-specific, high-performance optimization.

Building on this unified abstraction, LoongForge-Embodied provides a composable acceleration toolkit that combines reusable system-level optimization mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware strategies. Guided by the performance bottlenecks of individual workloads, the framework integrates efficient attention kernels [13, 15, 46], mixed-precision computation, and fused operators and optimizers to improve computational efficiency. Graph compilation [3] and configurable CUDA Graph capture [38] reduce execution overhead, while activation checkpointing [9] and parameter-efficient adaptation address memory constraints. Precomputation, caching, and asynchronous checkpointing further mitigate data-processing and I/O overhead. For distributed training, LoongForge-Embodied supports both Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) and Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) with FP8-based communication optimizations, reducing gradient synchronization traffic in DDP and parameter AllGather traffic in FSDP, particularly in bandwidth-constrained environments. Beyond communication compression, configurable synchronization and prefetching strategies improve computation–communication overlap. Rather than imposing a uniform optimization recipe, LoongForge-Embodied enables heterogeneous models to reuse shared acceleration mechanisms while retaining the flexibility to select architecture-specific implementations and hardware-aware configurations.

papers.title: On the Type E case of the Brown Wemyss realization conjecture
papers.abstract: We consider the remaining Type E case of the Brown-Wemyss numerical realization conjecture. The noncommutative splitting lemma and the Type A and D classifications of Brown and Wemyss leave two-generator cyclic potentials with cubic part $x^3$. For these remaining potentials, we construct geometric realizations under the hypothesis of radical growth dimension at most one. The construction combines marked ADE deformations and cyclic coordinate changes for lengths three, four, and six with a filtered finiteness argument in length five. Under the numerical growth hypothesis, cubic lower bounds exclude the other branches for every choice of formal tail. The resulting contractions have a regular source and a complete local cDV target. Finite-dimensional algebras are realized by threefold flops, and the sole growth-one algebra in this residual case is $\operatorname{Jac}(x^3+xy^3)$, for which we give a divisor-to-curve contraction.

papers.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
papers.abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.
papers.intro:
Recent advances in medical language and multimodal models have expanded AI support for patient consultation, clinical decision support, and medical document interpretation (Yang et al., 2026a, McDuff et al., 2025, Jiang et al., 2025). Models such as MedGemma demonstrate the value of adapting general-purpose models to medical knowledge and data (Sellergren et al., 2025). As these systems enter medical workflows, evaluating their outputs requires attention to both clinical correctness and the conditions governing their use. Responses may contain inappropriate recommendations, violate requirements governing medical practice, or compromise patient rights and professional conduct (Yang et al., 2026b, Draelos et al., 2026). These concerns motivate dedicated medical guardrails that identify risks and explain their judgments in context (Hakim et al., 2024, Gangavarapu, 2024).

Responses may contain inappropriate recommendations, violate requirements governing medical practice, or compromise patient rights and professional conduct (Yang et al., 2026b, Draelos et al., 2026). These concerns motivate dedicated medical guardrails that identify risks and explain their judgments in context (Hakim et al., 2024, Gangavarapu, 2024).

Existing guardrail research provides a foundation for this goal. General-purpose guardrails offer established approaches to broad content-safety classification (Inan et al., 2023, Han et al., 2024a, Zhao et al., 2025a, Team, 2026, Wu et al., 2024), but medical risks often involve specialized knowledge, patient context, and specific medical requirements that are difficult to assess using general content-safety criteria alone. Researchers have therefore developed guardrails for specific medical settings, including diagnostic workflows (Jain et al., 2025), clinical risk detection in telemedicine (Shi et al., 2026), and medical error detection, localization, and correction (Ma et al., 2026a). By examining clinical claims, identifying potential errors, and verifying relevant evidence, these approaches help detect medical risks that general safety classification may overlook. Building on this work, developing a unified guardrail for practical medical workflows requires addressing two further issues: risk coverage and the capabilities needed to support risk judgments.

Building on this work, developing a unified guardrail for practical medical workflows requires addressing two further issues: risk coverage and the capabilities needed to support risk judgments.

First, existing approaches primarily identify risks in specific settings or tasks, but risks in real medical interactions extend beyond the correctness of clinical content to include the boundaries of a system’s professional role and the protection of patient information and rights (Han et al., 2024b, Yang et al., 2024b). These requirements call for corresponding risk checks: detecting harmful dosage errors concerns medical safety; determining whether a system exceeds its authorized professional role concerns compliance; and checking whether a response discloses patient identity and medical conditions to unauthorized parties concerns privacy protection and medical ethics. These risks may coexist in one response but require different assessment criteria: clinical correctness establishes neither compliance with professional responsibilities nor adequate protection of patient privacy and rights. Detecting individual problems therefore cannot fully address the multiple risks within a medical interaction. A common assessment framework must preserve domain-specific criteria. Building on existing frameworks for medical ethics, patient safety, and trustworthiness assessment (Bian et al., 2025, Yang et al., 2024b, Ding et al., 2025), we consolidate assessment requirements across medical safety, compliance, and ethics. This enables a unified guardrail to identify risks in the same response and patient context using domain-specific criteria, while drawing on shared medical knowledge to support cross-domain judgments.

Second, cross-domain risk assessment also requires specialized medical capabilities that enable guardrails to identify specific risks in responses and verify the basis for their judgments. For responses generated from medical visual inputs, risks may arise from misinterpreting the source information or making medical claims unsupported by the image. Figure 2 illustrates these two problems. The first case concerns an incorrect interpretation of laboratory results: the reported lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) value of 204.50 U/L is incorrectly attributed to creatine kinase (CK), whose actual reported value is 39.00 U/L. The guardrail must correctly associate each test with its value to detect the inconsistency between the response and the original report and avoid overlooking the erroneous interpretation. This illustrates that medical multimodal entity understanding underpins the detection of such medical information errors. In the second case, the model claims that extraluminal contrast and free air are present in the CT image, but these claims lack visual support. Detecting such problems requires checking medical claims against image evidence and therefore calls for medical multimodal hallucination detection. For responses involving medical calculations, errors may occur during patient-variable extraction, formula selection, or calculation, as systematically evaluated by MedCalc-Bench (Khandekar et al., 2024). As shown in Figure 3, detecting an incorrect Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score requires checking the patient variables, formula, and calculated result. This illustrates the need for medical numerical reasoning to verify the correctness of score calculations.

papers.title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications
papers.abstract: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.

An agent reviewing a report may ask a peer to interpret a finding or delegate delivery of the report. An interpretation is a conversational reply. Delivery is an assigned business objective that may require a decision about the exact report and destination. An operator should be able to trace that decision to the assigned runner and the observed result. Process compliance depends on the applicable rules and evidence of the actions taken [9]. Inventory collection and ticket creation present different business logic with similar needs for assignment, authority, and evidence.

papers.title: Finitely supported mapping classes on infinite-type surfaces
papers.abstract: We study the topological closure of the group of mapping classes group with finite-type support on an infinite-type surface. Since every such mapping class fixes each end which is not a puncture, we have that the closure is contained in the pointwise stabilizer of infinite-type ends. A natural question is therefore when this inclusion is an equality, and if it is not, what must be added to obtain the full stabilizer. We prove that finitely supported mapping classes are dense in the stabilizer precisely when there is at most one end accumulated by genus and at most one end accumulated by punctures. We show that if we remove either of these conditions, we need to add puncture and/or handle shifts to topologically generate the stabilizer.

Shifts — homeomorphisms that translate a periodic pattern (handles, punctures, or more general subsurfaces) along a surface — appear repeatedly throughout the study of the big mapping class groups, which is part of why they are a natural object to understand on their own. In particular Abbott, Miller, and Patel [2] used compositions of shift maps — together with a pseudo-Anosov on a finite-type subsurface — to construct the first known loxodromic isometries of the relative arc graph for a broad class of infinite-type surfaces, extending an earlier construction of Bavard [5] for the plane minus a Cantor set. In follow-up work [1], the same authors show that composing a Dehn twist with a shift map already produces a loxodromic isometry. Lanier and Loving [10] used shifts to construct subgroups isomorphic to the restricted wreath product ℤ≀ℤ\mathbb{Z}\wr\mathbb{Z}. Their construction shows that every mapping class group of infinite-type surface contains a subgroup that is not virtually abelian and contains no nonabelian free subgroup, and hence does not satisfy the strong Tits alternative. They also exhibited examples that fail the classical Tits alternative.

papers.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
papers.abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

LLMs are now placed inside workflows that must decide something: whether an alert is benign, which value a document field holds, which action to take next. The output is consumed by code, not read by a person. Two requirements follow. The pipeline must know which decisions it may act on unattended (confidence gating), and when a decision is later questioned the record must show why it was accepted (auditability).

Sampling-based methods such as self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023) and semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024) meet the first requirement by drawing several samples and measuring their agreement. They cost 5 to 10 generations per item and reduce the evidence to a score; which answer is committed is a separate choice (the original semantic-entropy work scores a separately generated answer). We ask how much of their error-detection power a much smaller, fully specified procedure can recover, if the extra calls are spent on samples that make different mistakes rather than on more samples of the same distribution.

The procedure has three parts (Figure 1). (i) An anchor: the target model’s greedy answer, which is always the committed value. (ii) One or two checks, also greedy, chosen to reach the answer by a different route: the same model under an alternate prompt, or a model from a different family. (iii) A reconciler: a pure function that compares a declared decision field across the samples under a per-type equality rule and returns one of five outcomes. Only Agree is acted on automatically. Both components of the check are known in the hallucination-detection literature (Zhang et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2025); our contribution is a deterministic contract around them and a careful measurement of what it buys.

Both components of the check are known in the hallucination-detection literature (Zhang et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2025); our contribution is a deterministic contract around them and a careful measurement of what it buys.

A natural first design checks the anchor against a sample of the same model at temperature 0.8. Under matched scoring that design trails 5-sample semantic entropy by 7 points, because a model’s own samples tend to repeat its mistakes (Section 5.4); Appendix F records how the design evolved. Changing where the check comes from, not how many checks there are, is what closes the gap. We report the temperature-based design as an ablation. The same lesson applies to the baselines: semantic entropy computed over samples pooled from the target and a peer model improves on single-model semantic entropy at every budget. Compared with these cross-model baselines as complete pipelines, each committing its own answer, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled 3- and 5-sample semantic entropy differ by less than one point, with intervals that reach 1.2 points; compared as detectors of the anchor’s errors with the same tie-breaker, it is 3.9 points above pooled 3-sample entropy, 1.5 above 5 samples and +0.1+0.1 points [−0.6,+0.7][-0.6,+0.7] from 10 samples (sample counts are the baseline’s; the contract uses three calls). Most of that detector lead comes from where the three answers are drawn, not from the scoring rule: entropy over the same three greedy answers is only 0.6 points lower. We do not claim that anchor preservation or replayability is unique to the contract. Semantic entropy can score a separately generated answer (Kuhn et al., 2023), SAC3 assesses the target model’s own response (Zhang et al., 2023), and any baseline can store its samples and threshold for replay. What the contract fixes is the combination: a committed answer that never changes with sampling, an explicit five-way outcome in place of a threshold on a score, a confidence bounded by the anchor’s, and a specification small enough to be re-implemented from this paper.

papers.title: Statistical moments, risk weighting and percentiles of a loss distribution of a finite homogeneous credit portfolio; extending the Vasicek distribution
papers.abstract: The Vasicek distribution assumes an infinite portfolio of identical obligors and forms the basis of the Basel III/IV Risk Weighted Assets (RWA) calculation. We derive the central moments of the loss distribution for a finite number (n) of obligors. We use these moments to calculate percentiles of the fraction (x) of defaulted obligors, via the Cornish-Fisher expansion and via a weighting method. Both methods are based on scaling the standard deviation in x by a capital multiple. The weighting method assumes that the capital multiple is linear in the central moments and leads to an Extended Vasicek distribution. We apply this distribution in calculating an adjusted RWA for small portfolios. Simulations show that this adjustment is only relevant for small portfolios of less than 100 obligors and that the Extended Vasicek distribution allows analytical risk capital calculations for portfolios with different rating grades, even when the number of obligors per rating grade is small.

papers.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
papers.abstract: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

papers.title: Mahler measures and a cubic Dedekind zeta value in three dilogarithms
papers.abstract:
A general formula evaluates a three-variable Mahler measure at Heegner points of fundamental discriminant $-d$, with $d>3$ and $d\equiv3\pmod8$, using CM modular forms and ray class $L$-values. Together with the case $d=27$, it proves six identities conjectured by Zheng. The parameter at $d=163$ also occurs in a cubic Ramanujan-Sato series for $1/\pi$.
  For $C=\mathbb Q(a)$, where $a^3+2a-2=0$, an exact hyperbolic volume argument expresses the Dedekind zeta derivative $\zeta_C'(-1)$ in three Bloch-Wigner dilogarithms. The analogous identity for $C(\sqrt5)$ remains conjectural and is reduced to one explicit Bloch-group equality.

papers.title: Sheetwise stationarity for stationary unions of $C^{1,\alpha}$ graphs
papers.abstract: We prove that stationarity of a finite union of $C^{1,\alpha}$ graphs implies stationarity of each individual graph, in arbitrary dimension and codimension. The proof closely follows the approach of Minter and Stanbury \cite{MinterStanbury}, who also raised this question in their Remark~1.6. As in their paper, we give a proof that uses the planar frequency results of Krummel, Minter and Wickramasekera \cite{KMW26} (but avoids the centre manifold construction of that paper). We also rely on the Schauder estimates for $Q$-valued functions established in \cite{Luc26}.

papers.title: Hilbert schemes of points on plane curves via standard families
papers.abstract: We describe an approach to computing Hilbert schemes of points on embedded families of plane curves. This is achieved by introducing the notion of a standard family, and the associated Hilbert schemes are shown to be algebraic vector bundles over the Hilbert scheme of points on the plane. Any embedded family of plane curves lies in some standard family, which allows for the computation of the corresponding Hilbert scheme from that of the standard family. Further results on the geometry of these schemes are also collected.

Hilbert schemes of points on curves are fundamental to the study of curves; In particular, they are ubiquitous in enumerative geometry [13, 9, 5]. Interestingly, their homology is also connected to link invariants [15, 12]. The easiest case is the Hilbert scheme C[n]C^{[n]} of a smooth plane curve CC. In this case C[n]C^{[n]} is isomorphic to the symmetric power C(n)C^{(n)}, which is smooth of dimension nn. papers.title: Closed $G_2$-structures with fixed metric: compactness and almost-abelian fibres
papers.abstract: We study the space of closed $G_2$-structures inducing a prescribed Riemannian metric and orientation. On a compact seven-manifold, with a fixed Riemannian metric and orientation, we prove that the space of compatible closed $G_2$ structures inducing a prescribed spin-structure is homeomorphic to a real projective algebraic set defined by homogeneous quadratic equations in the kernel of the corresponding Dirac operator. The defining quadrics give a local analytic obstruction map and a \L ojasiewicz estimate that bounds the distance to the closed locus in terms of $\|d\varphi\|_{L^2}$. We also prove smooth compactness when the prescribed metrics converge smoothly, and strong $H^1$ compactness for sequences of compatible $G_2$-structures $\varphi_{j}$ satisfying $\|d\varphi_j\|_{L^2}\to 0$. In the invariant setting, the fixed-metric fibre of any seven-dimensional almost-abelian metric Lie algebra has at most four connected components, each a compact homogeneous space. We determine these spaces spectrally when the defining endomorphism is normal, and show that for a non-normal endomorphism the fibre is empty, one circle, or two circles. On compact quotients with symmetric bracket, sufficiently small torus fibres exclude all non-invariant harmonic spinors, so the invariant classification computes the full closed fibre.

papers.title: Evidence from a Multi-Regime Causal Discovery Benchmark: UCMT Algorithms, Comparative Performance, and Controlled Ablation Studies
papers.abstract: We present an internal, pre-registered evaluation of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family alongside established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, complemented by a separately pre-registered, controlled study of UCMT v2 Global components. The contribution is both empirical and methodological: a family-stratified comparison of three actively developed algorithm configurations and targeted evidence about which internal stages affect their outcomes. In the main benchmark, UCMT v2 Global has higher directed F1 than NOTEARS and DAGMA in selected real, semi-synthetic and Gaussian-network comparisons at the paired-run level, while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings. The BOSS-based UCMT v4 produces a CSuite-specific directed-F1 improvement over BOSS (mean paired difference +0.279; pair-level Holm p < 0.001), but the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188). In a separate fixed-skeleton ablation, UCMT v2 Global exceeds an adapted R^2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on standardized iSCM data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, dataset-level Holm p = 0.031); absolute orientation accuracy is 0.563 and there is no established broad advantage over RESIT, ANM or DirectLiNGAM. Controlled ablations show that sparsity and BIC-based refinement materially affect some outcomes, whereas the examined arbitration and automatic regime-selection mechanisms do not yield confirmed general improvements. We report performance shortcomings, multiple-testing correction, runtime costs, evaluation limitations and reproducibility checks. The results support UCMT as an implemented and empirically investigated algorithm family, not a claim of overall superiority, independent validation or demonstrated commercial impact.

papers.intro:
Causal discovery from observational and interventional data is evaluated on few real datasets with trusted ground truth [23, 8] and on many synthetic generators whose artefacts can be exploited [21]. We present an internal benchmark, pre-registered before execution, in which the UCMT family of algorithms is compared with established methods. The aim is to build a verifiable picture of where the UCMT family is useful, where it is not yet competitive, and which measured changes follow from its development. The public benchmark overview, methodology and comparative summaries are available at https://ucmtlabs.com/benchmarks. This page is a public results landing page, not a deposit of raw execution records or source code. No pooled ranking across families is produced. The paper offers three contributions: (i) a heterogeneous, family-specific comparison of v2 Global, v3 and a BOSS-based v4; (ii) separately pre-registered mechanism-level experiments on v2 Global; and (iii) an explicit translation of benchmark evidence into testable requirements for robust analytical software rather than unvalidated claims of business impact.

papers.title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

Humanoid robots could help people with a wide range of tasks in homes and workplaces. Many require whole-body loco-manipulation, in which the robot coordinates its steps and posture with its hand movements [17, 24]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models [5, 16, 31] and world action models [47, 22, 48] have shown that robots can learn diverse manipulation skills from demonstrations. For humanoids, however, the cost of whole-body teleoperation limits the range of tasks and environments represented in robot demonstrations [13, 49].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models [5, 16, 31] and world action models [47, 22, 48] have shown that robots can learn diverse manipulation skills from demonstrations. For humanoids, however, the cost of whole-body teleoperation limits the range of tasks and environments represented in robot demonstrations [13, 49].

Human experience of everyday activity offers a more scalable alternative to robot teleoperation. Recent work draws on the variety of activities and environments in these videos [46, 43] to pretrain manipulation policies [41, 52, 23]. Despite this diversity, visual observations alone provide no explicit targets for whole-body motion. Prior work therefore retargets recorded human motion to obtain robot action targets [7, 21]. However, differences in body proportions and joint structure can cause the resulting postures and hand trajectories to deviate from those in the human demonstration [2]. These deviations motivate retaining the original human motion as a training signal alongside the retargeted robot actions. Using that signal at scale requires egocentric video paired with synchronized whole-body motion across diverse tasks and environments. Yet many large egocentric datasets provide video alone or primarily track the head and hands [11, 15], while datasets such as Nymeria [28] offer only a few hundred hours of paired recordings.

papers.title: Algebraic matroids with non-algebraic duals exist in any positive characteristic
papers.abstract: We show that for every field $K$ of positive characteristic there exists an algebraic matroid $M$ over $K$ such that the dual matroid $M^*$ is not algebraic over any field. Our conceptual proof relies on the theory of matroids over one-dimensional algebraic groups. As an application, we deduce that the classes of supports of realizable volume polynomials and of realizable covolume polynomials differ in positive characteristic.

If a matroid is representable over some field KK, it is also algebraic over KK. Lindström showed in [14] that being algebraic over KK depends only on the characteristic of KK. In characteristic 00, every algebraic matroid over KK is representable over a field extension of KK [11]. In positive characteristic however, Ingleton described a matroid on 1111 elements of rank 33 which is algebraic over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} and has both the Fano and non-Fano matroids as restrictions; hence it is not representable over any field. It was only shown in 1975 that not all matroids are algebraic: Ingleton and Main proved that the Vámos matroid is not algebraic over any field [10].

papers.title: Held While Waiting: What LLM Agent Sessions Reserve on Serverless and Agent Runtimes
papers.abstract:
LLM agents spend nearly all their time waiting for the model. On Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, our agents waited a median of 2.7 seconds for each model reply, then computed for an estimated 5 to 40 milliseconds. AgentCore does not charge for CPU during the wait. But it reserves a separate environment, a virtual machine with its own memory, for every conversation, and keeps it reserved until the conversation is closed. So 1,000 conversations reserve 1,000 environments to do the work of 2 to 15 processor cores. A service runs out of environments long before it runs out of processing power.
  The shortage has two causes, and each has a fix. An environment stays reserved after its conversation ends: in the customer-service benchmark we ran, a conversation lasts 33 seconds on average, but its environment is held for 15 minutes more unless the client closes it. And an environment serves only one conversation, which is mostly waiting: in our simulation, 64 conversations sharing one environment need 59 times fewer environments, and 99 of every 100 replies are delayed by at most 40 milliseconds.
  The milliseconds are an estimate because they are hard to measure: a stubbed model, a timer around the model call, and steps run back to back each gave a plausible number that was too low. We show how to avoid all three. Of the two fixes, closing needs only the client. Sharing needs the platform, and of the agent runtimes we surveyed only one allows it, in part. They keep conversations apart because an agent runs tools, and sometimes code, chosen by a model. The open problem is to keep them apart without reserving an environment for each while it waits.
papers.intro:
Serverless platforms charge only while code runs. LLM agents fit that model poorly. An agent session spends almost all of its time waiting on a model, yet it holds an execution environment while it waits. A session proceeds in steps, each one model call plus the framework work around it. In our deployment, a step waits a median of 2.7 s on the model and computes for an estimated 5 to 40 milliseconds.

An agent session spends almost all of its time waiting on a model, yet it holds an execution environment while it waits. A session proceeds in steps, each one model call plus the framework work around it. In our deployment, a step waits a median of 2.7 s on the model and computes for an estimated 5 to 40 milliseconds.

One of the platforms built specifically for agents over the last two years, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, stops billing for CPU while a session waits on I/O (Amazon Web Services, 2026a). That addresses the cost of waiting, which was small to begin with: at published prices we calculate compute to be a few per cent of the model-token bill (Section 5). It does not, however, change what a waiting session holds. Agent runtimes give each session a dedicated, isolated environment for its whole life (Amazon Web Services, 2026n; Microsoft, 2026b), and count it against a session quota whether it is busy or idle (Amazon Web Services, 2026i). On these runtimes, what limits an agent workload is therefore less what it pays for processor time than how many isolated environments it holds, and for how long.

This paper characterises agent steps on serverless and agent runtimes, and measures that capacity. It makes four contributions.

This paper characterises agent steps on serverless and agent runtimes, and measures that capacity. It makes four contributions.

Agent runtimes, characterised (Sections 4, 5 and 6). First, we observe 3,549 steps of LangGraph and Strands agents serving a public benchmark, deployed on AgentCore and self-hosted. Second, we run our own CPU benchmark inside AgentCore and AWS Lambda, on the platforms’ own processors. Of the time a deployed agent step takes, only 0.2 to 1.5 per cent is computation; the rest is waiting on the model. A platform that gives each session its own environment holds that environment through the wait. At any moment, then, only 2 to 15 of every 1,000 held environments are using a processor, so for each core of work actually done the platform holds roughly 70 to 600 environments. A direct measurement of up to 400 concurrent sessions checks this calculation. A survey of nine platforms’ public documentation (our own; Section 6) shows where that ratio applies: the agent runtimes of AWS and Microsoft dedicate an environment per session, and Google’s shares one only when the agent’s code is asynchronous, while every runtime that shares environments by default is a general-purpose one (Amazon Web Services, 2026n; Microsoft, 2026b; Google Cloud, 2026a; Google Cloud, 2026b; Amazon Web Services, 2026j).

What isolation costs, and the cheapest fix (Section 7). In a simulation driven by the deployed workload, sharing 64 sessions per environment holds 59 times fewer environments than isolating each one, for at most 40 ms of added latency per step at the 99th percentile, against a 2.7 s model call. That fix needs the platform to change; the next needs only the client. A session left to the default 15-minute idle timeout, instead of being closed when its conversation ends, keeps its environment for the whole timeout, and the same traffic then holds 28 times more environments than when sessions are closed promptly. The multiple is simply the time an unclosed session is held over the time a closed one is, 933/33=28933/33=28 for our 33-second conversations, but it is the largest factor a client controls.

A measurement method, and three ways to get it wrong (Section 3). To measure a framework’s CPU per step without paying for thousands of model calls, and so that every run replays the same conversation with no seconds of network wait around each millisecond of computation, the model must be replaced with something fake. How it is replaced decides what is measured. Three mistakes each give a plausible but wrong number. (1) Replacing the model object with a stub skips the work of serialising the growing conversation, so framework CPU looks flat as conversations grow; faking only the network socket keeps that work. (2) Timing “the model call” in a deployed agent counts the client’s own serialisation and parsing as model time; by our estimate that hid most of the framework’s CPU in our deployed data. (3) Benchmarking steps back to back understates CPU: on our desktop, a step run after a wait of deployed length cost 1.9 to 4.7 times as much. Measured with the socket mock, framework CPU per step is linear in conversation size in both frameworks and on every processor we measured, though its constants vary more than fivefold.

Open problems for platform builders (Section 8). The main one is how to keep each session confined, as agent runtimes do today by giving it an environment of its own, without that environment sitting reserved while the session waits on the model. Today’s platforms offer one or the other, at least among the nine we surveyed: the agent runtimes confine each session in its own environment, and the runtimes that share environments confine per tenant rather than per session. Isolates and per-tool sandboxes point toward a middle ground (Section 8).

Two scoping statements frame everything that follows. First, the multiples we report count what the customer holds and pays for: environments, quota slots and billed memory. They are not the provider’s cost. A provider can pack many idle microVMs onto one machine, so a thousand held environments cost it far less than a thousand machines’ worth; by how much, we cannot see from outside. Our claims are about the customer’s side. Second, we do not argue that per-session isolation is a mistake. Agents run tools, and sometimes code, chosen by a model on a user’s behalf, and confining each session has real value. We measure its price.
